pages.title: The full Oracle stack, end to end
pages.description: How Fusion Cloud, Oracle Integration Cloud, and VBCS fit into one enterprise landscape — who talks to whom, through which protocols, and what each layer is responsible for.
headings: Identity and security across the stack
Stateless vs. orchestrated: two sample topologies
pages.content: The big picture Protocols between the layers Anatomy of one end-to-end request Identity and security across the stack Stateless vs. orchestrated: two sample topologies Anti-patterns that break this architecture Where to go next A. Simple & synchronous VBCS → Fusion B. Orchestrated & asynchronous VBCS → OIC → Fusion The big picture Here is the whole landscape in one picture. The pattern holds for almost every Oracle deployment — the only things that change are the modules in play and which side originates the data. Read it in layers: Follow a single action — "a supplier saves an expense request on the extranet portal" — all the way through the stack: Notice two important things: 1 OIC absorbed all the branching and error handling so the portal stays simple, and 2 the approval step is a process — OIC's Process Builder — not a hard-coded if/then in the page. Each layer has its own notion of "who is calling," and they connect through federated identity: Use for lookups and light reads. No durable state, no orchestration, lowest latency. Use for writes that need validation, enrichment, or a human approval before Fusion commits. The call returns quickly; the status round-trips afterward. Bottom layer — Fusion: owns master data and transactions. Its only doors for data are REST/SOAP services, FBDI file loads, and BIP reports. Middle layer — OIC: owns the moving of data. It talks to Fusion using REST and FBDI, talks to the world using ~100+ adapters, and exposes clean REST endpoints to anything internal. Top layer — VBCS: owns the experience. It consumes OIC endpoints and occasionally Fusion REST directly and renders pages for humans. See the pattern applied in the PO approval scenario . Refresh any term in the glossary . Drill into a layer: Fusion REST , OIC styles , or VBCS connections . The rule that keeps this architecture clean: VBCS asks, OIC does, Fusion stores. If the flow involves anything beyond a simple read, the logic belongs in OIC — not in your page's action chains. Never store shared Fusion passwords in your VBCS page or in browser code. Credentials belong in OIC connections or in OCI Secrets — the front end should only hold tokens . pages.title: Oracle Analytics Cloud (OAC)
pages.description: The modern cloud analytics service on OCI: data visualization, semantic models and classic dashboards, data flows, machine learning — and how OAC connects to Fusion Cloud via OAuth.
headings: Where OAC sits next to Fusion
pages.content: The two consoles — know both Core OAC capabilities Connecting OAC to Fusion OTBI → OAC migration Security & administration Where OAC sits next to Fusion Oracle Analytics Cloud OAC is the standalone, cloud-native analytics platform on OCI. Where OTBI is locked to one Fusion instance, OAC is a real platform: it connects to Fusion, databases, files, and SaaS APIs; preps and blends data; builds governed semantic models; and adds data-visualization and machine-learning. Think of it as the analytics layer for the whole enterprise , Fusion being one of many sources. OAC actually hosts two authoring paradigms, and teams rarely mix them up because they served different generations: There is a direct, supported path from OAC to Fusion Cloud data using OAuth — the same confidential-client pattern seen in the REST/OAuth material: Because both speak the same BI dialect, existing OTBI content can move to OAC rather than being rebuilt: DV is where OAC's future is being built — it is the default for anything new. The classic console exists so OBIEE/OTBI-style content analyses, dashboards, .rpd semantic models still runs on the cloud platform. This is a pull from OAC's side — OAC calls Fusion REST on your schedule — the inverse of Fusion pushing anywhere. Use it for cross-source blending Fusion + warehouse + file and for analytics that need OAC-specific capacity or ML. Vault the credentials; OAC stores the password in its secure wallet, not in scripts. OTBI subject areas can be connected from OAC via the Fusion OAuth connection above, so the same logical model is queryable in the cloud console. Dashboards/analyses can be recreated in OAC classic or rebuilt in DV — plan the move as a governed re-platform, not a copy. OBIEE on-prem .rpd files can be uploaded to OAC as semantic models see the OBIEE page for the migration path . You can also take Fusion data out via a data warehouse copy to ADW/object storage through an OIC or ODI pipeline and connect OAC to that . The choice is about volume and governance: REST pulls are easy but chatty; a warehouse copy is heavier to build and freshest-by-design. OTBI still remains the fastest route for in-instance questions. pages.title: OBIEE — On-Prem BI Enterprise Edition
pages.description: The on-prem classic: the .rpd repository and its three layers, BI Presentation Services and Answers, dashboards and the catalog, BI Apps, and the migration path from OBIEE to OAC.
headings: The architecture — where each piece lives
BI Applications (BI Apps) — the ERP/analytics pack
pages.content: The architecture — where each piece lives The .rpd and its three layers Answers, dashboards & the catalog BI Applications BI Apps — the ERP/analytics pack OBIEE and Fusion Migrating from OBIEE to OAC Where OBIEE fits today OBIEE Oracle Business Intelligence Enterprise Edition is the on-prem BI platform that OTBI and OAC both descend from. Fusion OTBI is effectively OBIEE-style analytics embedded in the cloud, and OAC is its cloud re-birth — so reading OBIEE content teaches you the grandparents of everything else in this section. If you only work on modern Fusion, you still need to recognize its artifacts, because they keep turning up. The repository is an offline-editable model the offline Admin Tool built of exactly three layers. Understand these and you understand the philosophy behind OTBI subject areas: The user experience is the ancestor of what you already know from OTBI: On-prem Oracle BI deployments are rarely naked OBIEE. Most ship as Oracle BI Applications : preconfigured subject areas Financial Analytics, Procurement and Spend Analytics, HR Analytics, Supply Chain Analytics fed by ODI ETL from EBS/JDE/PeopleSoft/Siebel. They are the direct ancestors of Fusion's delivered analytics: Two real-life pairings you will meet: Oracle's direction of travel is OBIEE → OAC, and the path is largely governed: Changes to the model happen offline, then a consistency check validates the model before load. That offline check-and-load ceremony is exactly why schema changes feel heavyweight in OBIEE-land. Answers — the ad-hoc analysis builder over presentation folders: columns, filters, groupings, pivots and charts. Dashboards — pages that arrange analyses and prompts for a role or workflow. Catalog — /Shared Folders governed and /My Folders personal , each folder access-controlled. BI Publisher — a companion server for pixel-perfect outputs driven by the same data. OTBI is OBIEE technology — the Fusion "Reports and Analytics" center is a curated, cloud-hosted OBIEE-like service. OBIEE experience transfers 1:1 to OTBI comfort. Fusion → on-prem OBIEE/OBI Apps — some estates still run enterprise OBIEE against Fusion data via BI connectors or by loading the Fusion warehouse into a BI-Apps-shaped on-prem model. When someone says "add a column to the report" in an OBIEE/OAC-classic world, the real work is often model changes — physical → business model → presentation — not the report itself. OTBI hides that plumbing because Oracle built the subject areas for you. The migration is a re-platform, not a lift . 'RPD uploads fine' does not mean the underlying data connections do — source credentials, refresh schedules, and report catalog permissions must all be re-established on OCI before users even sign in. Treat it as a project with its own test cycle, exactly like the report-modification walkthrough preaches. Component Role Repository .rpd The governed model: physical connections, business model, presentation layer BI Server The query engine that turns requests into database SQL BI Presentation Services The web application users touch: Answers, dashboards, catalog Catalog RPD-side Where analyses, dashboards and reports are stored BI Publisher server Pixel-perfect layouts on top of the same data Scheduler / Agent iBot Delivers/emails content on a schedule Layer Content Analogy Physical Actual database tables/columns and how to connect The 'real' schema Business Model & Mapping The logical model: dimensions and measures, with mappings to physical tables Subject-area mechanics Presentation The folders users actually pick from in Answers The subject area you see in OTBI real BI Apps layer Contains Data warehouse Star-schema tables fact + dimension that BI Apps populates ODI mappings The ETL that turns source-application tables into warehouse facts RPD functional The analytics subject areas on top of that warehouse Prebuilt dashboards Delivered 'out-of-the-box' report sets per domain out-of-the-box OBIEE asset In OAC .rpd repository Uploaded as a semantic model 12c .rpd is supported; 11g needs the migration validator first Answers analyses Recreated in classic dashboards or rebuilt in DV Dashboards Classic dashboards run in OAC; new work moves to DV BI Publisher reports Re-hosted or re-targeted at Fusion/BIP in the cloud BI Apps warehouse Leave on-prem, or re-point at Fusion/OAC-native models neutral 🗄️ Data sources Oracle/multi-DB · Essbase · files accent 🧩 BI Server's governed business model 🖥️ query engine — SQL to sources 🖼️ Presentation Services Answers · Dashboards · Catalog warning 🏢 OBIEE on-prem legacy estates · BI Apps · .rpd oic ☁️ OAC cloud DV · semantic models fusion 📊 OTBI in Fusion the same BI, curated for Fusion BDI / BI Apps ETL serves UI modernize embedded

pages.title: OTBI — Transactional Business Intelligence
pages.description: The analytics engine embedded in Fusion Cloud: subject areas, real-time vs warehouse facts, analyses and dashboards, drill-to-detail, the catalog, and the duties and data security that govern it.
headings: Subject areas — the model you query
Limits & the hand-off to other tools
Where OTBI sits in the stack
pages.content: Subject areas — the model you query Building an analysis Dashboards, catalog & delivered analytics Drill-to-detail KPI watchlist & monitoring Security model Limits & the hand-off to other tools Where OTBI sits in the stack OTBI Oracle Transactional Business Intelligence is Fusion's built-in ad-hoc analytics on transactional data. It is free, pre-secured, and always available in the same instance as your data — which is why the moment someone asks "how many invoices did we validate this week?" the answer is OTBI. Technically it runs Oracle BI web-technology embedded in Fusion, which is why it uses the OBIEE-family vocabulary. You never write SQL in OTBI. Instead you pick a subject area , the Oracle-delivered logical model for a domain, and drag its folders into the analysis: Subject areas come in two flavors, and knowing which one you are on explains refresh behavior: The analysis editor mirrors the OBIEE "Answers" experience you will meet again in OAC and on-prem OBIEE: Analyses get saved into the catalog and composed onto dashboards . Fusion ships a large collection of delivered analytics per module — clone, edit, and save to your own folder rather than rebuilding from scratch: OTBI's killer interaction: an aggregate can drill to the transaction — from "AP total" to the actual supplier invoice page in Fusion. This works because subject-area measures carry a drill-to-detail mapping to the transactional object, and the user's duty governs what they may then open. For "always-on" process metrics, Fusion's KPI module watches metric definitions and raises watchlist items when a KPI crosses a threshold — an operational layer on top of the same subject areas, not a separate tool. The practical consequence for implementers: giving someone "OTBI access" is really about the duty/role grants plus data security policies that scope the rows — a report can be perfectly built and show nothing to a user whose data access set excludes the ledger. Columns criteria — measures aggregate SUM/AVG/COUNT according to the model; dimensions slice them. Filters — like SQL WHERE , including SQL filters for expressions the editor cannot build. Prompts — runtime parameters; dashboard prompts drive several analyses at once. Pivot & graph views and conditional formatting highlight over-limit invoices live in the same analysis. The system automatically applies its palette of functions date, string, conversion for calculated columns. Two top-level areas: Shared Folders delivered + team reports and Users /My Folders personal scratch space . Best practice: never edit delivered reports in place — copy to /Custom/… and keep a migration path to non-prod the Modify a Report walkthrough shows the whole drill . Dashboards can embed analyses, prompts, and web content, and can be scheduled/emailed. Not pixel-perfect — no RTF layouts, bursting, or exact page formats; that is BI Publisher . Fusion data only — OTBI cannot query outside the instance; mixing sources is the OAC job. Performance ceiling — heavy queries go to the warehouse-backed subject areas; treat real-time subject areas like OLTP queries. Analyses can feed BIP data models for formatted output, and dashboards can be delivered on a schedule. The “Real Time” suffix in a subject area name is the tell. When a manager says “that balance is wrong”, check the subject area type first — a warehouse-backed answer that was refreshed last night will never match today's transactional reality. Drill-to-detail is what separates "list of numbers" from "actionable intelligence" in Fusion. When designing a dashboard, always keep the deepest level one drill away so users can resolve, not just observe. pages.title: Analytics — OTBI, OAC & OBIEE
pages.description: Oracle's BI family, one family tree: OTBI is the analytics engine embedded in Fusion, OAC is Oracle Analytics Cloud on OCI, and OBIEE is the on-prem classic they both descend from. This hub shows how they relate and which one answers which question.
headings: How Fusion data actually reaches these engines
pages.content: The family tree Decision guide — which engine when The shared vocabulary Learning path How Fusion data actually reaches these engines The "Reporting & Analytics" page chose the day-to-day tool per question OTBI, BI Publisher, Financial Reporting, Smart View . This pages covers the analytic engines behind those tools — OTBI, OAC, and OBIEE — how they are related, and how analytics work at enterprise scale. One sentence to remember: The honest rule: start in OTBI . It is already there, already secured by Fusion duties, and answers 80% of business questions in minutes. Graduate to OAC when you need data from outside Fusion, heavier preparation, or one analytics store for the whole company. Touch OBIEE when you meet a pre-OAC on-prem estate — and plan its migration. Once you know any one engine's words you know most of the others' — this is why OTBI, OAC's classic console, and OBIEE all feel familiar: It helps to picture the data flow once, because each engine sits at a different point in it: OTBI queries Fusion's transactional schema through prebuilt subject areas — either Real Time subject areas over live transaction tables or warehouse-backed subject areas over the Fusion analytics warehouse that refresh on schedule. OAC pulls Fusion data through a REST/OAuth connection or from the same warehouse and other sources. OBIEE on-prem usually reads a replicated copy of transactional data or the BI Apps warehouse that an ETL process e.g. ODI fills. OBIEE is the on-prem BI platform. OTBI is OBIEE-style analytics embedded inside Fusion . OAC is the modern cloud analytics service that can consume Fusion data alongside everything else. They share the same family DNA and the same vocabulary subject areas, analyses, dashboards, catalog . None of these engines read the source of truth blindly at all times — they read subject areas, warehouses, or replicated copies, and that is a refreshed view of the data. "Balance is off by one invoice" is usually a refresh-timing question, not a bug in the report. Engine Where it runs Signature strength Read the deep-dive OTBI Inside the Fusion Cloud instance Immediate questions on Fusion transactional data, no extra service OAC OCI — a separate cloud service Multi-source analytics, data prep, visualization, ML OBIEE Your own data center The on-prem classic with the RPD semantic layer; pairs with BI Apps Situation Use Why Ad-hoc question about Fusion data, answered today Built-in, duty-secured, near-real-time subject areas Combine Fusion with a data warehouse, Salesforce, files One service, many sources, data flows and prep Data-visualization storytelling, auto-insights, ML predictions OAC DV Drag-and-drop projects + machine-learning built in Fusion plus the wider enterprise in one governed model OAC + semantic model .rpd A single business model over many sources Reading or maintaining a legacy on-prem BI estate It is live in thousands of data centers; you must know the RPD ceremony Pixel-perfect invoices, statements, bank formats BI Publisher not these These engines analyze; BIP formats GL statements over ledgers Financial Reporting not these Account-structure statements, not analytics Term Meaning in every engine Subject area A logical queryable model e.g. 'AP Invoices Real Time' with folders of measures and dimensions Analysis Answers The ad-hoc query builder: columns, filters, grouping, aggregates, pivots, charts Dashboard A page of analyses and prompts, arranged for a role or process Prompt / filter A runtime parameter that narrows the query 'what period? which BU?' Catalog The folders where analyses, dashboards and reports are saved and secured Measures The numbers amounts, counts — aggregated with SUM/AVG/COUNT per the model Dimensions / hierarchy The way you slice Time, Business Unit, Supplier, Natural Account AP Invoices Real Time what period? which BU? accent 🏢 On-prem BI EE 11g/12c — the platform everything grew from fusion 📊 Inside Fusion — subject areas + analyses + dashboards oic ☁️ Oracle Analytics Cloud on OCI — DV, semantic models, ML embed modernize / move

pages.title: Approvals & Workflow
pages.description: Every Fusion business flow that needs a sign-off — AP invoices, purchase orders, expense reports, project spend — runs on Oracle BPM Workflow. This page explains approval rules, approval groups, the worklist, routing, and Groovy conditions.
headings: What runs on the approval engine
pages.content: What runs on the approval engine How an approval flows Core concepts Approval groups & routing Groovy conditions Where approval data lives Integration notes Next steps What runs on the approval engine How an approval flows A transaction submits to the workflow, a task is created in the approver's worklist, and the task routes through the configured path until it ends. Groups are the workhorses. A group holds members users or roles and defines how they vote: Business rules can route on any approval attribute using Groovy. The result returns which group/role handles the next step: Tasks are BPM instances. The commonly queried tables with the usual caveat to verify against your release : Documents submitted to approval are not final until the last task approves — always check the approval status before assuming a record is posted. A created AP invoice may sit in Requires Re-approval after a change — this is normal workflow behavior, not an error. OIC can query and act on approval tasks approve/reject/resubmit via the approval REST services, or notify approvers by email. Escalations and notifications are configured per flow — missing notifications usually mean a setup gap, not a data problem. Approvals gate the records described on the ERP Financials pages. Approval tasks are acted on inside OIC flows — see Integration Cloud . Worklist behavior ties into security roles who can approve . The attribute names here amount come from the transaction's workflow attributes — check the approval rule setup to see which are available for the flow you're configuring. For integrations, act on tasks through the worklist REST/service rather than the tables, and never rely on table-level access for approvals. pages.title: Core Concepts
pages.description: Flexfields, value sets, trees, attachments, Enterprise Scheduler, and approval workflows — the platform-level building blocks you must understand before any Fusion integration. These concepts cut across every module.
pages.content: Flexfields Value Sets Trees & Tree Structures Attachments & UCM Batch processing & ESS Approval workflows Next steps If modules are the where of Fusion, these concepts are the how . They are implemented once by the Fusion platform and used by every module, which is why a single concept a flexfield segment, for example can appear in Finance, Procurement, and HCM at the same time. None of them are optional reading for an integration developer. A flexfield is Fusion's way of letting each customer extend standard data structures without changing code. There are two kinds, and confusing them is a classic source of integration bugs: Key flexfields are composed of context-sensitive segments : depending on the context for example the operating unit or the account type , a different set of segments applies. When you read a record via REST you often get the segments as separate attributes e.g. Company , CostCenter ; when you load via FBDI you must concatenate them into the segment columns in the exact order the template defines. A value set is a named list that constrains what a flexfield segment or a profile option is allowed to hold. You will see them everywhere because they are the data dictionary behind most dropdowns in Fusion. Value sets are exposed as REST resources under vmValueSets , which is handy when you want to validate data before you send it, or to drive a VBCS dropdown from Fusion: A tree is a hierarchical grouping that Fusion uses when plain flat lists are not enough — for example organizing cost centers under regions, or storing a hierarchy of segments. The tree structure defines the node vocabulary which value set the nodes draw from and the tree version holds the actual hierarchy for a date range. You integrate against trees when a requirement says things like "roll up all sales cost centers to region level for reporting." You typically call the TreeManagementService REST resources treeDefinition , treeStructureDefinition , treeData to fetch the hierarchy, then walk it in your code. Trees are versioned, so a report that uses "as of" dates can read a historical version without disruption. Files attached to any Fusion object are not stored in the business table — they live in UCM Universal Content Manager . The public handling points are the documentResource REST endpoints, which let you upload, download, and delete files on most main objects. Uploading an attachment to a purchase order in REST parlance means POSTing the file, then attaching the resulting document ID back to the business object. With curl, a common pattern is a multipart POST to the document resource: The response returns a docId and a download URL. Store that docId in your integration metadata — you will use it later to fetch or delete the file. The Enterprise Scheduler Service ESS runs every background job in Fusion: FBDI imports, scheduled reports, and many module-specific processes. When you submit an FBDI load, ESS is what actually executes the import. ESS exposes a REST surface base erpintegrationservice where you submit jobs and, crucially, poll for status . The job status is available while the job runs and after it finishes, so batch integrations use a simple poll loop rather than a blocking call: The response envelope carries fields like completionMessage and a job status of SUCCEEDED , RUNNING , or FAILED . On failure, the payload also points you at the error CSV that ESS writes back to UCM. Many Fusion objects carry an approval step — a requisition needs a manager, an invoice needs an AP + finance approver. Historically that logic lives in Oracle Business Process the BPEL/SOA-based approval service that ships with Fusion. For new integrations Oracle increasingly routes these human steps through OIC Process , which extends and in time replaces parts of the native Fusion approval engine. You can still query approval state on the object itself — for reversible read paths check the object's status and the approvals REST resource — but if you need custom workflows with your own approver tables, plan to build them in OIC Process and trigger them from Fusion via events or REST. Independent — a standalone list "Payment Terms", "Countries" whose values carry optional effective dates and descriptions. Dependent — a second value set whose valid values depend on a value already chosen in another segment Province depends on Country . Table — values come from a SQL table at runtime; used when the list is huge or driven by another object. Validation type — the rules applied on top: format-only, pair-to-segment, special, or none. This determines whether a segment accepts free text or only listed values. Fusion-native: approvals configured per object; lifecycle states like PENDING_APPROVAL , APPROVED , REJECTED on the object. OIC Process: custom human tasks, approval hierarchies, and timeouts that you design and that call Fusion REST to apply the final state. Apply these concepts through the REST API fundamentals . See flexfields and ESS in action during FBDI loads . Check which module owns the object you need in application modules . The account flexfield format is the #1 FBDI failure . A value like 01-120-00000-000 must match the template's segment order and value-set-driven validations exactly, or the import job fails for '"Segment1" is not valid'. Check the concatenation separator and the number of segments on your instance before you build the file. ESS also accepts scheduling : you submit a job with a schedule or point it at an existing ESS schedule , so your "nightly FBDI load" can be driven entirely from Fusion rather than from OIC. pages.title: Costing Methods
pages.description: How an item's cost is determined in each organization: standard cost (a fixed planned amount) or actual cost (calculated from the transactions that happened). The choice defines every valuation, variance, and GL posting.
pages.content: Functional view Technical view Data flow — step by step Retrieve the data — SQL Worked example — standard cost variance Integration notes Next steps REST resources FBDI templates Read the Cost Management hub first. Functional view Standard cost fixes an item at a planned amount; variances between standard and actual are recorded separately. Actual cost FIFO, average, or specific values each movement from the transactions themselves. Cost Management applies one method per cost organization , and costs are maintained via cost updates / rollover . Method is the foundation: pick standard or actual per org before transactions run. Standard needs maintenance: run cost updates/rollover when prices change. Variances are important: purchase-price variance is how standard costing surfaces cost drift. Value before post: costs must exist before movements can create GL entries. Landed charges complicate cost — see Landed Cost . Back to the Cost Management hub . Read the Cost Management hub first. Column names follow the Fusion data dictionary naming. Confirm against your instance before relying on them. pages.title: Landed Cost
pages.description: Adding everything it costs to get goods onto your dock: freight, insurance, duties, and handling. Landed cost turns a supplier's invoice price into the item's true delivered cost — the number you revalue inventory and mark up from.
pages.content: Functional view Technical view Data flow — step by step Retrieve the data — SQL Worked example — freight on 10 chairs Integration notes Next steps REST resources FBDI templates Read Costing Methods — landed cost is an addition on top of the base cost. Functional view A PO says $150 per chair, but the real cost includes freight, insurance, and duty. Landed cost attaches those charges to receipts, distributes them across the received lines, and rolls them into the item's cost. The result: inventory is valued at the delivered cost, not the invoice price. Changes arrive late: freight bills come after receipts — expect cost adjustments post-receipt. Distribute correctly: charges must be spread across their receipt lines for the unit cost to be right. Import is the tool: bulk charges come via the Landed Cost Import FBDI. Back to the Cost Management hub . Cost value flows into Financials . Read Costing Methods — landed cost is an addition on top of the base cost. Column names follow the Fusion data dictionary naming. Confirm against your instance before relying on them. Resource What you can do with it r1 Create/read landed cost charges on receipts r2 Associate charges to receipt lines Template Purpose Must exist first f1 Bulk-load freight/invoice charges Receipts and / or supplier invoices to attach to Step What happens Where the data lands table 1 Goods are received at the base price t1 2 Landed cost charges freight, duty, insurance are added t2 3 Charges are distributed across the received lines t3 4 Cost is updated to the landed value t4 5 On-hand revalues and GL posts t5 neutral Base price supplier invoice amount warning Landed cost charges assigned to receipt lines success True cost revalues on-hand · posts variance + freight / insurance / duty distribute across lines SELECT chg.charge_id, chg.charge_type, chg.charge_amount, chg.currency_code, chg.status, i.item_number FROM landed_cost_charges chg LEFT JOIN landed_cost_distributions d ON d.charge_id = chg.charge_id LEFT JOIN egp_system_items_b i ON i.inventory_item_id = d.item_id WHERE chg.status = 'ACTIVE' ORDER BY chg.charge_type;

pages.title: Cost Management
pages.description: How inventory gets a monetary value. At period close (or at each transaction), Cost Management turns on-hand quantities into a balance-sheet value and expense — and posts that value into the GL. Understand cost and you understand where inventory, purchasing, and the ledger meet.
headings: Learning path — read in this order
pages.content: The business story Learning path — read in this order The processes Functional ↔ technical reference Configuration Data flow — step by step Integration notes Next steps Read the Inventory hub cost values on-hand and the Subledger Accounting page how inventory cost posts to the GL . The business story Pick any item with 100 units on hand — what is it worth? Cost Management answers that: it defines how an item's cost is computed costing method , maintains those costs over time, adds landed cost freight, insurance, duty , and posts the movements to the GL so inventory appears on the balance sheet. Costing is a method first: pick standard vs actual per organization before transactions exist. Cost before value: you need an item cost before movements can be valued. Landed cost waits on invoices: freight/duties often arrive after the receipt — expect adjustments. All roads lead to GL: cost posts inventory, COGS, and variance accounts to the ledger. Start with Costing Methods , then Landed Cost . Cost feeds the Financials ledgers. Read the Inventory hub cost values on-hand and the Subledger Accounting page how inventory cost posts to the GL . The sentence to memorize: inventory value = on-hand quantity × item cost , and every change to either side creates a GL entry. That's why cost and inventory are taught together. Cost Management REST resources live under the scmRestApi base and names vary by release — confirm against your instance's REST service catalog. Column names follow the Fusion data dictionary naming. pages.title: Document Sequencing
pages.description: The numbering engine behind legally significant documents: AR invoices, receipt numbers, and payment numbers. Sequences control gaps, ranges, and which documents get a number at all.
pages.content: What document sequencing does Core concepts Where numbering is applied Setup essentials Integration notes Next steps What document sequencing does Many documents must be numbered without gaps for tax and audit reasons. Fusion assigns a sequence to document types — like invoice, credit memo, or payment — so each gets the next number in a controlled range. Define document types for the business units that need them. Attach a sequence with a realistic range and effective dates. Use automatic entry for audit-sensitive docs; manual entry only for exceptions. Turn on gapless control only where law requires it — it slows processing. An import creating AR invoices must let Fusion assign the number — don't force your own. If you send a document number, the sequence may reject or ignore it — check the document type's entry type. Range exhaustion is a classic end-of-year failure: open a new sequence for the next period. Back to Core Concepts . Numbering failures in imports: FBDI errors . Seen in practice on the Receivables and Payables pages. Concept What it is Document type A category of documents that needs numbers Invoice, Credit Memo, Payment Document category Groups document types Accounts Receivable, Payments, Purchasing Sequence A numbered range e.g. AR-2025-0001 to AR-2025-9999 with effective dates Entry type Automatic system assigns / Manual user enters / None Gapless control Ensures numbers are used in order with no gaps strong audit requirement Range control Defines the numeric window the sequence may assign Module Documents that get sequences Receivables AR invoices, credit/debit memos, chargebacks, receipts Payables Payment numbers checks, EFT and invoice numbers if required Cash Management Bank transfers and other cash documents Purchasing Purchase orders where legal numbering is needed

pages.title: Enterprise Structures
headings: Why this matters before anything else
pages.content: Why this matters before anything else The concepts The relationships Why integrations must care Implementation order Underlying tables & SQL Next steps The organizational model that underpins every Fusion ERP transaction: ledgers , legal entities , business units , and the security that controls what each user can see MOAC . No integration is correct without knowing which business unit and ledger a document belongs to. breadcrumbs= , updated="February 2025" /> Why this matters before anything else Fusion is an organization-centric system. Every transaction — an AP invoice, a PO, an expense report — is owned by a business unit , reported through a legal entity , and accounted in a ledger . If you don't know the enterprise structure, you don't know which BU to send a document to, which ledger it posts to, or why a user can't see a record. The rules that make the model work: A new implementation builds the structure top-down, in this order: The structure lives in a small set of tables. Query them to answer "which BU/ledger/legal entity is this?": A business unit belongs to exactly one legal entity and reports to one ledger primary ledger . A legal entity can have many business units, but a business unit can be assigned to only one legal entity. The ledger owns the chart of accounts — all legal entities and BUs attached to it share that COA. Data access sets give GL users access to ledger balances; MOAC gives sub-ledger users access to a list of BUs. Every module page now makes more sense — see how documents need a BU in Payables . The chart of accounts behind ledgers is a core concept . Reporting reads these ledgers — see the reporting stack on the upcoming Reporting & Analytics page. pages.title: Driving ESS via REST (erpProcesses)
pages.description: Many integration flows end with a scheduled process: import the file, validate the invoices, create the accounting, post the journals. The erpProcesses REST resource is how you submit those jobs from OIC or custom code — and how you make a load 'finish' without a human clicking Run.
pages.content: Why this matters The resource Which jobs integrations drive most Submitting vs. polling Comparison with FBDI's automatic submission Security & privileges Integration notes Next steps A data load is rarely finished when the file uploads. In Fusion the sequence is usually: stage the data → run the import job → run the validation/accounting job → post . The erpProcesses REST resource lets you submit these Enterprise Scheduler Service ESS jobs programmatically, exactly as if a user had clicked "Submit" in the Scheduled Processes work area. The resource is erpProcesses under the FSCM REST API. It is a POST-only endpoint: you send a job name plus its parameters, and it returns the submitted job with an ID you can poll. The exact parameter names depend on the job. The reliable way to find them is the REST resource explorer in your instance see the Metadata Explorer tip on the REST API fundamentals page or the job's submission UI. Polling status works like the FBDI flow: the erpintegrationservice/scheduling/jobsStatus/ ' processId ' resource returns whether the job is queued, running, SUCCEEDED , or FAILED . Poll with a sensible interval and treat "partial success" imported some rows, rejected others as a state to handle explicitly. When you submit an FBDI ZIP via the erpintegrationservice/upload endpoint, the control file already names the import job — so one upload starts the import. But the downstream jobs validation, accounting, posting are still yours to drive. The two patterns work together: The integration user needs the job-role privileges that grant submitting these processes — for example Submit Scheduled Process , Import Payables Invoices , Load Interface File for Import , or the module-specific submit duties. An integration user that can read data but not submit processes will get an authorization error on the POST even though GET calls succeed. End-to-end automation — OIC can upload an FBDI file, poll its status, then submit the import job, then Create Accounting, all without a human. Load-order control — you decide when each step runs instead of hoping the UI job finishes first. Error containment — you can stop after import, inspect the interface table, fix rows, and only then run accounting. Chain, don't guess. Wait for the import job to finish before submitting Create Accounting — accounting over rows that are still importing creates wrong entries or errors. Parameters must match the job. A wrong or missing parameter fails the submission; validate parameter names against the job's submission UI or the resource explorer. Idempotent design. If you retry a submission, track the job ID so you do not run the same import twice. Period awareness. Many jobs fail when the period is closed — check accountingPeriodsLOV before submitting import/accounting jobs for a specific period. Learn the job lifecycle and failure modes on Scheduled Processes ESS . Understand what the interface tables stage in Interface Tables . See the pattern applied end to end in FBDI Integration with Fusion . Look up which job to submit for a task in the Tool Matrix . Create Accounting subledger accounting, module-agnostic is the single most common job a Financials integration drives. It turns the transaction data into accounting entries in XLA_AE_HEADERS / XLA_AE_LINES . See Subledger Accounting . pages.title: FBDI & ADFdi
pages.description: File-Based Data Import (FBDI) is Fusion's bulk, asynchronous loading path: a ZIP of CSV files plus an XML control file, uploaded to UCM and processed by Enterprise Scheduler Service. ADFdi is its end-user spreadsheet cousin. Learn the flow, the ZIP structure, and the gotchas.
headings: Fusion Data Loader vs FBDI vs ADFdi
pages.content: Why FBDI? The ZIP structure How to get templates Uploading and submitting Polling for status The FBDI catalog per module Fusion Data Loader vs FBDI vs ADFdi FBDI gotchas Next steps REST is perfect for a handful of records, but it falls over for bulk loads — importing 10,000 supplier invoices would take hours and hammer the service. That is exactly the job FBDI exists for: asynchronous, resume-friendly, batch import driven by a file Oracle can validate and process in the background. FBDI is the second pillar of Fusion integration and it exists for three concrete reasons: The same pipeline powers the interactive UI imports: the "Import and Export" jobs in the Navigator are FBDI templates underneath. If you learn one FBDI workflow you effectively know them all — only the template columns change. An FBDI submission is a single .zip with two kinds of files: The critical parts to read out of the control file are the importObjectName and importServiceName — that string is the job name you will reuse when uploading and when checking status. You rarely hand-craft an FBDI file. Oracle publishes the official templates with columns, dependencies, and notes as downloadable .xlsx files, so your pipeline should start by fetching the correct template and mapping your source columns onto it. The common download points are the ERP Integration Service REST template resources such as procurementCommonResources or the module-specific exportImportTemplates and the docs portal. As a rule of thumb: In practice most implementations one-time -download the template, verify it against their test instance, freeze it, and generate matching CSVs from that frozen layout. Once the ZIP is built you submit it with a multipart POST to the UCM dataloader endpoint. The essential parts are the file itself and the importConfigAttributes that name the job. A successful POST returns the ProcessId and the documents created in UCM. Keep that ProcessId — it is your handle for polling, and it will pinpoint the job in the Navigator's Scheduled Processes list. FBDI is asynchronous, so after submitting you poll ESS. The status resource lives under erpintegrationservice and takes the ProcessId from the upload response: The response tells you whether the job is queued, running, SUCCEEDED , or FAILED . On failure, Fusion writes an error CSV back to UCM with a row per failed record and a message you can diff against your source data. The completion message in the status response tells you how many records loaded versus failed — your integration should treat anything less than "all rows OK" as a partial success and handle it explicitly. These are the file-based imports Oracle documents for Financials guide File-Based Data Import FBDI for Financials . Every module page on this hub links back to the relevant rows. Names are release-stable, but always confirm the template exists in your instance's File Based Data Import folder before building a pipeline. The three terms are easy to blur. The distinction is who builds the file and who submits it : Practically: FBDI = you generate a file in OIC/ETL and submit it by REST. ADFdi = an accountant opens an Excel template in the UI and mass-edits expenses. Same validation pipeline underneath, different front doors. Bulk throughput — files move thousands of rows in one job where REST would need thousands of round-trips. Asynchronicity — the caller submits the file and walks away; ESS processes it, and you poll for the result. Nobody blocks on a long HTTP call. Built-in validation — Oracle ships a generic import pipeline HZ, AP, GL, HCM interfaces that catches bad rows and writes them to an error file instead of silently corrupting data. Data files — CSV/Excel sheets whose columns match the template exactly, including header row and required header codes like Segment1 , Segment2 for account segments. Control file — a .xml named to match e.g. loadInterfaceFile.xml that tells ESS which import job to run and which files feed it. Account flexfield format — the segment concatenation must match the template e.g. 01-120-00000 in exact order . Wrong segment order or stray hyphens fail validation with '"Segment1" is not valid'. Date formats — FBDI templates are picky YYYY-MM-DD or as the template specifies . Locale formats slip through intl and break the job. Required header codes — each template has mandatory columns like Source , Ledger , Date ; missing one fails the whole batch, not one row. Load order between objects — depend objects first. Suppliers and supplier sites must exist before you import invoices that reference them, and GL journals may depend on ledger setup. Plan the sequence in your orchestration. template version skew — a template from a different release URL version than your instance produces fields the pipeline ignores. Always re-validate after maintenance. See how OIC typically orchestrates the upload-and-poll pattern in OIC overview . Prep your data correctly with the core concepts — flexfields and value sets. Choose REST vs FBDI per call in REST API fundamentals . Look up which FBDI template to use for a task in the Tool Matrix . Column names in the CSV must match the template , including distinct CSV header codes for flexfields. Reordering or renaming a column silently shifts data into the wrong attribute — a classic reason a "successful" import loads garbage. Poll with a sensible cadence for example every 30–60 s and a maximum retry count. If the pod performing the job is busy, status may legitimately stay RUNNING for minutes on a large load. Two things consultants get wrong: Suppliers FBDI now ships with Procurement not the Financials guide , and GL journals load via Journal Import into GL_INTERFACE — there is no "journal" create REST resource. Both are covered on the module pages. FBDI offers no "undo." A loaded batch is a committed transaction in Fusion. Build a small test on your stage environment, verify counts and the error CSV, then promote the same file to production with the correct load order. pages.title: Financial Close & Consolidation
pages.description: The periodic close turns a messy month of transactions into audited financial statements. Sub-ledgers close first, transfer to the GL, the GL is revalued/translated/consolidated, and periods are finally closed.
pages.content: The close cycle Close steps in detail Why close status breaks integrations Close Manager Underlying tables & SQL Integration notes Next steps The close cycle Close runs bottom-up: sub-ledgers first, then the GL, then reporting. Everything downstream depends on everything upstream being finalized. Almost every "why did my import fail" question traces back to close state: Fusion ships Close Manager and Close Monitor to orchestrate this: a checklist of close tasks per ledger/BU, owners, statuses, and the ability to track the whole close. Many implementations run their close as a job set so the sequence executes automatically. Order matters: never post to a period mid-close; you'll corrupt the reconciliation and break sign-off. pages.title: Banks, Branches & Accounts
pages.description: Sets up the bank master data that every cash transaction touches. A bank account is the anchor: payments and receipts post to it, bank statements reconcile against it, and cash pools consolidate it.

Functional view Bank master data is a strict hierarchy: a bank has one or more branches , and a bank account lives on one branch. The account is what Cash Management, Payables, and Receivables actually transact on. Internal bank accounts are your own and get the full treatment: uses per business unit, payment documents, and GL mapping. External accounts belong to third parties for example a supplier's account and are only referenced. A bank account validation service can check account numbers IBAN/BIC style validation when the account is created or edited. Set up in this order — each level references the one above it. Where each step of the bank → branch → account → uses → documents chain lands. Run these against the Fusion database to pull back the bank master setup. Setting up a bank account is master data — it creates no accounting entries. The cash account on each bank account use decides where cash postings land in the GL. Order matters: bank → branch → bank account → uses → payment documents; each step references the previous one. No DELETE on the account: cashBankAccounts has no delete operation — deactivate rather than delete. Uses before transactions: a bank account use with a valid cash account combination must exist before payments or receipts can post for a business unit. Statement matching: bank statement imports match on bank + branch + account number, so keep these stable. Validation service: the bank account validation service checks account numbers on create/update — validate before you import. Back to the Cash Management hub . Statements for these accounts are imported via FBDI — see Bank Statements & BAI2 . Matched lines and cash positions build on this setup — see Reconciliation & Forecasting . A bank account with no use for a business unit cannot post cash transactions for that unit — finish the uses before loading payments or receipts. pages.title: Cash Management
headings: Deep dives — read in this order
Technical view — the Cash integration surfaces
pages.content: The business story Functional view Deep dives — read in this order Technical view — the Cash integration surfaces Configuration Data flow — step by step Retrieve the data — SQL Accounting SLA Reporting Integration notes Next steps Manages bank accounts and reconciles them. Cash Management ingests bank statements, matches them against internal cash transactions payments, receipts , and lets you reconcile balances. This hub is your starting point; the deep dives below cover each area in functional and technical detail. breadcrumbs= , , updated="August 2026" level="Foundation" /> Read Enterprise Structures ledger, business units , Payables payments , and Receivables receipts before this page. The business story Ask the CEO "how much cash do we have?" and the honest answer needs Cash Management. Every payment made and every receipt collected lands in a bank account ; the bank sends a statement ; Cash Management reconciles the two. It is the module that proves the money you think you have is actually in the bank. Cash Management sits between Payables money out and Receivables money in : the payments it issues and the receipts it collects are the same cash transactions a bank statement eventually lists — and the system matches the two sides together. Set up banks/accounts first, then statements, then reconciliation. If you integrate payments or receipts, the bank account is the anchor for everything else. Two facts that differ from older training material: there is no bankStatements REST create in current Fusion docs statements load via the Cash Management Bank Statement FBDI , and the correct REST names are cashBanks / cashBankBranches / cashBankAccounts . Bank accounts and their GL mapping come first; statements and reconciliation follow. Where each step of the bank account → statement → reconciliation chain lands in the underlying tables. Run these against the Fusion database to pull back whatever was created. Cash is the clearing point between payments/receipts and the GL bank account: Reconciliation marks a bank line matched or cleared — it doesn't create additional accounting, it confirms the transaction exists in the bank statement. Statements come from FBDI, not REST: the create path for statements is the Cash Management Bank Statement Data Import interface tables + ESS job . Bank account must exist before a statement import; match on bank + branch + account number. Reconciliation: after import, transaction matching is semi-automatic — plan for unmatched lines. Format matters: bank statement files custom/ISO 20022/BAI2 must map to the parse rule sets and transaction type mapping exactly. Back to the Financials hub . Payments and receipts come from Payables and Receivables . Statement staging is covered in Interface Tables . Read Enterprise Structures ledger, business units , Payables payments , and Receivables receipts before this page. Reconciliation creates no new accounting — it confirms transactions already posted. The goal is simple: the GL cash balance and the bank statement should eventually agree. Cash Management checks that what the company thinks is in the bank is actually in the bank . It matches the company's records against the bank statement. A bank account invisible to a user, or a statement that won't import, is almost always a setup/security issue rather than a data bug. Functional view Reconciliation matches unreconciled statement lines to open cash transactions — the payments issued by Payables, the receipts collected by Receivables, and external cash transactions entered directly. Matching can run automatically via matching rules or manually ; lines that don't match become exceptions , often cleared in mass reconciliation . Matching rules come first; positioning and forecasting sit on top of reconciled data. Where a statement goes from imported to reconciled and into the cash position. Run these against the Fusion database to inspect reconciliation state. Matching a statement line confirms an existing transaction — it doesn't re-post it. External transactions and fund transfers , however, do create GL entries. Trace the entries via XLA_AE_HEADERS / XLA_AE_LINES — see Subledger Accounting . No reconciliation REST: run matching through the Automatic Reconciliation job via erpProcesses . Expect exceptions: no rule set matches everything; design monitoring for the unmatched pool. External transactions: use cashExternalTransactions or the External Transactions Import FBDI for cash movements with no AP/AR source. Transfers: cashBankAccountTransfers moves cash between own accounts; physical pools actually transfer, notional pools only offset. A rule that is too loose over-matches; one that is too tight floods the exception list. Start with amount + date tolerances and add reference matching as the data allows. There is no REST create resource for reconciliation . Reconciliation is run by the Automatic Reconciliation job via erpProcesses ; external transactions and transfers are created through their own REST resources or FBDI. Functional view A bank statement is processed in stages: import → parse → validate → reconcile . The statement header carries the account and date range; statement lines carry each movement deposit, withdrawal, charge ; balances are carried alongside opening, closing, and per-line available balances . Configure the mapping and validation layer before importing real statements. Where a statement travels from the file to the reconciliation queue. pages.title: Order-to-Cash (O2C)
headings: Step by step — where the data lands
Worked example — one customer payment through O2C
pages.content: The business story The cycle at a glance Step by step — where the data lands The two automation engines Worked example — one customer payment through O2C Common failure points Integration notes Next steps AutoInvoice AutoCash & lockbox The cycle that turns sales into cash: order → shipment → AR invoice → AutoInvoice → receipt → lockbox → collections. It spans Receivables, Cash Management, and the GL, and it is where billing automation AutoInvoice and receipt automation AutoCash , lockbox live. breadcrumbs= , , updated="August 2026" level="Advanced" /> Read AutoInvoice , Receipts & Lockbox , and Collections first. The business story A customer orders, you ship, you bill, they pay, and you reconcile the cash. Order-to-Cash is the mirror image of Procure-to-Pay — where P2P spends money, O2C earns it. The two automation engines are AutoInvoice turns billing lines into AR invoices in bulk and AutoCash / lockbox turns bank payment files into applied receipts . AutoInvoice reads RA_INTERFACE_LINES_ALL , applies grouping rules what becomes one invoice and line ordering rules the order lines print , runs AutoAccounting derives accounts from customer and line , and creates the AR transactions. Rejected lines stay in the interface with a reason — the execution report tells you exactly what failed. Lockbox imports the bank's payment file into AR_PAYMENTS_INTERFACE_ALL . The Process Receipts Through Lockbox job creates receipts, then AutoCash applies them to open invoices using AutoMatch a weighted score on amount, reference, and date and your application rule sets . Customers first: party → account → site must exist before AutoInvoice runs. AutoInvoice is interface-driven: stage lines, run the import job, read the execution report — there is no "create invoice" REST for bulk. Receipts come from the bank: lockbox files are the reliable path; standardReceipts REST covers the small manual cases. Deferred revenue: if the sale spans periods, invoice with revenue rules and let the Recognize Revenue job release it. See the money-in side in Receivables . Follow the cash into the bank in Reconciliation & Forecasting . See the counterpart cycle that spends money: Procure-to-Pay . Read AutoInvoice , Receipts & Lockbox , and Collections first. The invoice: AutoInvoice creates AR invoice INV-1001 for $5,000 + $250 output tax = $5,250 due. Accounting: Dr AR trade receivable 5,250 · Cr Revenue 5,000 · Cr Output tax 250. The payment: the bank file shows $5,250 from "Customer Co" — AutoMatch scores it against INV-1001 amount matches and applies it in full. Accounting: Dr Cash/bank 5,250 · Cr AR trade receivable 5,250. The reconciliation: the bank statement line matches the receipt in Cash Management, and the receivable is cleared. It spans Procurement, Payables, Cash Management, and the GL — and it is the most common end-to-end flow consultants are asked to integrate. breadcrumbs= , , updated="August 2026" level="Advanced" /> Read Invoice Entry & Validation , Payments & PPR , and Reconciliation first. The business story Someone needs goods or services. The company buys them, receives them, gets billed, and pays the supplier. Each step moves through a different module, and each module has its own rules — an invoice cannot be paid until the PO exists, the goods are received, and the invoice is validated and approved. Every hop below shows the module, the table it lands in, and the integration surface you would use. Table names follow the Fusion data dictionary — confirm against your release. P2P breaks unless the invoice "agrees" with the PO and the receipt. Payables matches three documents: Order matters: supplier → PO → receipt → invoice. Each step validates the one before it. Two paths for invoices: a handful via invoices REST; thousands via the Payables Standard Invoice Import into AP_INVOICES_INTERFACE . Payments are a job, not a REST call: build the PPR and submit it via erpProcesses . Reconciliation is semi-automatic: plan for unmatched lines and define matching rules before go-live. See the money-out side in Payables . Follow the cash into the bank in Reconciliation & Forecasting . See the counterpart cycle that brings money in: Order-to-Cash . Read Invoice Entry & Validation , Payments & PPR , and Reconciliation first. If matching fails, Payables places a hold on the invoice and it stops in Requires Re-approval . See Holds & PO Matching . The PO: 2 × laptop at $600 each, tax 10%, supplier "Acme IT". The receipt: 2 units received → 3-way match possible. The invoice: $1,200 goods + $120 tax = $1,320 total. Validation passes within tolerance, PO and receipt match . Accounting SLA : Dr Equipment 1,200 · Dr Input tax 120 · Cr AP liability 1,320. The payment: PPR selects the invoice, builds an ACH file for $1,320, the bank statement clears it, and reconciliation marks it matched. pages.title: Record-to-Report (R2R)
headings: Step by step — where the data lands
Worked example — one month for a small company
pages.content: The business story The cycle at a glance Step by step — where the data lands Why the order matters Worked example — one month for a small company Common failure points Integration notes Next steps The cycle that turns transactions into financial statements: every sub-ledger event posts to the GL, the period closes in sequence, balances consolidate , and reports come out. It is the reporting layer on top of all other Financials activity and the cycle an accountant owns end to end. breadcrumbs= , , updated="August 2026" level="Advanced" /> Read Subledger Accounting , Period Close , and Journals & Posting first. The business story Everything that happens in the business — buying, selling, paying, receiving, depreciating — must end up in the ledger and then on a financial statement. Record-to-Report is the monthly loop that guarantees it: sub-ledgers post to the GL, the close sequence runs in the right order, and reporting finally produces the trial balance, income statement, and balance sheet. The heart of R2R is the close sequence : a specific order you follow every period, because each step depends on the one before it. The ordering collapses into the one sentence every accountant lives by: you cannot close a period with open transactions, and you cannot report before you close. More concretely: Accounting before close — Create Accounting must run for every sub-ledger event or the GL is missing entries. Posting before revaluation — revaluation only sees posted balances. Rates before translation — Translate Balances needs the period's rates. All done before consolidation — consolidating before the close finishes reports stale data. Drive the jobs, don't click them: Create Accounting, Post Journals, Revalue, Translate, and Open/Close are all erpProcesses submissions. Period status is the gate: query accountingPeriodsLOV before submitting anything that posts. Balances, not transactions, for reporting: reporting reads GL_BALANCES ; journal lines are the audit trail behind them. Interface tables first: journal feeds go into GL_INTERFACE and post via Import Journals — never insert into GL_JE_* directly. Master the close sequence on GL Period Close . Understand how any transaction becomes GL entries in Subledger Accounting . See the whole loop around R2R: Business Cycles . Read Subledger Accounting , Period Close , and Journals & Posting first. The Financial Close page covers the full close sequence and Close Manager; this cycle page shows how every sub-ledger plugs into it. 1. Sub-ledger posts: an AP invoice for $1,320 from P2P and an AR invoice for $5,250 from O2C create accounting entries and post to the GL. 2. New balances: GL_BALANCES now shows the accounts with period activity equipment +1,200, revenue +5,000, AP liability +1,320, AR receivable +5,250… . 3. Revalue: a €10,000 receivable at a 1.10 rate revalues — a $500 gain is journaled at 1.05. 4. Allocate: rent of $3,000 is spread across three departments at $1,000 each via an allocation journal. 5. Close: the period is closed; the trial balance ties debits = credits , and the P&L and balance sheet run. 6. Report: statements are produced in the Financial Reporting Center and reviewed before the ledger is locked. Functional view After submission an expense report moves through approval who must sign off , audit which reports get extra review , and finally reimbursement payment to the employee or card issuer through Payables . Cash advances and spend authorizations front-money the employee in parallel. Approval, audit, and reimbursement behavior is configuration, not code. Each setup gates a distinct part of the report lifecycle. Where each step of the submit → approve → pay chain lands in the underlying tables. Approval is asynchronous: submitted reports move through workflow and may need action — poll status before assuming the report is approved. Audit and holds gate payment: audit selection, payment hold rules, and risk indicators can block an otherwise approved report. Cash advances settle: advances are applied to lines and settled — an unsettled advance can block final reimbursement. Reimbursement is a Payables step: the report creates a payment request exposed via erpProcesses for Create Accounting and reimbursement jobs — verify names in instance that Payables then pays. A report that is approved but never reimbursed is usually a payment hold, a missing employee bank account, or a closed AP period — not a workflow failure. Functional view Corporate card programs model a card issuer VISA, MasterCard, American Express, Diners Club and the cards issued to employees. Card transactions arrive as files from the issuer, are imported and mapped to employees, and become card transactions that an employee either attaches to an expense report or reimburses directly. Card integration is configured in the Expenses card setup area: the program, the who-pays assignment, and the rules that interpret issuer files. Where each step of card file processing lands in the underlying tables. Run these against the Fusion database to inspect imported card transactions. The who-pays model decides the credit side of the entry. Trace entries via XLA_AE_HEADERS / XLA_AE_LINES — see Subledger Accounting . No public card FBDI: card files flow through the card program interfaces, not an FBDI template. Verify file-format requirements and job names against your instance. Mapping rules first: without issuer mapping rules, transactions land unmapped and never reach a report. Wait days: transactions are withheld for the configured wait days — do not expect them on reports immediately after import. Who-pays changes payment: company-pay reports pay the issuer; employee-pay reports reimburse the employee through Payables. Confirm the assignment per program. Tokenization & PGP: card data is tokenized per security setup, and card files are typically PGP-signed/encrypted — include key exchange in the project plan. Dual-currency transactions: transactions in a currency other than the reporting currency carry both amounts — be careful which amount feeds accounting. Back to Expenses . pages.content: The business story Functional view Deep dives — read in this order Technical view — the Expenses integration surfaces Configuration Data flow — step by step Retrieve the data — SQL Accounting SLA Reporting Integration notes Next steps Manages employee spend: expense reports , expense templates, policies, and approvals. An employee submits a report; it is approved; it feeds Payables for payment or a clearing account . This hub is your starting point; the deep dives below cover each area in functional and technical detail. breadcrumbs= , , updated="August 2026" level="Foundation" /> Read Enterprise Structures , Approvals & Workflow , and Tax before this page. The business story From a business trip to a team lunch to a foreign client dinner — people spend money on the company's behalf, and someone has to record, approve, and reimburse it. Expenses is that workflow: an employee submits an expense report , it's approved , and the money is paid back through Payables. Expense management is a workflow problem first: submit → approve → pay. The data model is built around the expense report one claim and its lines each spend , governed by templates and categories . Understand templates and policies first what can be claimed , then card programs where lines come from , then approval/audit/reimbursement what happens after submit . Expense data is served by REST resources under the expense* family. Note there is no "Import Expense Reports" FBDI in the current Financials FBDI guide — third-party expense data flows via XML export/import and a UCM upload under fin/expenses/import . Expense setups determine what a user can claim and where it posts. Where each step of the expense report → approval → payment chain lands in the underlying tables. Run these against the Fusion database to pull back whatever was created. An approved expense report creates entries through the sub-ledger accounting engine: Trace entries via XLA_AE_HEADERS / XLA_AE_LINES — see Subledger Accounting . Employee + category must exist : lines reject when the employee, category, or template is unknown. Approval is asynchronous : imported reports may enter "Needs Action" — poll status before paying. Period open: expense lines post to a period; closed periods block the import. Corporate cards: card feed integrations create lines from transaction files, then enrich them. No public expense FBDI: bulk data from third-party systems goes through the XML import / UCM upload path — verify the exact mechanism on your instance. Back to the Financials hub . Approved reports settle through Payables . Employee master data comes from HCM covered in a later module . Read Enterprise Structures , Approvals & Workflow , and Tax before this page. Expenses is a workflow module first: the money is small per line, but the approval and policy rules per diem, limits, receipt requirements are where the real complexity lives. Expenses handles the day-to-day spending of employees — travel, meals, supplies — from the report they file to the reimbursement they get back. Approved expense reports post to the GL and are settled through Payables — which is why an expenses integration usually also touches the AP payment process. A report that won't submit, or a line that posts to the wrong account, is usually a missing setup in one of these areas. pages.title: Templates, Expense Types & Policies
pages.description: The configuration layer that governs what employees can claim. Expense templates define the structure of a report, expense types and categories define what can be entered, and per-category policies enforce limits, mileage rates, per diem, and audit rules.

Template and policy names are shown as documented in Oracle's Using Expenses guide — verify against your instance. Functional view Three concepts are easy to confuse, so it helps to separate them. An expense template is the form an employee fills in; an expense type is the specific spend category e.g. Hotel, Airfare, Meal ; an expense category is the higher-level grouping that policies and accounts attach to. A template lists the expense types available on that report, and each type maps to a category that carries its accounting and policy defaults. Policy behavior is configuration, not code. Mileage and per-diem rules apply automatically when a matching line is entered, and audit rules fire on submit. Where each step of expense entry and policy enforcement lands in the underlying tables. Run these against the Fusion database to inspect expense lines and their category/type context. Lines post to the account mapped from their expense type → category . Entries come from the subledger accounting engine; trace them via XLA_AE_HEADERS / XLA_AE_LINES — see Subledger Accounting . Expense data entry is XML, not FBDI: Oracle's Using Expenses guide documents "Expense Report Data Flow Using a Third-Party Application," which uses XML export/import . There is no public 26C "Import Expense Reports" FBDI — confirm against your instance's FBDI guide before assuming one. Type must be on the template: lines reference an expense type that must exist and appear on the report's template, or the line is rejected. Policy evaluation is automatic: mileage, per-diem, and category limits apply on entry/submit — integration should expect policy result fields on the line. Read-only policy resources: policies are configured in the UI and exposed for GET only; do not try to create policy rules via REST. Per-diem is computed: request expensePerDiemCalculations before building lines so the correct allowance is carried onto the report. Back to Expenses . Card transactions become expense lines — see Corporate Card Programs . Submission and settlement workflows — see Approval, Audit & Reimbursement . Back to the Financials hub . Template and policy names are shown as documented in Oracle's Using Expenses guide — verify against your instance. A line posts to the account derived from its expense type → category mapping. Matching the template a report is created under is essential — lines that use types not on the template are rejected or removed. Most "why did this line reject" questions trace back to a missing per-category policy, an absent mileage rate for the date, or a type not on the template. Finish these setups before testing entry. These policy resources expose the configured rules for verification and integration awareness. They are GET only — create or update policies in the Expenses user interface. pages.title: Additions & Mass Additions
headings: Working example — submit Post Mass Additions
pages.content: Functional view Configuration Technical view Data flow — step by step Retrieve the data — SQL Accounting SLA Reporting Integration notes Next steps FBDI templates REST resources Working example — submit Post Mass Additions How assets get into the books: single manual additions, bulk mass additions fed from AP invoices, receiving, projects, or legacy systems, and construction-in-process that converts into a capitalized asset once complete — with capitalization thresholds gating every transfer. breadcrumbs= , , , updated="August 2026" level="Module" /> Read Asset Books & Setup books, categories, thresholds that an addition must pass , Driving ESS via REST erpProcesses how the Post Mass Additions job is submitted , and Payables if your mass additions come from AP invoices. Functional view An addition brings a new asset into an asset book at a cost. It can be entered one at a time in the Asset Workbench, or in bulk as a mass addition . Mass additions are the integration-facing path: source systems — AP invoices, receiving, projects, or a legacy asset register — supply the candidate lines, they are staged, and the Post Mass Additions process converts the valid lines into real assets. Source lines and source-line transfers. Each candidate line keeps a pointer to where it came from — the AP invoice, the receiving transaction, the project. That link "source line" is retained on the mass addition so the asset history can show the origin. Before posting, you can transfer source lines between mass additions or delete unwanted ones; only lines that survive to the post become assets. Capitalization thresholds gate the transfer. A line whose cost sits below the book's capitalization threshold — and is not forced to capitalize — is expensed instead, so it never becomes an asset. Low-value thresholds work the same way but route the value into a designated low-value category. For CIP, the threshold decides whether the completed project's cost capitalizes when it converts. The job turns valid FA_MASS_ADDITIONS rows into assets. Parameter names vary by job and release — read them from the job's submission UI or the REST resource explorer, and verify the exact names against your instance. Where each step of a mass addition lands in the underlying tables. An addition posts through Create Accounting for Assets : Events: asset addition and CIP conversion . Trace the entries via XLA_AE_HEADERS / XLA_AE_LINES — see Subledger Accounting . Converting legacy assets: when migrating from an old register, map your legacy category/method pairs to Fusion categories so the imported assets inherit the right books. Capitalizing CIP when complete: once all project costs are in and the unit is placed in service, run the CIP conversion — threshold check happens again at this point. Thresholds first: a line under the capitalization threshold is expensed, not capitalized — stage only what should become assets, or force the capitalize flag where intended. Post Mass Additions is the finish line: importing the FBDI only stages rows; nothing is an asset until the job runs and posts valid lines. Rejected rows stay in the line: rows that fail validation remain in FA_MASS_ADDITIONS with an error state — inspect, fix, and repost rather than reloading. Asset CRUD lives in SCM: for direct asset create/read, use the SCM / Asset Management REST guide fscmRestApi , not the Financials guide. Verify against your instance: sheet headers, ESS job parameters, and table columns all vary by release — confirm before building on them. Back to the Fixed Assets overview . Back to the Financials hub . Once assets exist, continue to Depreciation & Revaluation . Read Asset Books & Setup books, categories, thresholds that an addition must pass , Driving ESS via REST erpProcesses how the Post Mass Additions job is submitted , and Payables if your mass additions come from AP invoices. Assets added upon receipt is a special mode: an item received in inventory is simultaneously offered to Fixed Assets, so the receiving transaction and the asset addition are one continuous flow instead of a separate load. The Financials REST guide does not publish an assets resource — asset CRUD is under the SCM / Asset Management REST guide fscmRestApi . Most volume addition loads go through the Fixed Asset Mass Additions Import FBDI plus the Post Mass Additions ESS job instead. These are the underlying Oracle Database tables as documented in the Fusion data dictionary. Exact names and status columns can vary slightly by release — confirm against your instance's data dictionary before relying on them. Verify the column names in FA_MASS_ADDITIONS and FA_ADDITIONS_B especially the status field against your instance, and never query the Fusion database directly for production reporting — use OTBI or the REST API instead. Having trouble? See Fixed Assets troubleshooting for the most common failures and fixes.
