pages.title: Asset Books & Setup
pages.description: Everything that must exist before a single asset can be added: the asset books (corporate and tax), the depreciation calendars and fiscal years behind them, the conventions and capitalization thresholds that gate an addition, and the flexfields that name and locate every asset.
headings: Working example — look up books for an upload
pages.content: Functional view Configuration Technical view Data flow — step by step Retrieve the data — SQL Accounting SLA Reporting Integration notes Next steps REST resources FBDI templates Working example — look up books for an upload Read Enterprise Structures the ledger that asset books report to , Flexfields & Value Sets the asset, category, and location key flexfields , and the Fixed Assets overview before this page. Functional view An asset book is the rules holder for a set of assets: it carries the depreciation method, life, and conventions, and it answers to one General Ledger. A given asset is almost always tracked in more than one book at once — typically a corporate book that posts to the GL and one or more statutory or tax books that only report. Combining and transferring between books is routine, but transfers across ledgers carry additional accounting — the source book must be current on depreciation before the transfer runs. See Transfers, Retirements & Impairment . New assets get a default asset status from the category they are created under. If the category defaults are wrong for example a missing depreciation rule , every asset added under it inherits the same problem — fix categories before loading assets. Books and their supporting setups are configured in the Fixed Assets work area, before any mass addition is posted. The root service listing order is farfa → Fixed Asset in the REST resource explorer. Resource and field names vary slightly by release — verify them against your instance's REST resource explorer. Where each layer of the book setup lands in the underlying tables. Book setup itself creates no accounting entries. It only determines how later events post: the book's accounting method and the category's account defaults decide which GL accounts an addition, a depreciation run, or a retirement hit. The entries themselves are generated by Create Accounting for Assets and land in XLA_AE_HEADERS / XLA_AE_LINES — see Subledger Accounting . Setup first, load second: a mass addition against a book with no open calendar period or no category defaults will fail — finish books, calendars, categories, thresholds first. Books are UI-created: the Financials REST guide has no create endpoint for books — setup goes through Manage Asset Books. Only fixedAssetBooksLOV and fixedAssetCategoriesLOV GET exist there. Asset CRUD is elsewhere: creating asset records is done through the SCM / Asset Management REST guide fscmRestApi , not the Financials guide. Validate with the LOVs: before a bulk load, fetch fixedAssetBooksLOV and fixedAssetCategoriesLOV so the file only references books and categories that exist. Verify against your instance: resource names, book codes, and dictionary columns all vary by release — confirm before building integrations on them. Back to the Fixed Assets overview . Back to the Financials hub . Continue to Additions & Mass Additions — this is where the books you configured start getting used. Read Enterprise Structures the ledger that asset books report to , Flexfields & Value Sets the asset, category, and location key flexfields , and the Fixed Assets overview before this page. Because these setups are UI-driven there is no REST resource in the Financials REST guide that creates them , an integration typically reads the book and category setup to validate its uploads rather than writing to it. There is an important split to keep straight. The Financials REST guide farfa publishes only two read-only reference resources for Fixed Assets: fixedAssetBooksLOV and fixedAssetCategoriesLOV — both GET . There is no assets resource in the Financials book. Real asset CRUD creating, updating, reading asset records lives in the SCM / Asset Management REST guide fscmRestApi instead. Document those two sources as separate integrations. These are the underlying Oracle Database tables as documented in the Fusion data dictionary. Column names like BOOK_TYPE_CODE are plausible dictionary names — exact names and even which calendar table a release uses can vary, so confirm against your instance's data dictionary before relying on them. Verify the column names in FA_BOOKS and FA_CATEGORIES_B against your instance, and never query the Fusion database directly for production reporting — use OTBI or the REST API instead. Having trouble? See Fixed Assets troubleshooting for the most common failures and fixes. Book perspective What it does Corporate book Primary book for an asset; drives GL postings and managerial reporting Tax book Tracks the same asset under tax depreciation rules; usually reporting-only, not posted to the GL Multiple books One asset can live in several books simultaneously, each with its own cost, method, life, and convention Transfer between books Assets can move between books same ledger or different ledger , each move recorded as a transaction Setup concept What it controls Fiscal years The annual window a book recognizes; defined in a range before periods exist Asset calendar depreciation periods The periods a depreciation run can post to; opens/closes per book Prorate convention How much depreciation the first partial period takes mid-month, mid-quarter, next month, and so on Retirement convention How the period of a retirement/retired asset is handled for depreciation Capitalization threshold The cost below which an item is expensed instead of capitalized; low-value thresholds then place small assets in low-value categories Category and Category Key Flexfield Groups assets Machinery, Furniture… and drives the defaults each asset inherits Asset Key Flexfield The structured asset identifier tag, serial, description segments used to find and name assets Location flexfield Where an asset physically sits; pages.title: Depreciation & Revaluation
pages.content: Functional view Configuration Technical view Data flow — step by step Retrieve the data — SQL Accounting SLA Reporting Worked example — straight-line depreciation Integration notes Next steps ESS jobs FBDI templates Working example — run Calculate Depreciation How asset value is written off over time: the Calculate Depreciation run against each book's calendar, the depreciation methods and rules behind it, group depreciation, what-if projection, and revaluation with rules, value types, and price indexes. breadcrumbs= , , , updated="August 2026" level="Advanced" /> Read Asset Books & Setup the calendar and conventions a run posts against , Additions & Mass Additions , and Driving ESS via REST erpProcesses how the depreciation jobs are submitted . Functional view Depreciation is calculated per book, per period : the Calculate Depreciation run takes every asset in the book with an open depreciation period and writes the period's charge. The results aggregate per asset, and Create Accounting for Assets turns the run into journal entries that post to the GL. The result for any asset is driven by the depreciation rules and the book's default subcomponent rules : for assets made of subcomponents for example a machine with a rebuildable engine , the rule set describes how each subcomponent is treated and which method/life each gets. Revaluation restates an asset's cost and its accumulated depreciation so the books reflect current market or index values. It is governed by revaluation rules that define the value types book value, cost, accumulated depreciation, or gross value to revalue, the price indexes used, and how the revaluation gain or loss is accounted for. The parameter list and names vary by job and release — read them from the job's submission UI or the REST resource explorer and verify against your instance. After a successful run, submit Create Accounting for Assets to post the entries. Where the depreciation cycle lands in the underlying tables. Depreciation posts through Create Accounting for Assets : Trace the entries via XLA_AE_HEADERS / XLA_AE_LINES — see Subledger Accounting . Open period is everything: Calculate Depreciation only posts to an open period in the book's calendar — check it before every run. Run order: Calculate Depreciation → review the schedule → Create Accounting for Assets. Posting only happens at the accounting step. Projections are safe: the Depreciation Projection job is what-if and never posts — great for validating a rate or method change before committing. Units of production need data: units-based assets must have their actual units loaded Import Units of Production FBDI or the run undercharges. Revaluation impacts GL: revaluation entries hit asset, reserve, and expense accounts — verify the revaluation rules' accounts and value types first. Asset CRUD lives in SCM: direct asset maintenance goes through the SCM / Asset Management guide fscmRestApi ; verify resource and column names against your instance. Back to the Fixed Assets overview . Back to the Financials hub . Continue to Transfers, Retirements & Impairment . Read Asset Books & Setup the calendar and conventions a run posts against , Additions & Mass Additions , and Driving ESS via REST erpProcesses how the depreciation jobs are submitted . The Financials REST guide does not publish an assets resource — asset-level CRUD is under the SCM / Asset Management REST guide fscmRestApi . The depreciation cycle itself is driven by ESS jobs submitted through erpProcesses . These are the underlying Oracle Database tables as documented in the Fusion data dictionary. Which calendar table a release uses and the exact summary column names can vary — confirm against your instance's data dictionary before relying on them. Projections are produced by the Depreciation Projection job, not stored as book-of- record data — these queries give the basis to check them. Verify column names for example whether a release uses life_in_months against your instance, and never query the Fusion database directly for production reporting — use OTBI or the REST API instead. Having trouble? See Fixed Assets troubleshooting for the most common failures and fixes. Depreciation method How it writes off value Straight-line Equal annual expense spread over the asset's life most common default Declining balance Accelerated: a fixed rate applied to the remaining book value each period Units of production Expense proportional to actual usage/units versus the total expected units — fed by unit-of-production imports Life in Periods Specifies the depreciable life directly as a number of periods instead of years/months Annuity Level periodic amount that treats the asset as earning/lending a rate of return Capability What it does Deferred depreciation Postpones depreciation for assets not yet placed fully in service; released to expense on a later date Depreciation override Lets a user replace the calculated amount for a specific asset/period Unplanned depreciation Records an extra one-off charge for example a write-down of remaining value Group assets & group depreciation Depreciates a pool of similar assets together and computes a group rate; assets add into or retire from the group What-if depreciation analysis The Depreciation Projection job previews future charges without posting them Setup Why it matters Where it lives Depreciation pages.title: Fixed Assets
headings: Deep dives — read in this order
Technical view — the FA integration surfaces
pages.content: The business story Functional view Deep dives — read in this order Technical view — the FA integration surfaces Configuration Data flow — step by step Retrieve the data — SQL Accounting SLA Reporting Integration notes Next steps Tracks capital assets and their depreciation . Assets live in asset books, get added through the asset addition flow, and depreciate on a calendar held in the depreciation periods table. This hub is your starting point; the deep dives below cover each area in functional and technical detail. breadcrumbs= , , updated="August 2026" level="Foundation" /> Read Enterprise Structures ledger, asset books , Flexfields & Value Sets , and Financial Close how depreciation posts before this page. The business story Not everything the company buys gets used up in a month. A machine, a building, a vehicle lasts for years — and accounting has to recognize that it slowly loses value over that time. Fixed Assets tracks those big-ticket items: what was bought additions , and how its cost is written off each period depreciation . A company owns long-lived items. Each one is an asset that enters an asset book the rules holder via an asset addition , loses value per period through depreciation , and can later be transferred, adjusted, or retired. Every event is recorded in the asset history. Set up books and categories first, then additions/mass additions, then depreciation. The transactions page covers the back half of the asset lifecycle. One fact that surprises most consultants: the Financials REST guide ships only two Fixed Assets resources fixedAssetBooksLOV and fixedAssetCategoriesLOV , both read-only . Real asset create/update lives in the SCM / Asset Management REST guide, and the practical create path is the Fixed Asset Mass Additions Import FBDI. Fixed Assets is configured before any asset can be added or depreciated. Where each step of the asset → book → depreciation chain lands — including the calendar table FA_DEPRN_PERIODS that drives every depreciation run. Run these against the Fusion database to pull back whatever was created. Note the join through FA_DEPRN_PERIODS — it is the key to every depreciation query. The main FA events and their entries: Posting goes through the GL interface and XLA — see Subledger Accounting . Book-per-approach: assets belong to books; an integration typically writes to the corporate book used for GL posting. The calendar governs the run: depreciation can only post to an open period in FA_DEPRN_PERIODS — check open_period_flag before posting. Create path: additions are bulk-loaded via the Mass Additions FBDI and posted with the Post Mass Additions job — there is no Financials REST create for assets. Key fields: asset category drives capitalization rules — confirm available categories first. Depreciation start dates: the prorate/start date determines the first depreciation period. Back to the Financials hub . Depreciation posts flow into the GL journal world. Read Enterprise Structures ledger, asset books , Flexfields & Value Sets , and Financial Close how depreciation posts before this page. It's not inventory and it's not an expense: an asset is capitalized on arrival and its cost is released gradually as depreciation expense. That distinction is what Fixed Assets is all about. Fixed Assets tracks the big things a company owns that last for years — machines, vehicles, buildings — and slowly writes off their cost over time depreciation . The single most common FA failure — "no open period" — comes from the depreciation calendar. Check FA_DEPRN_PERIODS before every run. pages.title: Transfers, Retirements & Impairment
pages.description: What happens to an asset after it is added and depreciated: transfers and reclassification, retirement (partial or full) with reinstatement, impairments on cash-generating units, physical inventory cycles, and the transaction approvals that control it all.
headings: Working example — create accounting after a transaction
pages.content: Functional view Configuration Technical view Data flow — step by step Retrieve the data — SQL Accounting SLA Reporting Integration notes Next steps FBDI templates REST resources Working example — create accounting after a transaction Read Asset Books & Setup conventions that affect retirement proration , Additions & Mass Additions , and Depreciation & Revaluation . Functional view Once an asset exists it rarely sits still. Every change — a transfer to a new location or cost center, a category change, a partial or full retirement, a reclassification after an impairment review — is recorded as an asset transaction . Depending on your setups, these transactions require approval before they take effect. Retirements can be full or partial and trigger retirement depreciation : the asset is depreciated up to the retirement date using the book's retirement convention, then the net book value is written off. Reinstatement reverses that — the asset comes back with the remaining cost, reserve, and life it had before, so subsequent runs continue from where they left off. Each FBDI template above has a matching import process you submit through erpProcesses to turn interface rows into transactions. Process names and parameters vary by release — verify them against your instance's job submission UI and REST resource explorer. Where each step of a transfer/retirement/impairment lands in the underlying tables. Transactions post through Create Accounting for Assets : Trace the entries via XLA_AE_HEADERS / XLA_AE_LINES — see Subledger Accounting . Impairment: recorded on cash-generating units CGUs — a group of assets whose cash flows are independent. The impairment loss is allocated across the CGU's assets, and if the reason reverses, the loss can be reversed up to the recoverable amount. Physical inventory: counts are imported through the physical inventory interface, compared to the asset register, and corrective adjustments additions, retirements, or tag fixes are posted for the differences. Approvals: transaction approval rules can require a manager's sign-off on transfers, retirements, and reclassifications before the transaction is booked. Depreciation before the move: cross-ledger book transfers require the source book to be fully depreciated up to date — run Calculate Depreciation first. Retired status is book-level: an asset retires in one book and stays active in another — match on asset_id plus book_type_code , not on the asset alone. Reinstatement reverses the retirement: it restores cost, reserve, and life so the next run continues correctly — do not manually re-add a reinstated asset. Impairment is CGU-driven: allocate losses across the cash-generating unit, and respect the reversal cap recoverable amount when recording reversals. Interface imports need the import job: FBDI uploads only stage rows — the matching import process via erpProcesses converts them, then Create Accounting for Assets posts. Asset CRUD lives in SCM: direct asset transactions go through the SCM / Asset Management guide fscmRestApi ; verify resource, job, and column names against your instance. Back to the Fixed Assets overview . Back to the Financials hub . Retirement and impairment entries flow into the GL journal world. Read Asset Books & Setup conventions that affect retirement proration , Additions & Mass Additions , and Depreciation & Revaluation . As with additions and depreciation, the Financials REST guide does not publish an assets resource — asset-level CRUD is under the SCM / Asset Management REST guide fscmRestApi . Bulk transaction loads go through the Fixed Asset FBDI imports below, and accounting is generated with Create Accounting for Assets . These are the underlying Oracle Database tables as documented in the Fusion data dictionary. Exact names and status columns can vary slightly by release — confirm against your instance's data dictionary before relying on them. Verify the column names — especially the retirement status value in FA_BOOKS or FA_ADDITIONS_B , which can differ by release — against your instance, and never query the Fusion database directly for production reporting — use OTBI or the REST API instead. pages.title: Financial Accounting Hub (FAH)
pages.description: The module that lets transactions from other applications — or no application at all — become GL entries. FAH takes external/custom sub-ledger data, runs it through the subledger accounting engine, and posts into Fusion General Ledger: the integration-friendly door into the books.
headings: How FAH differs from a normal sub-ledger
Worked example — one external transaction to GL
pages.content: Functional view How FAH differs from a normal sub-ledger Technical view Data flow — step by step Retrieve the data — SQL Worked example — one external transaction to GL Integration notes Next steps Key surfaces Read Subledger Accounting FAH *is* SLA applied to external data , the GL hub , and Interface Tables before this page. Functional view Fusion's own modules Payables, Receivables… create their own XLA_ accounting automatically. FAH exists for the rest : a custom system, a legacy ledger, a third-party app, or an internally built sub-ledger that still needs proper accounting. Instead of building interface logic yourself, you feed FAH transactions and it runs the same subledger accounting engine — events, accounting methods, journal line rules — to produce validated entries that transfer to the GL. Where an external transaction and its entries land in the underlying tables. Events, not invoices: FAH is fed account-ready events; setup effort lives in the SLA mapping methods, rules, accounts , not in Fusion module screens. Reuse SLA knowledge: whatever you learned on XLA_ tables and accounting methods applies unchanged. Transfer is a job: creating entries is one step; transferring and posting them to the GL is driven as an ESS/erpProcesses job. Verify names: hub resources and transfer processes are version-specific — check the resource explorer on your instance. FAH runs on the engine explained in Subledger Accounting . Back to the GL hub or the Financials hub . Read Subledger Accounting FAH *is* SLA applied to external data , the GL hub , and Interface Tables before this page. The short version consultants memorize: FAH = bring external transactions into the Fusion accounting engine. It reuses all of SLA — events, methods, rules, XLA tables — so what you learn about subledger accounting applies directly. Accounting Hub resource names and the exact import/transfer process names vary by release the Financials REST guide documents the hub as accountingHub* resources . Confirm availability and names against your instance's resource explorer before building. These are the underlying Oracle Database tables as documented in the Fusion data dictionary. The hub's own transaction staging tables are release-specific — confirm against your instance. Column names follow the Fusion data dictionary naming. Confirm against your release before relying on them, and never query the Fusion database directly for production reporting — use OTBI or the REST API instead. The event: an external lending app sends "loan #8821 disbursed, $5,000". Mapping: the event type is mapped to an SLA accounting method; the rule derives Dr Cash-in-bank $5,000 · Cr Loan liability $5,000. Hub processing: SLA creates the entry in XLA_AE_HEADERS / XLA_AE_LINES . Transfer: the approved entry transfers to the GL and posts as a standard journal. Why FAH: the lending app never touches Fusion sub-ledgers — its only job is emitting the transaction; Fusion handles all accounting. Having trouble? Start with GL troubleshooting posting, periods, accounts — the same rules govern FAH-created entries. pages.title: Allocations & Recurring Entries
pages.description: Automated, formula-driven journals. Recurring journals repeat a fixed entry every period; allocations distribute costs and balances across segments using rules built in Calculation Manager.

Functional view Recurring journals post the same entry each period monthly accruals, fixed formulas with little or no formula logic. Allocations distribute cost or balances across segments — for example spreading one department's rent over several cost centers on a defined basis. Allocation rules are built in Calculation Manager , grouped into rule sets , and each rule is assembled from components POV, allocation, and formula components that reference variables . There is no dedicated create REST resource for allocation rules — rules are built in the UI Calculation Manager . Generation is an ESS job, and the recurring-like journals can also be loaded through the Journal Import FBDI. Where the generated allocation journals land in the underlying Oracle Database tables. Run this against the Fusion database to find the journals an allocation run generated. Allocations produce ordinary GL journals — a debit to the target account and a credit from the source basis. They do not pass through the sub-ledger accounting engine; they are GL journals from start to finish. Audit trails live in the allocation process output and the GL_JE_HEADERS description that identifies the rule that created them. Rules are UI, generation is API: build rule sets in Calculation Manager, then drive the Allocate Balances job from erpProcesses . Source/category: give allocation journals a dedicated journal source so they are easy to isolate in journalBatches , reports, and SQL. Audit: generated journals carry a description referencing the rule — preserve it when troubleshooting or reconciling. pages.title: Budgets & Budgetary Control
headings: Worked example — a department budget enforced
pages.content: Functional view Configuration Technical view Data flow — step by step Retrieve the data — SQL Worked example — a department budget enforced Integration notes Next steps Import and load surfaces How Fusion sets spend limits and enforces them at transaction time. Ledger budgets hold the planned amounts per account combination and period; budgetary control checks every document line against the remaining budget before it is approved — the accounting layer that makes a budget a hard limit instead of a report. breadcrumbs= , , , updated="August 2026" level="Module" /> Read the GL hub , GL Period Close the budget close step , and Subledger Accounting before this page. Functional view A budget is a plan: how much a department may spend on an account in a period. Fusion stores it as budget balances — a second set of balances beside the actuals in GL_BALANCES . Budgetary control makes that plan enforceable: when a document PO, expense report, AP invoice posts, the engine reserves the amount against the remaining budget and blocks the document if the reservation would exceed it. Budget control needs the ledger, a calendar, and a budget structure set up before the first document can be checked. Where a budget and its control events land in the underlying tables. Load order: open the budget period, load balances via FBDI, run Validate and Upload Budgets, then confirm the budget before documents are created. Reservations are the tricky part: with encumbrance on, POs/reservations consume budget before the invoice — integrations must treat a reject here as a budget error, not a data error. Reports monitor: Budget versus Actual runs in the Financial Reporting Center; OTBI exposes budget balances as a subject area. Rest is read-mostly: budget close queries budgetaryControlBudgetTransactions ; creation is FBDI + ESS, not REST create. Budgets close as part of GL Period Close . Back to the GL hub or the Financials hub . Read the GL hub , GL Period Close the budget close step , and Subledger Accounting before this page. Budgetary control is optional per ledger and per document type . Many implementations run budgets for reporting only no control ; control is switched on when the business wants hard enforcement at approval time. The REST surface for budgetary control is read-oriented in the 26C Financials guide — the create path for budget balances is the FBDI import followed by the Validate and Upload Budgets ESS job. Intercompany accounting keeps each entity's books balanced via the balancing segment and carries the receivable/payable between them. breadcrumbs= , , , updated="August 2026" level="Advanced" /> Read Enterprise Structures legal entity and balancing segment and Journals & Posting before this page. Functional view An intercompany transaction moves value from one legal entity to another. The balancing segment guarantees each company's books balance: every journal line carries a balancing segment value, and the intercompany engine offsets the due-to / due-from entry so no company is out of balance. Transactions flow outbound from the transferring entity and are received as inbound by the recipient, then transferred and settled . Agreements define the terms under which entities transact. Intercompany exposes REST resources for agreements and transaction sources, an FBDI import, and ESS jobs driven through erpProcesses . Where intercompany balances land in the underlying Oracle Database tables. Run these against the Fusion database to find intercompany balances and interface rows. Intercompany creates the offsetting due-to / due-from entries automatically so each legal entity balances. A purchase by one entity from another posts: Cross-ledger allocations and automated intercompany cross-charge for example, an AP invoice charged to another entity use the same balancing mechanism — entries land in GL_BALANCES per balancing segment. Balancing first: intercompany transactions require a valid balancing segment on every line — confirm the segment values before loading. Agreements via REST: create agreements with intercompanyAgreements before generating transactions under them. Bulk transactions: use the Intercompany Transaction Import FBDI and process the interface batches, then reconcile the interface. Multitier: transfer authorizations and settlement currency are set per agreement — model the chain before go-live, not during close. Reconcile: due-to and due-from must match per counterparty; differences surface as un-reconciled intercompany balances in GL. Back to the GL hub or the Financials hub . Intercompany cross-charge of AP invoices ties into Payables . Intercompany settlement runs as part of the close — see GL Period Close . Read Enterprise Structures legal entity and balancing segment and Journals & Posting before this page. Intercompany entries post to GL_BALANCES per balancing segment, so each company's trial balance stays balanced even though one entity pays another. The reconciliation view is the due-to / due-from balance per counterparty. Agreements are the REST-create surface; transaction creation itself is typically FBDI Intercompany Transaction Import or the UI. pages.content: Functional view Configuration Technical view Data flow — step by step Retrieve the data — SQL Accounting SLA Reporting Worked example — one journal through post Integration notes Next steps REST resources FBDI templates Working example — submit Import Journals Working example — read a journal batch How money moves into and around the general ledger. Journals are the batches of journal entry lines that post to accounts — and most GL integrations live or die on the journal import path, validation, and period status. breadcrumbs= , , , updated="August 2026" level="Module" /> Read Flexfields & Value Sets how the chart of accounts becomes per-segment accounts and Interface Tables before this page. Functional view A journal is a batch of journal entry lines that post to account combinations. Journals can be manual, recurring, allocation, revaluation/translation, or imported from a sub-ledger or an external system. Each batch has headers who/what/when and lines the per-segment debits and credits , and every line moves through a status chain before it touches balances. Journal-related setup is light but a missing piece silently changes where a journal posts. The create path for bulk journals is the Journal Import FBDI into GL_INTERFACE , driven by the Import Journals ESS job. The REST layer reads batches and patches limited attributes — there is no create journal over REST in the 26C Financials guide. Where a journal's life lands in the underlying Oracle Database tables. Run these against the Fusion database to find failed imports and posted journals. Journals created inside the GL manual, recurring, allocation, revaluation are written directly to GL_JE_HEADERS / GL_JE_LINES and are not SLA artifacts. Sub-ledger journals AP, AR, Expenses are first built by Subledger Accounting and then transferred into the same GL journal tables. Both paths update GL_BALANCES on post. Create path is FBDI: bulk journal loads go through Journal Import into GL_INTERFACE ; submit the job with erpProcesses . Period status: query accountingPeriodStatusLOV first — posting to a closed period rejects the batch. Balancing validation: by default a batch must balance; use suspense posting only when the business accepts it. Approval: if approval rules apply, journals stop at Approval Pending until a user or BPM workflow releases them. Reversals: set the auto-reverse flag on the imported journal to create the offsetting entry next period automatically. Back to the GL hub or the Financials hub . Cross-currency journals need rates — see Multi-Currency & Rates . The Interface Tables page details the GL_INTERFACE columns. Read Flexfields & Value Sets how the chart of accounts becomes per-segment accounts and Interface Tables before this page. Three behaviors matter most to integrations: reversal auto-reverse the next period, or a manual reversing entry , AutoPost post immediately when import succeeds instead of waiting for a user , and suspense posting post to a suspense account when an account combination is invalid, rather than reject the line . AutoPost only fires for criteria sets that match the imported journal source/category/date range . If nothing matches, journals stay Unposted and a scheduled Post Journals job — or a user — must post them. journalBatches is read/patch only. Do not build a create integration against it — the supported create path is Journal Import FBDI → Import Journals → Post Journals. Column names follow the Fusion data dictionary naming. Confirm against your release before relying on them. Column names follow the Fusion data dictionary naming. Confirm against your release before relying on them, and never query the Fusion database directly for production reporting — use OTBI or the REST API instead. Having trouble? Rates are the pivot: every cross-currency journal and every revaluation depends on a rate existing for the right date and rate type. breadcrumbs= , , , updated="August 2026" level="Module" /> Read Enterprise Structures ledger currency selection and Journals & Posting before this page. Functional view Every ledger has a functional currency . Transactions can be entered in a different entered currency and, if the ledger uses reporting currencies, converted to a third reported currency. Precision rules the decimals each currency carries. The key concepts: Rates are loaded through FBDI into GL_DAILY_RATES_INTERFACE and imported into GL_DAILY_RATES . Revaluation and translation run as ESS jobs driven by erpProcesses . The REST layer is read-only for rates. Where rates and converted balances land in the underlying Oracle Database tables. Run these against the Fusion database to check rates and revaluation/translation journals. Revaluation creates accounting entries to recognize unrealized exchange gains and losses. A typical revaluation posts: Translation produces translation adjustment entries including the cumulative translation adjustment for the reporting currency rather than cash gains and losses — it restates balances, it does not re-measure open items. Load rates before journals: cross-currency journals fail when no rate exists for the journal date under the rate type — load daily rates first. Rate type matters: confirm which rate type Spot, Corporate, User, Fixed the journal load or revaluation should use. Sub-ledgers feed GL: AP/AR convert in their own currency then post the converted journal to GL; supply the same rates to keep them consistent. Revalue at close: run Revalue Balances before translation and before closing the period, in the order your close sequence defines. Back to the GL hub or the Financials hub . Reporting currencies that hold converted balances — see Secondary Ledgers & Reporting Currencies . Where revaluation sits in the close cycle — see GL Period Close . Read Enterprise Structures ledger currency selection and Journals & Posting before this page. Rate types and dates are the first thing to check when a foreign-currency journal fails: the accounting engine converts at the rate for the journal date under the chosen rate type, and if none exists the journal rejects. pages.title: General Ledger (GL)
headings: Deep dives — read in this order
Technical view — the GL integration surfaces
pages.content: The business story Functional view Deep dives — read in this order Technical view — the GL integration surfaces Configuration Data flow — step by step Retrieve the data — SQL Accounting SLA Reporting Integration notes Next steps The system of record for financial balances. GL owns the chart of accounts account flexfield , the ledgers that define structure and currency, and the periods that control when posting is allowed. This hub is your starting point; the deep dives below cover each area in functional and technical detail. breadcrumbs= , , updated="August 2026" level="Foundation" /> Read Enterprise Structures ledgers, BUs, data access sets , Flexfields & Value Sets the chart of accounts , and Subledger Accounting before this page. The business story At the end of every month, someone in the business has to answer a simple question: "how are we doing?" The General Ledger is where that answer is written down. Every sale, purchase, payment, and receipt across the company eventually becomes a journal entry in the GL, posted to the right accounts for the right period — and those posted balances are what the financial statements are made from. The GL stores the finished numbers . It keeps the chart of accounts the list of account names , the journals that move money between them, and the periods that say when posting is allowed. Start with Journals & Posting if you are loading data, then multi-currency, then the ledger architecture topics. Period close pulls everything together. The biggest misconception in GL integration is that you create journals over REST. In current Fusion releases journals are loaded via the Journal Import FBDI into GL_INTERFACE , and the REST layer is mostly read/query plus LOV resources. The full catalog is on FBDI & ADFdi . The GL foundation is built top-down before any journal can post. Where a journal's life actually lands in the underlying Oracle Database tables. Full interface-table detail on Interface Tables . Run these against the Fusion database SQL Developer, DB access, or a read replica to pull back whatever was created. The GL receives two kinds of entries: journals created in the GL manual, recurring, allocations, revaluation, translation and journals created by sub-ledgers through SLA . Both land in GL_JE_HEADERS / GL_JE_LINES before posting updates GL_BALANCES . Period status is everything: posting to a closed period fails. Query accountingPeriodsLOV before running a journal load and choose the current open period. Segments must be real: each segment value must exist and combine into a valid, non-flagged account combination. Currencies: cross-currency journals need a valid exchange rate configured for the rate type and date. Create path is FBDI: bulk journal loads go through Journal Import into GL_INTERFACE ; use erpProcesses to drive Import Journals and Post Journals. Back to the Financials hub . Journal imports are a core part of the FBDI integration pattern . Understand the flexfields that define segments on the core concepts page. Read Enterprise Structures ledgers, BUs, data access sets , Flexfields & Value Sets the chart of accounts , and Subledger Accounting before this page. Think of the GL as the company's scoreboard : every other module does the playing, the GL keeps the score. The GL is the company's scorebook . Every sale and purchase gets written down here, and the totals become your financial reports. Every GL integration must know the account flexfield structure — how many segments and which are required — because journal lines are written per segment , not as a single "account string". Older training material shows journalEntries , generalLedgers , or accountingPeriods as REST create resources. Those are not in the official 26C Financials REST guide — confirm against your instance's resource explorer before building an integration on them. The three GL failures that dominate real projects — closed periods, invalid account combinations, and missing rates — all originate in these setups. These are the underlying Oracle Database tables as documented in the Fusion data dictionary. pages.content: Functional view Configuration Technical view Data flow — step by step Retrieve the data — SQL Accounting SLA Reporting Integration notes Next steps REST resources FBDI templates Working example — close an accounting period Working example — check a period status The GL mechanics that end a period: period status Open / Future-entry / Closed , the close sequence inside GL, consolidation into reporting currencies or a group ledger, clearing accounts , and year-end close. For the cross-module close sequence, see the Financial Close hub. breadcrumbs= , , , updated="August 2026" level="Advanced" /> Read Journals & Posting , Multi-Currency & Rates , and Secondary Ledgers before this page. Functional view Closing a GL period is a sequence, not a single action. The standard cycle runs daily rates → revaluation → translation → allocations → consolidation → closing journals → open/close periods . Period status controls everything: only open periods accept transactions, future-entry periods allow dates in the next period, and closed periods reject all posting. Year-end close transfers balances to retained earnings and opens the next year. Consolidation combines multiple ledgers reporting-only view, or balance transfer into a consolidation ledger . Period management is exposed through LOV resources for discovery and erpProcesses for the open/close jobs. Consolidation within GL uses maps configured in the UI plus balance transfer jobs. Where period state and close activity land in the underlying Oracle Database tables. Run these against the Fusion database to see period statuses and close activity. The GL close creates journals that are not SLA-driven: revaluation, translation, allocation, closing, and elimination entries are all GL journals written to GL_JE_HEADERS / GL_JE_LINES . Consolidation can be reporting-only a combined view, no journal or a balance transfer journals bring balances into a consolidation ledger . Status check before load: query accountingPeriodStatusLOV — never submit journals to a period that is not Open. Close via jobs: run Close / Open Accounting Period through erpProcesses ; re-opening a closed period requires administrator approval. Order matters: revalue before translate, translate before consolidate — follow the ledger's defined close sequence. Clearing accounts: a non-zero clearing account blocks a clean close — reconcile them before running Close Accounting Period. Budget close: validate and upload budgets, then close the budget period separately from the GL close. Back to the GL hub or the Financials hub . The full cross-module close sequence lives on Financial Close . Revaluation and translation steps are detailed on Multi-Currency & Rates . Read Journals & Posting , Multi-Currency & Rates , and Secondary Ledgers before this page. The cross-module close sequence sub-ledgers → GL → reporting is documented on Financial Close . This page covers the GL-specific period status mechanics and consolidation inside GL. Never close a period while sub-ledgers or GL processes are still posting to it — re-open requires an administrator and leaves the close audit trail inconsistent. Confirm against your release before relying on them, and never query the Fusion database directly for production reporting — use OTBI or the REST API instead. Having trouble? pages.title: Secondary Ledgers & Reporting Currencies
pages.content: Functional view Configuration Technical view Data flow — step by step Retrieve the data — SQL Accounting SLA Reporting Integration notes Next steps REST resources How one set of transactions can produce books for local GAAP, group GAAP, tax, and reporting in another currency. Secondary ledgers replicate accounting; reporting currencies add a converted balance view without a full ledger . breadcrumbs= , , , updated="August 2026" level="Advanced" /> Read Enterprise Structures ledger, legal entity, chart of accounts and Multi-Currency & Rates before this page. Functional view A primary ledger is the legal set of books. A secondary ledger keeps a parallel set of books that is derived from the primary by controlled replication same source accounting, adjusted at the journal level for the second GAAP . A reporting currency is not a full ledger — it holds converted balances only. Use secondary ledgers when you need journal-level differences tax vs book, local GAAP vs group GAAP ; use reporting currencies when you only need the same balances in another currency. There is no dedicated create REST resource for ledgers — setup is UI-based via Enterprise Structures. The REST layer lets you discover ledgers and read balances. Where transactions and balances land for each ledger type. Run these against the Fusion database to see ledgers and ledger-set assignments. Secondary ledgers share the sub-ledger accounting of the primary unless you choose adjusted accounting, in which case SLA rules run again for the second ledger and adjustments post as journals. Retained earnings and EMU conversion adjustments are generated by the ledger setup, not by source transactions. Discovery first: use ledgersLOV to find the ledger IDs your journals and balance queries should target — never hard-code them. Balance queries: ledgerBalances returns balances per ledger; filter on the secondary ledger or reporting currency explicitly. Go-live: verify reporting-currency balances right after go-live — a missing balance initialization shows up as zeros, not errors. Data access sets: a GL duty can only see ledgers its data access set grants, so REST users need access to each ledger they read. Back to the GL hub or the Financials hub . Reporting currencies depend on rates — see Multi-Currency & Rates . Ledger sets close together — see GL Period Close . Read Enterprise Structures ledger, legal entity, chart of accounts and Multi-Currency & Rates before this page. When to use which: reporting currency when the second GAAP is identical and only the currency differs; secondary ledger when you also need different chart of accounts, calendar, or period-level processing. Ledger sets group ledgers so a single close and single report covers several books. EMU European Monetary Union conversion is configured against the reporting currency as a fixed conversion rate so the transition to the euro restates balances without re-entering transactions. Ledger creation, secondary-ledger assignment, and balance initialization are UI processes under Enterprise Structures, not REST creates. Verify your integration's assumptions about secondary-ledger balances after go-live — a reporting currency that was not initialized will read as zero. Column names follow the Fusion data dictionary naming. Confirm against your release before relying on them. The ledger-set assignment tables such as GL_LEDGER_SET_NORM_ASSIGN vary by release and configuration — confirm exact names against your instance's data dictionary before relying on them. Having trouble? See GL troubleshooting for ledger and balance failures and fixes. pages.title: ERP Financials — hub
pages.description: The Financials suite covers everything that records money: General Ledger, Payables, Receivables, Cash Management, Fixed Assets, and Expenses. Each module has its own page covering the functional (business) and technical (REST + FBDI) view. This page ties the suite together.
headings: Learning path — read in this order
pages.content: The business story How the suite hangs together Learning path — read in this order The modules Functional ↔ technical reference table Integration patterns Integration-critical details Next steps 1 · Supplier onboarding Payables 2 · AP invoice import Payables 3 · GL journal import GL 4 · Expense sync Expenses + Payables The business story Every company runs on money in and money out , and every activity that touches money must be written down somewhere. That record-keeping is what Financials does: you buy Payables , you sell Receivables , you hold cash Cash Management , you own things that wear out Fixed Assets , your people spend on the company's behalf Expenses — and at the end of the month, all of it must roll up into one true picture: the General Ledger and its reports. Financials is a chain of sub-ledgers feeding a General Ledger . Every transaction starts in a sub-ledger and eventually posts to the GL, where the period is closed and reporting happens. The same order as the home page guide. Start at step 1 and follow down — later steps assume the earlier ones. Where a step links several pages, read them in the order listed. Each module page covers the functional view business objects, flows, setups , the technical view REST resources, FBDI templates, examples , a step-by-step data flow showing which Fusion table the data lands on at every step, and SQL queries to retrieve whatever was created. The fastest lookup for an integration developer: the business object, its module, the REST resource, and the FBDI template. External portal submits a supplier → OIC validates → creates the supplier via REST suppliers or bulk-loads the Supplier FBDI. The supplier must exist before the first invoice arrives. ERP/file/portal sends invoices → OIC stages them → AP Invoices FBDI load at night → OIC polls job status → processes the error file → re-submits rejected rows. For small volumes use apInvoices REST directly. Source system posts balances → OIC maps each row to GL segments → Journal Entries FBDI or journalEntries REST → verify the period is open before posting. Corporate card feeds create expense lines → OIC enriches employee/category → Expense Reports import → approved reports flow to Payables for payment. See how the same "functional vs technical" lens applies to core concepts flexfields, value sets, ESS . Combine these modules with the classic OIC pattern in FBDI integration with Fusion . Ground the REST examples with the REST API fundamentals page. The trick to learning Financials: every module is a sub-ledger feeding one general ledger . Learn one transaction end to end buy → pay, sell → collect and you understand how all six modules fit together — the Business Cycles do exactly that. Financials is the app where a company writes down what it earns and spends . Each module does one job — buying, selling, cash, assets, expenses — and at month-end it all comes together into the reports that say how the business did. You rarely write straight to the GL. Bulk supplier invoices feed Payables , customer money feeds Receivables , and only journals feed the GL directly. Each sub-ledger has its own acceptance rules approvals, open periods, business unit that will reject bad data. Foundations first, modules second, technical last. Skip a foundation page and the module pages will feel out of order. The sidebar and the Home page follow the same sequence. A few of these names changed between the EBS-era docs and current Fusion: legacy apInvoices , arInvoices , arReceipts and journalEntries REST resources no longer exist in the 26C Financials REST guide. pages.title: Holds & PO Matching
headings: Working example — release a hold via REST
pages.content: Functional view Configuration Technical view Data flow — step by step Retrieve the data — SQL Accounting SLA Reporting Integration notes Next steps PO matching levels REST resources Working example — release a hold via REST How Payables blocks invoices with holds and how invoice matching to purchase orders enforces price, quantity, and amount tolerances before an invoice can be paid. breadcrumbs= , , , updated="August 2026" level="Module" /> Read the Payables hub and Invoice Entry & Validation first. Matching assumes the purchase order, supplier site, and invoice already exist. Functional view A hold blocks an invoice from being paid until it is resolved. Holds are placed automatically by validation or matching, or manually by a user, and are released either automatically or after approval. PO matching compares invoice lines against the purchase order and optionally its receipts to catch price, quantity, and amount variances before payment. Hold workflow options: Set up tolerances and hold definitions before loading invoices that will be matched. Where the hold and matching lifecycle lands in the underlying tables. Run these against the Fusion database to inspect holds and matching status. Matching variances within tolerance can be recorded through variance accounts; holds themselves create no accounting entries. When a hold is released and the invoice posts, the entries are the standard invoice event — see Subledger Accounting . Automatic hold: placed by validation or matching when a rule fails. Manual hold: placed by a user on a specific invoice. Release: a hold can be released manually, by routing to approvers, or as part of a consolidated hold notification workflow. Hold blocks payment: an invoice with an open hold cannot be selected by a payment process request — check hold status before paying. Release via REST: use the invoiceHolds child resource create/update to add or release holds programmatically. Tolerances before loading: if you know lines will exceed tolerance, either pre-release the hold or fix the source data — otherwise the invoice stalls. No holds FBDI: you cannot bulk-load holds through an interface template; holds are placed by validation/matching or via REST. Back to Payables AP . Back to the Financials hub . Invoices that pass holds move on to Payments & PPR . Read the Payables hub and Invoice Entry & Validation first. Matching assumes the purchase order, supplier site, and invoice already exist. Tolerance is a percentage: rate, price, amount, and quantity tolerances can each be configured. Exceeding tolerance places a matching hold; within tolerance the line passes. Variances that pass tolerance can post to a configurable variance account. There is no dedicated holds FBDI in the Financials FBDI guide — holds are managed through the invoices REST resource, the work area, or ESS validation jobs, not through an interface template. The hold table name varies by release — query your instance's data dictionary for AP_HOLDS_ALL or AP_INVOICE_HOLDS before relying on it. Column names follow the Fusion data dictionary naming; confirm against your release. Column names follow the Fusion data dictionary naming. Confirm against your release before relying on them, and never query the Fusion database directly for production reporting — use OTBI or the REST API instead. Having trouble? pages.title: Invoice Entry & Validation
pages.description: How supplier invoices enter Fusion Payables, what validation does to them, and how to load and correct them with REST and FBDI. This is the page to read before building any AP invoice import.
headings: Worked example — one invoice with tax
Working example — create an invoice via REST
Working example — run the validateInvoice action
pages.content: Functional view Configuration Technical view Data flow — step by step Retrieve the data — SQL Accounting SLA Reporting Worked example — one invoice with tax Integration notes Next steps REST resources FBDI templates Working example — create an invoice via REST Working example — run the validateInvoice action Read the Payables hub first, plus Enterprise Structures business unit, legal entity and Flexfields & Value Sets account flexfield . Invoices fail validation when suppliers, tax codes, or periods are missing. Functional view An AP invoice is a bill to be paid. It has a header supplier, number, date, currency, terms , one or more lines what was bought , and distributions the accounts the charge posts to . Every invoice enters in status Entered , passes validation to Validated , and only becomes payable when Approved and Posted . Invoices come from several sources — most integrations use the first three: Validation behavior is driven by configuration, not code. Set these up before loading invoices. Where each step of an invoice import lands in the underlying tables. Run these against the Fusion database to inspect what the import produced. Entries come from the subledger accounting engine; trace them via XLA_AE_HEADERS / XLA_AE_LINES — see Subledger Accounting . Supplier before invoice: load Supplier FBDIs from the Procurement guide before invoice imports, or rows reject with "supplier not found". Stage → import → validate: FBDI only stages data; you must run Import Payables Invoices and Validate Payables Invoices to create and approve the invoices. Interface errors: rejected rows stay in the interface tables with an error message — query and fix them, then re-run the import. Idempotency: use a stable invoice number so retries do not create duplicates; the duplicate invoice tolerance also guards this. Prepayments: apply prepayments to PO invoices via the applyPrepayments action, or reverse with unapplyPrepayments . Back to Payables AP . Back to the Financials hub . Holds and PO matching constrain which invoices can be validated and paid — see Holds & PO Matching . Read the Payables hub first, plus Enterprise Structures business unit, legal entity and Flexfields & Value Sets account flexfield . Invoices fail validation when suppliers, tax codes, or periods are missing. A created invoice can sit in Requires Re-approval if a line fails validation. Integrations should poll invoice status and handle the rejection path explicitly rather than assuming the invoice is ready for payment. Most invoice import failures trace back to configuration: a supplier that was never loaded, a closed period, a missing tax code, or a duplicate invoice number. Finish configuration and pre-validate a few test invoices before bulk loading. Oracle 26C uses invoices and payablesInterfaceInvoices . Legacy names like apInvoices / apInvoiceLines are no longer valid in 26C — verify the resource names against your instance's REST service catalog before building. Supplier, Supplier Sites, Supplier Contacts, and Supplier Addresses FBDIs are in the Procurement FBDI guide, not the Financials FBDI guide — load supplier master from there before importing invoices. These are the underlying Oracle Database tables as documented in the Fusion data dictionary. Column names follow the Fusion data dictionary naming. pages.title: Payables (AP)
pages.description: Tracks money you owe. Payables manages suppliers, supplier sites, supplier invoices, and payments — and it is the most common Financials integration target because almost every company loads invoices from somewhere external. This hub is your starting point; the deep dives below cover each area in functional and technical detail.
headings: Deep dives — read in this order
Technical view — the AP integration surfaces
pages.content: The business story Functional view Deep dives — read in this order Technical view — the AP integration surfaces Configuration Data flow — step by step Retrieve the data — SQL Accounting SLA Reporting Integration notes Next steps Read Enterprise Structures business units, legal entity, ledger , Tax tax codes , and Flexfields & Value Sets before this page. The business story Everything the company buys — a supplier's goods, a consultant's services, a utility bill — arrives as a supplier invoice that eventually has to be paid . Payables is the module that manages that: it validates the invoice, matches it to what was ordered and received, and turns it into a payment out of the bank. It is the "money out" engine of the business. A supplier's bill, called an invoice , passes through a series of checkpoints before it can be paid: Entered → Validated → Requires Re-approval → Approved → Posted . Invoices that fail validation e.g. an invalid account flexfield get stuck and must be fixed or rejected — integration should handle that path explicitly. If you are integrating, start with Invoice Entry & Validation , then Holds & PO Matching , then Payments & PPR . Withholding tax applies when you pay suppliers in WHT countries. Note that the REST names changed between releases: current Fusion docs use invoices / payablesPayments , not the legacy apInvoices / apPayments from older training. Suppliers and their sites are created via the Supplier FBDI which ships in the Procurement FBDI guide . Set up in this order — skipping a step shows up later as a validation error. Where each step of the supplier → invoice → payment chain lands in the underlying tables. Run these against the Fusion database to pull back whatever was created. Every AP invoice produces accounting entries through the sub-ledger accounting engine. A standard invoice creates: Events: invoice creation and payment . Trace the entries via XLA_AE_HEADERS / XLA_AE_LINES — see Subledger Accounting . Supplier before invoice: bulk loads must run Supplier → Sites → AP Invoices in order, or invoices reject with "supplier not found". Validation state: a created invoice may sit in Requires Re-approval if lines fail validation — poll its status and handle the error file. Accounts: distributions need a valid account combination; supply each segment or a distribution combination ID. Interface-driven imports: bulk loads stage into AP_INVOICES_INTERFACE and need the Import Payables Invoices job to complete. Idempotency: use a stable invoice number so retries don't duplicate. Back to the Financials hub . The AP invoice import is the flagship example in FBDI integration with Fusion . Supplier master data feeds into the PO approval scenario . Read Enterprise Structures business units, legal entity, ledger , Tax tax codes , and Flexfields & Value Sets before this page. The one fact that rules AP integrations: you only ever pay an invoice that validated and got approved . Anything that fails validation — supplier, tax, period, account — stops in the workflow until fixed. Payables is how a company pays its bills . A supplier sends an invoice, you check that it's right, and the system pays it from the bank. Most AP integration failures trace back to missing suppliers, missing tax codes, or closed periods — finish these setups before loading anything. pages.content: Functional view Configuration Technical view Data flow — step by step Retrieve the data — SQL Accounting SLA Reporting Worked example — pay an invoice with a discount Integration notes Next steps REST resources FBDI templates Working example — submit a payment process request via ESS How approved invoices become payments through the Payment Process Request PPR , and how to create, format, and transmit payment files to your bank. breadcrumbs= , , , updated="August 2026" level="Advanced" /> Read the Payables hub and Invoice Entry & Validation first. Only invoices that are validated, approved, posted, and free of holds are payable. Functional view The Payment Process Request PPR is the engine that turns approved invoices into payments. You build a PPR, select the invoices to pay, validate the selection, generate a payment file in a defined format, transmit it to the bank, and confirm it. The lifecycle is driven by payment process profiles, payment methods, and payment formats. Payment file statuses and follow-up actions: Payment configuration lives under Payables payments setup and Cash Management bank accounts. Where the PPR lifecycle lands in the underlying tables. Run these against the Fusion database to inspect payments and PPR status. Trace entries via XLA_AE_HEADERS / XLA_AE_LINES — see Subledger Accounting . Reconciled payments also feed Cash Management . Payment file statuses: the file moves through stages as it is built, formatted, transmitted, and confirmed. Positive pay: a file sent to the bank listing issued checks so the bank can match presented items. Remittance advice: the supplier-facing notification generated with the payment file. Void / stop payments: reversing a payment or instructing the bank to stop one. Bank returns: unpaid or returned payments processed back from the bank. PPR is not created via REST: use the Submit Payment Process Request ESS job erpProcesses or the work area; paymentProcessRequests only supports GET/PATCH. Only clean invoices pay: the PPR excludes invoices on hold or not approved — verify status before expecting a payment. Formats are bank-specific: confirm the payment format and transmission profile PGP/FTP/bank connectivity match your bank before going live. Payment requests: external systems can feed the Payables Payment Request Import FBDI AP_PAYMENT_REQUESTS_INT to create invoices that the PPR can then pay. Back to Payables AP . Back to the Financials hub . Payments and bank statements reconcile in Cash Management . Withholding affects net payment amounts — see Withholding Tax & 1099 . Read the Payables hub and Invoice Entry & Validation first. Only invoices that are validated, approved, posted, and free of holds are payable. Payments can be cross-currency pay in one currency with funds in another and centralized across business units one treasury pays on behalf of many BUs . Both are configured through payment process profiles and payment documents. The paymentProcessRequests resource is GET/PATCH only — you cannot POST a new payment process request through REST. Submitting a PPR runs through the Submit Payment Process Request ESS job via erpProcesses or the work area. pages.content: Functional view Configuration Technical view Data flow — step by step Retrieve the data — SQL Accounting SLA Reporting Integration notes Next steps US 1099 reporting suite REST resources Working example — submit a tax reporting job via ESS Read the Payables hub and Invoice Entry & Validation first. Withholding is separate from VAT/GST input tax — it is tax deducted from a payment and remitted to the tax authority. Functional view Withholding tax WHT is deducted from supplier payments rather than charged on invoices. Payables calculates the WHT amount at invoice or payment time, creates a WHT tax line, pays the supplier net of withholding, and reports the withheld amounts for the tax period. WHT is configured once and applied automatically from then on. Where withholding calculation lands in the underlying tables. Run these against the Fusion database to inspect withholding balances. Withholding creates a payable to the tax authority rather than to the supplier: Trace entries via XLA_AE_HEADERS / XLA_AE_LINES — see Subledger Accounting . WHT affects payment amount: the net payment is the gross invoice minus withholding — reconciling bank files against gross invoice amounts will not match. Certificates before paying: a valid certificate or exception can reduce or waive WHT; confirm supplier certificate data before payment runs. Reporting jobs: income tax and 1099 outputs come from ESS jobs whose names vary — verify against your instance and schedule them per period. No dedicated WHT FBDI: withhold tax is set up via the work area and supplier master, not a Financials FBDI template verify in your instance . Back to Payables AP . Back to the Financials hub . AutoInvoice takes pre-staged billing lines from Oracle Applications or external systems, groups them by your business rules, validates every line, and creates AR transactions invoices, memos automatically. breadcrumbs= , , , updated="August 2026" level="Module" /> Read the Receivables hub and Subledger Accounting first. AutoInvoice assumes the customer party + account , transaction type, and remit-to address already exist. Functional view AutoInvoice is the interface-based billing engine: data is staged into interface tables, then the Import AutoInvoice process validates and converts each line into a real AR transaction. It exists because most billing volumes come from order capture, CPQ, or external systems — not from manual entry. Memo lines — extra descriptive or informational lines attached to a transaction for example a printed message — are also staged via the interface and get a line ordering so they print where you want them. Credit and debit memos flow through the same AutoInvoice engine: you set the transaction source and a transaction type whose class is credit or debit memo, and the import creates the memo instead of an invoice. Configure in this order so the import can find everything it validates against. Where each step of the billing chain lands in the underlying tables. Run these against the Fusion database to inspect the import outcome. Successful transactions create entries through the sub-ledger accounting engine: Accounts come from AutoAccounting unless overridden on the line. Trace entries via XLA_AE_HEADERS / XLA_AE_LINES — see Subledger Accounting . Stage, do not create: autoInvoiceInterfaceLines supports GET/PATCH only — bulk lines must come in through the AutoInvoice Import FBDI template. Rejects are the path: failed lines stay in RA_INTERFACE_LINES_ALL with STATUS and REJECT_REASON; read them, PATCH the fix, re-run the import. Pre-validate: customer, transaction type, and remit-to address must exist or the line rejects with "customer not found" style errors. Grouping and ordering: set grouping and line ordering rules before loading or your transactions assemble differently than the business expects. Post after import: run Create Accounting via erpProcesses or scheduled process after transactions are created. CPQ / orders: Oracle Applications billing feeds AutoInvoice automatically; external systems use the same interface tables. Back to Receivables AR . Back to the Financials hub . Once billed, the money comes in through Receipts & Lockbox . Deferred revenue on invoices is covered in Revenue & Credit Memos . Read the Receivables hub and Subledger Accounting first. AutoInvoice rejects lines when the customer, transaction type, or account is missing — finish these setups and pre-validate before any bulk load. Stage lines through the AutoInvoice Import FBDI template, then run the import via erpProcesses or the Scheduled Processes work area. Confirm resource availability against your instance. Credit checks assume customers exist with credit profiles. Functional view Credit Management decides whether a customer can get credit and whether an order or transaction is allowed to proceed. Advanced Collections takes over once a balance becomes delinquent: it ages the balance, duns the customer, assigns work to collectors through strategies, and tracks promises and disputes. A failed credit check over limit, or a scoring model decision can hold the order or open a credit case folder for review. In Advanced Collections, aging methods bucket overdue balances, dunning produces aged or staged letters, and collections strategies use scoring formulas and segments to decide what the collector does next. The collections dashboard reports CEI collection effectiveness index and DSO days sales outstanding alongside collector workload. Disputes are opened by the collector and resolved with adjustments. Set up credit and collections rules before the checks and dunning run. Where the credit and collections chain lands in the underlying tables. Run these against the Fusion database to inspect delinquent balances and credit data. Credit checks and dunning create no entries; the accounting appears when money moves or an adjustment posts through the sub-ledger accounting engine: Trace entries via XLA_AE_HEADERS / XLA_AE_LINES — see Subledger Accounting . Profile before credit check: establish credit profiles and scoring before orders run credit checks, or every order is held. Promises via POST: record promises to pay with collectionPromises and track fulfillment. Disputes: open with receivablesDisputes POST and resolve with adjustments read through receivablesAdjustments GET . Collected money is applied in Receipts & Lockbox . Dispute adjustments affect revenue — see Revenue & Credit Memos . Read the Receivables hub , Receipts & Lockbox , and Subledger Accounting first. Credit checks assume customers exist with credit profiles. pages.title: Receivables (AR)
pages.description: Tracks money owed to you. Receivables manages customers, customer accounts, AR invoices, and receipts — the mirror image of Payables. This hub is your starting point; the deep dives below cover each area in functional and technical detail.
headings: Deep dives — read in this order
Technical view — the AR integration surfaces
pages.content: The business story Functional view Deep dives — read in this order Technical view — the AR integration surfaces Configuration Data flow — step by step Retrieve the data — SQL Accounting SLA Reporting Integration notes Next steps Read Enterprise Structures business units , Tax , and Subledger Accounting before this page. The business story What keeps the lights on is money coming in . When a customer buys, Receivables issues an AR invoice the bill , tracks what they owe, and collects the receipt — whether from a lockbox, an electronic payment, or a check. It is the "money in" engine that completes the sale: no receipt, no cash. When a customer buys something, Receivables sends them a bill, called an AR invoice . When the customer pays, you record the money as a receipt and apply it to mark it against the invoice. The customer's details — party, account, site — must exist before anything can be invoiced. If you are integrating, start with AutoInvoice billing then Receipts & Lockbox cash in . Revenue and credit/collections are the advanced topics on top. Note that the REST names changed between releases: current Fusion docs use receivablesInvoices / standardReceipts , not the legacy arInvoices / arReceipts from older training. And AutoInvoice is driven through interface tables , not a REST create. Set up the billing and collection basics before creating customers or invoices. Where each step of the customer → invoice → receipt chain lands in the underlying tables. Run these against the Fusion database to pull back whatever was created. AR transactions create entries through the sub-ledger accounting engine: Trace entries via XLA_AE_HEADERS / XLA_AE_LINES — see Subledger Accounting . Business unit is required on AR transactions — include it or it defaults and may not be what you expect. Customer must exist first : bulk invoices reject when the customer account isn't found. AutoInvoice is interface-driven : stage into RA_INTERFACE_LINES_ALL , run Import AutoInvoice, then read the execution report for rejections. Invoice statuses matter : an invoice in Draft isn't valid for billing; check status after creation. Tax : if tax is enabled, lines may need tax codes/regimes, or validation fails. Back to the Financials hub . Receipts connect to Cash Management . AutoInvoice data staging is covered in Interface Tables . Read Enterprise Structures business units , Tax , and Subledger Accounting before this page. AR is the mirror image of AP: AP pays supplier invoices, AR collects customer invoices. Learn one and you already know the shape of the other. Receivables is how a company gets paid . You send the customer a bill, and when they pay, you record the money coming in. The customer hierarchy is party → account → site . Integrations must create or reference the right level: invoice at account level, address at site level. AutoInvoice rejects lines when the customer, transaction type, or account is missing — finish these setups and pre-validate before bulk loads. pages.content: Functional view Configuration Technical view Data flow — step by step Retrieve the data — SQL Accounting SLA Reporting Worked example — one receipt applied Integration notes Next steps REST resources FBDI templates Working example — create a receipt via REST Working example — run lockbox processing via erpProcesses How Receivables collects money against AR invoices. Receipts come in from banks via lockbox , from customers directly, or through automatic direct debit — then get applied to open transactions with AutoCash , AutoMatch , or manual rules. breadcrumbs= , , , updated="August 2026" level="Module" /> Read the Receivables hub , AutoInvoice , and Cash Management first. Applying receipts assumes the invoices already exist. Functional view A receipt class Customer, Misc, Short-term Debt and a receipt method define how money is received, remitted, and cleared. A receipt can be entered manually, created from a lockbox file, or generated automatically SEPA / ISO direct debit . Every receipt then needs to be applied to open transactions. Application exception rule sets catch borderline matches for review instead of auto-applying them. Cross-currency receipts convert to the invoice currency using the configured conversion rate type. Receipt-to-receipt applications move value between receipts for example reclassifying a misc receipt , and write-offs , chargebacks , and refunds are handled through adjustments. Reversing or unapplying a receipt returns its applications to the open transactions. Set up the money-in plumbing before receiving any payments. Where each step of the receipt chain lands in the underlying tables. Run these against the Fusion database to inspect receipts and their applications. Receipts create entries through the sub-ledger accounting engine: Trace entries via XLA_AE_HEADERS / XLA_AE_LINES — see Subledger Accounting . Lockbox first: bulk receipts stage into AR_PAYMENTS_INTERFACE_ALL and are only created when Process Receipts Through Lockbox runs. Interface rows fail loudly: rejected rows stay in the interface with reasons — read them, fix the mapping or data, and re-run. Direct creation: standardReceipts C/U/D creates receipts directly; you still apply them via REST, rules, or the work area . Unapplied needs owners: AutoCash / AutoMatch won't resolve everything — plan exception handling with application exception rule sets. Cross-currency and SEPA/ISO direct debit need the right receipt method, conversion type, and bank account setup before go-live. Adjustments: write-offs, chargebacks, and refunds are adjustments — read them via receivablesAdjustments GET . Back to Receivables AR . Back to the Financials hub . Billing that feeds these receipts starts in AutoInvoice . Cleared receipts flow into Cash Management . Chasing the money you haven't collected yet is Credit Management & Collections . Read the Receivables hub , AutoInvoice , and Cash Management first. Applying receipts assumes the invoices already exist. Receipt methods and bank accounts must line up — a receipt method with the wrong bank or clearance behavior produces remittance or reconciliation errors downstream in Cash Management. The Receivables Standard Receipt Import FBDI loads into AR_PAYMENTS_INTERFACE_ALL ; the receipts are only created when the Process Receipts Through Lockbox ESS job runs via erpProcesses or the Scheduled Processes work area .
