pages.title: Revenue & Credit Memos
pages.description: How Receivables defers and recognizes revenue on AR transactions, and how credit and debit memos adjust what a customer owes. Revenue policies, contingencies, scheduling rules, and the Recognize Revenue process drive when revenue is earned.
headings: Working example — create a credit memo via REST
Working example — run recognition via erpProcesses
pages.content: Functional view Configuration Technical view Data flow — step by step Retrieve the data — SQL Accounting SLA Reporting Integration notes Next steps REST resources FBDI templates Working example — create a credit memo via REST Working example — run recognition via erpProcesses Read the Receivables hub , AutoInvoice , and Subledger Accounting first. Revenue rules apply to invoices that already exist. Functional view Revenue policies decide when revenue is earned on a transaction. A revenue contingency makes recognition conditional on a future event — in Receivables the common case is payment-based recognition, where the contingency is removed as the customer pays. Event-based recognition ties recognition to a specific business event for example a delivered milestone . Revenue scheduling rules spread a transaction's value across periods. Credit and debit memos are AR transactions whose type class is a memo: they can reverse revenue or reduce the receivable. When a credit memo touches a line that was deferred, the deferred revenue on the credit memo is handled so the recognition books stay consistent. Sales credits and AutoAccounting derive the revenue accounts from customer and line attributes. Revenue Management RevMgmt sits on top for advanced contract accounting — Receivables hands it the transactions to analyze. Set up recognition behavior before invoices are created with contingencies. Where the revenue and memo chain lands in the underlying tables. Run these against the Fusion database to inspect memos and revenue recognition. Deferred and recognized revenue create entries through the sub-ledger accounting engine: Trace entries via XLA_AE_HEADERS / XLA_AE_LINES — see Subledger Accounting . No delete on memos: receivablesCreditMemos is create/update only — correct mistakes with another memo or an adjustment, not a delete. Defer first, recognize later: create invoices with the contingency, run Generate Revenue Schedules, then Recognize Revenue when the event occurs. Memos can carry deferred revenue: a credit memo touching a deferred line adjusts the schedule so recognition stays consistent. No revenue FBDI here: bulk memos go through AutoInvoice Import; revenue basis import is a separate module — verify in your instance. Accounts from AutoAccounting: revenue accounts are derived from customer/line attributes and sales credits unless overridden. Run in order: Generate Revenue Schedules → Recognize Revenue → Create Accounting via erpProcesses or scheduled processes. Back to Receivables AR . Back to the Financials hub . Collecting the invoices revenue was recognized on is Receipts & Lockbox . Revenue contingencies are payment-based — see Credit Management & Collections for the credit side. Read the Receivables hub , AutoInvoice , and Subledger Accounting first. Revenue rules apply to invoices that already exist. Contingency removal events must be assigned before the process can clear a contingency — without an assignment rule, deferred revenue sits on the schedule until someone intervenes. In the Oracle 26C Financials REST guide the memo resource is receivablesCreditMemos with create and update only — there is no delete on credit memos. Confirm resource availability against your instance. There is no dedicated revenue FBDI template in the Financials FBDI guide. Revenue basis data import is a separate module — verify the availability of any revenue-related interface template against your instance before relying on it. Run Generate Revenue Schedules before Recognize Revenue on newly created transactions, and Create Accounting afterward. pages.title: Flexfields & Value Sets
pages.description: Flexfields are Fusion's configurable data structures. The chart of accounts is one, and every 'extra field' on a form is another. Value sets define what values those fields accept. You can't understand an account combination or a custom field without them.
headings: Chart of accounts as a KFF
pages.content: The three kinds of flexfield Value sets Chart of accounts as a KFF Technical view SQL — find a valid value Integration notes Next steps The three kinds of flexfield Value sets A value set defines the valid values and their meaning for a flexfield segment or a descriptive attribute. The COA is a Key Flexfield. Its segments are account combinations , and each segment uses a value set. Three behaviors decide whether an account is valid: Segment qualifiers — mark which segment is the natural account drives account type, revaluation . Cross-validation rules — allow/deny specific segment combinations e.g. R&D dept can't use Cash accounts . Segment value security — who can enter/see which values data-level control . Flexfield metadata is configurable via REST commonValueSets , flexfield resources — read it to discover valid values at runtime. FBDI templates and imports use value sets too: a lookup value must exist before a load accepts it. Tables: value sets live in the FND_FLEX_VALIDATION_SETS / FND_FLEX_VALUES family; KFF structures in FND_ID_FLEX_STRUCTURES_B — data-dictionary names, confirm per release. An invalid account combination is the #1 FBDI rejection — validate segments before loading. When a UI shows a value a load rejected, check the value set, not the data file. Cross-validation rules break bulk loads that create new combinations — pre-create combinations. Ledgers use the COA: Enterprise Structures . Invalid accounts are a top error: FBDI errors . In practice, discovery is easier via the REST metadata commonValueSets resource than raw tables. Use SQL only when you have explicit data-access approval. Type Purpose Example Key Flexfield KFF A structured identifier made of segments Chart of accounts: Company.Department.Account.Subaccount Descriptive Flexfield DFF Extra fields attached to a form or object A 'Project Code' field on the supplier form Extensible Flexfield EFF Drillable, context-driven attributes analytical Product attributes in SCM or Financials Project Code Value set type How values are defined Independent A fixed list of values you define Dependent Values filtered by a parent independent value e.g. states per country Table Values come from a database table/view Translatable independent An independent list translated per language None Any value is allowed validation only -- Values for a value set e.g. the natural account segment SELECT fv.flex_value, fv.description, fv.enabled_flag, fv.start_date_active, fv.end_date_active FROM fnd_flex_values fv WHERE fv.flex_value_set_id = :value_set_id AND fv.enabled_flag = 'Y' ORDER BY fv.flex_value;

pages.title: Implementation & Data Migration
pages.description: How a Fusion ERP project actually happens: the implementation lifecycle, Functional Setup Manager (FAS), configuration packages, and the data migration playbook — the load order that makes a go-live clean.
pages.content: The implementation lifecycle Functional Setup Manager FAS Data migration — the playbook Choosing the load method Testing & go-live Integration notes Next steps The load order The implementation lifecycle Functional Setup Manager FAS FAS is the implementation cockpit. It organizes the work into: Migration has five phases, and order is what separates a clean go-live from a mess. Never load transactions before the reference and master data they depend on: Extract: pull legacy data suppliers, customers, open invoices, balances, assets . Map: map legacy codes to Fusion values segments, BU, ledger, category . Transform: reshape to the FBDI template / REST payload; build lookups for BU/ledger/tax. Validate: run your mapping rules on a sample before the full load. Load & reconcile: run FBDI, fix rejections, compare counts and totals to legacy sign-off numbers. SIT: integration flows against test data order: FBDI → validate → status → reconcile . UAT: business users validate functional setups with real scenarios. Parallel run: run both systems for one period and reconcile the difference. Cutover plan: freeze legacy → final extraction → load → reconcile → open periods → go live. Post go-live: track rejected rows, watch period close, confirm approvals behave. Reuse the same loader logic for migration and ongoing integrations — one code path, one set of fixes. Every FBDI load needs a reconciliation query count + totals — build it before go-live, not after. Keep a data dictionary of the Fusion tables/columns you load the module pages here are that dictionary . FBDI and ADFdi are the load engines — FBDI & ADFdi . Jobs behind every load — Scheduled Processes ESS . The structure you load into — Enterprise Structures . The three most common go-live disasters are all order problems: invoices loaded before suppliers, journals before the COA/accounts existed, and balances before periods were opened. Concept What it is Offering A licensed product group ERP, SCM, HCM, Financials… Functional area A workstream within an offering e.g. Payables, General Ledger Setup task A single configuration step define ledger, create BU, set up tax Setup group Configuration packaged for one ledger/BU assigned per org unit Implementation project Your project: which tasks, who owns them, status tracking Configuration package Export/import a setup between instances dev → test → prod Checklist/status Assigned, In Progress, Completed per task owner Method When to use it Examples FBDI Bulk, scheduled, needs an audit trail + error file Suppliers, invoices, journals, customers REST API Real-time or small volume, when the caller needs the ID back Create supplier, create invoice, check status ADFdi Ad-hoc spreadsheet loads by a power user Flexfield values, small master data fixes Application UI One-off manual entry during testing Setup tasks, test transactions neutral Plan scope, offerings, workstreams Configure FAS setup tasks per offering fusion Extend flexfields, reports, integrations Load data migration FBDI/REST Test SIT + UAT, parallel run success Go Live cutover, support 1 · Reference data flexfield values, calendar, tax codes 2 · Enterprise structures ledgers, legal entities, BUs, data access sets 3 · Accounting COA accounts, account combinations 4 · Master data suppliers, customers, items, employees, assets 5 · Open transactions AP invoices, AR invoices, POs, open expense reports 6 · Balances GL opening balances per period

pages.title: Interface Tables
pages.description: Every bulk load in Fusion works the same way: data is first staged into an interface table, then an import program validates and moves it into the real (base) tables. Learn the pipeline, the interface tables each module uses, and how to diagnose a load by looking at the right table.
headings: How a load flows through the tables
REST vs FBDI: both land in interfaces
When to look at the interface table
pages.content: The import pipeline The common interface tables How a load flows through the tables Reading rejection status REST vs FBDI: both land in interfaces When to look at the interface table Next steps Consultants often think a file or REST call writes straight to the business table — it does not. Fusion inserts into an interface table first. A scheduled program then reads those staged rows, validates them, and either moves them into the base tables or writes rejection reasons back. Until that program runs, nothing the user can see has happened. The key mental model: interface table = staging area, import job = the gatekeeper, base table = the real record . If a row is rejected you fix it in the interface table or the source file and re-run the import — you never edit base data directly. These are the staging tables behind the most common Financials loads. Exact names can vary slightly by release — confirm against your instance's data dictionary before writing code. Take a supplier invoice as the example — it is the pattern you will see in every module. Rejected rows carry a status and a reason in the interface table. The classic diagnostic query reads the interface table, not the base table: Some REST resources write directly to base tables create-a-record resources like invoices , while others populate the same interface tables a file would use: This is why a consultant must know both the resource and the job: a REST call may only stage data, and nothing reaches the business until the matching scheduled process executes. See Driving ESS via REST to submit those jobs programmatically. A load "succeeded" but nothing appeared — check the interface table; rows may still be pending import. Some rows failed — the error CSV is derived from the interface table; querying it directly gives you the same detail in a form you can join against source data. You want to know why AutoInvoice rejected a transaction — RA_INTERFACE_LINES_ALL holds the reason. Re-submitting after a fix — reset status columns per the import program's rules, or re-stage from the source. See how FBDI drives these tables in FBDI & ADFdi . Submit the import jobs from code in Driving ESS via REST erpProcesses . Each Financials module page now has its own data-flow section pointing at its interface tables. Interface tables are why FBDI can validate thousands of rows asynchronously and still tell you exactly which ones failed: rejection rows stay in the interface with a status and error column, and the error CSV is written from them. Do not treat these table names as guaranteed across releases. Oracle changes interface layouts between updates, and the safest source of truth is the data dictionary on your own instance SQL Developer on a read replica, or OTBI — not the docs page from last year. The most common rejection causes are the same across every interface table: invalid account combination, closed period, missing supplier/customer master, wrong date format, or a required column left empty. Fix the source , re-submit, and the same rows flow through cleanly. pages.title: Cycle Counting & Adjustments
pages.description: Keeping the book quantity true to the physical quantity. Cycle counting schedules small, frequent counts of a subset of items; adjustments post the difference between counted and on-hand. This is the reconciliation that keeps inventory (and its GL value) accurate.
pages.content: Functional view Technical view Data flow — step by step Retrieve the data — SQL Worked example — a count variance Integration notes Next steps REST resources FBDI templates Read On-hand & Transfers — a count corrects on-hand. Functional view Cycle counting counts a rotating sample of items rather than a full physical inventory. Each count compares the counted quantity with on-hand; if they differ, an adjustment approved brings on-hand to the counted value. Adjustments are also used directly to correct stock — for example after a return or a write-off. Approval gates the change: only approved adjustments alter on-hand. Reasons & accounts: adjustments need a reason that maps accounts for the GL entry. Rotate counts: cycle counting is designed to run continuously, not once a year. Inventory value flows into General Ledger via cost. Back to the Inventory hub . Read On-hand & Transfers — a count corrects on-hand. Column names follow the Fusion data dictionary naming. Confirm against your instance before relying on them. Resource What you can do with it r1 Create/read cycle counts and their entered quantities r2 Create approved adjustments that change on-hand Template Purpose Must exist first f1 Bulk-post adjustments built elsewhere Items, inventory orgs, adjustment reasons Step What happens Where the data lands table 1 A cycle count is created for an item/location t1 2 Counted quantity is entered t2 3 Variance vs on-hand is computed t3 4 Approved adjustment posts the difference t4 5 Cost/GL entries value the adjustment t5 neutral Schedule count rotate by class / location warning Enter counted qty compare to on-hand Approve adjustment reasons + accounts success On-hand updated + cost / GL entry variance SELECT t.transaction_id, t.transaction_type, t.transaction_quantity, t.transaction_date, t.reason_name, i.item_number FROM mtl_material_transactions t JOIN egp_system_items_b i ON i.inventory_item_id = t.inventory_item_id WHERE t.transaction_type IN 'Cycle Count Adjustment', 'Adjustment' AND t.transaction_date >= SYSDATE - 30 ORDER BY t.transaction_date DESC;

pages.title: Items & Item Master
pages.description: What an item is before it has any quantity. The item master defines every buyable and sellable thing — its attributes, how it's stocked or accounted for, and which organizations it's valid in. No on-hand, transfer, order, or receipt can exist without the item record first.
headings: Worked example — creating a new stock item
pages.content: Functional view Technical view Data flow — step by step Retrieve the data — SQL Worked example — creating a new stock item Integration notes Next steps REST resources FBDI templates Read the Inventory hub first. Items are the master data everything else references. Functional view An item is a distinct good or service. The item master is the shared catalog — EGP_SYSTEM_ITEMS_B in the data model — holding attributes like name, unit of measure, and whether it is stocked, purchased, or manufactured. Items are organized by item organizations where they're usable and inherit defaults from item templates based on item classes . Load items first, always: receipts, transfers, orders all validate against the item master. Organization is required: an item must be assigned to the org you transact in. Status gates transactions: Draft/Inactive items reject receipt and on-hand transactions. Attributes control behavior: a non-stocked item won't track on-hand; a lot-controlled one demands lot detail. With items defined, quantity can move — On-hand, Transfers & Reservations . Back to the Inventory hub . Read the Inventory hub first. Items are the master data everything else references. Column names follow the Fusion data dictionary naming. Confirm against your instance before relying on them. Concept What it is functional Item A distinct good/service with identifier, description, and unit of measure Item organization An organization or set where the item is defined/usable Item class Categories that group items and drive templates e.g. 'Purchased Item', 'Finished Good' Item template Default attribute values applied at creation Item attributes Flags controlling behavior: stocked, purchasable, sellable, serialized, lot-controlled Item status Draft, Active, or Inactive — only Active items are usable in transactions Purchased Item Finished Good Resource What you can do with it r1 Create/read items PIM REST resource — the primary create path r2 GET — read inherited defaults for validation Template Purpose Must exist first f1 Bulk-load item master from a legacy/ERP system Item class, template, and organization Step What happens Where the data lands table 1 Item is created UI, REST, or Item Import FBDI t1 2 Item is assigned to an organization t2 3 Status is set to Active t3 4 The item is now usable in transactions t4 -- Items in an organization, filtered to stocked purchasing items SELECT i.inventory_item_id, i.item_number, i.item_description, i.inventory_item_status_code, NVL org.stock_on_hand_qty, 0 AS on_hand_qty FROM egp_system_items_b i LEFT JOIN SELECT inventory_item_id, SUM quantity AS stock_on_hand_qty FROM mtl_on_hand_quantities_oif GROUP BY inventory_item_id org ON org.inventory_item_id = i.inventory_item_id WHERE i.inventory_item_status_code = 'Active' ORDER BY i.item_number;

pages.title: On-hand, Transfers & Reservations
pages.description: Where stock lives, how it moves, and how it gets set aside. On-hand is the running quantity per item per organization; transfers move it between orgs and subinventories; reservations commit available quantity to a sales order or project. This is the heart of inventory operations.
pages.content: Functional view Technical view Data flow — step by step Retrieve the data — SQL Worked example — 100 chairs, 30 reserved Integration notes Next steps REST resources FBDI templates Read Items & Item Master — on-hand only exists for defined, active items. Functional view On-hand is the current quantity an item has in an organization split by subinventory and locator . Available subtracts reservations — committed quantity — so availability is what a sale can actually promise. Transfers move quantity between orgs/subinventories; reservations set aside available stock for an order or project. Availability = on-hand − reserved: base order promising on this, not raw on-hand. Organization scopes everything: quantity is per inventory org and subinventory. Transfers are audited: they're inventory transactions with cost/GL impact — use reason codes. Reservation types matter: hard firm vs soft soft-reserved reservations behave differently. Reconcile the count in Cycle Counting & Adjustments . Back to the Inventory hub . Read Items & Item Master — on-hand only exists for defined, active items. Column names follow the Fusion data dictionary naming. Confirm against your instance before relying on them. Resource What you can do with it r1 GET — read on-hand by item/organization r2 Create transfers between orgs/subinventories r3 Create/read reservations against on-hand Template Purpose Must exist first f1 Bulk-load opening on-hand balances Items and inventory organizations Step What happens Where the data lands table 1 An on-hand transaction moves quantity receipt, transfer, adjustment t1 2 On-hand is maintained per item/org/subinventory t2c t2 3 A reservation commits available quantity to an order t3 4 Shipping consumes quantity — on-hand decreases t4 fusion On-hand what physically exists warning Reserved committed to orders/projects success Available what you can promise − reservations = SELECT i.item_number, o.inventory_org_id, o.subinventory_code, o.quantity_on_hand, o.quantity_reserved, o.quantity_on_hand - o.quantity_reserved AS available_qty FROM mtl_on_hand_quantities_oif o JOIN egp_system_items_b i ON i.inventory_item_id = o.inventory_item_id WHERE i.item_number = :item_number;

pages.title: Inventory
pages.description: How the goods a company buys and makes are stored, tracked, and moved. Inventory holds the on-hand picture behind every purchase, sale, and transfer — the quantifiable bridge between the money you spend (Procurement/Payables) and the revenue you earn (Order-to-Cash).
headings: Learning path — read in this order
pages.content: The business story Learning path — read in this order The processes Functional ↔ technical reference Configuration Data flow — step by step Integration notes Next steps Read the Procurement hub receiving puts goods into inventory and Order-to-Cash shipping pulls goods out of it . Inventory sits between the two. The business story Buying is only half the story — the goods have to live somewhere until they're sold. Inventory answers four questions about every item: what is it item master , how much do we have on-hand , where is it going transfers , and is the count right counting and adjustments . Item before quantity: you can't post an on-hand or transfer for an item that doesn't exist yet — load items first. Org matters: every quantity and transaction belongs to an inventory organization; pass the right one. Transactions are audited: inventory movements use reason codes and create cost/GL entries — treat them as accounting data. Counting is a reconciliation: cycle counting exists to keep on-hand true; expect adjustments after a count. Start with Items , then On-hand & Transfers , then Cycle Counting . Inventory connects to Order Management ship out and Procurement receive in . Read the Procurement hub receiving puts goods into inventory and Order-to-Cash shipping pulls goods out of it . Inventory sits between the two. Everything in inventory feeds cost : the on-hand quantity × the item cost is a balance-sheet value that eventually flows into the GL. That's why inventory transactions aren't just operational — they create accounting entries. Inventory REST resources live under the scmRestApi base and names vary by release — confirm against your instance's REST service catalog. Column names follow the Fusion data dictionary naming. Confirm against your instance before relying on them. Having trouble? See Cash Management for related cash flows, and watch this space for a dedicated Inventory troubleshooting page. pages.title: Walkthrough — change a BI Publisher or OTBI report and promote it to production
pages.description: The complete sequence for changing an existing Fusion report: understand what you're changing (BIP report or OTBI analysis), edit the definition, secure it, test, move it across environments, and publish to production with a rollback plan — the Fusion mirror of the OIC and VBCS walkthroughs.
headings: Phase 1 — Understand the report you are changing
Phase 5 — Migrate the report artifacts across environments
The full checklist (copy for your change)
pages.content: The journey at a glance Phase 1 — Understand the report you are changing Phase 2 — Edit the report definition Phase 3 — Secure the changed artifact Phase 4 — Test before promoting Phase 5 — Migrate the report artifacts across environments Phase 6 — Go live & monitor Rollback plan The full checklist copy for your change Next steps Your change is to reporting : a BI Publisher BIP report pixel-perfect output, bursting, schedule or an OTBI analysis/dashboard ad-hoc queries on subject areas . Fusion promotes report artifacts differently from setup or data — the pieces travel as catalog objects report definitions, data models, layouts, analyses with their roles and folder permissions , and every scheduled run is really an ESS job . Follow these phases in order. Reporting splits into two artifact families — identify which one you have before editing: Open the artifact and record before touching it: Edit the artifact where development happens — usually the non-production instance: A changed report inherits its security the same way it did before — but verify it, because edits can recreate artifacts or add new catalog folders: Reports move as catalog objects report definitions, data models, layouts, analyses , not as database rows. The disciplined sequence: Reports are lower-risk than data or setup because they are read-only artifacts — but plan the way back anyway: Catalog path — BIP addresses reports by path, not just name e.g. /Custom/Financials/AP/Invoices . Data source — the data model's SQL or Fusion data source; for OTBI, the subject area e.g. "Payables Invoices Real Time" . Schedule — is it scheduled? Then the run is an ESS job you must re-schedule in the target environment. Security context — which duties/roles and catalog folder grants let users see it see Reporting & Analytics . BIP: edit the data model add filters/columns , the layout RTF template in Word / eText for files , or the delivery email/bursting/FTP — then save the report definition. OTBI: edit the analysis add filters, columns, calculations or the dashboard layout, and save to the catalog. Keep the catalog path stable if other things reference it dashboards, scheduled jobs, integrations submitting the report via REST . Catalog folder access — confirm the report lives in a folder your intended users can open, and no unintended users gained access. Duties/roles — which duties can open BIP vs OTBI, and which subject areas they can query. Data security — the same ledger/BU/row filters apply see the reporting security model on the Reporting & Analytics page . Export the report definition and its data model/layout from the source environment, using the report catalog's upload/download in Reports & Analytics. Import into the target environment. Importing recreates the catalog entry; confirm the catalog folder and permissions survive the import re-apply catalog folder grants if the import landed in a different folder . OTBI: save and export the analysis/dashboard, import to the target catalog, and re-check its subject area references exist there. Re-create the schedule in the target environment — a schedule is part of the target instance's configuration, not the artifact itself; and if a data model or subject area differs between environments, re-validate the query. Run the Phase-4 checks again in the new environment before handing to production traffic. Keep the previous export/definition available; re-import it to restore the prior layout or analysis if the new output is wrong. If the change altered a catalog path , rollback must undo the path change and restore references — keep a note of old vs new path. A rolled-back schedule is just a re-scheduled job; confirm the old schedule parameters are restored, not duplicated. Know the engines you may touch — see Reporting & Analytics . Deliver report output through the integration layer — Oracle Integration Cloud . Support the schedule in ESS job errors . "Current artifact: BIP report /Custom/Financials/AP/Invoices , data model Payables Invoices , RTF layout, scheduled nightly via ESS, duty Payables Manager " is your safety net and rollback reference. Changing the catalog path breaks every reference to the report — integrations, scheduled jobs, and portal links. Prefer editing in place ; only move paths when the folder structure demands it, and update the references in the same change. Everything a report needs to run — the ESS job lifecycle, output vs log, retries — is on the troubleshooting pages ESS job errors if the run fails. The same advice as setup migration: reuse one path for publish and promote , and keep a document of the catalog paths + roles you moved so the next change is a replay, not a rediscovery. Reports never change the underlying data — so rollback is safe by nature. The real risk is a dangling reference : a path you moved or a subject area that no longer exists after rollback, which silently breaks scheduled jobs. Test the schedule after any rollback, not just the manual run. You're changing The artifact Where it lives BI Publisher report pixel-perfect / regulatory / bursted Report definition + data model + layout RTF/eText + delivery rules BIP catalog folder, e.g. /Custom/Financials/AP/Invoices OTBI analysis / dashboard ad-hoc queries Analysis on a subject area, laid out in a dashboard OTBI catalog folder Financial Reporting statement GL Row/column definition over a reporting tree Financial Reporting Center Check How Pass = The report runs Run it or run a scheduled ESS job in the test instance Output generated without error Output is correct Open the PDF/Excel/eText; compare to expected layout and data Data and layout match the requirement Parameters work Run with the prompts/hard-coded values used in production Parameter values resolve Delivery works Check email/FTP/bursting if configured Recipients got the right output Security holds Sign in as the report's actual audience Authorized users see it; others are denied Step Action Checkpoint 1 Import into production and verify the catalog path matches what references it References dashboards, jobs, integrations still resolve 2 Re-create the schedule and delivery email/FTP/bursting Schedule saved; delivery confirmed 3 Run one production request Output verified against prod data; parameters correct 4 Confirm security in production Correct duties/folders/data filters apply 5 Hand to business + monitor the report history Users see the new output; no regressions # Done? Identified the artifact BIP / OTBI / Financial Reporting and recorded its catalog path, data source, schedule, and roles ☐ Edited the definition data model/layout/analysis without changing the catalog path Verified security: folder access, duties, subject areas, data filters Tested in non-prod: runs, correct output, parameters, delivery, security Exported artifacts and imported to the target environment; folder/references verified 6 Schedule re-created in target; re-validated the query against that instance's data/setup 7 Published in production; production run verified; report history checked 8 Rollback artifacts and schedule restored; references confirmed neutral 1 · Understand BIP or OTBI · catalog path · who runs it fusion 2 · Edit the artifact data model / layout / analysis 3 · Secure it duties · catalog folder · subject area vbcs 4 · Test in dev/test run the report, check output 5 · Migrate artifacts export → import across environments success 6 · Go live & monitor schedule, delivery, rollback ready

pages.title: Application Modules
pages.description: Fusion Cloud is not one application — it is four families of applications (ERP, SCM, HCM, CX) sharing one platform. Each family exposes its own REST services, files, and business objects. This page maps the modules and the objects you are most likely to integrate with.
headings: Which module am I integrating with?
A common integration: import supplier invoices
The PR → PO → Receipt → Invoice flow
pages.content: The main application suites Financials in practice Procurement & Supply Chain HCM highlights CX Customer Experience Which module am I integrating with? Next steps A common integration: import supplier invoices The PR → PO → Receipt → Invoice flow When Oracle says "Fusion," it means a single cloud suite that happens to be sold and implemented in pieces. The technology is shared — one login, one REST framework, one file-loading engine — but the business objects are grouped into modules , and the module decides which REST base URL you call and which FBDI templates you use. Fusion ships as four suites. The first three are sold as Fusion ERP which groups Finance, Procurement, and Project Financials and Fusion SCM Supply Chain & Manufacturing . Fusion HCM and Fusion CX are separate product lines. As an integrator you will mostly care about which objects you touch, not the commercial packaging. Notice that modules share concepts: a customer appears in Receivables as a customer account , in OC Order Capture as a customer , and in CX as an account . One of the first things you do on any project is agree which module's copy is the source of truth. Financials is the most-integrated module in practice because everything money-related lands here. The objects you will see most often: For a handful of invoices you POST to the invoices REST resource. For thousands, you use the Payables Standard Invoice Import via FBDI template so ESS can process the batch asynchronously. Both paths end at the same place: an invoice in Payables that references a supplier, a site, and a set of distribution lines that carry the account segments. Procurement lives inside ERP and covers requisitions , purchase orders , and suppliers . SCM extends outward to inventory, order management, sourcing, and logistics. The object nearly every integration touches first is the supplier — it is master data you create before any buying can happen. A requisition is a request; once approved it is converted to a purchase order . When goods arrive, the warehouse records a receipt . When the vendor bills you, Payables matches the invoice against the PO and receipt — the famous three-way match . As an integrator you hook in at any of these points: creating POs, adding receipts, or importing supplier invoices. Fusion HCM manages people through several layers of structure. GitHub-style terminology aside, the objects map to real HR concepts: HCM has its own REST base URL. Note the difference from Financials: Fusion CX covers sales, marketing, and service. From an integration standpoint the key objects are on the sales side : CX uses the same REST framework but a different base: crmRestApi . In practice, many CX integrations are read-only extracts to a sales dashboard or a two-way sync of opportunities with a proposal tool. If you are still unsure, open the metadata explorer at the base URL while logged in: it lists every resource, and the resource name alone "…Payables…", "…HCM…", "…Sales…" usually gives the module away. General Ledger GL — the chart of accounts, account balances, and journal entries . Journal batches are posted in accounting periods ; an integration must find the open period before posting. Payables — supplier invoices and payments. The classic inbound integration is "import supplier invoices" from an external system. Receivables — customer invoices, credit memos, and receipts. Fixed Assets — asset books, additions, transfers, and depreciation runs. Expenses — expense report headers and lines, plus approval workflow. Workers — a person with one or more active assignments. In REST these are person and personProfile resources. Positions — an org-chart slot "Finance Manager, UK" that a worker occupies; you usually integrate positions, not just people. HR actions — the audited events hire, transfer, terminate that change a worker. hrActions is where status changes enter the system. Assignments — the specific job/org/location a worker fills on a date. Benefits & expenrollment — eligibility and enrollment records, including the fact that HCM also runs expense reports for employee travel. Leads — unqualified interest that can be routed and converted. Opportunities — a qualified pipeline deal with amount and close date. Customer accounts / contacts — the CRM representation of a party, shared with Receivables through the Customer Data Management CDM foundation. Learn the shared foundations in core concepts — flexfields, value sets, attachments, and Jobs. Master the mechanics of calling any of these modules in REST API fundamentals . Load bulk data into a module with FBDI & ADFdi . The single most useful habit: identify the module first . Almost everything else — the REST base URL, the templates, the security roles, the correct value sets — follows from knowing whether you are dealing with Financials, Procurement, SCM, HCM, or CX. The same versioned pattern 11.13.18.05 applies, but the resource family is hcmRestApi , not fscmRestApi . HCM also exposes SOAP services for example HCMWorkerService that some legacy integrations still use. When you are handed a requirement, the fastest way to decide the module is to look at the REST base URL in the service description or the delivered integration: fscmRestApi means ERP/SCM Finance, Procurement, Order Management ; hcmRestApi means HCM; crmRestApi means CX. The resource after the version — invoices , purchaseOrders , persons , opportunities — then tells you the exact module. Suite Business purpose Typical objects you integrate with ERP — Financials Account for money: general ledger, payables, receivables, fixed assets, expenses Journals, supplier invoices, payments, expense reports, budgets ERP — Procurement Buy things: requisitions, purchase orders, contracts, sourcing Requisitions, purchase orders POs , suppliers, supplier sites SCM Plan and move inventory and goods: inventory, orders, manufacturing, logistics Inventory items, order management OM orders, shipments, on-hand balances HCM Manage people: workforce structure, talent, payroll, benefits Workers, assignments, positions, HR actions, resumes, competencies CX Win and serve customers: sales, marketing, service, commerce Opportunities, leads, accounts/contacts, service requests neutral Source system ERP, portal, bank statements fusion Fusion Payables invoices · AP Invoice Import General Ledger journal entries in open period Requisition PR someone requests goods Purchase Order buyer turns PR into PO Receipt goods received against PO line success Invoice three-way match: PO + receipt + invoice REST or file validate + post approve ship bill curl -u "username:password" \\ -X POST \\ "https://yourinstance.oraclecloud.com/fscmRestApi/resources/11.13.18.05/invoices" \\ -H "Content-Type: application/vnd.oracle.resource+json; type=singular" \\ -H "REST-Framework-Version: 11.13.18.05" \\ -d ' ' curl -u "username:password" \\ "https://yourinstance.oraclecloud.com/fscmRestApi/resources/11.13.18.05/purchaseOrders?q=Status='OPEN'&limit=25" \\ -H "REST-Framework-Version: 11.13.18.05" https://yourinstance.oraclecloud.com/hcmRestApi/resources/11.13.18.05/persons?q=PersonNumber='00000001'

pages.title: Order Management
pages.description: How a customer order becomes a shipment. Order Management captures sales orders, schedules and fulfills them against available inventory, and hands the fulfilled lines to Shipping — the operational front half of the Order-to-Cash cycle that ends with an AR invoice.
headings: Learning path — read in this order
pages.content: The business story Learning path — read in this order The processes Functional ↔ technical reference Configuration Data flow — step by step Integration notes Next steps Read the Inventory hub on-hand is what gets shipped and Order-to-Cash where OM hands off to Receivables . The business story A customer orders — Order Management OM records it, checks inventory, schedules a fulfillment date, and the order flows toward shipping. Inventory is consumed, and the ship confirmation triggers the AR invoice that ends the Order-to-Cash cycle in Receivables. Customer & item first: order creation validates against customer and item master. Scheduling vs shipping: a booked order isn't shipped until fulfillment completes — poll status. Inventory is the constraint: availability on-hand − reserved decides promise dates. Ship triggers billing: the AR invoice comes after ship confirmation, not order entry. Start with Sales Orders & Fulfillment , then Shipping & Logistics . See the billing aftermath in Order-to-Cash . Read the Inventory hub on-hand is what gets shipped and Order-to-Cash where OM hands off to Receivables . The thing consultants remember: OM is where inventory quantity becomes customer service . A good order-prompting setup keeps bookings flowing; a good fulfillment setup ships them fast. OM/Shipping REST resources live under the scmRestApi base and names vary by release — confirm against your instance's REST service catalog. Column names follow the Fusion data dictionary naming. Confirm against your instance before relying on them. pages.title: Sales Orders & Fulfillment
pages.description: Order capture is the front of the Order-to-Cash cycle. A sales order records what a customer wants, scheduling turns that into a promise date, and fulfillment reserves inventory and moves the order to ship-ready. Understand this page and you understand how a sale becomes a shipment.
headings: Working example — create a sales order via REST
pages.content: Functional view Technical view Data flow — step by step Retrieve the data — SQL Worked example — a 5-unit order Integration notes Next steps REST resources FBDI templates Working example — create a sales order via REST Read the Order Management hub and the Inventory on-hand page. Functional view A sales order has a header customer, request date, destination and lines item, quantity, price . Scheduling checks availability and sets a promise date . Fulfillment reserves the item and prepares it for shipping. Status flows from Booked through Fulfilled to Shipped in Shipping . Validate up front: order lines reject on unknown customer/item or closed org. Poll, don't assume: a booked order isn't shipped until fulfillment finishes. Availability drives promise: watch on-hand minus reservations when promising dates. Ship = bill: the AR invoice follows ship confirmation, in Receivables. Ship-ready orders move to Shipping & Logistics . Back to the Order Management hub . Read the Order Management hub and the Inventory on-hand page. Column names follow the Fusion data dictionary naming. Confirm against your instance before relying on them. pages.title: Shipping & Logistics (WSH)
pages.description: The delivery engine that turns a ship-ready order into a shipped one. Shipping (WSH) groups fulfilled lines into deliveries, plans them into trips, packs and ships them — and the ship confirmation consumes inventory and triggers the AR invoice.
pages.content: Functional view Technical view Data flow — step by step Retrieve the data — SQL Worked example — shipping 5 chairs Integration notes Next steps REST resources FBDI templates Read Sales Orders & Fulfillment — shipping starts from ship-ready lines. Functional view Shipping takes fulfilled order lines and ships them. Key objects: a delivery groups lines going to the same destination, a trip plans routes, packing handles containers, and ship confirmation records that goods have left. On confirmation, inventory on-hand decreases and billing is triggered. Ship = consume: ship confirmation creates the inventory transaction that reduces on-hand. Billing waits on ship: the AR invoice arrives after ship confirmation, not order booking. Carriers matter: trip/carrier setup drives cost and tracking visibility. Shipped orders become AR invoices via Order-to-Cash. Back to the Order Management hub . Read Sales Orders & Fulfillment — shipping starts from ship-ready lines. Column names follow the Fusion data dictionary naming. Confirm against your instance before relying on them. pages.title: What is Oracle Fusion Cloud?
pages.description: Oracle Fusion Cloud is Oracle's suite of SaaS applications — ERP, SCM, HCM, and CX — built on a common technology platform. It is the 'system of record': the place where your master data, transactions, and approvals ultimately live.
headings: How Fusion is different from traditional E-Business Suite
Where Fusion sits in the enterprise
Business cycles at a glance — where every module plugs in
Key URLs and consoles you will use
The Financials / Supply Chain split in one table
pages.content: How Fusion is different from traditional E-Business Suite The Fusion technology stack Where Fusion sits in the enterprise The two integration pillars Business cycles at a glance — where every module plugs in Key URLs and consoles you will use Next steps 1. Service-based REST / SOAP 2. File-based FBDI The Financials / Supply Chain split in one table Fusion Cloud often just called Fusion or Oracle Fusion Applications is a set of cloud applications delivered as a service. Oracle runs, patches, and secures the infrastructure; your organisation gets fully managed modules for finance, procurement, supply chain, HR, and customer experience. Fusion Applications replaced the older Oracle E-Business Suite EBS as the flagship product line. The differences matter because they change how you integrate: Under the hood, Fusion is built on Oracle's own middleware. Knowing this stack explains a lot of the terminology you will see in the documentation: In a typical Oracle-centric landscape, Fusion is the hub, and OIC is the "nervous system" that moves data between Fusion and everything else: An integration developer works at the boundary between Fusion and OIC: connecting to Fusion services, transforming payloads, and orchestrating multi-step flows. A front-end developer builds VBCS pages that consume either Fusion services directly or OIC endpoints that hide the complexity. Every Fusion integration boils down to one of two patterns. Master both and you can handle almost any requirement. For small, synchronous, request-response calls — reading an invoice, creating a customer, or querying open POs. Each Fusion module exposes REST resources under a versioned URL space. For bulk, asynchronous, "no one is waiting on the result" loads — importing 10,000 supplier invoices. You upload a ZIP of CSV data plus an XML control file to UCM, and ESS runs an import job in the background. You will usually combine the two: OIC orchestrates and calls REST for the small stuff, but switches to FBDI for bulk . Modules are the tools; business cycles are the work. Everything on this site belongs to one of three end-to-end journeys: money you spend Procure-to-Pay , money you earn Order-to-Cash , and the reporting that wraps both around each month Record-to-Report . If you are ever unsure which module owns a task, the answer is "the part of the cycle doing the work right now." This is the map that answers the most-asked question — "is procurement part of supply chain?" Yes: procurement is the supply chain's buying stage . It meets Financials at the invoice, which is exactly where the P2P cycle crosses from SCM into Payables. Each cycle has a full step-by-step — table by table, REST/FBDI hop by hop — if you want the deep dive: Procure-to-Pay , Order-to-Cash , Record-to-Report . ADF Application Development Framework — the Java MVC framework that generates most Fusion pages. ADF also exposes the REST and SOAP services you consume. UCM Universal Content Manager — Fusion's document repository. Attachments you upload invoices, CVs are stored here. ESS Enterprise Scheduler Service — the job scheduler that runs FBDI loads, report generation, and other background processes. BIP Business Intelligence Publisher — the reporting engine that produces formatted documents PDF, Excel from data. Redwood — Oracle's new design system gradually replacing the older ADF look-and-feel in the user interface. Explore the application modules and what each one exposes. Learn the core concepts — flexfields, value sets, and attachment handling. Go deep on REST APIs and FBDI — the two pillars. The important mental model for an integration/UI developer: Fusion owns the data . Everything else in your ecosystem — an OIC integration, a VBCS page, an external web app — is either reading from Fusion or writing to Fusion. You rarely build "inside" Fusion; you build around it using its APIs and import/export files. Because you cannot run SQL against the Fusion database, every read and write must go through a supported channel: REST or SOAP services, FBDI file loads, or Business Intelligence Publisher reports. Real-world mix: an inbound invoice from a supplier portal lands in OIC. OIC validates it, calls Fusion REST to check the PO exists, then triggers an FBDI load to import the invoice in bulk at night. A VBCS page then shows the status. Procurement sources , Inventory stores , Order Management ships , Cost values — that is Supply Chain. Payables pays , Receivables collects , Cash confirms , GL scores , Assets depreciates , Expenses reimburses — that is Financials. They meet in the cycles: buy and pay P2P , sell and collect O2C , then report it all R2R . Open the REST base URL in a browser while logged in to Fusion — Oracle renders an interactive explorer showing every resource, its fields, and sample payloads. It is the fastest way to learn an endpoint. pages.title: Procurement
pages.description: The buying side of the business: how a need becomes a supplier payment. Procurement covers requisitions, purchase orders, suppliers, sourcing, and receiving — and it hands the result to Payables for the invoice and payment steps you already learned in P2P. This hub is the starting point; the deep dives below cover each area in functional and technical detail.
headings: Learning path — read in this order
pages.content: The business story Learning path — read in this order The processes Functional ↔ technical reference Configuration Data flow — step by step Integration notes Next steps Read Enterprise Structures business units, legal entity , Payables the invoice/payment side of the same flow , and it helps to have seen the Procure-to-Pay cycle first. The business story Someone needs something — a laptop, a service, raw material. Procurement is the discipline that turns that need into a paid invoice, in controlled steps: someone requests it requisition , a buyer orders it purchase order , the warehouse receives it receipt , and Payables pays the supplier's invoice . Procurement owns everything up to the receipt; Payables owns the invoice and payment. Where the procurement chain lands in the underlying tables. These are the purchase-side tables that feed directly into the Payables invoice tables you already know. Load order matters: supplier → supplier site → PO → receipt. Each step validates the one before it. Requisitions are two-path: self-service entry for users, or requisitionLines REST for external systems — then approval runs. POs can be created or updated via REST purchaseOrders ; bulk moves use the Purchase Order Import FBDI. Receiving closes the loop: without a receipt, 3-way match fails and the invoice is held. Different base URL: Procurement REST uses scmRestApi ; Financials uses fscmRestApi . Start with Requisitions , then Purchase Orders , then Receiving . See the whole money-out cycle in Procure-to-Pay . Back to the Financials hub or the home learning path . Read Enterprise Structures business units, legal entity , Payables the invoice/payment side of the same flow , and it helps to have seen the Procure-to-Pay cycle first. The three documents tie together through matching : Payables compares the invoice to the PO 2-way and the receipt 3-way before paying. So what Procurement creates — approved POs and accurate receipts — is what makes cleaner payments downstream. The Procurement REST resources live under the scmRestApi base e.g. purchaseOrders , not the Financials fscmRestApi . Confirm resource names against your instance's REST service catalog before building. Column names follow the Fusion data dictionary naming. Confirm against your instance before relying on them. Having trouble? See Payables troubleshooting for invoice/match issues, and watch this space for a dedicated Procurement troubleshooting page. pages.title: Purchase Orders
pages.description: The contract to buy. A purchase order (PO) names the supplier, the lines, the quantities and prices, and the charge accounts — and once approved it is the commitment Payables matches invoices against. Understand document types, lines, distributions, approvals, and change orders and you understand most procurement integrations.
headings: Worked example — a PO with budget check
Working example — create a PO via REST
pages.content: Functional view Technical view Data flow — step by step Retrieve the data — SQL Worked example — a PO with budget check Integration notes Next steps Approval & status REST resources FBDI templates Working example — create a PO via REST Read Requisitions and the Procurement hub first. The matching page in Payables explains how the PO is used to approve payment. Functional view The PO is the commitment : a legal promise to buy specific goods/services at agreed prices. It has a header supplier, site, terms, currency , lines item, quantity, price , and distributions the charge accounts . A PO can be created directly or converted from an approved requisition. Approving a PO requires funds/approval rules and — if budget control is on — a budget reservation . Status moves Incomplete → In Approval → Approved → Open / Closed . A PO cannot be received against until it is approved and open. Create path is REST or FBDI: purchaseOrders REST for small volumes; Import Purchase Orders FBDI for bulk. Supplier must exist first: PO creation rejects on a missing/inactive supplier site. Approved/open before receive: receiving against an unapproved PO fails. Accrual and budget: with accrual/budgetary control, a PO can reserve funds — plan the document type accordingly. Approved POs get received in Receiving . Back to the Procurement hub . Read Requisitions and the Procurement hub first. The matching page in Payables explains how the PO is used to approve payment. Column names follow the Fusion data dictionary naming. Confirm against your instance before relying on them. A PO "posts" to the GL only through accrual or the downstream invoice; the PO itself is a commitment encumbrance , not actual spend. Having trouble? See Payables troubleshooting invoice/match issues referencing the PO . Document type What it is Standard PO One-time purchase with defined lines — the common case Blanket PO Standing agreement; releases' draw down later no line commitment Contract PO Terms-only agreement; calls/expenses reference it Purchase requisition The request; becomes a standard PO on conversion Resource What you can do with it r1 Create/read/update PO headers and children — the REST create path r2 Create/read/update PO lines r3 Create/read PO distributions charge accounts proc POST — submit approval / AutoClose related ESS jobs if needed Template Purpose Must exist first f1 Bulk-create POs with headers, lines, and distributions Supplier + site, buyer, approved item/category, unit of measure Step What happens Where the data lands table 1 The PO is created converted from PR, entered, imported, or REST t1 2 PO lines carry item, quantity, price t2 3 PO distributions hold the charge accounts t3 4 Approval runs — status → Approved/Open t4c t4 5 Goods are received against open lines t5c t5 6 Payables matches the invoice to PO + receipt t6c t6 neutral From requisition approved PR → PO warning Approval document-level workflow success Approved → open ready to receive against Change orders amend lines / amounts or direct entry / import changes curl -u "integration.user:password" \\ "https:// .oraclecloud.com/scmRestApi/resources/latest/purchaseOrders" \\ -H "Content-Type: application/json" \\ -H "REST-Framework-Version" \\ -X POST \\ -d ' "SupplierId": 123456, "SupplierSiteId": 789123, "CurrencyCode": "USD", "BuyerId": 900001, "DocumentTypeCode": "STANDARD", "PaymentTermsName": "NET30", "Lines": ' SELECT h.po_header_id, h.segment1 AS po_number, h.document_status, h.document_type_code, h.currency_code, h.creation_date, s.supplier_name FROM po_headers_all h JOIN poz_suppliers s ON s.supplier_id = h.vendor_id WHERE h.creation_date >= SYSDATE - 30 AND h.document_type_code = 'STANDARD' ORDER BY h.creation_date DESC;

pages.title: Receiving
pages.description: How goods actually arriving turn into receipts. Receiving records what was received against a purchase order line, routes items to inventory or a destination, and produces the receipt the 3-way match (PO ↔ receipt ↔ invoice) depends on. It is the last Procurement step before Payables takes over.
headings: Working example — create a receipt via REST
pages.content: Functional view Technical view Data flow — step by step Retrieve the data — SQL Worked example — receiving 10 chairs Integration notes Next steps REST resources FBDI / interface tables Working example — create a receipt via REST Read Purchase Orders first — receipts are always recorded against an open, approved PO line. Functional view When goods arrive, the warehouse records a receipt : which PO line, how many, and where they go. Receiving can route items to inventory stocked items , to a destination expense/asset , or to inspection . A receipt can be created directly, via the receiving mobile/UI, or through the receiving interface tables that bulk loads use. Interface-driven for bulk: stage into RCV_HEADERS_INTERFACE / RCV_TRANSACTIONS_INTERFACE , then run the import. Over-receipt tolerance: configure receiving options so small variances don't fail the transaction. Returns & corrections: receiving also handles returns by creating negative transactions. Accrual: at period-end, un-invoiced receipts can accrue to the GL — expect accrual entries in period close. Receipts feed the Procure-to-Pay cycle's invoice step. Back to the Procurement hub . Read Purchase Orders first — receipts are always recorded against an open, approved PO line. Column names follow the Fusion data dictionary naming. Confirm against your instance before relying on them. A partial or over-receipt tolerance permitting records a different quantity than the PO line — which is exactly what makes 3-way match fail and the invoice get held. Having trouble?
