pages.title: Reporting & Analytics
pages.description: Fusion has four reporting engines and knowing when to use each is a core skill: OTBI for ad-hoc, BI Publisher for pixel-perfect delivered reports, Financial Reporting for GL statements, and Smart View for Excel. Plus how every scheduled report actually runs as a job.
headings: How a scheduled report actually runs
pages.content: Which tool do I use? OTBI — Oracle Transactional Business Intelligence BI Publisher BIP Financial Reporting & Smart View How a scheduled report actually runs Security model Next steps Running a report job REST-style Which tool do I use? Pick the engine by the question you're answering, not by habit. OTBI answers questions against the transactional data invoices, POs, expenses . You build analyses on subject areas logical models like "Payables Invoices Real Time" and lay them out in dashboards . BIP is the formatting engine behind all delivered Fusion reports invoice, statement, check, PO prints . You supply a data model SQL or a Fusion data source and a layout RTF, eText, XSL-FO, PDF, Excel , then schedule or run it as a report job. Financial Reporting Center is the GL reporting home: financial statements built with Financial Reporting Studio row/column layouts over ledger balances , opened in the web or Excel. Smart View is the Excel bridge for live ad-hoc against those structures. All of this rides on the same job engine: Subject areas define what you can query — one per area AP, AR, GL, Procurement, Expenses… . Drill-to-detail jumps from a metric to the underlying transaction page in the application. Security is via duties — a duty grants the subject areas and rows a user can see. Delivered analytics ship with dashboards; you clone, edit, and save to a catalog folder. OTBI results can feed BIP reports and be delivered on a schedule. Layout templates are built in Word RTF with fields and loops; eText for bank/regulatory files. Bursting splits one run into many outputs per BU, per manager, per email . Delivery to printer, email, FTP, WebDAV, UCM, or the report history. Invoked via ESS — every scheduled report is really a scheduled process job. BIP also exposes REST endpoints to submit/check report jobs from an integration. Financial statements are built from account structures and reporting trees , not SQL. Smart View connects Excel to the reporting structure for "what-if" and period-over-period analysis. Go deep on the engines behind OTBI in OTBI — Transactional BI , Oracle Analytics Cloud , and OBIEE . Reports are jobs — see how jobs work in FBDI & ADFdi . Data comes from the ledgers and tables covered in Enterprise Structures . Delivering report output is a classic OIC use case — see Oracle Integration Cloud . OTBI is not for pixel-perfect or multi-company statutory outputs — that is BIP's job. And OTBI reads a data warehouse subject areas , not the live transactional tables directly. The catalog path matters more than the report name — BIP addresses everything by its catalog path, e.g. /Custom/Financials/AP/Invoices . Question Tool Why Who's overdue? How many invoices this week? — ad-hoc a1 Interactive answers with filters, prompts, drill-to-detail Print invoice PDF with my logo / regulatory format a2 Pixel-perfect layouts RTF/PDF , bursting, delivery Send the same report to 100 managers automatically a3 Scheduled + bursted by BU/manager email Trial balance, income statement, balance sheet a4 GL account-based statements over ledgers Poke GL balances in Excel a5 Excel integration with live query Government-standard file e.g. tax file a6 XML/CSV templates + ESS delivery Layer Controls Example Duties/roles Which report tools and catalog folders a user can open Payables Manager duty Catalog Folder-level access to reports and analyses Only /Custom/Finance/AP Subject areas Which OTBI data a role can query AP Invoices Real Time vs full Financials Data security Which BUs/ledgers the data rows are filtered to Only DE business unit neutral Schedule Reports & Analytics → schedule fusion ESS Scheduled Process run BIP data model + layout Delivery PDF to printer / email / FTP / history Report history download from Reports & Analytics ESS job view curl -u "report.user:password" \\ "https:// .oraclecloud.com/xmlpserver/report/ " \\ -H "Content-Type: application/json" \\ -X POST \\ -d ' "parameterNameValues": , "outputFormat": "PDF", "reportRequestedBy": "integration.user" '

pages.title: REST API Fundamentals
pages.description: Every Fusion module exposes a consistent REST API built on the Oracle Application Development Framework (ADF). Learn the resource model, the mandatory REST-Framework-Version header, CRUD semantics, pagination, and the response envelope — and you can talk to any module.
pages.content: Resource model Reading data Writing data REST-Framework-Version Pagination Authentication & authorization Response envelope Metadata explorer tip Next steps Fusion REST is the first pillar of integration: synchronous, request-response calls for reading and writing individual records or small sets. Unlike the database which is forbidden or FBDI which is batch , REST is where you do the day-to-day work: look up a supplier, create a customer, update a PO line, read an invoice. Each module exposes a named set of REST resources , each with child resources for related records. A resource is addressable as a collection many records or an item one record . The URL shape is consistent everywhere: The most common operation is a GET on a collection with query parameters to filter, shape, and paginate the payload: To read one record you address the item directly and pass the primary key in the URL path. Finders are the alternative to ad-hoc q filters: Fusion ships dozens of named queries e.g. NameFinder that are faster and match what the UI uses. Fusion REST follows standard HTTP verbs, with one nuance on PATCH vs PUT: Writes use optimistic locking to avoid lost updates: read the ETag / If-Match-Token from a GET, then send it back in the If-Match header on PATCH/DELETE. If the record changed since you read it, Fusion rejects the write so you can decide what to do — rather than silently overwriting a colleague's edit. This custom header is Fusion's backward-compatibility contract. It tells the service which release behavior you expect: field sets, validation rules, and payload shapes for that version. Because the header and the URL version must agree, Oracle recommends you treat the version as a per-integration constant you configure once environment variable / connection property rather than hard-coding it per request. Collections never return "everything." A GET returns one page and a metadata envelope describing where you are. The two fields that matter for looping are totalResults only present if you ask with totalResults=true and hasMore / the links next page block. The canonical bulk-read pattern in OIC and VBCS looks like this: For very large extracts tens of thousands of records also set onlyData=true to strip the envelope from every item, and consider whether the job is better done as an FBDI pull or a BIP report streamed to file. Fusion REST accepts several authentication styles depending on where the caller lives: Authorization is not just "is the user real." The caller must hold the right job roles AND the data must pass the relevant data security policies . In other words: a valid login alone is not enough to read every record — the policies that govern rows for example "only own team records" still apply through the API. A collection GET returns a JSON envelope that wraps the actual payload. A sample for suppliers : Point a browser at the base URL — https://yourinstance.oraclecloud.com/fscmRestApi/resources/11.13.18.05/ — while logged in. Fusion serves an interactive explorer that lists every resource, its fields, valid query attributes, sample bodies, and even a live "try it" panel. It is faster and more accurate than hunting through PDFs, and it reveals added fields like custom flexfields that generic documentation never shows. base — your service instance, e.g. https://yourinstance.oraclecloud.com . moduleApi — fscmRestApi ERP/SCM , hcmRestApi HCM , crmRestApi CX . version — a release, e.g. 11.13.18.05 . You must match it with the REST-Framework-Version header. resource — the business object, e.g. suppliers , invoices , persons , opportunities . Basic auth — username and password over HTTPS. Simple; used by many integrations, but exposes a long-lived credential on every call. OAuth 2.0 client credentials — an access token minted from IDCS / OCI IAM. Tokens expire; recommended for OIC and VBCS service connections. Message protection — WS-Security-style signing used mostly with SOAP or with systems that can maintain certificate-based identity. See how these mechanics handle bulk data in FBDI & ADFdi . Ground the resource names in the application modules . Make sure the right roles back your API user in security & roles . Look up which REST resource to use for a task in the Tool Matrix . The REST-Framework-Version header is mandatory on every request . Omit it and you get an error; mismatch it with the URL version and the API may behave differently than you expect. When you upgrade the PPM patch-period maintenance that changes the available version, you update the header in one place and re-test — the API surface for the old version keeps working in the meantime. Never hard-code credentials in source code, connection strings, or browser-side code. Put them in OIC connections, OCI Vault/Secrets, or environment settings — and treat any leaked credential as compromised. Service accounts whose passwords expire are a top cause of "integrations broke at 3am" incidents. When a payload looks wrong, look at what you didn't ask for: with onlyData=false the envelope is what surprises people. Set onlyData=true on reads where you need the bare array. Parameter What it does Example limit Max records in this page limit=50 offset Skip N records paging offset=50 page 2 expand Include child collections expand=lines onlyData Return bare data, no metadata envelope onlyData=true totalResults Include the total record count totalResults=true q Query string filter operator-based q=Status='OPEN' orderBy Sort the results orderBy=LastUpdateDate finders Named, pre-built queries by key name limit=2&finder=NameFinder;SupplierName=\ OPEN Verb Semantics Body type Typical use POST Create a record in a collection singular resource JSON Create a supplier, invoice, or person PATCH Partial update of an item singular JSON with only changed fields Update one attribute without clobbering others PUT Full replace of an item complete resource JSON Rarely used; PATCH is preferred DELETE Remove an item may be disabled per object none Cleanup in test environments Field Meaning items The array of records in this page itemsCount Number of records in this page hasMore true if another page exists Overall count only when totalResults=true is passed links Navigation links self, canonical, next page, child resources / /resources/ / / ?. https:// .oraclecloud.com/fscmRestApi/resources/11.13.18.05/suppliers ^collection https:// .oraclecloud.com/fscmRestApi/resources/11.13.18.05/suppliers/300100220012345 ^item SupplierId .../suppliers/ /child/sites ^child collection curl -u "username:password" \\ "https://yourinstance.oraclecloud.com/fscmRestApi/resources/11.13.18.05/suppliers?q=SupplierName='ACME%'&limit=20&offset=0&totalResults=true" \\ -H "REST-Framework-Version: 11.13.18.05" curl -u "username:password" \\ "https://yourinstance.oraclecloud.com/fscmRestApi/resources/11.13.18.05/suppliers/300100220012345?onlyData=true" \\ -H "REST-Framework-Version: 11.13.18.05" curl -u "username:password" \\ -X POST \\ "https://yourinstance.oraclecloud.com/fscmRestApi/resources/11.13.18.05/suppliers" \\ -H "Content-Type: application/vnd.oracle.resource+json; type=singular" \\ -H "REST-Framework-Version: 11.13.18.05" \\ -d ' "SupplierName": "Acme GmbH", "SupplierNumber": "SUP-10023", "Addresses": ' offset = 0; pageSize = 100 loop: GET /resources/ / ?limit=pageSize&offset=offset&totalResults=true process page.items if page.hasMore == false → stop offset += pageSize "items": , "itemsCount": 1, "hasMore": false, "links": ,

pages.title: Scheduled Processes (ESS)
pages.description: Enterprise Scheduler Service (ESS) runs every background job in Fusion — FBDI imports, reports, depreciation, period close, and interface processes. If it isn't real-time, it's an ESS job. Learn the lifecycle, statuses, and how to drive it from code.
headings: What runs as an ESS job
pages.content: What runs as an ESS job The job lifecycle Core concepts Driving jobs from code Troubleshooting a failed job Integration notes Next steps What runs as an ESS job The job lifecycle Every job moves through the same states: ESS exposes REST so an integration can submit a job and poll its status. The supported resource is erpProcesses POST to submit a job by name, then poll its job status . Full walkthrough on Driving ESS via REST erpProcesses . Read the output first — it lists business errors rejected rows, invalid accounts . The log holds the technical trace; enable more logging to diagnose stack issues. Compare the parameter values from the failed run against the expected setup. Check dependencies: the supplier/period/account must exist before the job runs. Resubmit only the failed batch, not the whole load your loader should be resumable . ESS is asynchronous — never assume a submitted job has finished. Poll status, read output, then proceed. Idempotent loads matter: a retried import must not duplicate documents. Job sets encode your process order import → validate → post — reuse them instead of chaining individual jobs ad hoc. FBDI imports are the most common ESS jobs — see FBDI & ADFdi . Reports also run as jobs — see Reporting & Analytics . The close sequence is a job set — see Financial Close . Poll the returned job via the erpintegrationservice/scheduling/jobsStatus/ ' processId ' resource — and for FBDI imports, use the import's jobStatus field from the upload response see the FBDI page . Job Example Why it's a job FBDI import AP Invoices load File-based, asynchronous, big volume Reports Scheduled invoice report BIP engine runs as an ESS job Interface/PLSQL GL interface transfer Calls application APIs in a batch Period close Run depreciation, close periods Heavy, sequential, must be scheduled Web service job Publish-to-interface jobs Orchestrated by ESS Concept What it is Job definition The process itself a job type + job parameters , e.g. 'AP Invoice Import' Job type How the job executes: FBDI, Report, PL/SQL, SOA/BPM, Web service Job set Several jobs run in order with dependencies e.g. Import → Validate → Post Parameters Values the job needs: file name, period, BU, book type code Schedule Frequency: now, once, daily, on a calendar e.g. every night at 2am Output & log output.txt the result and the log file technical trace for every run Job status Succeeded / Warning / Error — plus detailed run status while running Retry & reschedule Re-run failed jobs without resubmitting data idempotent imports AP Invoice Import neutral Submit UI, ESS REST, or FBDI warning Scheduled waiting for its slot fusion Running In Progress success Succeeded / Warning / Error check output + log finish curl -u "integration.user:password" \\ "https:// .oraclecloud.com/fscmRestApi/resources/11.13.18.05/erpProcesses" \\ -H "Content-Type: application/json" \\ -H "REST-Framework-Version: 11.13.18.05" \\ -X POST \\ -d ' "processName": "Import Payables Invoices", "processType": "ESS", "parameters": , '

pages.title: Security & Roles
pages.description: Fusion is fully role-based: users and service accounts are granted job roles, duty roles, and privileges, and data security policies decide which rows they may actually see and change. This page explains the role hierarchy and how to configure an integration user that can do its job — and nothing more.
headings: Job roles vs data roles vs abstract roles
pages.content: How security is structured Job roles vs data roles vs abstract roles Data security REST service security Passwords & credentials vault Sign-on & federation Next steps Fusion's security model is the reason an integration "that works in the UI" often fails over REST, and vice versa. The API honors exactly the same roles and data policies as the web UI, so a service account is just a user whose roles happen to be tuned for machine access. Know the three layers below and you can predict most 403s before they happen. Fusion implements Role-Based Access Control RBAC as a strict hierarchy of role types. Nothing is granted at "user" level beyond the roles themselves: In practice your grant matrix is: assign a job role to a user , the job role "contains" the duty roles, and the duty roles carry the privileges. That is why a single line in user management can open dozens of functional doors. Fusion distinguishes three kinds of role that you will see in Setup & Maintenance and in the REST federation feeds: For service accounts you usually care about the job role functional capability and the data role scope . A user whose job role grants "Manage Suppliers" but whose data role scopes to only one business unit will see only that unit's suppliers over REST too. Job/duty/privilege decide what functions you may invoke. Data security policies decide which rows those functions may see. A policy is a condition evaluated against each record: for example Supplier is in 'Supplier BU' = Vision Ops or Role = 'ACCOUNTING_MANAGER' . The practical consequence for integration developers: Calling a REST resource requires more than API credentials: the acting user must hold the IT Security user profile and the relevant REST Service access — Oracle grants REST invocation through a duty called REST Service Invoke on the service account. In OIC the Fusion adapter stores these credentials in the connection and reuses them per call. FBDI submissions use the same identity model plus a UCM upload permission for the dataloader folder, so the job-role checklist applies there too. Fusion password policies force periodic expiry and often enforce complexity. An integration that hard-codes a Fusion password will silently break on rotation day — the most common cause of "the sync failed overnight" incidents. Fusion identity really lives in IDCS Identity Cloud Service / OCI IAM. Fusion users authenticate via SSO , and for organizational single sign-on Fusion acts as a SAML service provider : your IdP Azure AD, Okta, AD FS… issues assertions, IDCS maps them to Fusion users, and the session flows into both the UI and the REST/SOAP calls the browser makes. For automated process-to-process calls you usually skip SAML entirely and use OAuth client credentials directly from IDCS/OCI IAM — the token is your identity and scope is controlled there. Federation only matters when a human's session must map to a Fusion job role the "SSO user clicks and the API uses their identity" pattern . A service account needs a custom job role assembled from the exact duty roles and privileges the API calls demand — not a broad "all data" admin role. You must also ensure the account's data security contexts cover every org it touches. If Fusion applies a policy the account fails, you get a 403 even though the endpoint and credentials are correct. Test in a stage environment where you can inspect and adjust policies; a "works in dev, 403 in prod" difference is almost always a data policy difference between environments. Prefer OAuth 2.0 client credentials with tokens minted from IDCS / OCI IAM instead of basic passwords; tokens are short-lived and never sit in config. For the Fusion adapter in OIC, store credentials in the connection and rotate them in one place, not in every integration. If you must keep a password-based service user, use long expiry, rotate on a calendar reminder, and monitor for failed logins after every maintenance window. See the identity flows wired across the whole stack in end-to-end architecture . Protect the same boundary when calling REST in REST API fundamentals . Understand how OIC connections hold these credentials safely in OIC overview . A custom job role like zz_zhr_SR_PRIV is the community-standard naming for a "self-service" integration role: a narrowly scoped set of duties that gives an external system exactly the HR reads/writes it needs — nothing else. When in doubt, reproduce the failing call in the fscmRestApi metadata explorer in a browser where you are logged in as the same user. If the explorer succeeds and your OIC invocation fails, the gap is usually the connection's credentials — not the role setup. A service account whose password expires breaks every integration that uses it at once. Put expiry checks and a shared rotation step catalog or OIC connection, not the codebase into your runbook — and treat any credential that reaches source control as fully compromised. Level What it is Example Role A named set of duties/privileges assigned to a user Accounts Payable Manager, zz_zhr_SR_PRIV Duty role A functional grouping of one or more privileges Manage Supplier Invoices duty, Manage Workers duty Privilege The smallest unit of access to a function/data/entity Edit Supplier Invoice, View Person Role kind Purpose Job role The user's function; aggregates duties and privileges into one grant Payables Manager, zz_zhr_SR_PRIV Data role Couples a role with a data security context for example a business unit so the same job role can mean different access in different orgs Accounts Payable Manager — Vision Operations Abstract role A generic capability independent of function, e.g. 'Employee' or 'Partner' ESS employee self service , Mobile Sales Rep s function; aggregates duties and privileges into one grant", "Payables Manager, zz_zhr_SR_PRIV" , "Data role", "Couples a role with a data security context for example a business unit so the same job role can mean different access in different orgs", "Accounts Payable Manager — Vision Operations" , "Abstract role", "A generic capability independent of function, e.g. or neutral User / Service account job roles + data roles + abstract roles fusion aggregates duty roles groups privileges Privileges smallest unit of function access 1. User added to a job role with 'REST Service Invoke' duty 2. User assigned the specific REST resource duties it calls e.g. 'Manage Suppliers REST Service', 'Import Payables Invoices REST Service' 3. User's data roles scope to the business units it accesses 4. For SOAP: user has the corresponding SOA web-services permission

pages.title: Subledger Accounting (SLA)
pages.description: The engine that turns every transaction — an AP invoice, an AR receipt, a depreciation run — into GL journal entries. If you want to know why a number landed in a particular account, you read SLA.
headings: How a module flows through SLA
pages.content: What SLA is Core concepts How a module flows through SLA Where the entries live — SQL Configuration overview Integration notes Next steps What SLA is Fusion doesn't hardcode accounting. Each sub-ledger fires an event invoice created, invoice paid, receipt applied and SLA decides the entries using a configurable accounting method . That's why the same invoice can post differently across ledgers or legal entities — the method differs, not the event. Every accounting entry is an XLA record. To trace a transaction to its GL impact: Define the accounting method and its journal entry rule sets per event class. Assign the method to a ledger or legal entity per ledger in most implementations . Set account sources : natural accounts from distributions, constants, or derivation rules. Run Create Accounting an ESS job to generate AEs, then post. To "drill to detail" from a GL balance, trace: GL_JE_HEADERS → XLA_AE_HEADERS → source document. Accounting differences between ledgers are almost always the accounting method — compare methods first. AE status matters: incomplete entries explain missing balances before you suspect posting. See it in action per module: Payables and GL . The entries land in journals — General Ledger . If an entry is missing or wrong, start with the troubleshooting causes. The source document is linked to its AE via source_id_int_1 document id and the event_class_code . Exact column names follow the data dictionary — confirm per release. pages.title: Tax
pages.description: Fusion Tax (built on the Oracle E-Business Tax engine) manages indirect tax — VAT, GST, sales/use tax — on every transaction. Tax is configured as a regime hierarchy, determined by rules, and calculated by the tax engine at invoice time.
headings: Where tax attaches in a transaction
pages.content: How tax gets calculated The configuration hierarchy Where tax attaches in a transaction Underlying tables & SQL Integration notes Next steps How tax gets calculated Tax doesn't just sit on the invoice — it is determined by rules. The engine takes the transaction party, product, territory, dates and classifies it to find the right tax, status, rate, and accounts. Tax configuration lives in the ZX_* tables. Query them to trace what tax a transaction should carry: AP invoices: supplier + invoice tax code → tax engine calculates input VAT on each line/distribution. AR invoices: customer + item/product → output VAT / GST determined and calculated. POs & expenses: purchases carry tax too; expense lines may require a tax code. Tax lines flow to the GL through the same posting process XLA as the rest of the document. Invoice lines with a missing or invalid tax code fail validation — send the correct tax code per territory/entity. Rate selection is rule-driven, not hardcoded — two invoices can get different rates based on product/territory classification. Exempt/recoverable amounts depend on tax statuses and party fiscal classifications. Tax setups are per legal entity/BU — the same product can be taxed differently across your enterprise structure. Tax sits on the invoices covered in Payables and Receivables . Tax configuration is owned per legal entity — see Enterprise Structures . ZX_* is the EBS-era tax schema Fusion inherited. Column names follow the data dictionary naming — confirm against your release. Level What it is Example Tax regime The top level, usually one per country/tax area VAT, GST, Sales Tax Germany VAT Tax A type of tax within the regime output / input Output VAT sales , Input VAT purchases Tax status A legal category taxable, zero-rated, exempt Exempt supplies Tax rate The percentage, with effective dates 19% standard VAT, 7% reduced Tax rules Conditions that pick the tax/status/rate for a transaction If product = books then reduced rate Tax configuration owner The BU/legal entity profile that chooses which tax codes to use Acme DE BU uses Germany VAT Tax code configuration The visible code a user sees on the transaction VAT_DE_19_OUT Tax profile Per legal entity: default tax codes, calculation options, tax accounting Acme GmbH tax profile Table Holds Key columns t1 Tax regimes REGIME_CODE, REGIME_NAME, COUNTRY_CODE t2 Taxes within a regime TAX, TAX_NAME, REGIME_CODE, TAX_TYPE_CODE t3 Tax statuses TAX_STATUS_CODE, TAX_STATUS_NAME, TAX t4 Tax rates with effective dates TAX_RATE_CODE, TAX_RATE, EFFECTIVE_FROM, EFFECTIVE_TO t5 Determination rules RULE_NAME, TRX_CLASS, CONDITION..., RESULT_TAX, RESULT_RATE t6 Calculated tax lines on transactions ZX_LINE_ID, DOCUMENT_ID, TAX_LINE_AMOUNT, TAX_RATE, TAX_CODE neutral Classify party + product + territory + dates fusion Tax determination tax + status + rate matched Calculate tax lines, rates, exempt/recoverable amounts Accounts tax distributions post to the GL rule -- Rates for a tax, ordered by effective date SELECT r.tax_rate_code, r.tax_rate, r.effective_from, r.effective_to FROM zx_rates_b r WHERE r.tax = :tax_code ORDER BY r.effective_from; -- Calculated tax lines for a document SELECT l.document_id, l.tax_code, l.tax_rate, l.tax_line_amount, l.tax_currency_code, l.status_code FROM zx_lines l WHERE l.document_id = :document_id ORDER BY l.tax_line_id;

pages.title: Adapters & connectivity
pages.description: An adapter is OIC's pre-built knowledge of one protocol or product family. Pick the adapter, configure a connection, and OIC handles the protocol details — REST, SOAP, files, databases, SaaS APIs, queues, and OCI services. This page is the map of what reaches where.
headings: SaaS adapters — why they matter for Fusion work
Working example — file in, Fusion out
pages.content: The adapter families Protocol adapters in detail SaaS adapters — why they matter for Fusion work Messaging and OCI adapters Choosing the right adapter Connections are the risk surface Working example — file in, Fusion out Next steps You rarely write protocol code in OIC. Instead you choose an adapter — the pattern for speaking to a system — and create a connection — the concrete instance with an endpoint, credentials, and options. One adapter backs many connections; one connection serves many integrations. Adapters fall into groups by what they talk to. Each family has different concerns that change how you build the integration. These five adapters cover the majority of non-SaaS connectivity. Master the decision between them and you can handle almost any file- or protocol-driven requirement. Fusion work almost always pairs with other SaaS. These adapters generate the schema of the business object, so the map in your integration is prettily typed rather than a raw free-form payload: For bulky or high-volume data, adapters exist that decouple the integration from the consumer: When you hit "which one?" in a design, run down this list: Adapters are free; connections carry the risk. A connection bundles the endpoint, the credentials, the security policy basic vs agent + message protection , and the retry behavior. Treat connections like production secrets: Is it a SaaS app with a business object? Use its SaaS adapter. Is it a plain HTTP API? REST adapter. Is it a legacy web service? SOAP adapter. Is it a file exchange? FTP/SFTP or File, depending on where the file lives. Is it a database we query? Database adapter invoke only . Is it decoupled delivery? A messaging adapter: Streaming, MQ, or JMS. Is it an on-premises system? Add the connectivity agent and make the connection agent-based. Build a real flow with these adapters in orchestration . Secure every connection properly in security & auth . See the file-to-Fusion pattern end to end in FBDI integration . A Database adapter has no trigger — you cannot subscribe to a change in a table. If you need "when the DB changes", poll with a scheduled integration or use a change-data capture feed instead. Keep credentials out of the integration body — store them in the connection or an OCI secret and reference the connection, not the password, in the flow. Promote a connection as part of the package so new environments inherit the same configuration. Trigger: FTP/SFTP adapter polls /inbound/invoices/ for new CSV files. Logic: OIC reads the CSV, maps each row see mapping , and stages it for FBDI. Invoke: Fusion Applications adapter loads the staged rows, or the File adapter hands the ZIP to the FBDI pattern. Result: the supplier never touches OIC or Fusion; the file adapter is the whole front door. Family Adapters What changes in your integration SaaS Fusion HCM/ERP, Sales Cloud, Service Cloud, NetSuite, Salesforce, Workday, ServiceNow, Slack, Gmail, Oracle HCM Business objects and their fields; the adapter generates the schema Protocol REST, SOAP, FTP/SFTP, File, Database Oracle/third-party JDBC , JMS Endpoint style, authentication, and payload format OCI Object Storage, Functions, Streaming, Autonomous Database, OCI API Gateway OCI IAM, region and compartment, resource-type semantics Messaging OCI Streaming, Oracle MQ, Kafka, JMS queues Publish/consume semantics; batching and acknowledgement Partner / niche SAP, MFT, HL7, Oracle E-Business Suite Domain-specific formats and behaviors from SAP IDocs to health messages Adapter Speaks to Trigger or invoke Watch out for REST Any HTTP/JSON or XML API; OpenAPI import Trigger expose and invoke call Auth type, rate limits, large responses SOAP Any WSDL-based web service Invoke mostly; sometimes trigger WSDL 1.1/2.0 differences, namespaces, WS-Security headers FTP / SFTP File servers over FTPS/SFTP Trigger poll a folder and invoke put/get File presence, naming, and cleanup; key-based vs password auth File OCI Object Storage and file servers Trigger and invoke with file lifecycle Inbound/outbound directories, file naming conventions Database Oracle and third-party DBs over JDBC Invoke SQL — no trigger SQL injection surface, connection pools, elapsed-time limits Typical Fusion-neighbor use Fusion Applications The star: POs, invoices, payments, workers, journals through Fusion REST/SOAP Salesforce Opportunities and accounts that feed a sales-to-order cycle NetSuite Journal entries, transactions, or customer records syncing with Fusion Workday Worker/HR data feeding Fusion Finance or project setups ServiceNow Tickets that trigger procure-to-pay or fulfillment flows Pattern When to reach for it OCI Streaming Publish/consume an ordered stream of messages Telemetry-ish flows, event fan-out, decoupled microservices Oracle MQ / JMS Queue and topic semantics with acknowledges Reliable hand-off where a consumer must confirm processing OCI Object Storage Store and fetch files in buckets Staging bulk files for FBDI, archiving payloads, media interchange OCI Functions Trigger a serverless function as part of a flow Custom logic you do not want inside the integration

pages.title: Key concepts in Oracle Integration Cloud
pages.description: The vocabulary you need to work in OIC: connections and adapters, activation and runtime endpoints, lookups, on-premises agents, reusable libraries, and how integrations are organized.
pages.content: Connections and adapters The runtime & active endpoints Lookups Agents Libraries, schemas, and packages Projects and workspaces Next steps OIC leans heavily on a few recurring ideas. Once you understand that a connection is an adapter instance, that activation turns a design into a live endpoint, and that lookups keep translations out of your mappings, most of the console becomes instantly readable. An adapter is a pre-built connector that knows how to speak one protocol or to one product family. A connection is an instance of that adapter: you pick the adapter, then fill in the endpoint URL, credentials, and options. One adapter can back many connections, and a connection can be shared by many integrations. An integration in the designer is only a definition. Activating it publishes the design to the OIC runtime engine and creates a real, callable endpoint. An app-driven integration gets a REST URL under /ic/api/integration/v1/integrations/ ; a scheduled integration instead registers a job with OIC's enterprise scheduler that fires on the schedule you configure. The call is wrapped in a " " envelope; OIC unwraps it, runs the flow, and returns either 200 synchronous result or 202 Accepted asynchronous processing kicked off . A lookup is a two-column or multi-column runtime translation table. You define it once in the designer, then reference it inside a map. Because the translation lives outside your mappings, it can be maintained without redeploying the integration — and the same lookup can serve many integrations. The Oracle Connectivity Agent OCA — historically called the connectivity agent or on-premises agent — is a small runtime you install inside your own data center. It opens a secure, outbound-only tunnel back to OIC, which lets the cloud reach systems that have no public address: on-prem Flexcube or SAP, a warehouse database, an internal FTP box. Large integration portfolios repeat the same transformation logic over and over. OIC gives you three reuse mechanisms, from smallest to largest: As the portfolio grows, the console fills up. Projects are a hierarchy of folders that group integrations by business process, department, or release. They give you a place to organize without changing runtime behavior: Activate a new version, and OIC switches traffic to it. Deactivate, and the endpoint returns a hard 404 so callers fail loudly instead of silently. Each activation increments a version number . Older versions can be activated later as an instant rollback. Activating a scheduled integration starts it running on its schedule — but only starts it, so you can pre-validate before production go-live. Define the codes column and the meaning column; map the source field to the codes and read the paired meaning on the destination side. Typical example: Fusion stores a payment term as "01" , "02" … and you map it to "Immediate" , "Net 30" for an external portal. Lookups can be cached at runtime, so high-volume integrations should mark rarely changing tables as cacheable. Outbound-only — the agent initiates all connections to OIC, so you never need to expose inbound firewall ports. One agent group can serve multiple hosts ; use separate groups for separate environments prod vs. non-prod . The agent is a Java process on your server — renew its certificate regularly and watch the OPC alerts in Monitoring for a disconnect. Libraries — reusable map fragments and JavaScript snippets you import into a mapping. Fix a bug once in the library and every consumer picks it up on next deployment. Common schemas XSD/WSDL definitions used across multiple integrations, so payload contracts stay in one place. Packages — downloadable, importable solution bundles produced by Oracle and partners. The Fusion Financials packages, for instance, ship pre-built integrations for supplier invoices, payments, and GL entries that you import, configure with your connections, and activate. Learn the three ways integrations get triggered in integration styles . See the classic bulk pattern in FBDI integration . Keep integrations healthy with error handling and monitoring . Connection security policies decide whether the integration runs inside OIC "basic" or requires an agent and the extra handshake of message protection. For on-premises Fusion, agent-based connections are the norm; for SaaS targets you almost always use the plain non-agent connection. Never hard-code translations inside a mapping expression. The moment a code changes, three different integrations all silently break. Route every code through a lookup so one edit fixes the whole portfolio. For any on-premises target you must do all three: define an agent group , install the agent on the target host, and create the connection as agent-based . A non-agent connection to an on-prem system simply times out. A common convention: a "platform" project holds all shared libraries and schemas, while per-domain projects only contain integrations. New team members learn the convention in minutes instead of reading every flow. pages.title: Deployment & the environment lifecycle
pages.description: The lifecycle that takes a designed integration to production safely: export a package, import into the target environment, remap its connections and config variables, activate the right version, and roll back when needed. The discipline that makes 'go live' boring.
pages.content: The promotion loop Packages: the unit of transfer Config variables & connection overrides Versions, activation, and rollback Moving to production safely Segregation of duties an aside Next steps Nothing about OIC deployment is hard; the failure mode is forgetting a remap . A package moves cleanly, but every environment has its own endpoints, credentials, and schedules. Deployment is where you pay attention to those differences deliberately. A package bundles everything an integration or a whole project needs to travel: the flow XML, its lookups, dependencies, and the references that must be re-pointed on import. OIC separates the design value from the runtime value . Anything that differs between environments should be a config variable rather than a literal in the flow: An integration can hold several versions, and each activation switches which one serves traffic: Who may touch production matters as much as what is deployed. Production OIC tend to be guarded by roles that let operations deploy and monitor, but not redesign see security & auth . If development and production share a tenant, use projects and environment filtering to keep unconsumed designs out of the production workspace. Config variables — e.g. "ftp.inbound.dir" or "fusion.base.url" — are declared in the design and set per environment. Same package, different values. Connection overrides — on import you choose the version of each reference and the connections it should bind to. Editing a live integration creates a new draft version ; the draft does not affect runtime until you activate it. Activate publishes the chosen version. Deactivate makes the endpoint return a hard 404 — callers fail loudly instead of silently. On a bad release, reactivate the previous version — an instant rollback without a redeploy. Protect what you promote in security . Confirm what landed in monitoring . For the file-centric promotion story, see MFT . The integration artifact is identical in every environment. The connections and config values behind it are what differ — and what you must remap on import. A literal URL or credential left inside a map is a landmine: the package imports in production, works in dev, and fails only at the first real call. If a value varies by environment, make it a config variable at design time . Keep a printed checklist of the remap step. In a retrospective, most production incidents trace back to a skipped remap — connection, config variable, or schedule. See monitoring to watch it land. What's in a package What's not fix on import Integration definitions & versions Environment-specific connection details Lookup data Endpoint URLs and host names Map libraries and common schemas Usernames, passwords, OAuth secrets Tracking field definitions Schedules you re-assert per environment s in a package", "What Step What you verify Pitfall to avoid Import the package Structure and dependencies arrive intact Importing into the wrong environment Remap connections Every adapter points to the production target Leaving dev credentials live Set config variables URLs, directories, schedules match prod Default values from the package Validate with a test payload One real call succeeds end to end Skipping validation 'to save time' Activate Traffic switches to the new version Activating before validation Verify in Monitoring Instances appear with the expected tracking keys No tracking configured → invisible to save time neutral Dev design, map, test oic Test / UAT import + remap + validate success Production import + remap + activate export package promote

pages.title: Error handling and monitoring in OIC
pages.description: Why integrations fail, how to build fault handling into a flow, how to surface Fusion business errors cleanly, and how to use OIC Monitoring, resubmission, alerting, and retries.
pages.content: Why errors happen in integrations Fault handling in the integration Business errors from Fusion Monitoring & dashboards Alerting & audit Retry strategy best practices Next steps A healthy integration portfolio is not one where nothing ever fails — it is one where failures are visible, isolated, and recoverable . OIC gives you both the designer-side controls fault handlers, retries, routing and the runtime visibility Monitoring, alerts, resubmission . Integrations fail for a handful of recurring reasons. Knowing the category determines the remedy: Every invoke in the designer can get a fault handler : a branch that runs when the call fails, instead of the whole integration dying. Use it to diagnose, retry, and return a clean answer: The caller logs instanceId and errorCode and can look the instance up in Monitoring without reading logs. The trickiest failures are the ones where everything worked and Fusion still said no . When a REST create or an FBDI load rejects data — invoice total mismatch, missing reference, invalid combination — Fusion returns a business error , often as an attachment or a row in the import businessErrors file. OIC Monitoring is the operations console for everything you've deployed: Monitoring is reactive — alerts make it proactive. OIC can raise an integration error event on failure, and OIC lets you subscribe event subscribers email, custom REST, Slack-style webhooks to it: Retries are a safety net, and the net must be designed so it doesn't double your writes: Retry for transient errors: add a bounded retry with backoff on the invoke when the error is connectivity/timeout-class. Switch for error routing: inside the fault handler, branch on the fault code to decide whether to retry, resubmit, or escalate. Map the error to a response: translate the internal fault into a structured JSON the caller can parse — not a raw stack trace. Poison-message handling: when a payload keeps failing, park it log, quarantine file, or a correction process rather than retrying forever. Distinguish technical from business: a business error is a completed handshake with a data problem; it must be reported cleanly, not blindly retried. Capture the error text from the response and record it on the instance so Monitoring shows the reason at a glance. For FBDI, download and preserve the businessErrors file ; fix the affected rows and re-import only them. Resubmission is the killer feature: pick a failed instance, edit the request payload, and rerun it without rebuilding the integration. Set tracking fields e.g., invoice number on your integration so you can search by business key. Dashboard trends help capacity planning: growing durations mean a target is slowing down before it starts failing. Integration errors → event: a failed instance emits an event with integration code, instance ID, and error text. Audit logs capture activation, deactivation, and payload changes — keep them for compliance and post-mortems. Agent down alerts: watch OPC connectivity alerts; an offline agent fails every agent-based integration silently. Correlate: your alert should carry instanceId so support can jump straight into Monitoring. Idempotency for Fusion: where possible key the write on a business reference e.g., InvoiceNumber or check-before-create so a retry updates rather than duplicates. Exponential backoff: on transient errors, back off 5s → 25s → 125s instead of hammering at fixed intervals. Bounded retries: cap the attempt count; after the cap, surface the error through the fault path, not more retries. Retry the right thing: re-request the token if the fault is 401, retry the call if it is 503, and never retry a 4xx business validation. Refresh the building blocks that fail and recover: key concepts . Design faults into the flow shape with integration styles . Handle Fusion's own rejections in FBDI integration . Classify before you code. Transient failures network blips, timeouts deserve retries; permanent ones schema drift, bad data deserve alerts and a human — retrying those only creates duplicate mail. Treat business errors as data incidents , not code bugs. An automatic retry will reproduce them forever. Route them to a correction path a process task or a quarantine bucket where a human fixes the root data and re-submits once. Build a small reusable "retry invoke" pattern fault handler + backoff + cap and reuse it across integrations. Consistent retry behavior makes the whole portfolio predictable — and much easier to tune when one endpoint turns flaky. pages.title: FBDI integration with Fusion
pages.description: The File-Based Data Import (FBDI) pattern from OIC: stage data, build a CSV and control XML, upload to Fusion UCM, poll the ESS job, and surface the result — best for bulk, asynchronous loads.
pages.content: Why FBDI from OIC Approach overview Step-by-step flow in OIC The ZIP & control file Error handling in this pattern Performance & best practices Next steps FBDI File-Based Data Import is how Fusion ingests big, batch, async loads. From OIC the pattern is the same as from anywhere else — CSV + control XML in a ZIP, uploaded to UCM, processed by an ESS job — except OIC also orchestrates the whole journey and reports the outcome. Every REST create of an invoice or a worker is a round trip with overhead : connect, authenticate, validate one record, commit, respond. Past a few dozen rows, that is wasteful and slow. FBDI imports thousands of rows in a single file load , processed by Fusion's scheduler in one pass. The pattern is a loop: OIC collects data, packages it for Fusion, submits, and then waits for the scheduler to report back: Broken down into concrete designer steps, a typical FBDI integration looks like this: The ZIP must contain the data CSV and a small XML control file declaring the operation. The control file tells Fusion which action to take and which key identifies a row — critical for update vs insert semantics: FBDI rarely fails the whole load; it fails rows . Your integration must handle both levels: FBDI favors fewer, larger files . A late-afternoon window that collects everything and loads it once will beat ten small uploads: Throughput: one upload moves 10,000 supplier invoices where 10,000 REST calls would take hours and hammer rate limits. Fidelity to Fusion templates: every load maps onto a published Fusion template e.g., invoicesImport.zip , so validation is Fusion's own. Async by design: nothing blocks; you submit, poll, and report. Staging: the source data from a portal, SFTP, a query is normalized into the columns Fusion's template expects. Packaging: OIC writes the CSV and the control XML, zips them into something.zip , and uploads via the Fusion "load file" REST service. Polling: the response carries the ESS process ID; OIC polls jobsStatus until it reaches SUCCEEDED or FAILED . 1 · Create the integration with a Fusion Applications file adapter connection so OIC can talk to Fusion's UCM and ESS services. 2 · Stage the source: pull rows from your portal/DB/SFTP. If it is app-driven, the request payload is the staging area; if scheduled, run a query to gather changed rows. 3 · Build the payload: map your staged rows into a Fusion path that emits the CSV plus the control XML , then ZIP both. 4 · Upload: invoke Fusion's file load endpoint erpintegrations/upload with the ZIP and the record count. 5 · Parse the response: the upload returns an ESS process ID ; store it in a variable, instance tracking, or a log. 6 · Poll: loop on jobsStatus/ ` ` with a delay until the status is terminal, then branch on the outcome. action can be INSERT , UPDATE , MERGE , or DELETE . MERGE is the safe default when rows may exist already. The CSV must match the template columns exactly — including column order, if the template order is fixed. Download the current template rather than trusting an old copy. Date and number formats matter ; an invalid format silently becomes a row error, not a fail. Poll with delay and a max: loop on jobsStatus with, say, a 30-second delay and a sane upper bound large loads run long . Treat hitting the bound as a failure and raise an alert. FAILED status: the job object tells you the generic reason. Optionally resubmit once if the failure looks transient; then report. Business errors: Fusion records per-row rejections. Download the businessErrors file and attach it to the monitoring incident so a human can fix the offending rows and re-import just those. Alerts: raise an integration error on terminal failure so OIC Monitoring and event subscribers email, Slack see it immediately. Understand where FBDI sits among the styles in integration styles . Learn the quick-path REST alternative in REST & RESTful APIs . Report failures cleanly with error handling and monitoring . The rule of thumb: a handful of records → REST; hundreds or thousands → FBDI. Staying under the row count where REST is viable keeps your request/response integrations fast and your bulk flows efficient. Keep the same template version consistent between your staging map and Fusion. Oracle can add columns to templates over time; when they do, an older CSV can start failing validation with cryptic messages — update the formatter and re-test. Do Don't Load in large batches thousands of rows Micro-files of 5 rows each Use the current Fusion template columns Reuse last year's template blindly Poll with a backoff-aware delay Poll every second and hammer jobsStatus Also upload the control file and validate formats Ship only the CSV and hope Track the ESS process ID per instance Lose the process ID and be unable to poll t" rows= "Load in large batches thousands of rows ", "Micro-files of 5 rows each" , "Use the current Fusion template columns", "Reuse last year oic OIC Integration stage · build ZIP CSV + XML · poll fusion Fusion UCM file repository; returns process ID neutral ESS validates & imports each row Status back to OIC SUCCEEDED · FAILED · business errors upload ZIP ESS job runs jobsStatus InvoiceNumber importInvoices curl -X POST "https:// /fscmRestApi/resources/latest/erpintegrations/upload" \\ -H "REST-Framework-Version: 11.13.18.05" \\ -H "Authorization: Basic " \\ -F "processName=invoicesImport" \\ -F "fileName=invoices.zip" \\ -F "fileContent=@invoices.zip" # → 200 with

pages.title: OIC Gen 3 orientation
pages.description: Oracle Integration is now a generation-3 service: a new console, environment-based tenant, deeper OCI identity, and a different mental model from the classic gen 2 screens. This page orients you so tutorials and your own hands-on don't fight over which console is in front of you.
headings: How to tell which generation you are facing
pages.content: How to tell which generation you are facing What genuinely changed in gen 3 What pleasantly stayed the same Practical advice for learners Next steps Much of the OIC documentation and every third-party video shows the gen 2 console. If your tenant is gen 3 , the names are the same but the screens, navigation, and some provisioning steps differ. Learn to spot which generation you are on — that alone prevents hours of following the wrong tutorial. The core craft of integration work did not move: Environment-based tenancy — you run multiple OIC environments dev, test, prod under one region instead of separate instances. Your promotion story becomes "move a package between environments". OCI IAM — users, groups, and roles live in OCI IAM domains; fine-grained policies decide who can create connections, import packages, and activate integrations. OCI-wide connectivity — Object Storage, Functions, Streaming, Autonomous Database and the rest are first-class targets from the same console. Modern console — design, monitor, and insights sit in one refreshed UI. When a tutorial shows a navigation step that does not exist on your screen, check whether it is a gen 2 walk-through before concluding the tool moved. A connection in gen 3 still holds the endpoint and credentials — the concept is unchanged even though the "create connection" page looks different. Deployment moved from "spreadsheet of endpoints" to environment variables+config variables officially: see deployment . See how identity secures your console in security & auth . Keep the integration portfolio honest in deployment . Zoom out to the whole stack in architecture . The integration concepts — connections, mappings, orchestration, packages — are identical across generations. What changes is the shell : how you reach the console, manage environments, and handle identity. Everything else in this OIC section still applies. The fastest self-orientation: create a scratch Oracle Database Autonomous connection that pings /health , then a REST echo integration. If those two tasks feel comfortable in your console, gen 3's layout no longer slows you down. pages.title: Service limits & considerations
pages.description: The enforced limits Oracle Integration puts on payloads, concurrency, flow duration, and data — from the official service-limits documentation — plus the design considerations that turn those limits from footnotes into architecture decisions.
headings: Payload and file sizes — the fastest way to break a flow
Concurrency — what your message packs buy you
Connectivity that is not what it seems
When OIC is the wrong tool
pages.content: Payload and file sizes — the fastest way to break a flow Concurrency — what your message packs buy you Flow execution — durations and deadlines Loops, data, and strings Volume and scale ceilings Console and tenancy limits Retention and recovery Connectivity that is not what it seems When OIC is the wrong tool Next steps Some numbers here are hard service limits enforced by the platform — you cannot raise them. Others are design limits timeouts, loop bounds, character caps you must architect around. The official reference is Oracle's Service Limits documentation; this page distills the numbers a designer actually hits, sorted by what breaks first. Payload size is the limit people hit first, and the numbers vary a lot by adapter and by whether an endpoint is cloud-based, private, or behind the connectivity agent: Concurrent request limits come from your license type times the number of message packs . This is a business decision, not just a technical one: Beyond numbers, three adapter behaviors surprise designers: Synchronous ceiling: 2,000 concurrent requests; async ceiling: 1,000 . Async requests beyond the limit are queued , not rejected — the queue depth depends on your assigned packs. Parallel action branches count toward the sync concurrency: a parallel action with three branches needs two extra slots. Additional packs raise concurrency — the lever for high-concurrency requirements is commercial, not code. Database adapter is invoke-only — no trigger. Subscribe via polling or change-data-capture instead. No direct SQL to the Fusion database — Fusion's DB is forbidden to customers; read Fusion data through its services see Fusion overview . Agent paths are far smaller — 50 MB agent vs 100 MB cloud for the same structured payload. Know which path you are on. Revisit the strengths you are designing around in OIC overview . Confirm which edition and tenancy you are on in Gen 3 orientation . Keep the healthy patterns alive in monitoring . A rule of thumb from these tables: structured, schema-driven payloads stay under 50–100 MB; binary attachments and unparsed files can reach 1 GB; message queues top out at 10 MB. Design data movement with those three bands in mind. If a flow must run past the hour mark, a single synchronous or async integration is the wrong shape — split the work, run it on a schedule, or queue chunks. The 6-hour ceiling on async and scheduled flows is not negotiable. The decision rule stands: OIC owns orchestrated, governed flows between APIs and files. When the workload becomes bulk data engineering, streaming, or hosting, hand it to an OCI service and keep OIC on orchestration. pages.title: Mapping & data transformation
pages.description: Integrations rarely agree on shape. One side sends XML, the other wants JSON; one calls a field customerName, the other calls it name; one day it is 01, the next Net 30. Mapping is how OIC reshapes payloads — the single most common task in any integration.
headings: The map editor at a glance
Formats: XML, JSON, CSV and the envelopes
Working example — one invoice line through a map
pages.content: The map editor at a glance Map functions — the toolbox Flattening and unflattening Formats: XML, JSON, CSV and the envelopes XSLT under the hood Working example — one invoice line through a map Mapping best practices Next steps Direct assignment vs transformed A map connects a source element to a destination element. It sounds trivial; the craft is in the details: converting formats, looking up codes, splitting and joining records, and guarding against nulls. OIC's map editor generates XSLT under the hood, but you work visually — drag source to target, then use functions to transform the values. Open any map action in an integration and you see three areas: the source schema on the left, the target schema on the right, and the mapping expressions in the middle. A straight drag creates a direct assignment ; almost everything else wraps the source in a function. Functions are the real power. They fall into a few families; you will use the first three constantly. Sometimes the source nests data and the target is flat or the reverse . Two function families handle this: Every map sits between two payload shapes. Knowing which envelope you are in matters because the envelope rules change how you reach into the payload: OIC generates XSLT from your visual map. Knowing that helps you in three situations: reading the generated source when a map behaves unexpectedly, dropping in a custom XSLT map when a transform is too awkward to build visually, and understanding performance — recursive or unguarded XSLT can throttle a flow. The visual map and the generated XSLT stay in sync: change one and the other updates. Custom XSLT maps are the exception — you author the transform directly and OIC runs it as-is. Direct: source customerName → target name . Same value, same type. Transformed: source orderDate → target requiredDeliveryDate formatted as yyyy-MM-dd . Looked up: source "01" → lookup → target "Net 30" . Computed: source quantity × source unitPrice → target lineTotal . children" , "Attributes ↔ elements", "JSON attributes must become XML elements or vice versa", "REST JSON → Fusion SOAP" , /> For the classic portal → FBDI case you map the whole payload into the CSV structure that the import expects. That map usually pairs one source collection with a for-each that emits one CSV line per record — see FBDI integration for the end-to-end flow. Custom XSLT maps are the exception — you author the transform directly and OIC runs it as-is. Working example — one invoice line through a map Source: " " Target: Fusion REST expects supplierName , a numeric invoiceAmount , and a translated paymentTerms . The map: supplier → supplierName direct ; amount → invoiceAmount via a decimal function; terms → lookup → paymentTerms . Result: the integration receives a payload that Fusion will accept without rework — the classic job of an integration map. Mapping best practices Route codes through lookups — never hard-code translations in an expression. Guard nulls — a function on an empty source returns null; decide what the target should get explicitly. Use libraries for transforms reused across integrations; fix once, deploy everywhere. Keep dates typed until the last hop, then format — converting to strings early causes locale bugs. Name the map and test it — an unlabeled map in a 400-line flow is undebuggable in six months. See which adapters produce the payloads you will map. Read how maps plug into the flow toolbox in orchestration . Keep an integration healthy through a bad map with error handling . Test a function before relying on it: use the map test / preview pane with a sample payload. The most common mapping bug is a date format that looks right in preview data but differs in production. For the classic portal → FBDI case you map the whole payload into the CSV structure that the import expects. That map usually pairs one source collection with a for-each that emits one CSV line per record — see FBDI integration for the end-to-end flow. The map: supplier → supplierName direct ; amount → invoiceAmount via a decimal function; terms → lookup → paymentTerms . Result: the integration receives a payload that Fusion will accept without rework — the classic job of an integration map. pages.title: Managed File Transfer (MFT)
pages.description: A governed way to exchange files with trading partners: a host in the form of a dedicated service, scheduled delivery, encryption and signing with PGP, and end-to-end transfer status. MFT is the 'bank-quality' file channel that wholesale integrations use when a plain FTP drop is not enough.
headings: Why not just use the FTP adapter?
Working example — P2P in a banking context
pages.content: MFT at a glance Core building blocks Why not just use the FTP adapter? PGP in one paragraph Working example — P2P in a banking context Next steps Most file integrations are fine with an FTP or File adapter. Managed File Transfer adds the controls those adapters lack: a partner-facing host with a known address, who-is-allowed identities, guaranteed delivery, PGP encryption at rest and signing, and status visibility for a "did it actually arrive?" answer. Good question. The line is about who is responsible and what the partner expects : PGP Pretty Good Privacy is the encryption/signing scheme MFT uses. You generate a key pair — public and private. A partner encrypts to your public key so only your private key can open it, and signs with their private key so you can verify the file came from them. MFT manages these key pairs, so exchange definitions point at keys rather than a key-management project on your side. Connect the other file cases with adapters . Encrypt and identify correctly with security & auth . Govern the transfer lifecycle in deployment . Think of MFT as FTP with an audit trail, PGP, and an SLA . When a partner demands "tell me what happened to my file — and encrypt it", MFT is the answer. Key rotation is the silent killer of MFT setups. When an exchange "stops decrypting" overnight, it is almost always a rotated partner key that the exchange still references. Track expiry dates like a production SLA see also security . Exchange: each supplier uploads a signed, encrypted invoice file to the MFT host as a separate partner account. Verification: MFT checks the signature, decrypts with your key, and drops the plaintext into a pickup folder. Processing: a scheduled OIC integration reads the folder, maps it see mapping , and stages it for Fusion FBDI. Answerability: when a supplier asks "did you get it?", the MFT status screen answers with a timestamp instead of a shrug. Building block What it is What it buys you Host endpoint The partner-facing address where files are exchanged A stable contractual endpoint instead of chasing FTP paths Partner / user identities Who may connect, with credentials Controls which external identity can access which folder File transfer definitions The file pattern, folders, and flow per partner Packaged rules per exchange — no ad-hoc FTP politics PGP keys Encryption and signing key pairs Confidentiality and origin proof Schedule & alerts When transfers run, and notifications on failure SLAs a business can actually see Scenario FTP/SFTP adapter MFT Internal file pickup Fine — simple, fast Usually overkill Partner needs a fixed public endpoint No fixed SLA or reporting Designed for this Encryption mandated PGP You build it yourself Built-in key management 'Did the file arrive?' questions You improvise logs Native transfer status Large partner portfolios One-off scripts per partner One governed service Did the file arrive? neutral Trading partner submits through a public endpoint oic MFT service receives, stores, notifies Your integration pulls the file, processes it upload / signed / encrypted pickup / transformation

pages.title: Walkthrough — modify an integration and promote it to production
pages.description: The complete sequence for changing an existing OIC integration: understand the current flow, modify its mappings and actions, handle connections and config variables, test, deploy across environments, activate, and roll back — the OIC mirror of the VBCS edit walkthrough.
headings: Phase 1 — Understand the existing integration (do not skip)
Phase 2 — Edit the design (create a draft, don't touch production)
The full checklist (copy for your change)
pages.content: The journey at a glance Phase 1 — Understand the existing integration do not skip Phase 2 — Edit the design create a draft, don't touch production Phase 3 — Connections, config variables & secrets Phase 4 — Test before activating Phase 5 — Deploy across environments export → import Phase 6 — Activate in production & verify Rollback plan The full checklist copy for your change Next steps You have a live integration — say an invoicing flow built on the FBDI or REST pattern — and you must change how it works a new branch, an extra lookup, a different invoke . OIC's lifecycle has its own rhythm: drafts, versions, activation, packages, config variables, and environment promotion . Follow these phases in order; each ends in a checkpoint you can verify before moving on. The same rule as the VBCS walkthrough applies: read the flow you are about to change. In the integration designer: Editing a live integration creates a new draft version — production traffic keeps using the active version until you activate the draft. Make your change there: The design moves cleanly between environments; the connections do not. Handle them explicitly: OIC promotes integrations as packages or project/integration export/import . The disciplined sequence: If production regresses, roll back by activating the previous version of the integration: Open the integration and read the flow trace view outline end to end: trigger → maps → invokes → logic → end/error actions. Note the connections it uses adapter + credentials and any config variables it references — these are the pieces that differ per environment. Note the tracking fields and any global fault handler already in place, so your change composes with them. Check which versions exist and which one is active in each environment see deployment . Add a map to reshape data for the new option, a switch for the new branch, a lookup reference, or a new invoke to a connection — the full palette is documented on orchestration & the flow toolbox . Prefer config variables URLs, directories, schedules over hard-coded literals, so the same package works in every environment. Wrap risky steps in a scope with a fault handler; keep the global fault path intact so failures still reach the error hospital. Export the updated integration with its dependencies from the source environment. Import into the next environment dev → test, then test → prod . On import, OIC prompts you to remap connections and resolve config variables . Perform the remap deliberately — connection-to-target, variable values, and schedule — and run the Phase-4 checks again in the new environment. Do not activate to production traffic until the promoted build has passed in test. Keep the prior version addressable — do not delete it on activation. If the change added a config variable or a connection , confirm the target environment still has the old value/setup for rollback; do not remove them in the same change. After rollback, verify the error hospital shows no residual failures from the interim version, and the instance tracking still resolves. The actions you used while editing are explained in Orchestration & the Flow Toolbox . Deployment mechanics in Deployment & Lifecycle . Verify what landed in Monitoring & Tracking . Recording "current flow: trigger → validate map → invoke Fusion REST → log → return, using connection Fusion-Prod and variable fusion.base.url " is your safety net and your rollback reference. While you edit, the active version keeps serving — that is the safety guarantee. Never deactivate the production version "to make edits"; the draft model already isolates your work. A literal URL or credential baked into a mapping is the classic landmine: the package imports cleanly into production, works in dev, and fails on the first real call. If a value varies by environment, make it a config variable at design time . See monitoring & tracking for flow traces and message inspection — they are your debugger during this phase. Full mechanics — packages, connection overrides, config variables, and the promotion checklist — are on deployment & lifecycle . Remember the version mechanics from the docs: activating a version with the same identifier and same major version deactivates the previously active one. That is how rollback works — keep the prior version available to reactivate. Rollback reactivates the old flow, but any side effects it already produced created records, sent payments are not undone. Plan compensation if the new option wrote downstream data — the scopes/fault handlers guide has the pattern see orchestration . Item Why it matters Action Connections Each env has its own endpoints/credentials Confirm the draft references a connection that exists in the target env or use an override on import Config variables URLs, directories, schedules vary per env Declare them in the design; set values per environment on import — never hard-code a per-env value in a map Secrets Passwords, client secrets belong in the connection Keep credentials in the connection / OCI secrets, not in the flow body see security Tracking fields Observability depends on them Add/keep business identifiers so monitoring stays searchable Check How Pass = The flow runs Use the built-in test for REST/scheduled integrations, or invoke the draft endpoint The new branch/action executes end to end Mappings correct Inspect request/response payloads at each stage Shapes match; lookups returned the right values Faults handled Force a failure in the new path Fault handler and/or global fault catch it; error surfaces properly Tracking visible Check the instance in Monitoring Business identifiers present; instance searchable Step Checkpoint 1 Import into production and remap connections/config All references point at prod; no dev credentials remain 2 Validate one real call or run once for scheduled flows New behavior verified against prod data 3 Activate the new version Traffic switches to the new version same-version rule applies 4 Smoke-test a live instance in Monitoring Tracking fields visible; no spike of errors 5 Confirm parity Old happy path still works; new option behaves as accepted # Done? Read the existing flow, connections, config variables, tracking, and global fault handler — noted what they do ☐ Draft version edited map/action/lookup/branch without touching the active version Per-env values in config variables, secrets in connections — no hard-coded literals Tested the draft end to end with payload inspection and a forced failure Exported and imported to test; connections remapped; config resolved; re-tested 6 Change note written flow + connection + variable delta for rollback 7 Imported to production, remapped and validated with one real call 8 Activated; production smoke-test passed in Monitoring 9 Rollback plan recorded reactivate prior version; stateful side effects considered neutral 1 · Understand read the flow & its dependencies oic 2 · Edit the design draft: map / action changes 3 · Handle connections & config remap + variables per env vbcs 4 · Test before activating validated in the source env 5 · Deploy package → import dev → test → prod success 6 · Activate & verify production, with rollback ready

pages.title: Monitoring, tracking & observability
pages.description: Every run of an integration is an instance. This page is about seeing those instances clearly: tracking fields so you search by the business key you already know, dashboards and traces for diagnosis, and message inspection when something went wrong mid-payload.
headings: The unit of visibility: the instance
Tracking fields — visibility by business key
pages.content: The unit of visibility: the instance Tracking fields — visibility by business key Flow traces Message inspection & resubmission Dashboards, alerts & reports Observability best practices Next steps The Monitoring area turns the runtime into a searchable record of every execution. The difference between "we can find it" and "we can't see anything" is decided before a flow ever runs — by the tracking fields you define. Every time a trigger fires, OIC records an instance with a lifecycle. Monitoring lists instances; you filter and open one to inspect every step it took. A tracking field is a value from the payload you declare as a searchable key. If you track PO_Number , the monitoring search box accepts that PO number and lists every instance that touched it. Open an instance and OIC shows its flow trace — the ordered list of stages, each with duration, status, and payload snapshots. This is the fastest diagnostic tool: When an instance failed, the question is almost always "what exactly did the target receive?" Message inspection lets you open the messages exchanged at each connection — request body, response, status code. Once the cause is clear, a properly built integration can be resubmitted after the fix without re-entering data: Track the business identifier your callers already use — invoice number, PO number, employee ID — never an internal OIC ID. A flow can carry several tracking fields; keep it to the two or three an operator would actually type. Assign the value early in the flow, before the first invoke, so a failed request is still searchable. Which stage failed — the trace highlights it; the stage's fault handler if any shows what it decided. Where time went — a long invoke reveals a slow target; a long map suggests a heavy transform. What was sent — inspect the request/response payload at any stage. Dashboards — at-a-glance counters: completed, aborted, and faulty instances per integration over time. Alerts — notify on fault thresholds e.g., more than N failed instances in an hour to Slack or email. Reports — packaged or custom reports on instance outcomes, volumes, and durations, for weekly operations review. Define tracking fields on day one; search is only as good as the keys you track. Keep a log stage at decision points so traces answer "why this branch?" without opening payloads. Alert on the business symptom missed invoices , not just on instance counts. Package the dashboards/reports with the integration so a new environment inherits the same views. Fix what you see in error handling . Track the right keys — build them into the flow in orchestration . Promote the same visibility into production in deployment . Instance status is what your ops team monitors. The error handling page tells you how to fix failures; this page tells you how to see them first. Tracking fields are cheap to add and expensive to retrofit. Every new integration should define at least one before its first go-live. Payload inspection can include sensitive data — limit the log / tracing level to what you need and review access to Monitoring accordingly. See security . Find: ops searches Monitoring by the supplier's batch reference and sees the scheduled instance in Aborted . Traces: the flow trace shows the Fusion invoke returned 403 — not the map. Inspect: message inspection shows the exact token error → the client secret was rotated see security . Recover: update the connection, resubmit the instance, verify it completes, and set an alert so the next rotation never waits for a user. Open the stage, read the fault Message inspection What did we actually send/receive? Check request vs response payloads Resubmission Can this finish now?
