pages.title: What is Oracle Integration Cloud?
pages.description: Oracle Integration Cloud (OIC) is Oracle's integration-platform-as-a-service (iPaaS). It connects Fusion and hundreds of other systems using pre-built adapters, orchestrated flows, and process automation — all configured in a visual designer rather than handwritten code.
headings: The OIC console and its building blocks
What OIC actually runs for you
A typical OIC flow, end to end
When to choose OIC vs. a plain API call
pages.content: The OIC console and its building blocks What OIC actually runs for you The three integration styles A typical OIC flow, end to end When to choose OIC vs. a plain API call Next steps OIC is the middle layer of the Oracle stack. If Fusion is the system of record and VBCS is the front end, OIC is the plumbing that makes them talk. It handles connectivity, transformation, routing, scheduling, error handling, and even human approval flows. OIC is accessed through a set of related consoles in the same cloud subnet. Each one targets a different kind of developer: When you activate an integration, OIC deploys it to a runtime engine and exposes it as an endpoint you can call from anywhere. That means your integration instantly becomes an API — which is exactly how VBCS talks to it. Every integration you build is one of three "styles." They differ in what triggers the flow. Consider a supplier submitting an invoice on your external portal. Here is the OIC journey: OIC receives the request, calls a Fusion REST endpoint to verify the PO and supplier, uses a lookup to map payment terms, stages the data to an FBDI file, and submits it to Fusion's ESS. On completion, it notifies the portal. You watch the whole thing in OIC Monitoring. Activate an integration to publish it. An app-driven integration gets a REST endpoint URL; a scheduled one gets an enterprise scheduler entry. Packages let Oracle ship full solutions e.g. "Fusion to NetSuite GL" that you import and configure instead of building from scratch. Agents extend OIC into your own data center to reach on-premises systems Oracle databases, SAP, files on your network through a secure outbound-only tunnel. Lookups act as runtime lookup tables e.g. map "01" → "Active" so you never hard-code translations in your mappings. Dig into key concepts — connections, agents, lookups, libraries. Understand the three styles in depth in integration styles . See the classic Fusion pattern in FBDI integration . Think of OIC as "integration as configuration." You draw the integration, map the fields visually, choose the adapter, and OIC generates the underlying runtime for you. You still can drop in custom code JavaScript / XSLT mappings, Groovy in processes , but the default path is low-code. You don't strictly need OIC for simple Fusion reads — VBCS can call Fusion REST directly. But the moment you need transformation, orchestration, scheduled sync, or error tolerance , OIC earns its place: it keeps that complexity out of your front-end code. pages.title: Process automation with OIC
pages.description: Model human approval workflows in OIC's Process Builder: BPMN-style components, approval patterns, data flowing through task assignments, and how processes talk to integrations and VBCS pages.
pages.content: OIC Process Builder Process components Approval patterns Integrating processes with integrations & pages Groovy & scripting When process vs. integration Next steps Integrations move data; processes move decisions . OIC's Process Builder models human-in-the-loop workflows — approvals, reviews, exception handling — as diagrams that route a payload from person to person with an audit trail. You draw a process like a flowchart BPMN-flavored : a start event , a chain of user tasks assigned to people or roles, service tasks that call out to REST/integrations, gateways that branch the flow, and an end event . Every process lives in a process application a project-like container , and each task keeps an instance and audit history — who saw it, when, and what they decided. Most processes are a few approval patterns composed together. The data associations connecting tasks are what carry the REST payload along the diagram — map request fields into the task's temporary variables, and map the approver's answer back out. Processes expose their start and task endpoints over REST, which is exactly how VBCS surfaces an inbox: Beyond mapping, process tasks can run embedded Groovy snippets — useful for enrichment computing an approver from a rule , validation, and light formatting. Groovy can read process variables and call out to REST: The overlap confuses new OIC users. Use the decision differently from the overflow reasoning: Single approver: one person or role sees the task; their approve/reject ends the branch. Routing by amount: a business rule checks the request total — under $5,000 auto-approves, between $5k and $50k goes to the manager, above $50k escalates to finance + director. Sequential approvals: task B waits for task A e.g., manager first, then finance . Parallel approvals: several groups review the same payload at once; the gateway re-combines their verdicts all-approved vs. any-rejected . A VBCS page binds a table to this task list service, so approvers get an online "approvals" dashboard built from the same REST task API. The process can also brake on an integration call : after approval, a service task invokes your OIC integration that performs the Fusion write. Call the process start from an integration's fault path too — e.g., "FBDI row rejected → start a correction process for a human." Enrichment: set the assignee from a participant table before the user task. Logic you don't want as a gateway: a one-line computation that avoids adding a decision node. Keep Groovy small and side-effect-free ; heavy orchestration belongs in the integration, not a script. Ground the integration side in key concepts . Learn how a process hands work off via REST endpoints . Watch failing processes and their instances in error handling and monitoring . The distinction between a task and a decision is worth internalizing: tasks involve people; decisions are automatic. A business rule can pre-filter "no approval needed" and skip straight to the end, saving your approvers time. Keep the process data-light : pass a reference an ID plus the fields the reviewers actually need, and let a service task fetch the rest from Fusion REST when the decision is made. Reviewers see a clean form, and you avoid stale copies of large payloads. Orchestrate-in-integration when the flow is automatic — transform, call, no human ever looks at it. Approve-in-process when a human must review and decide . The robust pattern combines them: the integration does the work and hands the interesting cases to a process; the process, on approval, invokes the integration again to complete the write. Each tool does what it does best. Component Purpose Typical configuration Start event Receives the initial payload REST service, JMS/message, or a scheduled start User task Shows work to a human, waits for a decision Accepts payload via data associations; assignee/role Service task REST Calls an integration or REST endpoint mid-flow OIC integration invoke or any REST service Business rule Evaluates data and returns a decision Route by approval amount, region, or product line Decision / gateway Branches the diagram EXCLUSIVE for the old approver's verdict Approval task Structured single/multi-approver task Sequential or parallel routing, due dates End event Closes the instance Optionally throws the result back to the caller oic restService · message · schedule Business rule / decision route by amount, role, region form rendered in VBCS, assignee approves Service task call integration / Fusion REST instance closes with outcome payload approve path decision result curl -X GET "https:// /ic/api/bpm/v1/ws/workflow/task/list" \\ -H "Authorization: Bearer " # → 200 # "taskList": # # #

pages.title: REST and RESTful APIs in OIC
pages.description: Consume Fusion REST from OIC, expose integrations as clean REST endpoints, understand the request/response envelope, and secure your endpoints with OAuth 2.0 client credentials.
pages.content: Consuming Fusion REST from OIC Exposing integrations as REST Request/response envelope Authentication for your endpoints Pagination & large payloads Versioning & change management Next steps REST is the lingua franca of OIC. You use it in three directions: consuming Fusion's REST services on the invoke side, exposing your own integrations as REST endpoints on the trigger side, and securing those endpoints so only authorized callers get in. Inside an integration, talk to Fusion through the Fusion Applications adapter which knows the module's REST resources or the lower-level REST adapter . Both let you import a resource definition, configure authentication, and then map into the payload. When you create an integration with a REST/HTTP trigger and activate it, OIC auto-generates a public endpoint. The URL pattern is versioned and predictable: OIC app-driven integrations expect the incoming JSON in a " " wrapper and return results wrapped in " " : The integration trigger's request parameter is this entire envelope; you map from request into the target payload, and map your output into response . Keep the envelope shape stable across versions so callers don't break. The standard for machine-to-machine callers is OAuth 2.0 client credentials against OCI IAM or Identity Cloud Service on older tenancies : Fusion REST returns collections with limit / offset paging and links. OIC handles large payloads with a scanner: Every activation creates a new version of the integration and republishes the endpoint — callers hit the newest active version automatically. Treat that as a discipline, not a trap: Import the resource: the Fusion adapter lets you browse and select a resource e.g., invoices , suppliers and request its JSON schema. Authentication: basic a service account or OAuth 2.0 client credentials. Prefer OAuth where Fusion's OAuth client support is enabled. Map it: once the schema is loaded it appears in the mapper like any other payload — drag fields across, add lookups and expressions. Every Fusion REST call should send the REST-Framework-Version header that matches your instance; OIC carries it automatically from the adapter configuration. /ic/api/integration/v1/… is the OIC integration REST namespace; /activate/invoke marks the live activation of the integration whose code is in the path. The Content-Type: application/vnd.oracle.resource+json header tells OIC the payload is the standard request envelope , not a raw body. Inbound auth is configured at design time basic, OAuth, or access-token . Choose the level that matches who calls — VBCS service connections, partners, or anonymous. Create an OAuth client in OCI IAM with the proper scopes, grant access to the OIC instance, and use the returned client ID/secret in grant_type=client_credentials . Tokens are short-lived and signed; pass them as Authorization: Bearer and refresh before expiry. For private-key flows JWT client assertions instead of a shared secret , you sign a JWT with your key and submit client_assertion — it eases rotation because there is no client secret to rotate. Use the Fusion adapter's query with pagination settings — the adapter issues the paged reads and exposes an iterator in the mapper. For very large transfers, hand off to FBDI or Object Storage instead of streaming one giant REST response through memory. Prefer fields filters to fetch only the columns you need; big payloads cost time and quota. See how orchestration shapes an endpoint in integration styles . Switch to the bulk channel when rows pile up: FBDI integration . Debug slow or failing invokes in error handling . For simple reads with no orchestration, VBCS can call Fusion REST directly and skip OIC entirely. OIC earns its place when you need chained calls, transformation, retries , or a stable endpoint that hides Fusion's schema version churn. Never embed a client secret in browser code or a VBCS page. The page should use an SSO/OAuth authorization-code flow or a proxied connection; the client- credentials secret belongs in OIC connections or OCI secrets. Practice Why it matters Keep the envelope contract stable Callers compile against ; breaking it breaks them Activate new versions consciously Old versions remain available for instant rollback Keep integrations in version control The console stores versions; your repo stores source + docs Deprecate, then delete A path that callers still hit should return a clear message Test activation in a sandbox first Catching a bad map before production activation POST https:// /ic/api/integration/v1/integrations/ImportSupplier/activate/invoke Content-Type: application/vnd.oracle.resource+json Authorization: Bearer → 200 "response": "request": "supplierNumber": "SUP-10023", "payload": curl -X POST "https:// /oauth2/v1/token" \\ -H "Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded" \\ -d "grant_type=client_credentials" \\ -d "scope=urn:opc:resource:consumer::all" \\ -d "client_id= " \\ -d "client_secret= " # → 200

pages.title: Security & authentication
pages.description: Every connection in OIC has an identity, and every exposed endpoint must be protected. This page maps the auth types, the credential vault, certificates, OAuth 2.0 flows, and the roles that decide who can build, run, and manage integrations.
headings: Application roles that gate the console
pages.content: Application roles that gate the console Authentication types on a connection Where secrets live Protecting the endpoints you expose Agents and message protection Keys, certificates, and rotation Next steps Security in OIC sits in four layers: who may use the cloud service roles , what identity a connection presents to a target auth types , where secrets live key stores and the credential vault , and how a caller is admitted to your exposed endpoint security policies . OIC authorization is role-based. Oracle ships roles you grant to users or user groups: Each connection carries the credentials the target expects. Match the auth type to the target's contract: OIC keeps secrets out of your flow and your code: An activated app-driven integration is a real, callable URL. You control who can call it: For on-premises targets, the connectivity agent opens an outbound-only tunnel to OIC. Two security controls matter there: Certificates are the source of most OIC "sudden break" incidents. Keep a hygiene rule: Credentials stored in the connection — the normal place for passwords and client secrets. They travel with the connection but stay out of the integration body. OCI Vault / secrets — for Gen 3 and OCI-based setups, store sensitive values centrally and reference them. Key stores — hold the certificates and keys used for signing, TLS, and PGP. Renew them on a schedule; a lapsed cert is a classic "works in dev, fails in prod" cause. Agent-based connection — the target is only reachable through the agent group you install on-premises. Message protection — integrity/encryption over the tunnel for sensitive payloads; the agent and OIC exchange credentials and the connection is marked accordingly. Apply auth types when you pick adapters in adapters . Watch tokens and instances in monitoring . Ship the secured portfolio safely in deployment . The exact role names and what each grants vary slightly by OIC edition gen 2 vs gen 3 — see the Gen 3 page . The principle holds on both: least privilege — give the user only the role the job needs. In Fusion you almost always choose OAuth 2.0 client credentials : register an integration client in the Fusion console, put the client id/secret in the connection, and let OIC handle token acquisition and refresh. Never paste a token into the integration body — it expires and the flow breaks silently. Setup: OAuth 2.0 resource owner policy; a VBCS page uses a service connection with its client id and secret. Call: VBCS exchanges the client credentials for an access token and calls the trigger endpoint with Bearer . Result: the integration stays private to your apps — no token in page code, no open endpoint. When an integration that worked fails with 401 / 403 or a cert error overnight, check rotation first: an OAuth secret or certificate was likely rotated at the target and the connection still holds the old value. It is rarely "the integration". Role Sees / can do Typical owner Service Administrator Everything: environments, agents, packages, all integrations OIC platform admin Integration Administrator Create, edit, activate, and manage integrations Integration lead Integration Developer Design and test integrations within allowed projects Developer/consultant Integration Ops / Monitor Start/stop, view instances, resubmit — but not redesign Operations analyst Insights / Reporting Read dashboards and packaged reports Ops or business Auth type What it sends Used for Basic Username/password Legacy endpoints and many on-prem systems Bearer token Authorization: Bearer REST APIs that issue a token OAuth 2.0 client credentials Exchanges a client id/secret for an access token Modern SaaS: Fusion, Salesforce, NetSuite, OCI OAuth 2.0 resource owner User's credentials traded for a token APIs that act on behalf of a user Mutual TLS mTLS Present a client certificate to the server High-assurance partner APIs, banks Certificate / key Sign or decrypt with a stored key SOAP WSS, signing, MFT/PGP Security policy Who can invoke When to choose No security open Anyone with the URL Internal demos only — never production Basic auth Caller sends username/password Systems that cannot do OAuth A registered client's token The standard for production API-to-API Custom / policy-based Your own authorization policy When entitlement logic lives outside OIC Asset Purpose Renew before Connectivity agent cert Identity for the agent tunnel Its expiry in OPC TLS truststore Server-side certs you trust Server migration / cert change at the target Signing key / PGP key Signing and file encryption Partner key rotation schedule Integration client secret OAuth token acquisition Fusion/OCI console rotation window # Quick check that a connection's OAuth credentials are still valid curl -s -X POST "https:// .identity.oraclecloud.com/oauth2/v1/token" \\ -u " : " \\ -H "Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded" \\ -d "grant_type=client_credentials&scope=urn:opc:idm:__myscopes__"

pages.title: Integration styles and when to use each
pages.description: Every OIC integration is app-driven, scheduled, or event-driven. Understand the three styles, how to build each one, and how to pick the right trigger for your use case.
pages.content: The three integration styles Building an app-driven integration Scheduled integrations Event-driven with Fusion business events Choosing the right style Next steps Synchronous vs asynchronous The single most important design decision in OIC is what starts the flow . Everything downstream — the mapping strategy, the fault handling, the way other systems call back — follows from the trigger you choose. OIC categorizes integrations by trigger into three styles. Most teams mix all three in one portfolio. The app-driven request/response style is the workhorse: a caller sends data and expects a structured answer. In the designer the flow is always the same shape: Deciding whether the caller should wait is the real architectural choice: A scheduled integration has no incoming request . Instead, OIC's enterprise scheduler wakes it up on a cron-like schedule — every hour, nightly, the first Monday of the month — and the flow performs the work end to end on its own. Scheduled integrations are the natural home for bulk data movement and for "reconciliation" flows that correct what real-time styles missed. Fusion publishes Business Objects events when the state of a business object changes — a PO is approved, an invoice is rejected, a worker is hired. OIC can subscribe to those events and react the instant they fire, with the event payload delivered directly into the integration. When a requirement arrives, classify it with these questions before opening the designer: Synchronous — the integration runs to completion, then returns the result in the HTTP response. Use it when the caller needs a value immediately a lookup, a single-record create whose ID informs the next step . Asynchronous — the trigger takes the request, returns 202 Accepted right away, and the flow continues in the background. Use it for slow or batched work FBDI loads, multi-step orchestrations . Callers poll a status endpoint or receive a callback instead of blocking. Pull what changed: the classic pattern is to query the source with a date-range predicate e.g., Fusion REST with lastUpdateDate > :lastRun , then upsert the delta into the target. Operate in batches: read a page, process it, remember a bookmark, and resume next run. Never reprocess the whole table. Schedule granularity: OIC supports schedules down to minute-level repeats plus a scheduler service similar in spirit to Fusion's Enterprise Scheduler for calendar e.g., monthly on day 5 patterns. Overlap guard: if a run is still going when the next one is due, OIC you can signal the previous deployment so you know a run is late — monitor duration, not just success. The trigger is the Fusion Applications event adapter configured to consume a specific business event; no polling server side needed. Because it is push — not poll — latency is real-time , and the downstream systems get notified only when something actually changed. Events carry a payload and event context who, when, which object . Map that payload straight into your downstream calls. Is someone waiting on the result , and does it involve more than a single call? → App-driven . Is it bulk , nightly , or "process everything since midnight"? → Scheduled . Is it a notification of change "when X happens, tell Y" ? → Event-driven . Refresh the grounding vocabulary in key concepts . Apply the app-driven style to bulk Fusion loads in FBDI integration . Expose a style over a clean API in REST & RESTful APIs . The styles are not a framework you have to fit into — they are a vocabulary . The same integration can even be cloned and activated with a different trigger if the requirement changes. A common anti-pattern is making an asynchronous workload synchronous "just to be simple." The caller times out at ~90 seconds; big imports fail. If the work can take longer than a few seconds, return 202 and poll . Example: a supplier invoice is approved in Fusion. The "Supplier Invoice Approved" business event fires, OIC picks up the payload, looks up the invoice in Fusion REST to enrich it, and posts the payment-window data to the bank portal. No polling, no schedule — the event is the schedule. Two rules cover most decisions. Writes to Fusion that need orchestration — use app-driven. Bulk window loads — use scheduled. If a write also needs human approval, hand the request to a process see process automation and let the process continue the flow when approved. Style Trigger When to use Example App-Driven / Orchestration An incoming request REST, SOAP, file, DB event A caller waits for a result; you orchestrate multiple steps A PO arrives from a portal; OIC validates and imports it into Fusion Data-Driven / Scheduled A time-based schedule ESS-like job Bulk, periodic, no one waiting on the response Every night, GET changed suppliers from Fusion REST and sync downstream Event-Driven A change notification pushed from a system React in real time to something that already happened Fusion fires a business event when a PO is approved; OIC notifies the next system neutral 🌐 External portal · app · scheduler · webhook oic REST / SOAP / file adapter Map validate · transform · lookup Invoke Fusion file/SOAP invocation to a Fusion resource vbcs Response 200 result · 4xx business error POST /invoke request payload canonical form result or fault

pages.title: Official use cases
pages.description: The ten use cases Oracle documents for Oracle Integration — from AI-guided invoice creation to B2B order-to-cash — summarized faithfully so you can see what a finished integration looks like before you build your own.
headings: 5 · Extract Data Using OCI AI Services
pages.content: At a glance The capability cards 1 · Create Invoices 2 · Update Invoices 3 · Procure to Pay 4 · Order to Cash 5 · Extract Data Using OCI AI Services 6 · Employee Recruitment 7 · Respond to Messages 8 · Stage Reports from Fusion Applications 9 · Sync Versus Async Integrations 10 · Disaster Recovery Simulation Patterns to take away Next steps Steps from the Oracle use case Oracle's getting-started guide walks through ten realistic automations. Together they show the full range of what Oracle Integration can orchestrate: AI services for extraction and analysis, human-in-the-loop approvals, robotic process automation for systems without APIs, B2B / EDI document exchange, decisions for routing, and a knowledge base for policy. This page preserves each one's steps so you can recognize the patterns when you meet them in your own work. Each use case bundles a few building blocks. Recognize these before reading the steps: Vendors send invoices as email PDFs or SFTP uploads ; OIC turns them into ERP invoices with as little manual effort as possible. The counterpart automation: bulk-correct existing invoices so nothing is updated by hand. Your company a product manufacturer orders parts from a supplier through EDI over AS4, and every message is tracked by OIC's B2B component. A retailer orders from you the manufacturer ; you fulfill, bill, and collect — also over EDI/AS4. A single upload becomes an ERP decision — fully or partially automated by AI and policy. An agentic AI assistant runs an end-to-end recruiting workflow from the uploaded resumes to references. Customer communications are analyzed, then answered automatically or routed to a human. Fusion reports are copied to File Server so other systems or people can use them without opening Fusion. The decision that shapes nearly every integration you design — and Oracle's official stance mirrors the one this site teaches: Not a business flow but an operational discipline: regularly prove that your OIC DR plan works before it is needed. Find new invoices — on a schedule email or on a File Server system event SFTP upload . Extract invoice data — the integration calls OCI Document Understanding to pull the PO number and PO amount. Review extracted data — if the confidence score is below 1, a human-in-the-loop task asks an employee to compare the extract against the invoice and approve or correct it. Confirm the PO amount — a robot opens the legacy procurement system no APIs , finds the original PO, and reports whether the authorized amount matches the billed amount. Approve the purchase — a decision checks the amount against the auto-approval limit; above the limit, a human task approves, and can approve or reject any item in natural language e.g. "new desk chairs yes, espresso machine no" . Create the invoice — the integration creates the invoice in Oracle Cloud ERP using the ERP Cloud Adapter. Find an invoice — an integration passes a set of invoice numbers, amounts, and supplier names to a robot data often comes from a staged Fusion report — see use case 8 . Verify the invoice — the robot checks that number, amount, and supplier match the passed values. Update and repeat — on a match the robot updates the invoice, then moves to the next one. Place an order — you upload an EDI file to File Server; integrations send 850 Purchase Order and receive an MDN confirmation. Receive updates — a receive integration validates the order, sends 997 Functional Acknowledgment , translates the file with the B2B schema, and writes the PO to Oracle Cloud ERP via the ERP Cloud Adapter; the supplier accepts with 855 PO Acknowledgment . Shipment and invoice — the sequence of 856 Advance Ship Notice and 810 Invoice messages, each acknowledged. Send payment — the order is paid on receipt of the goods. Receive an order — the retailer uploads an EDI 850 Purchase Order to File Server; you confirm receipt with MDN . Process the order — a receive integration validates it, sends 997 , translates to ERP XML, and writes the PO to Oracle Cloud ERP with the ERP Cloud Adapter; you accept with 855 . Shipment and invoice — 856 Advance Ship Notice and 810 Invoice , each acknowledged by the retailer. Receive payment — you collect for the order. Upload an invoice — an employee uploads a PDF to File Server; a File created system event fires. Extract data — an event-triggered integration calls OCI Document Understanding for items and amounts, then OCI Generative AI builds a prompt like "Approval needed for a keyboard that costs $22 and a mouse that costs $19." Decide and update ERP — OCI Generative AI Agents RAG compares the prompt against the uploaded company expense policy: auto-approve within limits, auto-reject disallowed purchases, or route a human-in-the-loop task to a manager with the extracted data. Receive scores — a hiring manager uploads resumes to a chat interface. The agent uses integrations for OCI Document Understanding classify + extract resumes , job-description analysis, and knowledge-base policy retrieval; a decision scores candidates; OCI Language AI checks for bias. Scores and bias analysis return to the chat. Schedule interviews — the manager picks candidates; the agent calls integrations to create profiles in Oracle Cloud HCM and to email candidates a calendar link for choosing an interview time. Check references — the agent calls an integration that starts background-check/reference verification for the top candidate s . Analyze a message — an integration detects the communication email, social post, review and calls AI services for sentiment and the product/feature mentioned. Send a response — a decision picks the best next step: send an automated reply, route to the right employee via human-in-the-loop for a custom response, create a help-desk ticket, or even compute a value like churn risk. Update enterprise applications — an integration writes the engagement to the CRM using application-specific adapters. Generate a report — e.g. a pay-period report of invoices that still need manual updates in Fusion. Copy to File Server — an integration runs on a Fusion report event or on a schedule and stages the report. Use it downstream — archive it, access it without Fusion, distribute it to stakeholders, send it to an on-premises app, or feed it to the Update Invoices robot use case 2 . Create a business continuance strategy — define roles and responsibilities, document the failover plan, and build in reviews and audit. Perform a DR simulation — periodically fail over to the other instance and fail back, implementing the documented process. Conduct an operational site rotation optional — switch to a different center of operations e.g. every ~6 months so failover is a muscle you use, not a rumor. Files are often the trigger — File Server + system events start most of these flows. AI extracts, a decision routes — Document Understanding or Generative AI reads unstructured input; a decisions component picks the branch. Humans only where the rules are — human-in-the-loop tasks sit at low-confidence extractions and above-limit approvals, not on every step. No APIs → a robot — the legacy procurement system appears only because it has no API; expect RPA where integration can't reach. ERP Cloud Adapter is the endpoint — Oracle Cloud ERP is written to via the application-specific adapter at the end of most financial flows. Build the pieces these flows use in orchestration and mapping . See the pattern behind use cases 3 and 4 in FBDI integration . Keep a portfolio of flows like these healthy in monitoring . The B2B/EDI documents in this page run over the AS4 protocol and use standard EDI document types: 850 Purchase Order, 855 PO Acknowledgment, 856 Advance Ship Notice, 810 Invoice, 997 Functional Acknowledgment, and MDN Message Disposition Notification. This is the same P2P business cycle the Financials site covers — but here it is executed as B2B message exchange instead of API calls. See Procure-to-Pay for the finance side of the same story. The mirror image of Procure-to-Pay from the supplier's seat. See Order-to-Cash for the finance-side cycle. Note the difference from use case 1: here the policy lives in a knowledge base RAG that OIC consults at runtime; in use case 1 the approval limit is evaluated by a decision rule. This is the same sync/async trade-off covered in detail on the orchestration page — the official use case confirms the guidance in exactly these terms. This use case assumes Oracle-managed disaster recovery . Customer-managed DR is also available but has its own supported/unsupported list — confirm which model your tenancy uses before you plan around it. pages.title: PO Approval Scenario
pages.description: A concrete, step-by-step walkthrough of a purchase order request flowing through the stack — from a buyer's form in VBCS, through OIC orchestration and approval, back to a refreshed portal status.
pages.content: The business case The end-to-end flow Step 1 - The VBCS page Step 2 - OIC integration Step 3 - Approval process Step 4 - Status callback Error scenarios Key takeaways Next steps The business case A buyer who does not have access to Fusion needs to raise a purchase order. They open a VBCS portal — an extranet form — and submit their request. The request does not go straight to Fusion: it lands in OIC , which validates it, looks up supplier data, and creates a draft PO in Fusion . The PO then enters an OIC approval process where the buyer's manager signs off. Once approved, the status flows all the way back to the portal so the buyer sees "Approved" without ever logging into Fusion. Four layers participate, and each owns one job: Trace the request through its five stops. Every hop is an Arrow label you can watch in OIC Monitoring: The portal is a VBCS page built around a page variable called poRequest . The form binds directly to it, so whatever the buyer types is the payload that leaves the page: When the buyer clicks Submit , an action chain fires: it runs a Call Rest Endpoint action against the OIC service connection. The service connection hides the endpoint URL and the OAuth token, so the page only needs to send the variable and await a response. The hit arrives at an app-driven integration exposed as a REST endpoint. OIC's first job is to confirm the supplier actually exists in Fusion. It makes a GET against the supplier resource: If a supplier record returns, OIC enriches the payload : a lookup maps the supplier's payment terms code to the human name, and the amounts carry over untouched. It then POSTs to Fusion to create the PO in draft, gets a Fusion PONumber back, and stashes it in a variable for the approval step. Next the integration hands off to an OIC Process Builder flow. The gate is a business rule on the order total: The data association between the integration and the process carries the whole PO payload — supplier, lines, total, and the PONumber — so the approval screen shows the manager exactly what they are signing off on. The manager can approve, reject, or request changes; the outcome becomes the process result. When the process completes, control returns to the integration, which does two things: Back in the page, the action chain wasn't waiting synchronously for the approval — it returned as soon as the PO was accepted. The portal refreshes or polls a small status endpoint that OIC keeps current, and the buyer's card flips to "Approved" or "Rejected" . The same flow, when things go wrong — these are the cases you will actually chase in OIC Monitoring: VBCS portal: collects the request and shows the result. It never touches Fusion directly. OIC integration: receives the request, validates the supplier against Fusion REST, enriches it with payment terms, and creates the PO. Fusion: holds the PO as the system of record, in pending approval status. OIC process: runs the human approval task and reports the final status back to the portal. Supplier: the supplier number or name the buyer wants to purchase from. Line items: item, quantity, and unit price for each line. Amount: the total, used later to decide whether the order needs a manager. Currency: ISO code such as USD or EUR . Payment terms: left blank on purpose — OIC fills it from a lookup. Under $5,000 , the PO is auto-approved — no human in the loop. At or above it, the flow creates a manager approval task and assigns it by the buyer's reporting line: manager task . Updates Fusion: approves or rejects the pending PO so the status written by Step 2 becomes final. Notifies the portal: fires the callback return path so VBCS learns the outcome. See how this scenario fits the wider landscape in architecture . Learn why this is an orchestration style in OIC styles . Wire the portal side with VBCS connecting . Read how failures like the ones above look from the inside in OIC errors . Every one of these failures leaves an entry in OIC Monitoring with the exact stage and payload. Get into the habit of matching an error message back to the arrow in the diagram above — the culprit is always the last step that actually ran. The rule that keeps this scenario clean: VBCS asks, OIC does, Fusion stores. The portal never formats the data or approves the order; OIC owns validation, enrichment, and the human gate; Fusion is the only place the PO truly exists. Failure Where it surfaces OIC behavior Supplier not found OIC integration, Stage: GET suppliers Fusion returns 404; OIC routes to a fault handler that logs the reason and returns a clean error to the portal Fusion rejects the PO OIC integration, Stage: POST createPO Fusion returns a business error in the payload; OIC marks the instance as failed and shows the Fusion message in Monitoring Approval task times out OIC process, Task Process escalates to a second approver or ends with a timeout status that the callback relays to the portal vbcs VBCS Portal buyer submits PO form oic OIC Integration validate supplier via Fusion REST fusion PO created, pending approval OIC Process manager approval task Portal Update page refresh shows 'Approved' Approved POST /invocations REST lookup task assignment callback "supplierNumber": "SUP-10023", "currency": "USD", "paymentTerms": null, "lines": , , "totalAmount": 6700.00 curl -u "username:password" \\ "https://yourinstance.oraclecloud.com/fscmRestApi/resources/11.13.18.05/suppliers?finder=SupplierFindAll;number=SUP-10023" \\ -H "REST-Framework-Version: 11.13.18.05"

pages.title: Advanced querying
pages.description: Hierarchical CONNECT BY queries, PIVOT and UNPIVOT, regular-expression functions, LISTAGG string aggregation, and reading JSON and XML straight from SQL.
headings: Hierarchical queries: CONNECT BY, START WITH, LEVEL, PRIOR
Reading JSON and XML in SQL
pages.content: Hierarchical queries: CONNECT BY, START WITH, LEVEL, PRIOR PIVOT and UNPIVOT Regular expressions LISTAGG — string aggregation Reading JSON and XML in SQL These are the "shape-shifting" tools: turn rows into a tree hierarchies , turn columns into rows unpivot or vice versa pivot , aggregate strings, and reach into JSON or XML without leaving SQL. They are the difference between writing five queries and writing one. Oracle's native way to walk a parent/child tree in one statement. Every row gets a LEVEL — how deep it sits — and PRIOR refers to the parent row in the current-to-previous comparison: PIVOT rotates rows of category values into new columns — the classic "counts per region as columns" report: UNPIVOT is the reverse — take several columns you want to treat as one dimension: Oracle's regex functions search, extract, and rewrite text with patterns. They are per-row single-row and are the escalation when LIKE is too blunt: LISTAGG concatenates values within a group into one string — "list the order IDs for this customer separated by commas": Modern Oracle stores JSON in an IS JSON -checked column and lets you pull fields out in plain SQL. The deep dive is the JSON & XML page , but the shape you will see daily: And XML with XMLTABLE XMLTYPE-typed columns when you integrate with legacy XML feeds — the PL/SQL page shows the XMLTYPE handling side. Consider the MODEL clause — Oracle's spreadsheet-like "if/then across rows" engine — as the very last tool to reach for; it is powerful, obscure, and rarely worth the learning curve versus a self-join or analytic function. Direction matters: PRIOR employee_id = manager_id walks down parent → children ; PRIOR manager_id = employee_id walks up. Cycles A reports to B who reports to A cause infinite loops — add NOCYCLE and handle CONNECT_BY_ISCYCLE . The ANSI alternative — recursive WITH — is on the subqueries page ; both produce a tree, pick whichever your shop standardizes on. The famous LISTAGG limit: the output is a VARCHAR2 and hits the 4,000-byte ceiling or 32,767 in extended mode with ORA-01489 on big groups. The 19c+ ON OVERFLOW TRUNCATE / ON OVERFLOW ERROR clauses give you control; for genuinely huge strings pre-aggregate or use JSON_ARRAYAGG . Keyword Meaning START WITH Which rows are the roots of the tree CONNECT BY How a child relates to its parent PRIOR The parent side of the connection used in the CONNECT BY + SELECT LEVEL Depth: 1 at the root, 2 at first children, … ORDER SIBLINGS BY Order rows at the same level within the tree Function What it does REGEXP_LIKE col, pattern TRUE if the string matches the pattern REGEXP_SUBSTR col, pattern, start, occ Extracts the matching substring REGEXP_REPLACE col, pattern, replacement Replaces matches group refs with \\1 REGEXP_INSTR col, pattern Position of the first match SELECT LPAD ' ', 2 * LEVEL - 1 || full_name AS employee, LEVEL FROM employees START WITH manager_id IS NULL -- who is the root? CONNECT BY PRIOR employee_id = manager_id; -- child.manager_id = parent.employee_id SELECT * FROM SELECT r.region_name, o.order_id FROM orders o JOIN customers c ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id JOIN regions r ON r.region_id = c.region_id PIVOT COUNT order_id -- what to compute FOR region_name IN 'West' AS west, 'East' AS east -- value -> column ; SELECT * FROM sales_totals UNPIVOT amount FOR quarter IN q1, q2, q3, q4 ; -- each row becomes 4 rows with a quarter name column -- Rows that are a 10-digit or 3-3-4 phone number SELECT * FROM contacts WHERE REGEXP_LIKE phone, '^\\ ? 0-9 \\ ? -. ? 0-9 -. ? 0-9 $' ; -- Normalize to 555-123-4567 SELECT REGEXP_REPLACE phone, '\\ ? 0-9 \\ ? -. ? 0-9 -. ? 0-9 ', '\\1-\\2-\\3' AS normalized FROM contacts; SELECT c.customer_name, LISTAGG o.order_id, ', ' WITHIN GROUP ORDER BY o.order_id AS order_list FROM customers c LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.customer_id GROUP BY c.customer_name; -- Orders with a JSON attributes column SELECT o.order_id, JSON_VALUE o.attributes, '$.shipment_tracking' AS tracking, JSON_QUERY o.attributes, '$.packages' AS packages FROM orders o WHERE o.attributes IS JSON;

pages.title: Analytic / window functions
pages.description: OVER, PARTITION BY, window ordering, ROWS/RANGE frames, ROW_NUMBER, RANK, DENSE_RANK, LAG, LEAD, running totals and moving averages, FIRST_VALUE, LAST_VALUE, NTILE, PERCENT_RANK, and CUME_DIST.
headings: The anatomy: OVER (PARTITION BY … ORDER BY … frame)
LAG and LEAD — look at neighboring rows
pages.content: The anatomy: OVER PARTITION BY … ORDER BY … frame Ranking: ROW_NUMBER, RANK, DENSE_RANK LAG and LEAD — look at neighboring rows Running totals and moving averages FIRST_VALUE, LAST_VALUE NTILE, PERCENT_RANK, CUME_DIST These are the single most career-changing feature in Oracle SQL. An analytic window function computes a value per row while looking at a neighborhood of rows: "rank each order within its customer", "each row's share of its region total", "the 7-day moving average". Unlike GROUP BY , they do not collapse rows — every input row stays in the output, with its computed number attached. Every analytic function ends in an OVER clause with three parts: LAG reaches into the previous row of the same partition; LEAD the next . Instant "change vs last month" and "next expected item": The frame decides which rows feed the window. With ORDER BY the default frame RANGE BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW gives running totals; a sliding ROWS window gives moving averages: Jump to the first or last row of the frame — often used to attach a benchmark: The distribution quartet for buckets and percentile reports: PARTITION BY is "GROUP BY for analytics" — it does not reduce output rows. An ORDER BY inside OVER does not affect the final output order; it only defines the order the function sees. Both take col, offset, default — offset 1 by default LAG x = LAG x,1,NULL . The result of one analytic feeds the next : nesting to compute a lagged aggregate as above is idiomatic. ROWS counts physical rows; RANGE groups equal ORDER BY values — subtle, keep to ROWS for sliding windows. Moving averages on non-contiguous dates mislead — order the frames by the actual date value, not row position. "Top N per group" here: biggest order per customer, top 3 invoices per supplier is the single most useful analytic pattern in business SQL. It replaced the old correlated-subquery mess entirely — the optimizer even gets a hint dedicated to it TOPN . LAST_VALUE notoriously returns the current row unless you widen the frame to ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND UNBOUNDED FOLLOWING — one of Oracle's best-known analytic surprises. When you mean "last over the whole partition", spell the frame out. Part What it does Default PARTITION BY col Split rows into groups; the function runs within each partition One partition = whole result set ORDER BY col Order rows inside each partition rankings, running totals need it Not needed for simple aggregates frame ROWS/RANGE Which rows count: all, up to current, a sliding window For ORDER BY queries: so far up to the current row Function Ties Classic use ROW_NUMBER No ties — each row gets a unique number arbitrary among equals Top-N per group RANK Ties share a rank, then GAP 1,1,3 Leaderboards, competition-style DENSE_RANK Ties share a rank, no gap 1,1,2 Close-ranked reports, bands Frame Rows included ROWS BETWEEN 2 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW Current row + the two before ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW Everything up to current running total RANGE BETWEEN CURRENT ROW AND UNBOUNDED FOLLOWING Everything from current to the end ROWS BETWEEN 3 PRECEDING AND 3 FOLLOWING Symmetric sliding window What it returns Use NTILE n Bucket number 1..n Quintiles/deciles of spend, A–E rating bands PERCENT_RANK Relative rank 0..1 between rows Percentile-style position CUME_DIST Cumulative distribution rows ≤ current ÷ total 'What % is below this value' What % is below this value SELECT o.customer_id, o.order_id, o.total_amount, SUM o.total_amount OVER PARTITION BY o.customer_id AS customer_total, ROW_NUMBER OVER PARTITION BY o.customer_id ORDER BY o.total_amount DESC AS rank_in_customer, LAG o.total_amount, 1 OVER PARTITION BY o.customer_id ORDER BY o.order_date AS prev_order_amount FROM orders o; SELECT customer_id, order_id, total_amount FROM SELECT o.customer_id, o.order_id, o.total_amount, ROW_NUMBER OVER PARTITION BY o.customer_id ORDER BY o.total_amount DESC AS rn FROM orders o WHERE rn = 1; -- "top N per group": change 1 to N SELECT TRUNC order_date AS day, COUNT * AS orders, LAG COUNT * OVER ORDER BY TRUNC order_date AS prev_day_orders, COUNT * - LAG COUNT * OVER ORDER BY TRUNC order_date AS day_change FROM orders GROUP BY TRUNC order_date ; SELECT TRUNC order_date AS day, SUM COUNT * OVER ORDER BY TRUNC order_date ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW AS running_total, AVG COUNT * OVER ORDER BY TRUNC order_date ROWS BETWEEN 2 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW AS avg_3_days FROM orders GROUP BY TRUNC order_date ; SELECT c.customer_name, FIRST_VALUE o.order_date OVER PARTITION BY o.customer_id ORDER BY o.order_date AS first_order FROM orders o JOIN customers c ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id; SELECT customer_id, SUM total_amount AS spend, NTILE 4 OVER ORDER BY SUM total_amount DESC AS quartile FROM orders GROUP BY customer_id;

pages.title: Basic querying
pages.description: SELECT, DISTINCT, column aliases, arithmetic and string literals, the WHERE filter, ORDER BY sorting, and the three ways to limit the rows Oracle returns: FETCH FIRST, OFFSET, and the legacy ROWNUM.
headings: SELECT and the logical order of execution
Limiting rows: FETCH FIRST, OFFSET, and ROWNUM
pages.content: SELECT and the logical order of execution The basic SELECT Column aliases Arithmetic and string literals WHERE — the filter ORDER BY Limiting rows: FETCH FIRST, OFFSET, and ROWNUM A SELECT is a question: which columns, from which table, under which filter, in what order, and at most how many rows. Oracle evaluates a query in a fixed order that is worth learning once, because every error you hit alias in WHERE , ORDER BY not matching traces back to it. You write clauses with columns first, but conceptually Oracle processes them in this order: An alias renames the output column, which matters when a column is an expression or the name is awkward. Use double quotes to keep case, spaces, or special characters: Columns can be combined with + - * / and text with the concatenation operator || . In the SELECT list, literals are written in single quotes: WHERE applies row-by-row comparisons. It can use the operators you will see in depth on the filtering page; here is the basic shape and one regex-free trap-free example: Sort with ORDER BY , ascending ASC , default or descending DESC . You can sort by a column name, an alias, a position, or an expression: "Top ten" queries in modern Oracle use FETCH FIRST . The older ROWNUM approach predates it and has a famous footgun, so both appear here. And a quirk to remember: Oracle's optimizer performs this row cutoff at the end, so a top-N optimizer hint can still avoid sorting everything — that is what makes FETCH FIRST so fast on big tables. SELECT * is fine for exploration, but name columns explicitly in real code — the report survives someone adding a column later. DISTINCT deduplicates the whole selected row combination , not just the first column. SELECT DISTINCT customer_id, region_id is different from SELECT DISTINCT customer_id . Arithmetic on NULL yields NULL — there is no "skip the missing value" by default. That is why expressions like qty * price quietly disappear when either is NULL. Integer / division is not integer: 7 / 2 = 3.5 in Oracle, unlike many languages. Use TRUNC / ROUND to shape the result. Date arithmetic in Oracle is in days : order_date + 30 is 30 days later. To add months, use ADD_MONTHS see single-row functions . Character literal compare is case-sensitive by default, and the rules become surprising in WHERE — that is the next page's territory. Sort multiple keys left to right; order is stable within the first key. NULLs sort last on ASC and first on DESC default Oracle behavior . You can override with NULLS FIRST / NULLS LAST . Sorting by a character column uses the session's linguistic collation unless you specify COLLATE — accents and case handling differ by database setting. Because aliases are created at step 5, you cannot use a column alias inside WHERE or GROUP BY — but you can in ORDER BY , which runs after SELECT . SELECT customer_name AS name FROM customers WHERE name = 'X' fails; ... ORDER BY name works. In Oracle, an unquoted alias is stored uppercase NAME , and a quoted alias keeps exactly what you typed Credit Limit . Reference a quoted one with the same quotes, or you will get ORA-00904 . ROWNUM is assigned before sorting — so SELECT * FROM orders WHERE ROWNUM does not give you the five biggest orders; it gives five arbitrary rows usually in insert order and then sorts them. For correct "top N", nest: SELECT * FROM SELECT * FROM orders ORDER BY total_amount DESC WHERE ROWNUM . Prefer FETCH FIRST and keep ROWNUM for legacy code and the techniques on the advanced pages. Step Clause What it does 1 FROM Pick the table s and join them 2 WHERE Discard rows that fail the filter 3 GROUP BY Collapse rows into groups see grouping page 4 HAVING Discard whole groups that fail 5 SELECT Compute the output columns and aliases 6 Sort the final rows 7 FETCH FIRST Cut the result down to N rows SELECT customer_name, credit_limit -- the columns you want FROM customers -- the table WHERE region_id = 1; -- keep only matching rows SELECT * FROM orders; -- every column, every row SELECT DISTINCT customer_id -- one row per distinct customer FROM orders; -- NULLs count once SELECT customer_name AS name, credit_limit AS "Credit Limit" FROM customers; SELECT order_id, total_amount * 1.10 AS total_with_tax, 'Order ' || order_id AS order_label, DATE '2026-08-15' AS anchor_date FROM orders; SELECT customer_name, credit_limit FROM customers WHERE credit_limit >= 10000 -- numeric comparison AND region_id IN 1, 3 ; -- membership test SELECT customer_name, credit_limit FROM customers ORDER BY credit_limit DESC; -- biggest first SELECT order_id, customer_id, total_amount FROM orders ORDER BY customer_id, total_amount DESC; -- customer asc, amount desc within each -- Top 5 biggest orders SELECT order_id, total_amount FROM orders ORDER BY total_amount DESC FETCH FIRST 5 ROWS ONLY; -- Page 2 of the same list rows 6..10 SELECT order_id, total_amount FROM orders ORDER BY total_amount DESC OFFSET 5 ROWS FETCH NEXT 5 ROWS ONLY; -- With a percentage, for sampling SELECT * FROM customers FETCH FIRST 10 PERCENT ROWS ONLY;

pages.title: Constraints & data integrity
pages.description: PRIMARY KEY, FOREIGN KEY, UNIQUE, NOT NULL, CHECK, default values, enabling and disabling constraints, and the cascading delete behaviors that protect your relationships.
pages.content: The five types Table-level declaration with names Default values Enabling and disabling constraints Cascading delete behavior Constraint lookup dictionary queries A constraint is a rule the database enforces automatically on every insert and update. Constraints are how the schema stays healthy even when a careless script writes to it — which is far more robust than "remember to check in the application". Each rule can be declared inline with the column or at table level with a name . Named, table-level constraints are what survive in production schemas — you can find, drop, and re-enable them later: A default is not a constraint but the two live together at column definition. It fills the column when an INSERT omits it; it does not prevent NULL from being inserted explicitly: The dictionary lets you disable rules with DISABLE and re-enforce later with ENABLE — the standard choreography for a huge migration that loads messy historical data: What happens when you delete a parent row that children still reference? The foreign key decides, via ON DELETE : DISABLE NOVALIDATE / ENABLE NOVALIDATE / ENABLE VALIDATE control whether existing rows are scanned. Default ENABLE validates old rows too. Disabling a PK/unique constraint also drops its backing index — the load need not maintain it — then enabling recreates it a big win for bulk load time . The flip side: a disabled constraint protects nothing . Re-enable as the last step of the migration, and check the dictionary after: Primary, unique, and foreign keys generally create an index automatically Oracle builds one for a PK/unique constraint . NOT NULL and CHECK create none. That is why querying "hard by primary key" is fast even with no hand-written index. The error a bad insert throws — ORA-02290: check constraint SCHEMA.CK_ORDERS_AMOUNT violated — names the rule. Unnamed constraints end up auto-generated things like SYS_C00988 that tell you nothing. Name yours. Choose cascade deliberately . A blanket ON DELETE CASCADE on a financial table is how one innocent DELETE FROM customers deletes every order, every line, and every allocation beneath it — with no warning and no rollback hope once committed. Prefer the default refuse wherever audit matters. Constraint Rule it enforces Example declaration PRIMARY KEY Column s uniquely identify each row; cannot be NULL order_id NUMBER PRIMARY KEY FOREIGN KEY Value must exist in the referenced parent column, or be NULL customer_id REFERENCES customers customer_id UNIQUE No two rows share the value NULLs allowed, multiple email VARCHAR2 100 UNIQUE NOT NULL Column must always have a value customer_name VARCHAR2 60 NOT NULL CHECK Values must satisfy the boolean expression total_amount NUMBER CHECK total_amount >= 0 ON DELETE clause Deleting parent row Typical use default Refused with ORA-02292 integrity constraint violated — child exists Protect financial/audit data ON DELETE CASCADE Children deleted with the parent Order → order lines cleanup ON DELETE SET NULL Children's FK set to NULL column must be nullable Keep history, unlink parent CREATE TABLE orders order_id NUMBER, customer_id NUMBER, order_date DATE DEFAULT SYSDATE, total_amount NUMBER 12,2 , CONSTRAINT pk_orders PRIMARY KEY order_id , CONSTRAINT fk_orders_cust FOREIGN KEY customer_id REFERENCES customers customer_id , CONSTRAINT ck_orders_amount CHECK total_amount >= 0 ; CREATE TABLE orders order_id NUMBER PRIMARY KEY, order_date DATE DEFAULT SYSDATE, -- omitted -> now status VARCHAR2 10 DEFAULT 'OPEN' -- omitted -> 'OPEN' ; ALTER TABLE customers DISABLE CONSTRAINT fk_cust_region; -- load 5M rows fast -- ... bulk load ... ALTER TABLE customers ENABLE CONSTRAINT fk_cust_region; -- re-check everything SELECT constraint_name, constraint_type, status FROM user_constraints WHERE status = 'DISABLED'; CREATE TABLE order_lines line_id NUMBER PRIMARY KEY, order_id NUMBER CONSTRAINT fk_lines_order REFERENCES orders order_id ON DELETE CASCADE, -- delete order -> delete its lines ... ; -- Alternative: keep lines, clear the FK order_id NUMBER REFERENCES orders order_id ON DELETE SET NULL SELECT c.constraint_name, c.constraint_type, -- P, R, U, C, V check/view , or O c.status, cc.column_name FROM user_constraints c LEFT JOIN user_cons_columns cc ON cc.constraint_name = c.constraint_name AND cc.table_name = c.table_name WHERE c.table_name = 'ORDERS';

pages.title: Oracle data types
pages.description: VARCHAR2, CHAR, NUMBER, DATE and TIMESTAMP with time zones, CLOB, BLOB, RAW, ROWID — and the NULL / three-valued logic trap that bites every beginner.
headings: Date and time: DATE vs TIMESTAMP
pages.content: Character types: VARCHAR2 and CHAR Numeric type: NUMBER Date and time: DATE vs TIMESTAMP Large objects: CLOB and BLOB RAW and ROWID NULL and three-valued logic Every column declares a data type , and Oracle is strict about it: you cannot store 'abc' in a NUMBER column, and you cannot compare a string column to a number without an implicit conversion. Learning the core types — and which one to reach for — removes the most common beginner errors. Oracle's workhorse numeric type is NUMBER precision, scale — a floating-range decimal that stores integers and fractions alike: The second-most common data-type mistake in Oracle is treating "dates" as strings. A DATE always stores both date and time accurate to the second ; a TIMESTAMP adds fractional seconds; add WITH TIME ZONE or WITH LOCAL TIME ZONE for time-zone awareness. When a value does not fit in VARCHAR2 whose practical size limits are 4,000 bytes, or 32,767 in the extended datatypes mode , Oracle offers LOB types: Two types you will meet mostly in diagnostics and hash storage: NULL means unknown / missing — it is not the empty string and not zero. This creates three-valued logic : every comparison is TRUE , FALSE , or UNKNOWN . Do not reach for INTEGER , FLOAT , or NUMBER 38 out of habit under Oracle — NUMBER covered with an explicit precision is almost always the right choice, and BINARY_DOUBLE / BINARY_FLOAT exist only for float math and are rarely the right call for application data. For money, NUMBER 10,2 -style scales are conventional; the database rounds on insert if you exceed the scale. On insert you can rely on the default format DD-MON-YYYY in many sessions, but you should never write TO_DATE '15-08-2026','DD-MM-YYYY' implicitly — always give both the literal and the format mask the conversion functions page shows TO_DATE / TO_TIMESTAMP properly . SYSDATE is the current date+time of the database session; SYSTIMESTAMP is the same with time-zone and fractional seconds. Time-zone data is where record-keeping systems come unstuck: store TIMESTAMP WITH TIME ZONE when the moment in absolute time matters a flight departure , LOCAL when only the local wall-clock time matters a business day . RAW n — fixed-length binary data, typically up to 2,000 bytes. Used for stored hashes and identifiers where hex/binary values must survive unaltered no character -set conversion . ROWID — the physical address of a row inside a table, e.g. AAAE2XAAFAAAAClAAA . ROWIDs are pseudo-columns, not something you store for long; they point at a specific physical location and change when the row moves see Oracle-specific SQL . You cannot find NULLs with = NULL ; you must use IS NULL / IS NOT NULL . This is the single most common NULL mistake. WHERE keeps a row only when the filter evaluates to TRUE — rows where the condition is UNKNOWN are excluded, so a NOT IN against a subquery that returns a NULL matches nothing explored on the filtering page . Aggregates skip NULLs: COUNT * counts all rows, COUNT col counts only non-null values of that column. The NVL / COALESCE family replaces NULL with a fallback — covered in single-row functions . VARCHAR2 stores the value and ignores trailing spaces, but CHAR pads them. A CHAR 5 column holding 'AB' actually holds 'AB ' , which has caused more than one mysterious WHERE comparison failure. Prefer VARCHAR2 unless you have a concrete reason not to. A common pattern: store the document metadata in real columns file name, size, uploaded date and the bytes only in the BLOB . That keeps queries fast and the BLOB untouched until actually needed. The practical nightmare this causes: a junction "where credit_limit " misses every customer whose limit was never set. The fix is either WHERE credit_limit , or — better — a NOT NULL constraint and a default, so "no value" becomes an explicit number. Type Meaning When to use VARCHAR2 n Variable-length string, up to n characters; uses only as much storage as the value needs byte semantics by default in most setups Almost everything: names, descriptions, emails, codes CHAR n Fixed-length string, always padded with blanks to exactly n characters Rarely — only for short, always-full values like fixed format codes and flags Declaration Holds Example value Note NUMBER Any number up to 38 digits 12345.6789 No bounds — full precision NUMBER 8 Integers up to 8 digits 12345678 Scale 0: integer NUMBER 10,2 10 significant digits, 2 decimal places 12345678.12 Classic money column NUMBER 3,-2 Rounded to hundreds 12300 Negative scale rounds to the left of the point Example DATE Day + time to the second 2026-08-15 14:30:00 TIMESTAMP 6 Day + time to microseconds 2026-08-15 14:30:00.123456 TIMESTAMP WITH TIME ZONE Timestamp + offset or named zone 2026-08-15 14:30:00 +02:00 TIMESTAMP WITH LOCAL TIME ZONE Stored normalized to database zone, displayed in session zone 2026-08-15 12:30:00 shown in your session zone INTERVAL A span of time, not a point INTERVAL '2' MONTH 2 Contents Typical use Caveat CLOB Character large object text Long free-text notes, documents, JSON/XML strings over 4 KB Cannot be indexed with a regular B-tree; use full-text or JSON/XML indexes BLOB Binary large object Files, images, PDFs, encryption payloads Never in WHERE or ORDER BY without conversion NCLOB National character large object Unicode text over 4 KB Same caveats as CLOB Expression Result when credit_limit IS NULL credit_limit = 1000 UNKNOWN not found by = credit_limit < 0 UNKNOWN credit_limit 1000 credit_limit IS NULL TRUE credit_limit IS NOT NULL FALSE NULL = NULL UNKNOWN — always!

pages.title: Database foundations
pages.description: What a database, schema, table, row, column, and key actually are, how SQL is carved into DDL / DML / DCL / TCL, the data dictionary, and the tools you will type SQL into — SQL Developer and SQLcl.
headings: SQL statement categories: DDL, DML, DCL, TCL
Oracle tools: SQL Developer and SQLcl
Schemas in a real enterprise database
pages.content: Database, schema, table, row, column Primary keys and foreign keys SQL statement categories: DDL, DML, DCL, TCL Oracle tools: SQL Developer and SQLcl The data dictionary Schemas in a real enterprise database Next up Everything in this section depends on one simple idea: relational data is stored in tables , and SQL is the language you use to read and change it. Before the first query, it is worth being precise about the vocabulary, because words like "schema" and "database" mean particular things in Oracle that differ from other products. In Oracle, a database is the physical storage: the files and memory structures that a running database instance manages. Inside it live schemas , which are logical containers owned by users. This is a common source of confusion because in MySQL a "schema" is basically a "database" — in Oracle the words are different. Keys are how the database keeps relationships trustworthy. A primary key PK uniquely identifies every row in a table — it must be non-null and unique. A foreign key FK is a column or set of columns that references the primary key of another table, enforcing a parent–child relationship: The foreign key is what stops you from inserting an order for a customer that does not exist, and it is what lets the database cascade or clean up related rows when a parent is deleted. The constraints page covers the full rules including what happens on delete . SQL is split into four families. You meet one rule from each almost immediately: DML can be rolled back , DDL commits implicitly , DCL manages who can do what , and TCL is the transaction itself . Two tools matter for writing SQL against an Oracle database, and both are free: The SQL text is identical across tools — the tools only change how you run it, see the results, and inspect the execution plan the performance page uses DBMS_XPLAN , available from SQLcl and SQL Developer alike . Oracle describes itself to you through the data dictionary — a set of read-only views owned by SYS that answer questions like "which tables exist", "what columns does this table have", and "what privileges does this user hold". Because it is a meta-layer, many dictionary views come in three families: A production Oracle database is never one flat pile of tables. It is many schemas with clear ownership, sometimes for separate applications sharing one database: This layout is exactly the pattern the integrations and Fusion tables in the rest of this hub rely on — separate owners keep privileges minimal and make it clear who is responsible for each object. Schema — the collection of objects owned by one user: tables, views, sequences, synonyms, indexes, procedures. The schema name is the owner's username. Table — a named collection of rows sharing the same fixed set of columns . Each column has a data type see the data types page . Row — one record or "tuple": one value for every column. Column — one attribute of a record, e.g. customer_name . Learn the data types before you write your first CREATE TABLE in Oracle data types . Write your first queries in basic querying . Because a schema is owned by a user, fully-qualified names look like HR.EMPLOYEES — schema HR , table EMPLOYEES . When you reference a table without a prefix, Oracle uses your current schema . Oracle executes implicit commits before and after many DDL statements. If you UPDATE a thousand rows and then run CREATE INDEX before committing, the update is committed too — DDL cannot be rolled back and it commits your open work. The dictionary is your documentation when someone hands you an unknown schema: scan USER_TABLES first, drill into USER_TAB_COLUMNS for the column list, then USER_CONSTRAINTS to see the keys. The Oracle-specific page returns to these views in detail. Key Guarantees Example Primary key Every row is uniquely identified, and no key value is NULL orders.order_id Foreign key Every value must exist in the referenced parent's primary key orders.customer_id → customers.customer_id Family Expands to Verbs You use it when… DDL Data Definition Language CREATE, ALTER, DROP, TRUNCATE, RENAME Building or changing the structure: tables, indexes, views, synonyms DML Data Manipulation Language SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE, MERGE Reading or modifying the rows inside existing tables DCL Data Control Language GRANT, REVOKE Giving users the right to run DML/DDL on objects TCL Transaction Control Language COMMIT, ROLLBACK, SAVEPOINT Making your DML permanent or undoing it Tool What it is When to use it SQL Developer A full GUI client: worksheet, data grids, explain plan viewer, PL/SQL debugger Interactive development, exploring the data dictionary, debugging SQLcl A command-line client like SQL*Plus, modernized with history, formatting, spooling, and scripting Scripted/automated work, CI pipelines, quick checks in a terminal Prefix Scope Examples USER_* Objects you own USER_TABLES, USER_TAB_COLUMNS, USER_VIEWS ALL_* Objects you can access yours + privileged others ALL_TABLES, ALL_OBJECTS, ALL_INDEXES DBA_* Everything, requires DBA privileges DBA_TABLES, DBA_USERS, DBA_TAB_PRIVS Schema Typical content Used by HR Employees, departments, jobs Human-resources app and the standard HR sample schema APPS Application metadata, seeded data, FND tables Oracle E-Business Suite style multi-schema setups STAGE Landing tables for imports ETL/integration jobs that load then transform REPORT Views and summary tables Reporting tools that should never see raw tables accent 🗄️ Database Instance + datafiles + redo logs one per server oic 👤 Schema owned by a user HR · APPS · SCOTT — one container per user success 📋 Tables regions, customers, orders — plus views, indexes, … contains -- SQLcl / SQL*Plus / SQL Developer worksheet — identical SQL SELECT region_name, COUNT * AS customer_count FROM regions r JOIN customers c ON c.region_id = r.region_id GROUP BY region_name ORDER BY customer_count DESC; -- What tables exist in my schema? SELECT table_name FROM user_tables ORDER BY table_name; -- What columns does ORDERS have, and what are their types? SELECT column_name, data_type, data_length, nullable FROM user_tab_columns WHERE table_name = 'ORDERS' ORDER BY column_id;

pages.title: DDL — database objects
pages.description: CREATE, ALTER, DROP, TRUNCATE, RENAME; tables and temporary tables; and the object family you define once and query forever: views, sequences, synonyms, indexes, and constraints.
headings: The object family you will define every week
pages.content: The five verbs CREATE TABLE Temporary tables ALTER TABLE DROP and TRUNCATE The object family you will define every week DDL Data Definition Language builds or changes the structure itself — not the rows, the containers. It is immediate, permanent, and commits your open work, which is the one behavioral difference you must never forget. Each major verb gets its own example below, and the dedicated object types — constraints, views, sequences, indexes — each have a full page of their own. The full shape of a table definition — columns with types, inline constraints, and a default — was previewed in the data types and foundations pages. The canonical form: Oracle temporary tables hold data visible only to the session or transaction that wrote it — a scratchpad for complex multi-step logic inside a PL/SQL program or a batch flow: ON COMMIT PRESERVE ROWS keeps the data for the whole session; ON COMMIT DELETE ROWS empties it at each commit. Unlike other databases, the table definition is shared — only the rows are private. Change the shape of an existing table — add, drop, or modify columns, and manage constraints. Constraint-specific work is on the constraints page : These look alike and act very differently: Beyond tables, DDL creates the objects everything else in this section uses: The pattern to internalize: data lives in tables; everything else is metadata and speed . Views and synonyms shape how people see the data, indexes and partitions shape how fast the database finds it, and constraints shape what the data may be . Constraints get names — named constraints are debuggable, unnamed are not. DEFAULT fills the column when an insert omits it, but does not make it NOT NULL . Simpler CREATE TABLE x AS SELECT ... "CTAS" builds a table from a query — the fast way to clone or snapshot rows but it does not copy constraints or indexes . CREATE TABLE t AS SELECT ... is one of the most-used DDL statements in migration work. Remember it copies data and column nullability but not keys, constraints, defaults, or indexes — you re-create those afterwards. Both are DDL, so both commit your open work and neither can be rolled back normally. Oracle recently added real "recoverable" purge options on FLASHBACK-Friendly tables, but the default expectation in production is: TRUNCATE and DROP are final. Add PURGE to DROP TABLE to skip even the recycle bin. Verb What it does Example CREATE Define a new object CREATE TABLE … / CREATE INDEX … / CREATE VIEW … ALTER Change an existing object ALTER TABLE … ADD column / ALTER TABLE … ENABLE constraint DROP Remove the object permanently DROP TABLE … PURGE TRUNCATE Delete all rows, keep the structure TRUNCATE TABLE staging_load RENAME Rename an object RENAME employees TO staff DROP TABLE TRUNCATE TABLE Rows Gone Structure Kept Rollback-able? No unless recycle bin No Triggers Dropped Bypassed none fire Speed N/A Very fast — drops storage to free space tables Typical use Retire unused objects Reset a stage/reload table before a new load Object What it is Defined by Full page View A stored SELECT shown as a table CREATE VIEW ... AS SELECT ... views Sequence A number generator IDs CREATE SEQUENCE ... sequences & identity Synonym An alias pointing at another object CREATE SYNONYM ... FOR ... oracle-specific / security Index A fast-lookup structure for a table's columns CREATE INDEX ... indexes & performance Constraint A data-integrity rule on columns In CREATE TABLE / ALTER TABLE ... ADD constraints CREATE TABLE orders order_id NUMBER PRIMARY KEY, customer_id NUMBER NOT NULL CONSTRAINT fk_orders_cust REFERENCES customers customer_id , order_date DATE DEFAULT SYSDATE, total_amount NUMBER 12,2 NOT NULL CHECK total_amount >= 0 ; CREATE GLOBAL TEMPORARY TABLE stage_sums region_name VARCHAR2 30 , total NUMBER ON COMMIT PRESERVE ROWS; -- PRESERVE / DELETE options -- Only this session sees its own rows; cleared at session end. ALTER TABLE customers ADD region_code VARCHAR2 2 ; ALTER TABLE customers MODIFY credit_limit NUMBER 14,2 ; ALTER TABLE customers DROP COLUMN region_code; -- or mark a column unused first fast, reversible-ish then drop it ALTER TABLE customers RENAME COLUMN credit_limit TO credit_cap; CREATE VIEW active_customers AS SELECT customer_id, customer_name FROM customers WHERE void_date IS NULL; CREATE SYNONYM cust FOR customers; -- now "cust" works everywhere CREATE INDEX idx_cust_name ON customers customer_name ;

pages.title: DML — changing data
pages.description: Insert, update, delete, and the workhorses around them: MERGE upserts, INSERT ALL and multi-table inserts, INSERT ... SELECT, and RETURNING INTO to get values back.
pages.content: INSERT UPDATE DELETE MERGE — upsert in one statement INSERT ALL and multi-table inserts RETURNING INTO DML changes the rows inside tables that already exist. None of it is permanent until you COMMIT — that sentence, and what it implies for multi-statement bank transfers, is the substance of the transactions page . Here is the syntax. Insert rows with an explicit column list best practice or positionally. Omitting a column means "use its default or NULL": INSERT INTO ... SELECT loads a whole result set — the canonical "copy from one table to another" and the meat of data migrations: Update changes the values of existing rows by pattern. The WHERE you forget is how you update the whole table: Delete removes whole rows. Because a DELETE can trip a foreign key e.g. deleting a region that customers still point at , the constraints page covers ON DELETE CASCADE / ON DELETE SET NULL : MERGE updates a row that exists and inserts one that does not, in a single pass — the standard way file-based loads reconcile incoming data against existing rows: INSERT ALL pushes one source row into several target tables at once, and INSERT FIRST adds an IF/ELSE ladder: INSERT FIRST is the classic "routing" statement — each source row goes into the first branch whose condition matches: RETURNING INTO hands values from the row you just changed straight back into PL/SQL variables — typically to fetch a generated key you do not know yet for identity columns, see the sequences page : The ON condition decides match; when it matches more than one source row per target row Oracle raises ORA-30926 . Dedupe the source first. WHEN MATCHED THEN UPDATE / WHEN NOT MATCHED THEN INSERT are the two usual branches; there is also DELETE inside the matched branch for reconcile-style cleanup. There is no "are you sure?" In SQL*Plus and SQLcl you can set SET DEFINE tricks, and SQL Developer supports "commit on close" prompts — but the reliable discipline is count first : SELECT COUNT * … WHERE … the exact filter before UPDATE / DELETE , then verify SQL%ROWCOUNT after. For purging massive chunks of a table, DELETE in batches or well-designed TRUNCATE , which is DDL and drops the data outright — see the DDL page for why TRUNCATE is fast, permanent, and not rollback-able. RETURNING works with INSERT , UPDATE , and DELETE — for BULK statements arrays you use BULK COLLECT INTO , which we keep for the PL/SQL page .
