INSERT INTO customers customer_id, customer_name, region_id, credit_limit VALUES 101, 'Acme Corp', 1, 50000 ; -- Fewer columns: credit_limit defaults to NULL INSERT INTO customers customer_id, customer_name, region_id VALUES 102, 'Beta Ltd', 2 ; INSERT INTO orders_archive order_id, customer_id, order_date, total_amount SELECT order_id, customer_id, order_date, total_amount FROM orders WHERE order_date < DATE '2025-01-01'; UPDATE customers SET credit_limit = credit_limit * 1.05 WHERE region_id = 1; -- only Western customers -- DANGER: no WHERE -> every row, same value UPDATE customers SET credit_limit = 0; DELETE FROM orders WHERE order_id = 999; -- "1 rows deleted" — verify ROWCOUNT before commit MERGE INTO customers c USING SELECT customer_id, credit_limit FROM staged_limits s ON c.customer_id = s.customer_id WHEN MATCHED THEN UPDATE SET c.credit_limit = s.credit_limit WHEN NOT MATCHED THEN INSERT customer_id, customer_name, credit_limit, region_id VALUES s.customer_id, 'NEW via merge', s.credit_limit, NULL ; INSERT ALL INTO orders_archive order_id, total_amount VALUES order_id, total_amount INTO orders_flagged order_id, total_amount VALUES order_id, total_amount SELECT order_id, total_amount FROM orders WHERE total_amount > 10000; INSERT FIRST WHEN total_amount >= 10000 THEN INTO orders_large order_id, total_amount VALUES order_id, total_amount WHEN total_amount >= 1000 THEN INTO orders_medium order_id, total_amount VALUES order_id, total_amount ELSE INTO orders_small order_id, total_amount VALUES order_id, total_amount SELECT order_id, total_amount FROM orders; DECLARE v_id NUMBER; BEGIN INSERT INTO orders customer_id, total_amount VALUES 42, 1234.56 RETURNING order_id INTO v_id; DBMS_OUTPUT.PUT_LINE 'New order id: ' || v_id ; END;

pages.title: Filtering
pages.description: The full comparison toolkit: =, <>, >, <, >=, <=, AND/OR/NOT, IN and NOT IN, BETWEEN, LIKE with the % and _ wildcards, IS NULL and IS NOT NULL, and EXISTS / NOT EXISTS.
headings: AND, OR, NOT — and the precedence trap
IS NULL and IS NOT NULL
pages.content: Comparison operators AND, OR, NOT — and the precedence trap IN and NOT IN BETWEEN LIKE and wildcards IS NULL and IS NOT NULL EXISTS and NOT EXISTS , >, =, WHERE decides which rows survive. The operators here are the words every business question gets translated into — "customers who have not reordered", "orders in the last week", "products whose name contains 'Pro'". Each operator has a NULL-rich trap, so the examples deliberately poke at them. Combine conditions with AND both must hold , OR either may hold , and NOT invert . NOT binds tightest, then AND , then OR — and the order surprises people: IN is a list membership test — shorthand for a chain of = with OR . NOT IN is its logical inverse, but NOT IN plus a NULL in the list becomes the classic empty-result surprise: BETWEEN a AND b is inclusive on both ends : x BETWEEN 10 AND 20 is x >= 10 AND x . It is not a "between but excluding the edges" operator. For dates, remember the DATE column carries a time component — WHERE order_date BETWEEN DATE '2026-08-01' AND DATE '2026-08-31' misses anything on the 31st after midnight. The robust pattern is a half-open range: LIKE does pattern matching on strings with two wildcards: % = any sequence of characters including none , _ = exactly one character. The correct way to test for missing values: EXISTS tests whether a subquery returns at least one row. It evaluates to TRUE/FALSE, never NULL, which makes it immune to the NOT IN trap and usually the fastest way to express "has at least one X": ESCAPE lets you search for the wildcard characters themselves: LIKE '50\%' ESCAPE '\' matches a literal 50% . Case matters: LIKE 'tech%' will not match TechCorp . Wrap in LOWER / UPPER on both sides if you want case-insensitive, at a performance cost the index page shows why . A leading wildcard '%...' cannot use a normal B-tree index efficiently — a classic performance smell. Never equate a value to NULL with = NULL — that is always UNKNOWN , so the condition silently matches nothing. Use IS NULL / IS NOT NULL . When in doubt, parenthesize. Mixed AND / OR without brackets is the most common "why is my count wrong" bug in SQL. If the subquery feeding a NOT IN can return NULL, prefer NOT EXISTS below — it has no such trap. This single rule avoids a whole class of production bugs. Inside an EXISTS subquery the SELECT list is irrelevant — convention is SELECT 1 . And because ExISTS stops at the first matching row, it is usually faster than COUNT * > 0 against a large child table. Correlations like this are the heart of the subqueries page . Operator Meaning Example = Equal region_id = 3 or != Not equal Oracle accepts both credit_limit 0 > / < Greater / less than total_amount > 500 >= / <= Greater-or-equal / less-or-equal total_amount >= 500 Pattern Matches 'A%' Anything starting with A '%A%' Anything containing A '_A%' Any character, then A, then anything '%o' Anything ending in o A% %A% _A% %o SELECT order_id, total_amount FROM orders WHERE customer_id = 42 AND total_amount >= 100 AND total_amount < 1000; -- inclusive/exclusive range -- Intended: region 1 OR region 3 AND over 500 SELECT order_id FROM orders WHERE region_id = 1 OR region_id = 3 AND total_amount > 500; -- Reality: region_id = 1 OR region_id = 3 AND total_amount > 500 -- Fix: parenthesize the OR WHERE region_id = 1 OR region_id = 3 AND total_amount > 500; SELECT customer_name FROM customers WHERE region_id IN 2, 4 ; -- regions 2 or 4 -- The trap: if any returned region is NULL, this returns ZERO rows SELECT customer_name FROM customers WHERE region_id NOT IN SELECT region_id FROM regions ; -- Because: x NOT IN 1, 2, NULL ==> x 1 AND x 2 AND x NULL -- ... AND UNKNOWN ==> never TRUE SELECT order_id FROM orders WHERE total_amount BETWEEN 100 AND 500; -- 100 and 500 included WHERE order_date >= DATE '2026-08-01' AND order_date < DATE '2026-09-01' -- exclusive upper bound SELECT customer_name FROM customers WHERE customer_name LIKE 'Tech%' -- starts with Tech OR customer_name LIKE '% Systems'; -- or ends with ' Systems' -- Customers with no credit limit set SELECT customer_name FROM customers WHERE credit_limit IS NULL; -- Orders that are not voided a non-null flag SELECT order_id FROM orders WHERE void_date IS NOT NULL; -- Customers with at least one order SELECT c.customer_name FROM customers c WHERE EXISTS SELECT 1 FROM orders o WHERE o.customer_id = c.customer_id ; -- Customers with no order yet safe version of NOT IN SELECT c.customer_name FROM customers c WHERE NOT EXISTS SELECT 1 FROM orders o WHERE o.customer_id = c.customer_id ;

pages.title: Grouping & aggregate functions
pages.description: COUNT, SUM, AVG, MIN, MAX; GROUP BY and HAVING; and the reporting workhorses ROLLUP, CUBE, and GROUPING SETS with GROUPING and GROUPING_ID.
headings: GROUP BY — one row per distinct group
pages.content: The five core aggregates GROUP BY — one row per distinct group HAVING — filtering groups, not rows ROLLUP, CUBE, GROUPING SETS GROUPING and GROUPING_ID Aggregates collapse many rows into one number. The moment your question is "how many", "total", or "average" — grouped by something — you are writing aggregate SQL. The two mistakes that dominate here are confusing WHERE with HAVING , and forgetting GROUP BY only survives with aggregates on the column list. GROUP BY collapses rows that share the listed columns and lets you aggregate within each group. The rules that cause the classic ORA-00979 : WHERE filters rows before grouping; HAVING filters groups after aggregation. You cannot put an aggregate in WHERE : The same question "filter after grouping" also works for group membership: HAVING COUNT * > 1 finds duplicate keys, a daily check on data loads: These three extend GROUP BY to produce the subtotal rows that reports overwhelmingly want. They appear in reporting and analytics: A subtotal row produced by ROLLUP shows NULL in the rolled-up columns — but NULL can be a real value too. GROUPING col returns 1 when the row is a subtotal for that column and 0 otherwise, letting you label rows safely: Every column in the SELECT list must be either a grouped column or inside an aggregate — nothing else. Use the grouped column's raw name, not its alias, in GROUP BY . You group by a column you do not even need to output, so you can aggregate by things you keep hidden. SUM total_amount on a table whose column is entirely NULL returns NULL , which then poisons anything downstream. Wrap with NVL SUM total_amount , 0 when a zero result is the meaning you need. GROUPING_ID returns a packed number for many columns at once e.g. GROUPING_ID a, b = 0 for detail, 3 for the grand total and is what analytic tools use to tag result rows. Tuple-ish — treat it as the multi-column cousin of GROUPING . Aggregate What it returns NULL behavior COUNT * Number of rows Counts every row, even all-NULL COUNT col Number of non-NULL values in col Skips NULLs SUM col Total of the non-NULL values Skips NULLs; all-NULL → NULL not 0 AVG col Average of the non-NULL values MIN col Smallest value MAX col Largest value Extension Produces Typical use ROLLUP a, b Grouped rows + subtotals rolling up the columns a+b, a, grand total Monthly revenue + yearly totals CUBE a, b Every combination of subtotals a+b, a, b, grand total Multi-dimensional drill-down reports GROUPING SETS a , b Exactly the grouped sets you list, no more Two separate summaries in one pass SELECT COUNT * AS order_count, SUM total_amount AS revenue, AVG total_amount AS avg_order, MIN total_amount AS smallest, MAX total_amount AS largest FROM orders; SELECT r.region_name, COUNT o.order_id AS orders_count, SUM o.total_amount AS revenue FROM orders o JOIN customers c ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id JOIN regions r ON r.region_id = c.region_id GROUP BY r.region_name ORDER BY revenue DESC; SELECT r.region_name, SUM o.total_amount AS revenue FROM orders o JOIN customers c ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id JOIN regions r ON r.region_id = c.region_id WHERE o.order_date >= DATE '2026-01-01' -- drop rows first GROUP BY r.region_name HAVING SUM o.total_amount >= 5000 -- then drop groups ORDER BY revenue DESC; SELECT region_name, COUNT * FROM regions GROUP BY region_name HAVING COUNT * > 1; SELECT r.region_name, COUNT * AS customers FROM customers c JOIN regions r ON r.region_id = c.region_id GROUP BY ROLLUP r.region_name ; -- Rows: Westerners / Easterners / NULL, grand total -- The NULL subtotal row is exactly why GROUPING matters below SELECT CASE WHEN GROUPING r.region_name = 1 THEN 'ALL REGIONS' ELSE r.region_name END AS region, COUNT * AS customers FROM customers c JOIN regions r ON r.region_id = c.region_id GROUP BY ROLLUP r.region_name ;

pages.title: Indexes & performance
pages.description: B-tree, bitmap, and function-based indexes; composite indexes; EXPLAIN PLAN and DBMS_XPLAN; full table scan vs index scan; nested loops, hash join, and merge join; statistics and the optimizer; and the bind-variable habit.
headings: Full table scan vs index scan — and the selectivity test
pages.content: What an index is Index types Explain plan and DBMS_XPLAN Full table scan vs index scan — and the selectivity test Join methods Statistics and the optimizer Bind variables Avoiding functions on indexed columns The optimizer turns your SELECT into a plan — choices like "full table scan or slow index probe", "hash join or nested loops". You cannot make Oracle fast by wishing; you make it fast by giving the optimizer good indexes, true statistics, and predictable expressions. This page is the vocabulary for that conversation. An index is a separate structure holding sorted copies of some columns plus a pointer to the row. The database uses it to jump to matching rows instead of scanning every row. The cost: every insert/update/delete must also maintain the index. The plan is how you argue with facts. The modern route avoids the old EXPLAIN PLAN FOR buffers and reads the live plan straight back: What to read in the plan output, top down: The optimizer picks per selectivity how many rows pass vs exist . An index that would return 90% of a small table is slower than just reading the table — the optimizer knows, and so should you when you look at a plan and see a FULL scan on a small table. That is often correct, not a bug. The optimizer guesses from statistics gathered by DBMS_STATS — row counts, distinct values, histograms. Stale statistics produce comically wrong plans. Refresh them after large loads: Oracle prepares statements once and reuses the plan while values change — if you use bind variables instead of splicing constants: The single most common performance self-sabotage: wrapping a column in a function in WHERE , so the index on the raw column is unusable: Bitmap indexes shine in analytics and die on frequent DML — heavy single-row updates block them. Keep them to read-mostly warehouses. A composite index's leading column dominates: an index region_id, created_dt serves filters on region_id efficiently and region_id, created_dt together, but a filter on created_dt alone cannot use it well. Order your columns: equality first, then range. Operation — TABLE ACCESS FULL bad for selective filters , INDEX RANGE SCAN / INDEX UNIQUE SCAN good , joins as NESTED LOOPS / HASH JOIN . Rows / Bytes / Cost columns and, with ALLSTATS LAST , the actual Rows used — divergence between estimated and actual is your smoking gun. Note at the bottom a warning when the optimizer had stale stats. Automated stats jobs exist, but a big overnight load that changes table size materially still deserves a targeted gather. Histograms matter for skewed columns; they are gathered automatically but check the plan note if you suspect them. On LOWER name equality use a function-based index — CREATE INDEX i ON t LOWER name — and match the expression exactly. The NVL col, 0 and TO_DATE -wrap-RANGE patterns from earlier pages are the same disease. Nested loops degrade fast if the optimizer underestimates the driver — that is the #1 reason a "fast" query explodes as data grows, and the first thing DBMS_XPLAN 's actual-vs-estimate comparison exposes. Applications that generate a fresh SQL string per value cause hard parsing : each query is compiled, serially-ish, and the shared pool thrashes. Bind-variable-native drivers JDBC/Oracle Client, SQLcl scripts with & substitution handled server-side avoid it. The exception that proves the rule: data-skewed columns may deliberately want literals via SQL_PLAN_MANAGEMENT adaptive plans. Scan reports for function-wrapped indexed columns and LIKE '%…' leading wildcards — together they account for more "why is this query slow" tickets than any other symptom. Index type Design Best for B-tree Standard balanced tree on key values Selectivity, equality and range lookups on most columns Bitmap One bit vector per distinct value Low-cardinality columns gender, status in warehouse reads Function-based Index on an expression: LOWER name , TRUNC date Queries that always filter by a function of the column Composite Multiple columns in one index Queries whose WHERE/ORDER use several columns together Plan step When the optimizer chooses it TABLE ACCESS FULL Filter selects a large share of rows, or there is no useful index INDEX UNIQUE SCAN Lookup by primary/unique key — at most one row INDEX RANGE SCAN Selective non-unique or range lookup — few rows INDEX FAST FULL / SKIP SCAN Covering or low-selectivity access on mostly-empty ranges Method Strategy Good when NESTED LOOPS For each outer row, probe the inner table via index Small driving set + indexed inner; few returned rows HASH JOIN Build a hash of one side; probe with the other Large joins with no usable index on the inner MERGE JOIN Sort both sides, then merge Pre-sorted or range join inputs CREATE INDEX idx_cust_region ON customers region_id ; CREATE INDEX idx_orders_total ON orders total_amount DESC ; DROP INDEX idx_orders_total; SELECT index_name, column_name FROM user_ind_columns; EXPLAIN PLAN FOR SELECT customer_name FROM customers WHERE credit_limit > 10000; SELECT * FROM TABLE DBMS_XPLAN.DISPLAY ; -- Better: from the actual run SQLcl / SQL Developer display this natively SELECT * FROM TABLE DBMS_XPLAN.DISPLAY_CURSOR FORMAT => 'ALLSTATS LAST' ; EXEC DBMS_STATS.GATHER_TABLE_STATS USER, 'ORDERS' ; -- or the draw-all plan EXEC DBMS_STATS.GATHER_SCHEMA_STATS USER ; -- In PL/SQL the :name binds automatically: SELECT customer_name FROM customers WHERE region_id = :r; -- Hard-coding literals re-parses and can suffer literal explosion SELECT customer_name FROM customers WHERE region_id = 1; -- Index on order_date is IGNORED: SELECT * FROM orders WHERE TRUNC order_date = DATE '2026-08-15'; -- Same idea, index-friendly: SELECT * FROM orders WHERE order_date >= DATE '2026-08-15' AND order_date < DATE '2026-08-16';

pages.title: Joins
pages.description: Inner, left/right/full outer, cross, and self joins; equi vs non-equi joins; the ANSI JOIN ... ON syntax; and how to recognize the legacy Oracle outer-join operator (+) you will find in old code.
headings: ANSI JOIN vs the old Oracle (+) syntax
Choosing the join in one table
pages.content: Setting the scene: the data Inner join — only matching rows Left / right / full outer joins Cross join Self join Equi and non-equi joins ANSI JOIN vs the old Oracle + syntax Choosing the join in one table A join combines rows from two tables by matching values — usually a parent's primary key against a child's foreign key. The only hard part is deciding which rows survive when a match is missing . That decision is what separates INNER, OUTER, and the rest. The examples use the running schema. A customer belongs to a region via region_id , and orders belong to customers. Two regions have customers; one region is empty; one customer has no region; one customer has no orders — which buys us every join case at once. An inner join keeps rows that have a match on both sides. Rows without a key match simply vanish: An outer join keeps the unmatched rows of one or both sides, padding the other side's columns with NULL : A cross join produces every pair of rows — no condition at all. It is the Cartesian product and grows explosively N×M rows , so it is only for generating combinations or testing: Joining a table to itself is how you pair each row with another row in the same table — employees with their manager, cities with neighboring cities. The trick is aliasing: Read it as "for every a , find a different b in the same region." Self-joins with WHERE / ON filters give you pairings, hierarchies, and "next similar row" logic. Almost every join matches on = — that is an equi join . When you need a range or an inequality instead, it is a non-equi join : Non-equi joins are how you attach a "which tier" answer to every row — but they cannot use a plain B-tree foreign key, so watch the plan the performance page covers why . The modern form you have just seen — JOIN … ON — is the ANSI standard and what all new code should use. It also works for outer, cross, and self joins, and the join condition is explicit and local to the join. Legacy code from before Oracle 9i expresses an outer join with + placed on the side that is missing values — the "optional" side. The full outer example rewritten: INNER JOIN and just JOIN are the same thing. Because JOIN is a start-of-clause keyword and , -comma joins behave identically, join type and join method do not decide the plan — the optimizer does. Write what you mean. When an outer join does match, the non-matching side comes back NULL — so filtering with WHERE r.region_name = 'West' silently turns your outer join back into an inner one it drops the NULL rows . Move the filter into the ON clause or use IS NULL deliberately e.g. "customers with no orders" : WHERE o.order_id IS NULL . Read + fluently but never write it: the ANSI form is clearer, handles FULL OUTER which + cannot , and avoids the notorious "ORA-01417: a table may be outer joined to at most one other table". Every shop-standard is ANSI joins today. Join Keeps Classic use LEFT OUTER JOIN All left rows + matches All customers, even region-less RIGHT OUTER JOIN All right rows + matches All regions, even empty ones FULL OUTER JOIN All rows from both sides Find unmatched on either side I need… Write… Result Rows that exist on both sides INNER JOIN … ON Matching pairs only All of the left, plus what matches LEFT JOIN … ON Left rows with NULL padding on the right Both sides, even unmatched FULL OUTER JOIN … ON Everything, NULLs on whichever side fails Every combination N × M rows Rows compared within one table JOIN table t2 ON … Pairs inside the same table SELECT c.customer_name, r.region_name FROM customers c INNER JOIN regions r ON r.region_id = c.region_id; -- Every customer must have a matching region row or it is dropped SELECT c.customer_name, NVL r.region_name, 'No region' AS region FROM customers c LEFT JOIN regions r ON r.region_id = c.region_id; SELECT c.customer_name, r.region_name FROM customers c CROSS JOIN regions r; -- N customers × M regions = expensive SELECT a.customer_name AS customer_a, b.customer_name AS customer_b, r.region_name FROM customers a JOIN customers b ON b.region_id = a.region_id JOIN regions r ON r.region_id = a.region_id WHERE a.customer_id b.customer_id ORDER BY r.region_name; CREATE TABLE payment_brackets lower_bound NUMBER NOT NULL, upper_bound NUMBER NOT NULL, fee NUMBER ; SELECT o.order_id, pb.fee FROM orders o JOIN payment_brackets pb ON o.total_amount >= pb.lower_bound AND o.total_amount < pb.upper_bound; SELECT c.customer_name, r.region_name FROM customers c, regions r WHERE r.region_id + = c.region_id; -- + marks the side that may be absent

pages.title: JSON, XML & modern Oracle SQL
pages.description: JSON columns and IS JSON, JSON_VALUE, JSON_QUERY, JSON_TABLE, XML data and XMLTYPE, and SQL macros — the modern Oracle database beyond the relational model.
pages.content: JSON columns and IS JSON JSON_VALUE, JSON_QUERY, JSON_EXISTS JSON_TABLE — JSON as rows XML data and XMLTYPE SQL macros 23c Oracle stopped being "just rows and columns" a long time ago. You can store a JSON document in a column, query inside it with dot-syntax and functions, load XML from old integrations into XMLTYPE , and even write SQL macros that act like template queries. Knowing how far you can push this decides whether "unstructured" data stays out of your database or in it, usefully. A JSON column 23c or a CLOB with a CHECK col IS JSON constraint stores one JSON document per row, validated on write: Pull a scalar out of a document with JSON_VALUE , get an object or array back with JSON_QUERY , and test for existence with JSON_EXISTS — all using dot notation paths: JSON_TABLE shreds a JSON array into relational rows — the bridge that lets you JOIN a document against ordinary tables: It behaves like a lateral inline view: for each order row, produce one output row per array element. This is how you write genuinely relational queries over JSON payloads. The XML counterpart — used where SOAP feeds, B2B messages, and old interfaces still speak XML: store documents as XMLTYPE , query them with EXTRACT / EXTRACTVALUE older or XMLTABLE modern : A SQL macro is a PL/SQL function the optimizer expands into your query at parse time — write a reusable fragment once, and get inlined logic with proper optimizer visibility in every caller. The pattern you'll see: a "scalar" macro returning an expression: IS JSON validates syntax at insert; queries can also test WHERE attributes IS JSON . There is fast JSON full-text style query support via JSON indexes and the JSON_EXISTS / JSON_VALUE family below. Prefer XMLTABLE over the legacy EXTRACT / EXTRACTVALUE — the latter have been deprecated-ish for years. Modern Oracle is JSON-first for new schemas; XML skills remain vital for the SOAP-era systems still running in enterprises. The classic pairing mistake: JSON_VALUE at the end of an object path gives NULL it wants a scalar ; JSON_QUERY at the end of a scalar path gives NULL it wants a container . If a lookup "silently" returns nothing, check which one you used. Macros differ from ordinary functions in one crucial way: the optimizer sees the body , so it can prune, reorder, and index accordingly. An ordinary PL/SQL function in a query is a black box that silently blocks some optimizations. Reaching for a macro is the modern fix and the PL/SQL page has the function basics . Function Returns NULL when… JSON_VALUE A scalar value text/number/date Path missing or a JSON object/array at the end JSON_QUERY A JSON object or array as JSON Path missing or a scalar at the end JSON_EXISTS TRUE/FALSE whether the path matches N/A -- 21c style: CLOB with a JSON check CREATE TABLE orders order_id NUMBER PRIMARY KEY, attributes CLOB CONSTRAINT ck_orders_json CHECK attributes IS JSON ; -- 23c native: -- order_id NUMBER PRIMARY KEY, attributes JSON SELECT o.order_id, JSON_VALUE o.attributes, '$.shipment.courier' AS courier, JSON_QUERY o.attributes, '$.packages' AS packages, CASE WHEN JSON_EXISTS o.attributes, '$.fraud_flag' THEN 'flagged' ELSE 'ok' END AS fraud FROM orders o; SELECT o.order_id, p.tracking_no, p.weight_kg FROM orders o, JSON_TABLE o.attributes, '$.packages * ' COLUMNS tracking_no VARCHAR2 20 PATH '$.tracking', weight_kg NUMBER PATH '$.weight' p; SELECT x.order_no, x.amount FROM orders_xml o, XMLTABLE '/order' PASSING o.doc COLUMNS order_no NUMBER PATH 'number', amount NUMBER PATH 'total' x; CREATE FUNCTION tax_amount amt NUMBER RETURN VARCHAR2 SQL_MACRO SCALAR IS BEGIN RETURN 'amt * 0.10'; -- optimizer folds this into the query END; SELECT order_id, tax_amount total_amount AS tax FROM orders;

pages.title: Oracle-specific SQL
pages.description: DUAL, ROWID and ROWNUM, NVL and DECODE, CONNECT BY, date and number format models, USER and SYS_CONTEXT, and the USER_ / ALL_ / DBA_ data dictionary views.
pages.content: DUAL ROWNUM and ROWID NVL, NVL2, NULLIF, DECODE CONNECT BY Date and number format models USER and SYS_CONTEXT Data dictionary views These are the pieces that mark a statement as distinctly Oracle . Some are quirks you must read in other people's code the + join, DECODE , others are daily tools unique to Oracle DUAL , ROWNUM , data dictionary views . Knowing them separates "writes SQL" from "writes Oracle SQL". DUAL is a one-row, one-column dummy table used when you need a SELECT with no real table — running functions and literals: The null-handling quartet and Oracle's home-grown conditional were covered in depth on the single-row functions page . The shorthand: NVL a,b = "a unless NULL, then b"; DECODE x, a, r1, b, r2, def = equality-dispatch. You will see both everywhere in existing code, and you will write COALESCE and CASE instead. The tree-walker is the advanced querying page's subject; the Oracle-only bits to remember here: START WITH , LEVEL , PRIOR , ORDER SIBLINGS BY , and CONNECT_BY_ROOT / CONNECT_BY_ISCYCLE pseudo-columns for root tracking and cycle detection. Format models are the mask vocabulary you hand to TO_CHAR / TO_DATE and the NLS session settings. The most used: SYS_CONTEXT reads values any application namespace can set — this is the hook Virtual Private Database uses to restrict rows per session e.g. salesperson sees only their own accounts . The foundational three families plus the most-called siblings all appear on the foundations page . A practical quick-reference for the work-week: Since Oracle 23c you can often write SELECT SYSDATE; without FROM dual — but FROM dual works in every version and is what legacy code expects. Keep writing it. Prefer FETCH FIRST for new code the basic-querying page covers it . ROWNUM survival skill is for reading legacy scripts, and ROWID for quick de-dupe surgery where no unique key exists. A format mask literal that is not a recognisable element must be quoted: TO_CHAR SYSDATE, 'YYYY"Q"Q' . And vague display formats fail silently in surprising ways once the raw value drifts — always pair TO_DATE with the matching mask. When troubleshooting, always ask the dictionary first — the answer to "why is this insert slow / why this error" is usually one dictionary lookup away from a concrete fact instead of folklore. Pseudo-column What it is Gotcha ROWNUM A running number assigned as Oracle returns each row Assigned BEFORE sorting — a top-N trap unless you nest ROWID The physical address of the row on disk Changes when the row moves; never a durable key Element Meaning Example output DD-MON-YYYY Day – month abbrev – year 15-AUG-2026 DD/MM/YYYY Day/month/year locale-neutral 15/08/2026 HH24:MI:SS 24-hour time with seconds 14:30:00 YYYY-MM-DD ISO date 2026-08-15 FM Trim padding FMMonth FM 'Month' → 'August' YYYY-MM-DD\ HH24:MI Literal characters in quotes 2026-08-15T14:30 Month August 9 / 0 Digit placeholders 0 pads, 9 leaves blank 999.99 $ Currency symbol $1,234.50 , Thousands separator 1,234 S Sign placement, front or trailing MI S9999 / 9999MI View Answers USER_TABLES / ALL_TABLES Which tables exist, rows, blocks, logging USER_TAB_COLUMNS Columns, types, nullability, defaults USER_CONSTRAINTS / USER_CONS_COLUMNS Keys and rules and which columns they cover USER_INDEXES / USER_IND_COLUMNS Indexes and what they index ALL_OBJECTS Everything you can see, across schemas, with object type DBA_USERS Database accounts privileged USER_SEQUENCES Sequences and their CACHE/MAXVALUE settings SELECT SYSDATE FROM dual; -- today SELECT USER FROM dual; -- your schema name SELECT 60 * 24 * 60 AS minutes FROM dual; -- WRONG intent: five arbitrary rows then sorted SELECT * FROM orders WHERE ROWNUM SELECT MIN ROWID FROM customers x WHERE x.customer_id = c.customer_id ; SELECT TO_CHAR SYSDATE, 'DD-MON-YYYY HH24:MI' FROM dual; SELECT TO_CHAR 1234.5, '$999,999.99', 'NLS_CURRENCY=USD' FROM dual; SELECT USER FROM dual; -- schema name e.g. HR SELECT SYS_CONTEXT 'USERENV', 'SESSION_USER' FROM dual; -- logged-in user SELECT SYS_CONTEXT 'USERENV', 'DB_NAME' FROM dual; -- database instance

pages.title: Learning Oracle SQL — where to start
pages.description: SQL is the language you use every time you touch an Oracle database: asking questions of tables, changing rows, defining objects, and tuning how the database answers. This section walks the full roadmap — from schema and SELECT to analytic functions, partitioning, and PL/SQL — with every example written for a real Oracle database.
headings: A single worked example that carries through
Quick reference: the four SQL statement families
pages.content: The learning path A single worked example that carries through Quick reference: the four SQL statement families The pages are ordered so each builds on the previous one. Work through the foundations first what a table is, what the data types mean , then querying, then joins and subqueries, and only then move to the object-definition and performance topics. The whole section is written against an Oracle database — SQL*Plus, SQL Developer, or sql in SQLcl — so every example runs as-is. Several pages reuse the same small schema so you can follow one story from first SELECT to analytic query. It models a simplified sales table that an order-to-cash process might own: The regions → customers → orders chain is a classic one-to-many parent → child relationship, and it reappears in the joins, subqueries, DML, and index pages so the examples stay concrete. Every statement you write falls into one of these categories. Knowing the family tells you whether the statement can be rolled back DML yes, DDL no and who is allowed to run it. You do not need an installed Oracle database to start. SQLcl and SQL Developer connect to any free Oracle Database Free 23ai instance, and the Oracle Live SQL website lets you run many of these examples in the browser. The data dictionary views used here USER_TABLES , ALL_OBJECTS , … exist in every version. Learn without breaking things. Examples throughout this section include UPDATE , DELETE , MERGE , TRUNCATE , DROP , and trigger code. They are illustrative and version-dependent — run them only against a disposable learning instance a throwaway schema or a free practice database , never production. The pages with data-destroying statements mark them with DANGER callouts so you can spot them at a glance. Want a copy-paste runnable dataset? The DML page includes an INSERT block that populates these three tables with enough rows for the later examples. A common beginner trap in Oracle: pay attention to DDL's implicit commit . Running CREATE INDEX in the middle of a batch permanently commits all the work you did before it — which is usually not what you wanted. Family What it does Verbs Transactional? DDL Define and change database objects CREATE, ALTER, DROP, TRUNCATE, RENAME, COMMENT Commits implicitly; cannot be rolled back DML Query and modify the rows inside tables SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE, MERGE SELECT is read-only; the rest are part of your transaction DCL Grant and revoke security privileges GRANT, REVOKE Commits implicitly TCL Control your transaction COMMIT, ROLLBACK, SAVEPOINT These are the transaction itself CREATE TABLE regions region_id NUMBER PRIMARY KEY, region_name VARCHAR2 30 NOT NULL ; CREATE TABLE customers customer_id NUMBER PRIMARY KEY, customer_name VARCHAR2 60 NOT NULL, region_id NUMBER REFERENCES regions region_id , credit_limit NUMBER 12,2 ; CREATE TABLE orders order_id NUMBER PRIMARY KEY, customer_id NUMBER NOT NULL REFERENCES customers customer_id , order_date DATE DEFAULT SYSDATE, total_amount NUMBER 12,2 NOT NULL ;

pages.title: Partitioning & large data
pages.description: Range, list, hash, and interval partitioning; partition pruning; local vs global indexes; and parallel SQL basics for big tables.
pages.content: The methods Partition pruning Local and global indexes Parallel SQL basics When a table grows past a few hundred million rows, Oracle can split it into partitions — separate physical segments that still expose one table name to SQL. You query the same way; the optimizer just touches only the partitions it needs partition pruning . Partitioning is the difference between a table that slows everyone down and one that quietly gets faster. Or the hands-off INTERVAL variant that makes the monthly partition the moment you insert its first row: When the WHERE references the partition key, the optimizer can restrict its work to a subset of partitions — often one. That is the whole performance point: the query "touches only January" even if the table holds ten years' rows: A local index lives inside each partition and is pruned with it. A global index is one structure spanning every partition — useful when you need a unique key on a column that is not the partition key. Remember the interaction with maintenance: a global index can degrade when you DROP PARTITION without updating it. For genuinely heavy reads — aggregating a whole big table, a full scan — the parallel query feature splits the work across multiple server processes. The optimizer decides parallelism from table/partition degree and the PARALLEL hint: Parallelism shines on big full scans; it hurts on tiny OLTP lookups setup overhead swamps the gain . Don't hard-wire high degrees: honor the datafile/partition degree set by the DBA, or let the hints pick. Parallel DML ALTER SESSION ENABLE PARALLEL DML for big loads exists but adds locks/transactions complexity — treat it as a DBA-level skill. A filter that does not reference the partition key forces a full scan of every partition unless another index covers it . Design the partition key around your most common query filters — for orders that is the date. Real-world recipe for a large table: RANGE or INTERVAL partition by date → most queries prune to one partition → local indexes match the keys you query within a partition → a parallel full scan for the quarterly analytics job. That combination is how data-warehouse tables stay responsive at the hundreds-of-GB scale. Method Rows go into a partition by… Best for RANGE A column's value falling into a range DATEs, IDs Time-series: orders by month LIST An explicit value list Region codes, status values HASH A hash of the partition key spread evenly Even distribution, when no natural list/range works INTERVAL RANGE, but new partitions created automatically 23ai/12c Never-miss-a-month append-only data Index type Scope Note Local index One index per partition, aligned with it Dropping/adding a partition maintains only its own index — the usual choice for partitioned tables Global index Covers all partitions in one index across the table Non-partitioned index on a partitioned table; global-partitioned indexes also exist CREATE TABLE orders order_id NUMBER, customer_id NUMBER, order_date DATE, total_amount NUMBER 12,2 PARTITION BY RANGE order_date PARTITION p2024 VALUES LESS THAN DATE '2025-01-01' , PARTITION p2025 VALUES LESS THAN DATE '2026-01-01' , PARTITION pfuture VALUES LESS THAN MAXVALUE ; CREATE TABLE orders order_id NUMBER, customer_id NUMBER, order_date DATE, total_amount NUMBER 12,2 PARTITION BY RANGE order_date INTERVAL NUMTOYMINTERVAL 1, 'MONTH' PARTITION p_initial VALUES LESS THAN DATE '2025-01-01' ; SELECT * FROM orders WHERE order_date >= DATE '2026-01-01' AND order_date < DATE '2026-02-01'; -- Partition Pruned: p2026-01 SELECT /*+ PARALLEL o, 4 */ region_id, COUNT * FROM orders o GROUP BY region_id;

pages.title: Blocks, variables & scope
pages.description: The DECLARE / BEGIN / EXCEPTION / END skeleton, anonymous blocks, comments and DBMS_OUTPUT.PUT_LINE, variables and constants, %TYPE and %ROWTYPE anchoring, bind variables, and how scope flows through nested blocks.
pages.content: Block structure Anonymous blocks Comments and output Variables, constants, initialization %TYPE and %ROWTYPE — anchor to the schema Bind variables Scope: local, global, package Every PL/SQL program is a block . Learning the block's skeleton first makes every later topic procedures, packages, triggers feel like variations on it. This page also settles the variable rules that govern everything you write — including the %TYPE / %ROWTYPE anchoring that is a PL/SQL signature skill. A block that is not stored in the database runs once and is gone — that is an anonymous block . It is the scratchpad: testing logic, running ad-hoc SQL, wrapping a multi-step job in a script: DBMS_OUTPUT.PUT_LINE writes to the server message buffer that the session displays. It is for development and small volumes — for production logging you use your own tables or DBMS_APPLICATION_INFO see the performance page , never PUT_LINE on huge loops. The single most valuable PL/SQL habit. Instead of guessing a column's type, you anchor your variable to it — if the table changes, your code follows: Outside PL/SQL-anonymous names, : variables in dynamic SQL and SQLcl are bind variables : placeholders the server parses once and fills per call the performance rule from the SQL section . In a PL/SQL script you can declare them with VARIABLE : Inside standalone PL/SQL you rarely need VARIABLE — your v_ variables are the in-memory values, and bind variables come back into play with EXECUTE IMMEDIATE and applications that drive PL/SQL from Java/Python. SET SERVEROUTPUT ON makes DBMS_OUTPUT visible; without it nothing prints. Anonymous blocks cannot be called by other code — turn them into procedures/functions when other code must invoke them. They are perfect for one-off PL/SQL in a migration script or a test harness. Variable naming convention v_ , constant c_ , parameter p_ , cursor c_ / cur_ — shops differ but naming is expected. CONSTANT values cannot be reassigned; declaring them documents intent and lets the compiler catch mistakes. Don't initialize in DECLARE with expressions that fail e.g. a SELECT — keep that in BEGIN. %TYPE tracks a single column's type, precision, nullability. %ROWTYPE gives you one record with all columns — dot-reference them as v_row.column . SELECT * INTO v_row works because the record's column list matches the table — the reason anchoring is safer than spelling out dozens of scalars. A nested block may shadow an outer name by redeclaring it — then both "exist" but the inner one wins. Shadowing is legal and a common source of "why did my variable change" bugs. The compiler will often warn; don't rely on that — avoid reusing names. Section Mandatory? Contents DECLARE No Variables, constants, types, cursors BEGIN ... END Yes The executable statements — the only required pair EXCEPTION Error handlers covered on the exceptions page labels Optional > labels and trailing / in SQL*Plus/SQLcl Scope Visible where Lives where Local Only inside the block that declares it and nested blocks A block's DECLARE section Global-ish Visible to nested blocks declared beneath it An outer block's DECLARE, seen by inner blocks Package-level Across every program in the package, for the session A package spec's or body's declarations Subprogram parameter Inside that procedure/function only The IN/OUT parameter list s DECLARE section" , "Global-ish", "Visible to nested blocks declared beneath it", "An outer block s or body DECLARE v_message VARCHAR2 50 := 'Hello'; -- declarations optional BEGIN DBMS_OUTPUT.PUT_LINE v_message ; -- executable statements EXCEPTION WHEN OTHERS THEN -- handlers optional DBMS_OUTPUT.PUT_LINE SQLERRM ; END; / SET SERVEROUTPUT ON DECLARE v_count NUMBER; BEGIN SELECT COUNT * INTO v_count FROM orders; DBMS_OUTPUT.PUT_LINE 'Total orders: ' || v_count ; END; / DECLARE v_x NUMBER := 42; BEGIN -- single-line comment /* multi-line comment */ DBMS_OUTPUT.PUT_LINE 'x = ' || v_x ; DBMS_OUTPUT.PUT_LINE 'x*2 = ' || v_x * 2 ; END; / DECLARE v_name VARCHAR2 60 := 'Acme'; -- initialized at declaration v_total NUMBER 12,2 DEFAULT 0; -- DEFAULT also works v_created DATE := SYSDATE; v_status VARCHAR2 10 ; c_tax_rate CONSTANT NUMBER := 0.10; -- a constant: never changes BEGIN v_status := 'OPEN'; -- assignment uses := DBMS_OUTPUT.PUT_LINE v_name || ' ' || v_status ; END; / DECLARE v_name customers.customer_name%TYPE; -- exactly the column's type v_row customers%ROWTYPE; -- a record with every column BEGIN SELECT customer_name INTO v_name FROM customers WHERE customer_id = 101; DBMS_OUTPUT.PUT_LINE v_name ; -- %ROWTYPE: fetch the whole row into the record SELECT * INTO v_row FROM customers WHERE customer_id = 101; DBMS_OUTPUT.PUT_LINE v_row.customer_name || ' / ' || v_row.credit_limit ; END; / VARIABLE v_amt NUMBER BEGIN :v_amt := 5000; -- assign through the colon END; / SELECT customer_name FROM customers WHERE credit_limit >= :v_amt; DECLARE v_outer NUMBER := 10; BEGIN DECLARE v_inner NUMBER := 20; BEGIN DBMS_OUTPUT.PUT_LINE v_outer ; -- 10 — outer is visible here DBMS_OUTPUT.PUT_LINE v_inner ; -- 20 — own variable END; -- v_inner is gone here; referencing it is a compile error END; /

pages.title: Bulk processing
pages.description: BULK COLLECT, FORALL, the LIMIT clause, SAVE EXCEPTIONS and SQL%BULK_EXCEPTIONS — and why row-by-row processing is the number one PL/SQL performance sin.
headings: BULK COLLECT — fetch many rows at once
FORALL — one statement over a collection
LIMIT — chunk the fetch for memory
The before-and-after that makes this real
pages.content: BULK COLLECT — fetch many rows at once FORALL — one statement over a collection LIMIT — chunk the fetch for memory SAVE EXCEPTIONS and SQL%BULK_EXCEPTIONS The before-and-after that makes this real The most consequential performance decision in PL/SQL is context switching : every time your block talks to the SQL engine, both engines hand off. A loop that runs one UPDATE per row pays that overhead per row. Bulk processing collapses the switch into one pass — BULK COLLECT to fill memory, FORALL to push it back — and routinely turns 100k-row programs from minutes into seconds. An ordinary FOR rec IN SELECT ... row loop fetches one row each iteration. BULK COLLECT pulls the whole result into a collection in one go: The DML twin of BULK COLLECT: one FORALL executes the same statement once per element without a per-row round trip: A BULK COLLECT of a million rows loads a million rows into memory. To bound memory and allow periodic commits, chunk with LIMIT : By default a bad row inside FORALL aborts the whole statement. SAVE EXCEPTIONS makes FORALL keep going, collecting failures into SQL%BULK_EXCEPTIONS , which you walk afterwards: BULK COLLECT works with SELECT , cursor FETCH , and EXECUTE IMMEDIATE . Each column shares its own collection, or use a record collection for whole rows. Always co-Gather any RETURNING with BULK COLLECT INTO so the affected row values come back together. FORALL cannot be used with SELECT that is BULK COLLECT's job and itself performs DML only. It is also usable with INSERT ... VALUES using a collection, and its RETURNING pairs with BULK COLLECT INTO . LIMIT + COMMIT in a loop is the canonical high-volume batch pattern: bounded memory, short row locks, and a natural restart point. It is the production-grade successor to the row-by-row loop everyone starts with — and the Fusion/OIC-style bulk loads you will be asked to write follow exactly this shape. First ask "can this be one UPDATE ?", because a set-based statement beats even bulk loops. When the row logic genuinely must live in PL/SQL decision after reading a value, an external call, a counter , reach for BULK COLLECT + FORALL and chunk with LIMIT . Attribute / clause Meaning SAVE EXCEPTIONS Keep going past per-row errors in FORALL instead of aborting SQL%BULK_EXCEPTIONS Array of for every failed element SQL%ROWCOUNT after FORALL Rows changed across the whole bulk Pattern Context switches Typical shape Nested-loop per row UPDATE inside FOR rec... N many Slow to very slow at scale SET-based single UPDATE ... WHERE no loop at all 1 Fastest when the logic is pure SQL BULK COLLECT + FORALL chunks with LIMIT A handful per chunk The right tool for imperative per-row logic at scale DECLARE TYPE t_ids IS TABLE OF orders.order_id%TYPE; v_ids t_ids; BEGIN -- the slow way mental model — don't run 100k rows like this FOR rec IN SELECT order_id FROM orders LOOP NULL; -- one context switch per row END LOOP; -- the bulk way: one fetch, all rows in memory SELECT order_id BULK COLLECT INTO v_ids FROM orders; DBMS_OUTPUT.PUT_LINE 'fetched ' || v_ids.COUNT || ' ids' ; END; / DECLARE TYPE t_ids IS TABLE OF customers.customer_id%TYPE; v_ids t_ids := t_ids 101, 102, 103 ; BEGIN FORALL i IN v_ids.FIRST .. v_ids.LAST UPDATE customers SET credit_limit = COALESCE credit_limit, 0 + 100 WHERE customer_id = v_ids i ; DBMS_OUTPUT.PUT_LINE 'updated ' || SQL%ROWCOUNT || ' rows' ; END; / DECLARE CURSOR c_orders IS SELECT order_id, total_amount FROM orders WHERE status = 'PENDING'; TYPE t_rows IS TABLE OF c_orders%ROWTYPE; v_batch t_rows; BEGIN OPEN c_orders; LOOP FETCH c_orders BULK COLLECT INTO v_batch LIMIT 1000; -- one batch EXIT WHEN v_batch.COUNT = 0; FORALL i IN 1 .. v_batch.COUNT UPDATE orders SET total_amount = v_batch i .total_amount * 0.9 WHERE order_id = v_batch i .order_id; COMMIT; -- checkpoint per batch END LOOP; CLOSE c_orders; END; / DECLARE TYPE t_rows IS TABLE OF customers.customer_id%TYPE; v_ids t_rows := t_rows 101, 102, 103, 99999 ; -- one bad id BEGIN FORALL i IN v_ids.FIRST .. v_ids.LAST UPDATE customers SET credit_limit = 100 WHERE customer_id = v_ids i SAVE EXCEPTIONS; -- don't stop on the bad row EXCEPTION WHEN OTHERS THEN IF SQL%BULK_EXCEPTIONS.COUNT > 0 THEN FOR j IN 1 .. SQL%BULK_EXCEPTIONS.COUNT LOOP DBMS_OUTPUT.PUT_LINE 'row ' || SQL%BULK_EXCEPTIONS j .ERROR_INDEX || ' error ' || SQL%BULK_EXCEPTIONS j .ERROR_CODE ; END LOOP; ELSE RAISE; END IF; END; /

pages.title: Collections
pages.description: Associative arrays, nested tables, and VARRAYs — the three PL/SQL collection types — and the methods COUNT, FIRST, LAST, NEXT, DELETE, and EXTEND that manage them.
headings: Collections as parameter and return types
pages.content: The three types The core methods Iterating with FOR ... IN Collections as parameter and return types A collection is PL/SQL's array — a set of values of one type, indexed and iterated in code. Collections are the data structure behind the bulk page's BULK COLLECT / FORALL : bulk loading needs a collection to land into. Choosing the right collection type matters less than knowing the methods — the methods are where the daily work happens. For dense collections, the FOR -loop with 1 .. COUNT works; for sparse ones iterate v.FIRST .. v.LAST only if fully dense, otherwise stick to the NEXT walk. There is also the newer FOR i IN INDICES OF v that visits only populated indexes: Collections shine as IN OUT parameters and function returns — a procedure can accept a whole set of "things to insert" in one argument. Define the type in a package spec so callers share it: This is the stepping stone to the bulk page: pass a punched list of primary keys once, and FORALL drives it at database speed instead of row-by-row calls. Associative arrays are in-memory only — they cannot live in a database column. Nested tables and VARRAYs can be column types as a table's element column , which is how you store an "answer list" inside a row. Reading v_days 2 after DELETE raises NO_DATA_FOUND collections reuse that exception . Guard every risky read with IF v_days.EXISTS 2 THEN — and never assume a collection is dense. INDICES OF needs the collection populated by a BULK COLLECT or with keys already set and is the sparse-friendly cousin of VALUES OF . When in doubt, the FIRST/NEXT walk always works. And for the pattern "collection → row change", that is the FORALL territory of the bulk page . Type Index Shape Best for Associative array Index-By NUMBER or VARCHAR2 you define Dense or sparse, no order guarantee In-memory lookup tables keyed by name/id fastest for lookups Nested table Dense 1..n by default, can delete → sparse Like a set; grows/shrinks via methods General-purpose lists; storage as a database column type VARRAY variable-size array Dense 1..n, fixed maximum size Fully dense once declared max size Small, ordered, fixed lists days, segregation checklists Method What it gives you COUNT Number of populated elements FIRST / LAST Lowest / highest index that has a value NEXT n / PRIOR n Next / previous index after n walks sparse collections safely EXISTS n TRUE if index n holds a value your way to check before DELETE DELETE Remove all / DELETE n one / DELETE m,n a range — turns collections sparse EXTEND Add one / EXTEND n n empty slots nested tables and VARRAYs only TRIM Drop trailing elements nested tables and VARRAYs only DECLARE TYPE t_as IS TABLE OF VARCHAR2 20 INDEX BY PLS_INTEGER; -- assoc array TYPE t_nt IS TABLE OF NUMBER; -- nested table TYPE t_var IS VARRAY 5 OF VARCHAR2 10 ; -- varray, max 5 v_assoc t_as; v_nt t_nt := t_nt ; -- initialize empty collections v_var t_var := t_var 'Mon', 'Tue' ; BEGIN v_assoc 1 := 'West'; -- associative array: any index v_assoc 50 := 'East'; DBMS_OUTPUT.PUT_LINE v_assoc 50 ; END; / DECLARE TYPE t_tbl IS TABLE OF VARCHAR2 10 ; v_days t_tbl; v_i PLS_INTEGER; BEGIN v_days := t_tbl 'Mon', 'Tue', 'Wed', 'Thu' ; v_days.DELETE 2 ; -- now sparse: Tue is gone DBMS_OUTPUT.PUT_LINE 'count = ' || v_days.COUNT ; -- 3 v_i := v_days.FIRST; WHILE v_i IS NOT NULL LOOP DBMS_OUTPUT.PUT_LINE 'day = ' || v_days v_i ; v_i := v_days.NEXT v_i ; -- always move via NEXT END LOOP; END; / DECLARE TYPE t_arr IS TABLE OF VARCHAR2 10 INDEX BY PLS_INTEGER; v_arr t_arr; BEGIN v_arr 10 := 'x'; v_arr 20 := 'y'; v_arr 30 := 'z'; FOR i IN INDICES OF v_arr LOOP -- 10, 20, 30 — skips the gaps DBMS_OUTPUT.PUT_LINE i || '=' || v_arr i ; END LOOP; END; / CREATE OR REPLACE PACKAGE pkg_ids AS TYPE t_id_list IS TABLE OF NUMBER; -- public collection type PROCEDURE process p_ids IN t_id_list ; END; /

pages.title: Control statements
pages.description: IF / ELSIF / ELSE, CASE, the three loop forms (basic LOOP, WHILE-LOOP, FOR-LOOP), and the exit and skip verbs — EXIT, EXIT WHEN, and CONTINUE.
pages.content: IF / ELSIF / ELSE CASE The three loops EXIT, EXIT WHEN, CONTINUE Labeled loops for nested exit PL/SQL's control flow is classic structured programming: selection IF / CASE and repetition LOOP . The surface is simple, but two habits decide whether your loops are safe: always having an EXIT path, and knowing which loop form to pick for work over cursors and collections which the cursors and collections pages build on . Two forms. The simple CASE matches one expression to values; the searched CASE evaluates arbitrary conditions: The three loop-control verbs, each with a WHEN form: When you must escape several levels e.g. "stop scanning this grid early" , label the outer loop and EXIT to it by name: It is ELSIF one word, no E — the "E" missing is the classic typo. Each branch ends with END IF; — easy to miss when nesting. Conditions evaluate top-down; the first TRUE branch wins. NULL in a condition goes to ELSE — three-valued logic applies here too IF v_x with v_x NULL is not FALSE, it falls to ELSE/ELSIF . If simple CASE matches none of its WHEN s and there is no ELSE , it raises CASE_NOT_FOUND . Give searched CASE an ELSE or ensure a truthy branch . The classic infinite loop is the bare LOOP with no EXIT path — plan the exit before writing the body. And remember FOR -loop counters are read-only: assigning j := 5 inside a FOR j loop is a compile error. For pure SQL problems, ask first whether a loop is even needed — many "loop over a table" programs in Fusion/ORM-land are really an UPDATE ... SET ... WHERE in disguise. The performance page hammers this point. Form When it runs Use it for basic LOOP ... END LOOP Body runs until an EXIT Anything with an explicit, early exit; cursor fetch until no more rows WHILE condition LOOP Only while the condition is TRUE Unknown count, condition-checked before each pass FOR i IN min..max LOOP Counter runs the range once Known count; all-NUMBER counters Verb What it does EXIT; / EXIT WHEN cond; Leave the loop entirely immediately / when the condition is true CONTINUE; / CONTINUE WHEN cond; Skip to the loop's next iteration EXIT loop_label; Leave a specifically labeled outer loop from inside nested ones DECLARE v_amount NUMBER 12,2 ; v_size VARCHAR2 10 ; BEGIN v_amount := 1500; IF v_amount > 10000 THEN v_size := 'LARGE'; ELSIF v_amount > 1000 THEN v_size := 'MEDIUM'; ELSE v_size := 'SMALL'; END IF; DBMS_OUTPUT.PUT_LINE v_size ; -- MEDIUM END; / DECLARE v_status VARCHAR2 10 := 'APPROVED'; v_note VARCHAR2 30 ; v_amount NUMBER := 2500; v_rating VARCHAR2 10 ; BEGIN -- simple CASE: one expression, many values v_note := CASE v_status WHEN 'OPEN' THEN 'still open' WHEN 'APPROVED' THEN 'ready to pay' ELSE 'other' END; -- searched CASE: conditions win v_rating := CASE WHEN v_amount >= 10000 THEN 'premium' WHEN v_amount >= 1000 THEN 'standard' ELSE 'basic' END; DBMS_OUTPUT.PUT_LINE v_note || ' / ' || v_rating ; END; / DECLARE i NUMBER := 1; BEGIN -- FOR: known count, implicit counter FOR j IN 1 .. 3 LOOP DBMS_OUTPUT.PUT_LINE 'for ' || j ; END LOOP; -- WHILE: condition at the top WHILE i 3; -- leave when the condition holds DBMS_OUTPUT.PUT_LINE 'basic ' || i ; i := i + 1; END LOOP; END; / DECLARE v_sum NUMBER := 0; BEGIN FOR i IN 1 .. 10 LOOP CONTINUE WHEN MOD i, 2 = 0; -- skip even numbers v_sum := v_sum + i; -- only odds summed = 25 END LOOP; DBMS_OUTPUT.PUT_LINE 'sum of odds: ' || v_sum ; END; / DECLARE v_found VARCHAR2 1 := 'N'; BEGIN > FOR i IN 1 .. 3 LOOP FOR j IN 1 .. 3 LOOP IF i = 2 AND j = 2 THEN v_found := 'Y'; EXIT outer_loop; -- jump out of BOTH loops END IF; END LOOP; END LOOP; DBMS_OUTPUT.PUT_LINE 'found at inner cell? ' || v_found ; END; /

pages.title: Cursors
pages.description: Implicit cursor attributes (SQL%ROWCOUNT, SQL%FOUND, SQL%NOTFOUND), explicit OPEN / FETCH / CLOSE cursors, cursor FOR loops, parameterized and return cursors, FOR UPDATE with WHERE CURRENT OF, and SYS_REFCURSOR ref cursors.
headings: Cursor FOR loops — the recommended default
FOR UPDATE and WHERE CURRENT OF
pages.content: Implicit cursors and their attributes Explicit cursors — OPEN, FETCH, CLOSE Cursor FOR loops — the recommended default Parameterized cursors FOR UPDATE and WHERE CURRENT OF Ref cursors — SYS_REFCURSOR A cursor is PL/SQL's handle for "a query, processed row by row". SQL already ran FOR rec IN SELECT ... loops on earlier pages; here you meet the full ceremony — because understanding it explains how to drive queries, count what changed, and hand result sets to other programs. Every SQL statement PL/SQL runs is an implicit cursor , named SQL capital . After a DML or SELECT INTO you can inspect what it just did: When you must manage the fetch yourself — process a batch, stop early, or page — declare the cursor, then run the lifecycle manually: The FOR -loop cursor opens, fetches, and closes implicitly — this is what production code writes: A cursor can take IN parameters no OUT , so one cursor serves many filter values: Two paired tools for "read a row, then safely update just the row you are looking at" — FOR UPDATE locks the rows as you read them; WHERE CURRENT OF cursor points an UPDATE at the row the loop currently holds: A ref cursor is a variable that holds a cursor — the typed SYS_REFCURSOR is the generic, referenceable kind. It is how a procedure returns a result set to a caller a Java app, a report tool, another PL/SQL program : Ref cursors also drive dynamic SQL results — the OPEN cursor FOR dynamic_statement USING binds form returns whatever the string queries, which is what data APIs and report backends commonly rely on. Explicit cursors support c_orders%ROWCOUNT , %FOUND , %NOTFOUND , %ISOPEN — note the cursor name , not SQL . Forgetting CLOSE leaks a cursor handle; always close, ideally behind the FOR -loop shortcut next. SQL%ROWCOUNT refers to the most recent SQL statement — read it immediately after, because the next statement resets it. A FOR -loop cursor or a SELECT ... BULK COLLECT is what you reach for 95% of the time. The manual OPEN/FETCH/CLOSE exists for special needs — nested control, early termination, or dynamic statements. And when the loop's query is small enough that row-by-row processing is wasteful, prefer the bulk page's FORALL . FOR UPDATE holds row locks until commit/rollback — the same lock behavior as the transactions page. Use it only when you genuinely intend to change the rows, and commit promptly so the locks do not block the rest of your estate. The rule that keeps cursors simple: FOR -loop cursors for internal iteration, WHERE CURRENT OF only under FOR UPDATE , and SYS_REFCURSOR when you must hand a result set out of a subprogram. Attribute Returns SQL%ROWCOUNT Rows affected by the last DML / opened by SELECT SQL%FOUND TRUE if the last statement affected at least one row SQL%NOTFOUND The opposite of SQL%FOUND SQL%ISOPEN FALSE for implicit cursors; TRUE while an explicit cursor is open BEGIN UPDATE customers SET credit_limit = credit_limit * 1.1 WHERE region_id = 1; DBMS_OUTPUT.PUT_LINE SQL%ROWCOUNT || ' customers raised' ; IF SQL%NOTFOUND THEN DBMS_OUTPUT.PUT_LINE 'Nothing matched - check the filter!' ; END IF; END; / DECLARE CURSOR c_orders IS SELECT order_id, total_amount FROM orders WHERE total_amount > 1000; v_id orders.order_id%TYPE; v_total orders.total_amount%TYPE; BEGIN OPEN c_orders; -- 1. open LOOP FETCH c_orders INTO v_id, v_total; -- 2. fetch a row EXIT WHEN c_orders%NOTFOUND; -- 3. stop at the end DBMS_OUTPUT.PUT_LINE v_id || ' = ' || v_total ; END LOOP; CLOSE c_orders; -- 4. close END; / BEGIN FOR rec IN SELECT order_id, total_amount FROM orders WHERE total_amount > 1000 LOOP DBMS_OUTPUT.PUT_LINE rec.order_id || ' = ' || rec.total_amount ; END LOOP; END; / DECLARE CURSOR c_reg p_region NUMBER IS SELECT customer_name FROM customers WHERE region_id = p_region; BEGIN FOR rec IN c_reg 1 LOOP DBMS_OUTPUT.PUT_LINE 'West: ' || rec.customer_name ; END LOOP; FOR rec IN c_reg 2 LOOP DBMS_OUTPUT.PUT_LINE 'East: ' || rec.customer_name ; END LOOP; END; / DECLARE CURSOR c_cust IS SELECT customer_id, credit_limit FROM customers WHERE region_id = 1 FOR UPDATE; -- lock rows we will change BEGIN FOR rec IN c_cust LOOP IF rec.credit_limit IS NULL THEN UPDATE customers SET credit_limit = 1000 WHERE CURRENT OF c_cust; -- updates ONLY this row END IF; END LOOP; COMMIT; -- release the locks END; / CREATE OR REPLACE PROCEDURE get_orders p_cursor OUT SYS_REFCURSOR IS BEGIN OPEN p_cursor FOR SELECT order_id, total_amount FROM orders WHERE total_amount > 1000; END; / -- caller SQLcl : VARIABLE cur REFCURSOR EXEC get_orders :cur ; PRINT cur;

pages.title: SQL inside PL/SQL
pages.description: SELECT ... INTO, running INSERT / UPDATE / DELETE / MERGE from PL/SQL, transaction control (COMMIT/ROLLBACK/SAVEPOINT), and dynamic SQL with EXECUTE IMMEDIATE.
headings: DML statements — direct and with RETURNING
pages.content: SELECT ... INTO DML statements — direct and with RETURNING Transaction control — COMMIT, ROLLBACK, SAVEPOINT Dynamic SQL with EXECUTE IMMEDIATE The point of PL/SQL is that SQL is a first-class citizen inside the block — no string-building, no driver, just write the statement. But the rules are stricter than in a tool: a SELECT must fetch into variables, and the cardinality must be exactly one row unless you handle the two famous exceptions. This page is that contract. A query in PL/SQL needs a destination. SELECT ... INTO fetches exactly one row into variables or a %ROWTYPE record: PL/SQL inherits the whole transaction model from the transactions page . The disciplined pattern for a long batch: work in chunks, checkpoint with COMMIT , and keep a SAVEPOINT to roll back only a bad chunk: When the statement itself must be assembled at runtime — unknown table names, dynamic filters, DDL — use EXECUTE IMMEDIATE . It parses and runs a string, and the USING clause binds values so they never end up in the SQL text: Zero rows raises NO_DATA_FOUND . More than one raises TOO_MANY_ROWS . DML in PL/SQL behaves exactly like the SQL pages describe — constraints, defaulting, and all. RETURNING ... INTO grabs values from the affected row without a second query its basic use was on the DML page; for collections you pair it with BULK COLLECT , see the bulk page . These statements touch the same transaction as everything else in the session — nothing commits unless you say so. USING binds values safe ; table/column names cannot be bound and must be whitelisted. DDL via EXECUTE IMMEDIATE commits your open transaction — the DDL rule from the transactions page applies. For multi-row dynamic reads, EXECUTE IMMEDIATE ... BULK COLLECT INTO the bulk page is the pattern. Longer/more flexible dynamic runs use the OPEN cursor FOR ... USING ref-cursor form — the cursors page . SELECT INTO demands exactly one row — that is a hard rule: Zero rows raises NO_DATA_FOUND . More than one raises TOO_MANY_ROWS . Both are handled or ignored on the exceptions page . A query that "selects into no variable" outside the block is fine; inside PL/SQL the INTO is mandatory. Commit deliberately : at well-chosen checkpoints, not after every row, and not from deep inside a shared helper that other callers may be mid-transaction on. The rule of thumb that keeps packages composable: the outermost caller owns the COMMIT . Dynamic SQL is where SQL injection happens. Values go through USING ; object names get validated against a hard-coded allow-list e.g. IF v_tbl NOT IN 'ORDERS','CUSTOMERS' THEN RAISE_APPLICATION_ERROR ... ; . Never concatenate a user-supplied string straight into the SQL text. DECLARE v_row customers%ROWTYPE; v_name customers.customer_name%TYPE; BEGIN SELECT * INTO v_row FROM customers WHERE customer_id = 101; DBMS_OUTPUT.PUT_LINE v_row.customer_name ; SELECT customer_name INTO v_name FROM customers WHERE customer_id = 102; DBMS_OUTPUT.PUT_LINE v_name ; END; / DECLARE v_id customers.customer_id%TYPE; BEGIN -- INSERT INSERT INTO customers customer_id, customer_name, region_id VALUES seq_customers.NEXTVAL, 'Acme Corp', 1 ; -- UPDATE with an expression based on a variable UPDATE customers SET credit_limit = credit_limit * 1.05 WHERE customer_id = 101; -- DELETE DELETE FROM order_lines WHERE order_id = 999; -- MERGE: reconcile staged data MERGE INTO customers c USING staged_customers s ON c.customer_id = s.customer_id WHEN MATCHED THEN UPDATE SET c.credit_limit = s.credit_limit WHEN NOT MATCHED THEN INSERT customer_id, customer_name, region_id VALUES s.customer_id, s.customer_name, s.region_id ; -- RETURNING captures generated / changed values UPDATE customers SET credit_limit = 20000 WHERE customer_id = 101 RETURNING credit_limit INTO v_id; DBMS_OUTPUT.PUT_LINE 'new limit ' || v_id ; END; / DECLARE v_count NUMBER := 0; BEGIN FOR rec IN SELECT * FROM staged_rows ORDER BY row_id LOOP SAVEPOINT before_row; -- bookmark for this row only BEGIN INSERT INTO customers customer_id, customer_name VALUES rec.id, rec.name ; v_count := v_count + 1; EXCEPTION WHEN OTHERS THEN ROLLBACK TO SAVEPOINT before_row; -- undo THIS row, keep the rest log_error rec.id, SQLERRM ; END; END LOOP; COMMIT; END; / DECLARE v_sql VARCHAR2 200 ; v_cnt NUMBER; v_tbl VARCHAR2 30 := 'ORDERS'; BEGIN -- dynamic SELECT with a bind value and an INTO v_sql := 'SELECT COUNT * FROM ' || v_tbl || ' WHERE total_amount > :x'; EXECUTE IMMEDIATE v_sql INTO v_cnt USING 100; DBMS_OUTPUT.PUT_LINE 'big orders: ' || v_cnt ; -- dynamic DML v_sql := 'DELETE FROM ' || v_tbl || ' WHERE customer_id = :id'; EXECUTE IMMEDIATE v_sql USING 999; -- DDL cannot be bound — only hard-coded after whitelisting! EXECUTE IMMEDIATE 'TRUNCATE TABLE ' || v_tbl; END; /

pages.title: Exception handling
pages.description: Predefined exceptions (NO_DATA_FOUND, TOO_MANY_ROWS, ZERO_DIVIDE), the WHEN OTHERS catch-all, user-defined exceptions, RAISE and RAISE_APPLICATION_ERROR, and the SQLCODE / SQLERRM detail functions.
headings: WHEN OTHERS — the safety net and the sinhole
pages.content: The EXCEPTION section Predefined exceptions User-defined exceptions RAISE_APPLICATION_ERROR — the friendly error WHEN OTHERS — the safety net and the sinhole SQLCODE and SQLERRM — error details Exceptions are how PL/SQL fails deliberately . An unhandled error stops the block and propagates outward to the caller; a handled one lets your program choose what happens next. Good PL/SQL is written around "what can go wrong here" — this page is that section of the block. Order matters: PL/SQL scans the handlers top-down for the first match. Put the specific ones first and WHEN OTHERS last — it is a catch-all, and if it comes first nothing else ever fires. Declare your own exception, then RAISE it — clean domain errors without error-code litter: To surface a clean error message to the caller an API, an integration, a screen , use RAISE_APPLICATION_ERROR with a code between -20000 and -20999 . This is what applications actually catch: The caller receives ORA-20001 or ORA-20999 , etc. with your text — the standard way exceptions cross the PL/SQL ↔ application boundary. Inside a handler, SQLCODE is the numeric error code e.g. -20001 , 1403 for no-data-found and SQLERRM is the message text. There is also the modern DBMS_UTILITY.FORMAT_ERROR_BACKTRACE for the line stack: Remember inside a loop : NO_DATA_FOUND thrown by a SELECT INTO terminates the whole block, not just the iteration — it does not behave like "skip this row". Guard with COUNT * first or handle inside a nested block. WHEN OTHERS that just prints and returns makes errors disappear — the batch "completes" while rows quietly failed. The two acceptable uses: 1 log-then- RAISE to keep the error visible, or 2 intentionally swallow-and-continue a scoped error you have thought about. Anything else is data loss in waiting. A RAISE inside a handler re-raises the very error being handled; RAISE_APPLICATION_ERROR creates a new one. And an exception inside a nested block that is not handled locally propagates outward until a block handles it — so an outer WHEN OTHERS catches everything beneath it. Structure your outer boundaries accordingly. Exception Raised when NO_DATA_FOUND SELECT INTO finds no rows; a collection element is uninitialized TOO_MANY_ROWS SELECT INTO finds more than one row ZERO_DIVIDE Division by zero DUP_VAL_ON_INDEX An insert/update violates a unique constraint VALUE_ERROR A conversion or size error e.g. putting 'x' into a NUMBER INVALID_NUMBER A string can't convert to a number in SQL context CASE_NOT_FOUND A simple CASE matches no WHEN and has no ELSE TOO_MANY_... / PROGRAM_ERROR Internal engine conditions x Detail function Returns SQLCODE The error number negative for Oracle errors SQLERRM The full error message DBMS_UTILITY.FORMAT_ERROR_BACKTRACE Where the error actually occurred, line by line DBMS_UTILITY.FORMAT_ERROR_STACK The stack of exception handlers the error traveled DECLARE v_name customers.customer_name%TYPE; BEGIN SELECT customer_name INTO v_name FROM customers WHERE customer_id = 101; DBMS_OUTPUT.PUT_LINE v_name ; EXCEPTION WHEN NO_DATA_FOUND THEN DBMS_OUTPUT.PUT_LINE 'No such customer' ; WHEN TOO_MANY_ROWS THEN DBMS_OUTPUT.PUT_LINE 'Duplicate keys - the query is not unique' ; WHEN OTHERS THEN DBMS_OUTPUT.PUT_LINE 'Unexpected: ' || SQLERRM ; END; / DECLARE e_limit_exceeded EXCEPTION; -- user-defined exception v_limit NUMBER 12,2 := 15000; BEGIN IF v_limit > 10000 THEN RAISE e_limit_exceeded; END IF; EXCEPTION WHEN e_limit_exceeded THEN DBMS_OUTPUT.PUT_LINE 'Credit limit over 10k — adjust.' ; END; / DECLARE v_customer customers.customer_id%TYPE := 101; v_count NUMBER; BEGIN SELECT COUNT * INTO v_count FROM orders WHERE customer_id = v_customer; IF v_count > 5 THEN RAISE_APPLICATION_ERROR -20001, 'Customer ' || v_customer || ' has too many open orders: ' || v_count ; END IF; END; / EXCEPTION WHEN OTHERS THEN log_error SQLCODE, SQLERRM ; -- your own audit table RAISE; -- re-raise the SAME error END; / EXCEPTION WHEN OTHERS THEN DBMS_OUTPUT.PUT_LINE 'CODE : ' || SQLCODE ; DBMS_OUTPUT.PUT_LINE 'MSG : ' || SQLERRM ; DBMS_OUTPUT.PUT_LINE 'WHERE: ' || DBMS_UTILITY.FORMAT_ERROR_BACKTRACE ; END; /

pages.title: Files & external integration
pages.description: Reading and writing server-side files with UTL_FILE, DIRECTORY objects and their privileges, calling REST services, and processing JSON and XML from PL/SQL.
pages.content: UTL_FILE and DIRECTORY objects Calling REST services JSON processing from PL/SQL XML processing PL/SQL is not confined to the database: it can read and write files the database server can see, call REST endpoints, and process JSON and XML. For Fusion/OIC-style work the JSON-processing half is where most of the day-to-day value sits — integration payloads arrive as JSON and leave as JSON, and PL/SQL is often the engine validating and transforming them. UTL_FILE reads/writes files on the database server's filesystem — not a client's hard drive. The file path comes from a DIRECTORY object, a schema object mapping a logical name to an OS path, which the DBA creates and grants: Oracle offers several HTTP-capable packages; which one you may call depends on the version and edition. The APEX_WEB_SERVICE family is the friendliest for JSON: The essential modern skills — matching what integration work asks for: And the other direction — JSON arrives, you shred it into rows and push it to a table typically inside a FORALL per the bulk page : The legacy counterpart — SOAP-era integrations still speak it. XMLTYPE columns, XMLTABLE to shred, DBMS_XMLDOM /XPath for manipulation: Why a DIRECTORY and not a path string? Because raw server paths are a security hole — the grant is the guard. Key routines: FOPEN , PUT_LINE , GET_LINE , FCLOSE ; also FREMOVE and FGETATTR for cleanup/inspection. File errors surface as UTL_FILE -specific exceptions INVALID_PATH , WRITE_ERROR , ACCESS_DENIED — read the message from SQLERRM . Front-run the DBA directory + privileges when a procedure says it will write files — that is the "storage is somewhere else" reality of file-based loads. Generate JSON — JSON_OBJECT / JSON_ARRAY , and JSON_OBJECTAGG over rows. Parse JSON — JSON_VALUE , JSON_QUERY , and JSON_TABLE the SQL page has the full set . Validate — JSON_EXISTS and IS JSON check it is well-formed before you trust it. REST from the database is a network+latency decision, not just a code one: a loop calling a web service per row is the single most expensive program shape possible. Design the remote call to accept a batch the bulk page's philosophy applied to HTTP , and remember this needs outbound ACLs/network access the DBA approves. The modern guidance leans on JSON for new contracts and XML only for the SOAP/B2B that will not go away. Whichever side you sit on, the pattern is identical: type → shred → store and query → assemble → emit , with the shapes nailed down by JSON_TABLE / XMLTABLE and the SQL macros page for reuse. Package / facility When to use APEX_WEB_SERVICE Simple REST GET/POST with JSON/CLOB, easy headers; commonly available with an APEX install UTL_HTTP Lower-level HTTP with full request control — everywhere Oracle runs, but more code DBMS_CLOUD Autonomous Database / 23ai Native REST, object storage, and external tables in the cloud database OCI queues/events Async messaging when REST is not the right shape -- DBA creates the directory and the logical name CREATE DIRECTORY OUT_DIR AS '/u01/app/outbound'; GRANT READ, WRITE ON DIRECTORY OUT_DIR TO app_user; -- then PL/SQL writes with it DECLARE v_fh UTL_FILE.FILE_TYPE; BEGIN v_fh := UTL_FILE.FOPEN 'OUT_DIR', 'orders.csv', 'W' ; UTL_FILE.PUT_LINE v_fh, 'order_id,amount' ; UTL_FILE.PUT_LINE v_fh, '101,500' ; UTL_FILE.FCLOSE v_fh ; END; / DECLARE v_body CLOB; BEGIN v_body := APEX_WEB_SERVICE.make_rest_request_b p_url => 'https://api.example.com/customers/101', p_http_method => 'GET' ; DBMS_OUTPUT.PUT_LINE DBMS_LOB.SUBSTR v_body, 4000, 1 ; END; / DECLARE v_json CLOB; BEGIN SELECT JSON_OBJECT 'request' VALUE JSON_OBJECT 'customerId' VALUE c.customer_id, 'name' VALUE c.customer_name, 'orders' VALUE SELECT JSON_ARRAYAGG JSON_OBJECT 'orderId' VALUE order_id, 'amount' VALUE total_amount FROM orders o WHERE o.customer_id = c.customer_id RETURNING CLOB INTO v_json FROM customers c WHERE customer_id = 101; DBMS_OUTPUT.PUT_LINE DBMS_LOB.SUBSTR v_json, 4000, 1 ; END; / DECLARE v_payload CLOB := ' "lines": , '; BEGIN INSERT INTO order_lines order_id, sku, qty SELECT 1001, jt.sku, jt.qty FROM JSON_TABLE v_payload, '$.lines * ' COLUMNS sku VARCHAR2 10 PATH '$.sku', qty NUMBER PATH '$.qty' jt; END; / DECLARE v_xml XMLTYPE; v_id NUMBER; BEGIN v_xml := XMLTYPE ' 101 ' ; SELECT TO_NUMBER x.number INTO v_id FROM XMLTABLE '/order' PASSING v_xml COLUMNS number VARCHAR2 20 PATH 'number' x; DBMS_OUTPUT.PUT_LINE v_id ; END; /

pages.title: Packages
pages.description: Package specification vs body, public vs private objects, package-level variables and the initialization block, why real projects are built around packages, and the built-ins DBMS_OUTPUT, UTL_FILE, and DBMS_SCHEDULER.
headings: Why real projects are built on packages
Common built-in packages you will actually use
pages.content: Specification vs body Public vs private Package variables & the initialization block Why real projects are built on packages Common built-in packages you will actually use A package bundles related procedures, functions, types, and variables into one deployable, grantable unit. Standalone programs exist, but production Oracle code is organized into packages almost without exception — because they deliver encapsulation, overloading, shared state, and one-grant deployment that loose procedures cannot. A package is two files : the specification the public contract and the body the implementation . They are compiled separately and can even be re-deployed separately: A package can hold session-level state : variables declared in the spec or body persist for your whole session between calls — and the body may run an initialization block the first time the package is touched: Calling convention: package_name.program_name . Anything only declared in the body is private — invisible to callers, which is how you hide internals. The spec is a contract; grant EXECUTE on the package and the whole surface becomes available. Encapsulation — a stable public API over a swappable engine. Deployment as one unit — grant EXECUTE ON pkg once; no per-procedure grants. Overloading — only possible inside packages the procedures page showed it . Shared, session-cached data — lookup tables loaded once into memory per session. Matching the vendor pattern — Fusion/OIC integration code calls DBMS_* packages constantly; your own code belongs in packages so it looks like the platform's. Design rule that keeps packages healthy: the specification exposes the what , and everything volatile lives in the body. Change the body all you like; callers depending on the spec rarely notice. This is exactly why Oracle ships DBMS_* as packages — you inherit a stable API around a swappable engine. Package state is per session and reset at session end, not per package compile — and it is shared by every program in the package. That is perfect for caches and counters, and a subtle bug source if you reuse one "global" variable for two purposes. Visibility Declared in Can callers use it? Public The package specification Yes — the documented API Private Only the package body No — implementation detail, changeable without breaking callers Package What you use it for Look out for DBMS_OUTPUT PUT_LINE/PUT — server-side debugging output Only visible with SERVEROUTPUT ON; not for production logging UTL_FILE Read/write server-side files via directories Needs a DIRECTORY object + OS privileges files page DBMS_SCHEDULER Create OS-independent jobs, schedules, programs Job failures surface in DBA_SCHEDULER_JOB_RUN_DETAILS DBMS_APPLICATION_INFO Set the session/client info strings for monitoring The instrumentation tool the performance page recommends DBMS_MVIEW / DBMS_REFRESH Refresh materialized views Plumbing behind Fast Refresh settings DBMS_STATS Gather optimizer statistics The single best performance lever there is -- SPECIFICATION: what the world may call CREATE OR REPLACE PACKAGE pkg_finance AS FUNCTION total_spend p_customer NUMBER RETURN NUMBER; PROCEDURE apply_credit p_customer NUMBER, p_amount NUMBER ; c_default_limit CONSTANT NUMBER := 1000; -- public constant END pkg_finance; / -- BODY: how it actually works CREATE OR REPLACE PACKAGE BODY pkg_finance AS v_calls NUMBER := 0; -- PRIVATE package variable FUNCTION total_spend p_customer NUMBER RETURN NUMBER IS v_total NUMBER; BEGIN SELECT NVL SUM total_amount ,0 INTO v_total FROM orders WHERE customer_id = p_customer; RETURN v_total; END; PROCEDURE apply_credit p_customer NUMBER, p_amount NUMBER IS BEGIN UPDATE customers SET credit_limit = NVL credit_limit,0 + p_amount WHERE customer_id = p_customer; v_calls := v_calls + 1; END; END pkg_finance; / SELECT pkg_finance.total_spend 101 FROM dual; -- public use CREATE OR REPLACE PACKAGE pkg_config AS PROCEDURE get p_key VARCHAR2, p_value OUT VARCHAR2 ; END; / CREATE OR REPLACE PACKAGE BODY pkg_config AS v_cache DATE; -- package variable: lives for the session PROCEDURE get p_key VARCHAR2, p_value OUT VARCHAR2 IS BEGIN p_value := p_key; -- real impl reads a config table END; BEGIN -- package initialization block v_cache := SYSDATE; -- runs once per session, at first touch END; / BEGIN DBMS_SCHEDULER.CREATE_JOB job_name => 'J_REFRESH_REPORTS', job_type => 'PLSQL_BLOCK', job_action => 'BEGIN pkg_reports.refresh_all; END;', start_date => SYSTIMESTAMP, repeat_interval => 'FREQ=DAILY; BYHOUR=2', enabled => TRUE ; END; /

pages.title: PL/SQL — from blocks to production code
pages.description: The procedural language Oracle runs inside the database itself: blocks and variables, control flow, cursors, procedures, functions, packages, triggers, collections, bulk processing with BULK COLLECT and FORALL, plus performance, security, and deployment.
headings: The anatomy of every PL/SQL program
The one rule that governs everything
