pages.content: The learning path The anatomy of every PL/SQL program The one rule that governs everything SQL asks questions; PL/SQL executes logic. Since PL/SQL runs inside the Oracle database — beside the data, with full transaction control — every program you write here is deployed, granted, compiled, and secured the same way a table is. This section takes you from a first anonymous block to the stored programs real projects ship and maintain, ending with the bulk-processing and security skills that separate junior code from production code. Every PL/SQL program — anonymous block, procedure, function, trigger — shares the same skeleton. Learn the skeleton once and every page that follows is just "what goes in each section": PL/SQL and SQL share the same transaction . Procedures that run DML change the caller's transaction — there is no hidden commit of your own, and you COMMIT or not deliberately. That single fact, learned on the transactions page , is why production PL/SQL guidelines are full of "commit in the caller, never deep inside" advice. If your goal is Oracle Fusion / OIC work , weight your time toward these pages: procedures & functions , packages , cursors , exception handling , bulk processing , dynamic SQL in the SQL-inside-PL/SQL page , and the files & JSON page — that is the exact skill set integration developers are asked for. The EXCEPTION section turns errors into handled outcomes. A block without one simply raises the error to its caller. Nested blocks each may carry their own handlers, and an exception not handled locally propagates outward — that is the whole mental model of error flow in PL/SQL. Section Goes inside… Typical contents DECLARE optional Before BEGIN Variables, constants, cursors, types BEGIN The executable section Assignment, control flow, SQL statements EXCEPTION optional After the executable statements WHEN NO_DATA_FOUND THEN … handlers END; The close of the block Optional labels; trailing / in SQL*Plus/SQLcl

pages.title: Performance & best practices
pages.description: Avoid SQL inside loops, prefer bulk operations, proper exception handling and logging, avoiding unnecessary commits, using bind variables, and instrumentation — the habits that make PL/SQL production-ready.
headings: 1. Don't run SQL inside a loop
2. Use bulk operations for high-volume data
6. Instrumentation — the code should tell you how it ran
pages.content: 1. Don't run SQL inside a loop 2. Use bulk operations for high-volume data 3. Exceptional handling and logging 4. Avoid unnecessary commits 5. Bind variables 6. Instrumentation — the code should tell you how it ran The checklist The first things you will be taught and interviewed on about PL/SQL performance are these: don't put SQL in a loop, do it in bulk, log like you mean it, commit deliberately, and bind everything. This page is that checklist — each rule shown twice: the anti-pattern and the fix. This is the bulk page in one line: fetch with BULK COLLECT , change with FORALL , chunk with LIMIT , and let SAVE EXCEPTIONS keep a failed batch diagnosable. At 100k+ rows there is no excuse for per-row context switches. Production PL/SQL logs to a table , not the screen. A common pattern simplified uses a shared logging helper called from an outer WHEN OTHERS : Each COMMIT forces a disk write and releases locks. The habits: In PL/SQL, variable := value statements already bind implicitly — the discipline bites in EXECUTE IMMEDIATE and when text gets concatenated. Rule: values via USING , never by string assembly : When a batch takes 40 minutes, someone needs to know where . Oracle's native instrumentation is DBMS_APPLICATION_INFO , which any DBA can see live: An AUTONOMOUS_TRANSACTION log writes and commits independently of the failing business transaction — so the audit survives the rollback. Log the who/what/when : proc name, message, error code, timestamp, and any business key you were processing. Don't blanket-swallow: log for observability, but let RAISE preserve the error journey to the caller. Commit at the boundary — the outermost caller owns the COMMIT; a helper buried mid-transaction that commits can strand the caller's still-open work. Chunk commits for long batches the bulk-page LIMIT+COMMIT pattern to bound undo and row locks. Never commit in a loop, in a trigger, or "just in case". Combine with V$SQL_MONITOR -style watching: the DBA can see "AP_PAYMENT_BATCH / PHASE 2" taking 30 minutes. A small app_run_log plus DBMS_APPLICATION_INFO is the whole observability story most batches need. Rule of thumb: if a query mentions the outer loop's row, it is a correlated subquery that the whole loop could have answered in one pass. Rewrite as a join reads or a FORALL writes . The bulk page showed why row-by-row is the #1 sin. Rule Why Where learned No SQL in loops; set-based or bulk Context switching costs per row bulk page BULK COLLECT / FORALL / LIMIT One pass instead of thousands Log to a table; autonomous + RAISE Audit survives rollback; errors stay visible exceptions page Commit at boundaries, chunk big loads Lock and undo hygiene transactions page Bind values, never concatenate Plan reuse + no injection SQL-inside-PL/SQL page Instrument with DBMS_APPLICATION_INFO Deployers/DBA can see progress live this page -- ANTI-PATTERN: one SELECT per iteration FOR rec IN SELECT customer_id FROM customers LOOP SELECT COUNT * INTO v_cnt FROM orders WHERE customer_id = rec.customer_id; -- N queries! END LOOP; -- FIX: one query that answers for everyone SELECT c.customer_id, COUNT o.order_id INTO ... -- bulk or join — solve it set-based once CREATE OR REPLACE PACKAGE pkg_audit AS PROCEDURE log_run p_proc VARCHAR2, p_msg VARCHAR2, p_code NUMBER ; END pkg_audit; / CREATE OR REPLACE PACKAGE BODY pkg_audit AS PROCEDURE log_run p_proc VARCHAR2, p_msg VARCHAR2, p_code NUMBER IS PRAGMA AUTONOMOUS_TRANSACTION; -- logger's COMMIT is independent BEGIN INSERT INTO app_run_log proc_name, msg, err_code, at_ts VALUES p_proc, p_msg, p_code, SYSTIMESTAMP ; COMMIT; -- commits only the log row END log_run; END pkg_audit; / -- business code calls it once at the boundary, then re-raises EXCEPTION WHEN OTHERS THEN pkg_audit.log_run 'PROCESS_ORDERS', SQLERRM, SQLCODE ; RAISE; END; / -- BAD: builds fresh text per value EXECUTE IMMEDIATE 'SELECT COUNT * FROM orders WHERE total_amount > ' || v_amt; -- GOOD: bind the value EXECUTE IMMEDIATE 'SELECT COUNT * FROM orders WHERE total_amount > :amt' INTO v_cnt USING v_amt; BEGIN DBMS_APPLICATION_INFO.SET_MODULE module_name => 'AP_PAYMENT_BATCH', action_name => 'PHASE 1: VALIDATE' ; -- ... phase 1 ... DBMS_APPLICATION_INFO.SET_ACTION 'PHASE 2: APPLY' ; -- ... phase 2 ... DBMS_APPLICATION_INFO.SET_ACTION NULL ; END; /

pages.title: Procedures & functions
pages.description: CREATE / REPLACE / EXECUTE / DROP, the IN / OUT / IN OUT parameter modes, default parameters, function return types, calling functions from SQL, and overloading.
headings: Procedures — and the IN / OUT / IN OUT modes
pages.content: Procedures — and the IN / OUT / IN OUT modes Default parameters Functions and return types Calling functions from SQL Overloading DROP and REPLACE Procedures do things; functions return values. Both are stored in the database, callable from SQL, applications, and other PL/SQL. The distinction matters more in Oracle than most languages because of one hard SQL-rule, and the parameter modes govern how data travels in and out. Parameters can carry defaults, letting callers omit them — the classic pattern for optional switches: Oracle supports positional in order and named param => value notation. Overlapping both is allowed but ugly — pick positional for short lists, named when skipping defaults. Functions that are pure no DML, no side effects can run inside SELECT — that is what makes customer_spend customer_id above work. But there are rules, and they matter for the performance page : Like most languages, PL/SQL lets the same name back different signatures — the compiler picks the version by argument count/types. Overloading only works inside a package : The function must behave as a pure function — a SELECT with no DML. If it must be callable from SQL, declare it WITH DETERMINISM 19c+ or keep it side-effect free; otherwise the optimizer cannot fold/prune calls. Calling a function in a WHERE on indexed columns blocks index use the SQL page's warning unless it's function-based-index friendly. An OUT parameter holds no trustworthy value when the procedure raises an exception mid-way — code the error path explicitly as the WHEN NO_DATA_FOUND above does , and never read an OUT expecting the pre-call value. Keep the overloaded versions behaving similarly — two process_order functions that do unrelated things is a maintenance trap. Use overloading for "same operation, different input flavor", not as a naming hack. Prefer CREATE OR REPLACE over DROP … CREATE : the former keeps existing object grants and is a single atomic step. The security & deployment page covers what happens to dependents and how compile warnings flow through. Mode Data direction Default? Typical use IN Into the procedure read-only Yes The inputs; cannot be assigned OUT Out of the procedure No Return values, e.g. OUT p_error, OUT result set IN OUT In, changed, and back out again Accumulators and 'update this value' parameters update this value Return type Notes Scalar NUMBER, DATE, VARCHAR2, BOOLEAN BOOLEAN return cannot be used directly inside plain SQL %TYPE / %ROWTYPE / records Return a fetched row as one result Typed collections / SYS_REFCURSOR/table type Return whole result sets listed on the collections page CREATE OR REPLACE PROCEDURE adjust_credit p_customer IN customers.customer_id%TYPE, p_amount IN NUMBER, -- read only p_new_limit OUT customers.credit_limit%TYPE, -- caller gets this p_count IN OUT NUMBER -- in, incremented, handed back IS BEGIN UPDATE customers SET credit_limit = NVL credit_limit, 0 + p_amount WHERE customer_id = p_customer; SELECT credit_limit INTO p_new_limit FROM customers WHERE customer_id = p_customer; p_count := p_count + 1; -- IN OUT: changes flow back to the caller EXCEPTION WHEN NO_DATA_FOUND THEN p_new_limit := -1; END adjust_credit; / DECLARE v_customer NUMBER := 101; v_limit customers.credit_limit%TYPE; v_count NUMBER := 0; BEGIN adjust_credit v_customer, 500, v_limit, v_count ; DBMS_OUTPUT.PUT_LINE 'new limit ' || v_limit || '. calls=' || v_count ; END; / CREATE OR REPLACE PROCEDURE run_report p_report VARCHAR2, p_format VARCHAR2 DEFAULT 'PDF', p_once BOOLEAN DEFAULT TRUE IS BEGIN DBMS_OUTPUT.PUT_LINE p_report || ' as ' || p_format ; END; / BEGIN run_report 'AP_AGING' ; -- uses both defaults run_report 'AP_AGING', 'CSV' ; -- format only, default once run_report 'AP_AGING', p_once => FALSE ; -- named notation END; / CREATE OR REPLACE FUNCTION customer_spend p_customer NUMBER RETURN NUMBER IS v_total NUMBER; BEGIN SELECT NVL SUM total_amount , 0 INTO v_total FROM orders WHERE customer_id = p_customer; RETURN v_total; EXCEPTION WHEN NO_DATA_FOUND THEN RETURN 0; END; / -- call from SQL SELECT customer_name, customer_spend customer_id AS spend FROM customers; CREATE OR REPLACE PACKAGE pkg_orders AS PROCEDURE process_order p_id NUMBER ; PROCEDURE process_order p_name VARCHAR2 ; -- overload: same name, diff type END pkg_orders; / CREATE OR REPLACE PACKAGE BODY pkg_orders AS PROCEDURE process_order p_id NUMBER IS BEGIN DBMS_OUTPUT.PUT_LINE 'by id ' || p_id ; END; PROCEDURE process_order p_name VARCHAR2 IS BEGIN DBMS_OUTPUT.PUT_LINE 'by name ' || p_name ; END; END pkg_orders; / BEGIN pkg_orders.process_order 7 ; -- NUMBER version pkg_orders.process_order 'Acme' ; -- VARCHAR2 version END; / -- REPLACE re-creates atomically keeps grants — the daily dev loop CREATE OR REPLACE PROCEDURE my_proc ... ; -- DROP removes DROP PROCEDURE my_proc; DROP FUNCTION my_func;

pages.title: Records & object types
pages.description: User-defined records and table-based %ROWTYPE records, plus an introduction to object types and object methods with the MAP / ORDER / MEMBER methods that power custom SQL types.
headings: Records inside collections — the workhorse shape
Object types and methods — the advanced layer
pages.content: User-defined records Table-based records with %ROWTYPE Records inside collections — the workhorse shape Object types and methods — the advanced layer A record bundles several values of possibly different types under one name — PL/SQL's struct. Records combine naturally with the collections page: a table of records TABLE OF t_my_rec is the shape you want for "many rich rows in memory". Object types take records a step further into database-first classes. When the record must match a query's output — not just one table — you have two idioms, each with a distinct feel: This is precisely the intermediate form the bulk page turns into a BULK COLLECT / FORALL : query into an array of records, then push it to the table in one shot. Object types are Oracle's database-visible classes: a type with attributes, stored like a schema object, with methods defined alongside. They are heavier machinery than records — used for genuinely object-shaped domains and for custom column/table types: Record fields can be anchored with %TYPE — the same schema-tracking habit as variables. A record is copied whole: v_scores := v_c; — no per-field copies. %ROWTYPE the blocks page is a one-liner record that mirrors a whole table. "Object types going too deep" is a known Oracle anti-pattern — schema-on-records plus JSON reduces the need for full object modeling. The useful level for most projects: a TYPE ... IS RECORD in a package for in-memory shapes, and reserve CREATE TYPE ... OBJECT for domain columns you genuinely store and query the JSON/SQL macros pages show the modern, lighter alternative . Idiom Shape comes from Use when %ROWTYPE record One table Fetching a whole row with SELECT * or a cursor FOR row SELECT col, col INTO record Exact declarations Projecting a subset into a hand-defined record Method kind What it means MEMBER Runs on an object value; sees SELF STATIC Runs without an instance — type-level utility MAP Returns a scalar Oracle uses to ORDER/COMPARE values ORDER Compares two objects when MAP is not usable CONSTRUCTOR Creates an initial value default exists, or custom DECLARE TYPE t_cust IS RECORD name customers.customer_name%TYPE, region regions.region_name%TYPE, score NUMBER 3 DEFAULT 0 ; v_c t_cust; -- one record v_scores t_cust; -- same shape again BEGIN v_c.name := 'Acme Corp'; v_c.region := 'West'; v_c.score := 95; DBMS_OUTPUT.PUT_LINE v_c.name || ' / ' || v_c.region || ' / ' || v_c.score ; END; / DECLARE v_row customers%ROWTYPE; -- whole table row BEGIN SELECT * INTO v_row FROM customers WHERE customer_id = 101; DBMS_OUTPUT.PUT_LINE v_row.customer_name ; -- projected: a record that only carries two columns v_projected.name := v_row.customer_name; v_projected.limit := v_row.credit_limit; END; / DECLARE TYPE t_row IS RECORD cid customers.customer_id%TYPE, name customers.customer_name%TYPE ; TYPE t_rows IS TABLE OF t_row; -- collection OF records v_list t_rows := t_rows ; BEGIN v_list.EXTEND; v_list 1 .cid := 1; v_list 1 .name := 'One'; v_list.EXTEND; v_list 2 .cid := 2; v_list 2 .name := 'Two'; FOR i IN v_list.FIRST .. v_list.LAST LOOP DBMS_OUTPUT.PUT_LINE v_list i .cid || ' ' || v_list i .name ; END LOOP; END; / CREATE OR REPLACE TYPE address_t AS OBJECT street VARCHAR2 60 , city VARCHAR2 30 , postcode VARCHAR2 10 , MEMBER FUNCTION label RETURN VARCHAR2 -- member method: runs on a value ; / CREATE OR REPLACE TYPE BODY address_t AS MEMBER FUNCTION label RETURN VARCHAR2 IS BEGIN RETURN self.street || ', ' || self.city; -- SELF = the current value END; END; / -- use it in a table column and read owned methods in SQL SELECT a.home_address.label FROM customers c, TABLE c.address_books a; -- illustrative: object columns & collections

pages.title: Security & deployment
pages.description: Definer rights vs invoker rights (AUTHID), grants for procedures and packages, dependencies and recompilation, compile errors and warnings, and source-controlled deployment scripts.
pages.content: Definer rights vs invoker rights AUTHID Grants for procedures and packages Dependencies and recompilation Compile errors and warnings Source control and deployment scripts A stored program is only useful if people can run it safely and the right version ships everywhere. This page is the boundary between "I wrote a procedure" and "the organisation trusts and deploys that procedure" — AUTHID rights, explicit grants, dependency management, and compile hygiene baked into a promotion pipeline. When a procedure runs, whose privileges decide what SQL is allowed inside it? That is the AUTHID question, and it is Oracle's single most security-relevant PL/SQL switch: Granting EXECUTE controls who may run the program; grant on the package covers its whole surface: PL/SQL objects record dependencies: a procedure touching customers is "dependent" on it. Change the table and the dependent becomes INVALID ; Oracle recompiles it on next use, or you force a recompile: A failed CREATE OR REPLACE leaves the object compiled-with-errors . The compiler also surfaces warnings the compiler sees during PLW checks. The three commands for the review loop: PL/SQL ships as files the CREATE scripts — so it belongs in Git exactly like the rest of the codebase, and promotion is a scripted, tested play: Grant EXECUTE , never direct table DML, when the package is your API. Roles vs direct grants: roles group entitlements and are changed everywhere at once. Object-level audit: ALL_TAB_PRIVS shows which role holds EXECUTE on what. Files, not the live — one file per object or per package pair: spec + body , versioned. Idempotent promotable — CREATE OR REPLACE everywhere, so rerunning the script is safe. Environments in steps — dev → test → prod, each with its own schema/grants/git tag. Compile-and-check gate — run the file, then verify USER_ERRORS is empty and objects are VALID. Rollback strategy — keep the previous file s /tag; CREATE OR REPLACE with the old version restores behavior data-schema changes still need a plan . DEFINER rights are how you hand users a "trusted wrapper" around tables they may not touch directly — but the same mechanism silently endows every caller with the owner's power for that procedure. Audit what each definer-rights program does; a careless EXECUTE to a broad role is how privilege leaks. Package bodies are invalidated less often than package specs — one more reason to keep logic in the body: changing the body often recompiles quietly, changing a spec signature can ripple through every caller. Make friendly errors a habit: a bad CREATE in a script should stop the deployment, not leave a "compiled with errors" object that silently old-version executes. Check USER_ERRORS for the count before promoting. Tie it together: AUTHID DEFINER + a package + a role + an idempotent file + a compile gate is the exact artifact an Oracle shop runs through its pipeline hundreds of times. That combination — not any single keyword — is what "production PL/SQL" means. Mode Runs SQL as… Effect AUTHID DEFINER default The owner of the procedure Callers run with the owner's privileges — the classic trusted-wrapper pattern AUTHID CURRENT_USER invoker The caller current user Callers' own privileges apply — safer for shared objects, needs grants on every table s privileges — the classic trusted-wrapper pattern" , "AUTHID CURRENT_USER invoker ", "The caller current user ", "Callers CREATE OR REPLACE PROCEDURE pay_vendor p_inv NUMBER AUTHID CURRENT_USER -- invoker rights IS BEGIN -- inside here, SQL runs with the CALLER's privileges: -- the caller must hold UPDATE on the tables used UPDATE ap_controls SET paid_flag = 'Y' WHERE invoice_id = p_inv; END; / CREATE ROLE app_processor; GRANT EXECUTE ON pkg_finance TO app_processor; -- one grant, whole API GRANT app_processor TO staff01, staff02; -- the inverse REVOKE EXECUTE ON pkg_finance FROM staff02; SELECT object_name, object_type, status FROM user_objects WHERE object_type IN 'PROCEDURE','FUNCTION','PACKAGE','TRIGGER' AND status = 'INVALID'; -- force recompile also after changing the underlying table ALTER PACKAGE pkg_finance COMPILE BODY; -- or: ALTER PROCEDURE COMPILE -- the classic one-command sweep for a pushed change EXEC DBMS_UTILITY.COMPILE_SCHEMA USER ; -- errors on the last creation SHOW ERRORS; -- persistent view of both SELECT * FROM user_errors WHERE name = 'PKG_FINANCE'; -- compiler warnings optional strictness ALTER SESSION SET PLSQL_WARNINGS = 'ENABLE:ALL'; -- 01_package_spec.sql git, tagged v2.1 CREATE OR REPLACE PACKAGE pkg_finance ... ; -- 02_package_body.sql CREATE OR REPLACE PACKAGE BODY pkg_finance ... ; -- 03_grants.sql GRANT EXECUTE ON pkg_finance TO app_processor; -- post-run check fail the play if any rows : SELECT COUNT * FROM user_errors; -- expect 0

pages.title: Triggers
pages.description: BEFORE, AFTER, and INSTEAD OF triggers; INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE triggers; row-level versus statement-level; the :OLD and :NEW records; auditing triggers; and the mutating-table error with its fix.
headings: Row-level vs statement-level — and the mutating-table error
pages.content: Timing and level :OLD and :NEW Auditing triggers Row-level vs statement-level — and the mutating-table error INSTEAD OF triggers on views The production checklist A trigger is stored PL/SQL that fires automatically when a DML statement happens against a table — no application has to remember to call anything. That is their power and their risk: they run inside the same transaction, so every trigger error and every slow trigger is every insert/update/delete. A trigger is defined by two independent axes, which combine into four classic kinds: In a row-level trigger the record has two halves: :OLD holds the row's values before the change, :NEW after. What each : record contains depends on the event: The most common real-world trigger: copy who/what/when into an audit table on every change a lightweight alternative to full AUDIT , and a pattern Fusion-style apps rely on : FOR EACH ROW means per affected row; without it the trigger runs once per statement . Statement-level triggers cannot see :OLD / :NEW , which is also why they are the safe home for "after this whole batch, do X". A view is usually not updateable in complex cases. An INSTEAD OF trigger intercepts the DML on the view and lets you write the real implementation: Move the query to a statement-level AFTER trigger which runs when the table is quiet — read :OLD / :NEW only inside a row trigger, then aggregate there afterwards. Use a compound trigger row-section + after-statement-section to collect per-row data safely. Disable for bulk loads — triggers fire per row; a trillion-row load through a row trigger will not get faster. Never hide DML-heavy logic in a trigger — it becomes invisible to every caller and every plan. Name triggers and track them via USER_TRIGGERS — an unknown trigger is how "who changed that column" mysteries start. Use ALTER TRIGGER … DISABLE/ENABLE and optimizer hints like NO_QUERY_TRANSFORMATION deliberately, not as a habit. A BEFORE row trigger can change :NEW to fix values before the row is written — the stamping pattern below. It cannot modify :OLD , and AFTER row triggers cannot change :NEW at all. Audit inside the same transaction means the audit row commits or rolls back with its source — that is usually the desired guarantee "audit cannot lie" , but it also couples your audit write to every business transaction's performance. The famous ORA-04091 mutating-table error : a row-level trigger on table T cannot query T itself "ORA-04091: table T is mutating, trigger may not read or modify it" . While a row trigger runs, the table is in flux. The standard fixes: Move the query to a statement-level AFTER trigger which runs when the table is quiet — read :OLD / :NEW only inside a row trigger, then aggregate there afterwards. Use a compound trigger row-section + after-statement-section to collect per-row data safely. BEFORE AFTER INSTEAD OF ROW-level FOR EACH ROW Run per row, before the change — stamp/modify :NEW Run per row, after the change — audit/log Only valid on views — replace the DML the view cannot do STATEMENT-level default Run once for the whole statement, before Run once for the whole statement, after Only valid on views Event :OLD :NEW INSERT All NULL no old row The row being added UPDATE The pre-change row The post-change row may be modified by the trigger DELETE The row being removed All NULL CREATE OR REPLACE TRIGGER trg_orders_audit BEFORE INSERT OR UPDATE OR DELETE ON orders -- the events FOR EACH ROW -- the level BEGIN DBMS_OUTPUT.PUT_LINE 'row touched' ; END; / CREATE OR REPLACE TRIGGER trg_orders_before BEFORE INSERT OR UPDATE OF total_amount ON orders FOR EACH ROW BEGIN IF :NEW.total_amount > 0 AND :OLD.total_amount > 100000 THEN raise_application_error -20010, 'Order value change too big' ; END IF; END; / CREATE TABLE customers_audit aud_id NUMBER GENERATED BY DEFAULT AS IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY, customer_id NUMBER, old_limit NUMBER 12,2 , new_limit NUMBER 12,2 , action VARCHAR2 6 , changed_by VARCHAR2 30 , changed_at TIMESTAMP ; CREATE OR REPLACE TRIGGER trg_customers_audit AFTER UPDATE OR DELETE ON customers FOR EACH ROW BEGIN INSERT INTO customers_audit customer_id, old_limit, new_limit, action, changed_by, changed_at VALUES :OLD.customer_id, :OLD.credit_limit, :NEW.credit_limit, CASE WHEN :NEW.customer_id IS NULL THEN 'DELETE' ELSE 'UPDATE' END, USER, SYSTIMESTAMP ; END; / CREATE OR REPLACE TRIGGER trg_orders_compound FOR INSERT OR UPDATE ON orders COMPOUND TRIGGER v_rows NUMBER := 0; AFTER EACH ROW IS BEGIN v_rows := v_rows + 1; -- safe: just counting the row END AFTER EACH ROW; AFTER STATEMENT IS BEGIN -- the table is not mutating here — safe to query orders DBMS_OUTPUT.PUT_LINE 'orders changed: ' || v_rows || ' — total now ' || total_order_count ; END AFTER STATEMENT; END trg_orders_compound; / CREATE OR REPLACE TRIGGER trg_v_customers INSTEAD OF INSERT ON v_customer_regions FOR EACH ROW BEGIN INSERT INTO customers customer_id, customer_name, region_id VALUES :NEW.customer_id, :NEW.customer_name, :NEW.region_id ; END; /

pages.title: Security
pages.description: Users and roles, system vs object privileges, GRANT and REVOKE, profiles and password concepts, synonyms for controlled access, and row-level security with Virtual Private Database.
pages.content: Users and roles System vs object privileges GRANT and REVOKE Profiles and password concepts Synonyms for controlled access Row-level security / Virtual Private Database VPD Database security is a story of two lists : who users and the roles they hold and what the privileges attached . Almost everything in this page reduces to keeping those two lists small and deliberate — the database enforces them hard, which is precisely why the rights you grant here are the ones an auditor asks about. A user is an account; a role is a named bundle of privileges you grant to users. Roles are what let you manage hundreds of accounts without hundreds of GRANT statements: The wrinkle: CREATE TABLE is a system privilege you may create tables in your own schema , but working on someone else's table is an object privilege on that table. A profile sets account limits — password rules, lifetime, failed-login locking. It applies to a user, not to a schema: A synonym is a private alias. Used well, it both shortens names and, more importantly, hides where an object really lives — so you can relocate tables without breaking every query: Synonym + revoke is the controlled-access recipe: the user sees employees , never HR.PAY_ROLL_RAW — and if the real table must move, the pointer changes, the users do not. Object privileges control which tables ; VPD controls which rows . A policy function appends a WHERE to every SQL against the table, driven by SYS_CONTEXT values the Oracle-specific page introduced SYS_CONTEXT : Never hand out DBA casually — it is the everything-role. Role membership can be default always active or granted on demand; quiz yourself on which privileges are "role-granted" when a user shows a surprising capability. Account lifecycle: lock unused accounts ALTER USER … ACCOUNT LOCK , rotate passwords, and revoke roles when people change jobs. Grant the minimum — SELECT where reading suffices, not SELECT+ALL. WITH GRANT OPTION lets the grantee re-grant; use it only when you mean delegation. Dictionary check: USER_TAB_PRIVS shows what you hold on which object. VPD applies invisibly and centrally — you cannot forget the WHERE. That is its power and its danger: code that writes through the policy sees only its own rows. Row-level restrictions can also be built with views the "views as security" pattern — simpler, but easier to bypass than VPD. Enable AUDIT traces for privileged roles; data-touching SQL before role changes is the usual audit ask. PUBLIC means everyone, forever, and auditing it is hard. Grants to PUBLIC old demos and sample setups do this constantly are a classic security finding — check ALL_TAB_PRIVS WHERE grantee = 'PUBLIC' before going live. The DEFAULT profile ships permissive no expiry . Organizations that care apply versions of the above globally; anyone who inherits DEFAULT should expect an audit flag. Kind Scope Examples System privilege Actions on the database as a whole CREATE SESSION, CREATE TABLE, CREATE ANY VIEW, ALTER ANY TABLE Object privilege Actions on a specific table/view/etc. SELECT on HR.EMPLOYEES, UPDATE on custom extras, EXECUTE on a procedure CREATE USER sales_app IDENTIFIED BY StrongPass123; CREATE ROLE sales_read_role; GRANT CREATE SESSION TO sales_app; GRANT sales_read_role TO sales_app; GRANT SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE ON customers TO sales_app; GRANT EXECUTE ON pkg_payments TO billing_clerk; REVOKE UPDATE ON customers FROM sales_app; -- remove read-write -- The recursive version: grant with ADMIN OPTION passes it on GRANT SELECT, UPDATE ON customers TO app_owner WITH GRANT OPTION; CREATE PROFILE app_user_profile LIMIT FAILED_LOGIN_ATTEMPTS 5 PASSWORD_LOCK_TIME 1 PASSWORD_LIFE_TIME 90 PASSWORD_REUSE_MAX 5 PASSWORD_VERIFY_FUNCTION VERIFY_FUNCTION_11G; -- complexity check ALTER USER sales_app PROFILE app_user_profile; GRANT SELECT ON hr.employees TO reporting; CREATE PUBLIC SYNONYM employees FOR hr.employees; -- reporting now runs "SELECT * FROM employees" -> hr.employees -- If the table moves to REPORTING schema, only the synonym changes. -- The policy body is a PL/SQL function returning a WHERE-clause string CREATE OR REPLACE FUNCTION restrict_sales schema_name VARCHAR2, table_name VARCHAR2 RETURN VARCHAR2 IS BEGIN RETURN 'owner = SYS_CONTEXT ''APP'', ''SALES_REP'' '; END; BEGIN DBMS_RLS.ADD_POLICY 'SALES', 'CUSTOMERS', 'sales_policy', 'SALES', 'RESTRICT_SALES', 'SELECT, UPDATE' ; END;

pages.title: Sequences & identity columns
pages.description: CREATE SEQUENCE, NEXTVAL and CURRVAL, the CACHE/CYCLE/INCREMENT settings that bite you at scale, and the 12c+ identity columns that automate the whole pattern.
headings: CACHE, CYCLE, INCREMENT — the settings that bite
pages.content: CREATE SEQUENCE and NEXTVAL / CURRVAL CACHE, CYCLE, INCREMENT — the settings that bite Identity columns 12c and later Every table needs unique keys, and Oracle generates them with sequences — independent, concurrency-safe number generators. They are the classic pattern behind the primary key you have been seeing as NUMBER PRIMARY KEY . Since 12c, an identity column wires a sequence to a table automatically. An identity column makes the sequence invisible — the database generates the value automatically on insert. It is now the recommended default for new tables' keys: For bulk imports that carry their own IDs say, from the source system , use BY DEFAULT for the identity — an import can supply order_id and the database keeps generating fresh ones for everything new. NEXTVAL gives the next number and moves the sequence forward; CURRVAL reads the last NEXTVAL your session fetched. Calling CURRVAL before any NEXTVAL raises ORA-08002 . Sequences are gap-ok : rolled-back inserts, crashes, and CACHE changes all burn numbers. If you need truly gapless numbering you are in document sequencing territory Oracle's DBMS-friendly "gapless" tools , not sequences. Because NEXTVAL is called during the statement, you can use it in an INSERT ... SELECT to number every row of the batch. The two design decisions that matter: don't use CYCLE for primary keys reused numbers silently collide with old rows , and keep CACHE moderate. A huge CACHE e.g. 1,000 is great for bulk load speed but on an instance crash your key space jumps by that many unused numbers. Under the hood an identity column creates a sequence look it up via USER_TAB_IDENTITY_COLS . The difference from doing it by hand: the tie to the table is automatic, so you cannot accidentally hand-number two tables from one shared sequence — the classic bug when you write the sequence pattern manually. Setting Default What it does Gotcha INCREMENT 1 Step between numbers negative counts down Negative for descending IDs START WITH MINVALUE? First number returned Rarely needed after 12c identity CACHE 20 Pre-allocates numbers in memory for speed Gaps on instance-crash numbers are lost, not reused NOCACHE / ORDER No pre-allocation / guarantee of order across sessions ORDER costs performance on RAC CYCLE NOCYCLE Wrap around when MAXVALUE is hit CYCLE can duplicate IDs unless MINVALUE set carefully — usually avoid MAXVALUE 10^27 Upper boundary Overshoot throws ORA-08004 unless CYCLE Mode Behavior GENERATED ALWAYS Insert can never supply the value; Oracle always generates it GENERATED BY DEFAULT Gives a value unless the INSERT explicitly provides one good for data migration BY DEFAULT ON NULL Like BY DEFAULT but also fills when the insert passes NULL CREATE SEQUENCE seq_orders START WITH 1 INCREMENT BY 1 CACHE 20; -- Ask for the next number: oracle assigns it, guaranteed unique INSERT INTO orders order_id, customer_id, total_amount VALUES seq_orders.NEXTVAL, 42, 500 ; -- Read the value THIS session just got no call to NEXTVAL - it errors otherwise SELECT seq_orders.CURRVAL FROM dual; CREATE TABLE orders order_id NUMBER GENERATED BY DEFAULT AS IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY, -- rows get 1,2,3... without any NEXTVAL customer_id NUMBER, total_amount NUMBER 12,2 ; INSERT INTO orders customer_id, total_amount VALUES 42, 500 ; -- order_id is filled for you 1, next 2, ...

pages.title: Set operators
pages.description: UNION, UNION ALL, INTERSECT, and MINUS (Oracle's EXCEPT) — combining whole result sets vertically, plus the column and ordering rules that make them fail.
headings: UNION vs UNION ALL — the cost difference
INTERSECT and MINUS — the reconciler's tools
pages.content: The four operators The column rules UNION vs UNION ALL — the cost difference INTERSECT and MINUS — the reconciler's tools Joins combine tables side by side more columns . Set operators combine result sets one under another more rows . You use them for "which customers appear in either list", "which products we stopped selling", and reconciliation questions where two systems' outputs must be compared. Both queries must return the same number of columns with compatible types . The column names used for output come from the first query. Violations throw ORA-00933 or ORA-01790 : The classic mistake is writing ORDER BY inside one leg — ordering belongs at the very end and applies to the whole result: UNION must sort or hash the whole result to find and drop duplicates. UNION ALL merely appends — no sort. On large sets that is the difference between a fast query and an expensive one: These two are gold in data-quality work: compare what two systems think and find the differences in one statement. If the two legs cannot overlap distinct key ranges , use UNION ALL and skip the sort. If you need the count of distinct rows, UNION is the real meaning — keep it. MINUS is Oracle's name for what other databases call EXCEPT . New versions of Oracle actually accept EXCEPT as a synonym, but legacy scripts say MINUS — know both. Output column names come from the first leg , so aliases you set on the second leg are ignored for naming. Don't fight it — name things in leg one. Rule of thumb: "did I mean duplicates-or-not?" If duplicates are fine or impossible, UNION ALL is almost always the better choice on big data. INTERSECT and MINUS compare the whole selected row, not just the key. If the two systems disagree only on balance , the row shows up in both MINUS legs with different values — which is exactly what your reconciliation wants to see, but "changed" vs "new" rows need a full join plus NULLIF or DECODE to separate. Operator Rows returned Dedup? Meaning UNION Rows in A or B Yes Everything, once UNION ALL No Everything, duplicates kept INTERSECT Rows in both A and B The overlap MINUS Rows in A but not B The difference Oracle's EXCEPT SELECT customer_id FROM customers WHERE region_id = 1 UNION SELECT customer_id FROM customers WHERE region_id = 2; SELECT customer_name, 'has orders' AS status FROM customers WHERE EXISTS SELECT 1 FROM orders o WHERE o.customer_id = customers.customer_id UNION ALL SELECT customer_name, 'no orders' AS status FROM customers WHERE NOT EXISTS SELECT 1 FROM orders o WHERE o.customer_id = customers.customer_id ORDER BY status, customer_name; -- one ORDER BY at the end -- What BOTH sources believe INTERSECT SELECT account_id, balance FROM new_system INTERSECT SELECT account_id, balance FROM old_system; -- What the new system thinks but the old one does not MINUS SELECT account_id, balance FROM new_system MINUS SELECT account_id, balance FROM old_system;

pages.title: Single-row functions
pages.description: Functions that return one result per input row: character (UPPER, SUBSTR, INSTR, TRIM, REPLACE…), number (ROUND, TRUNC, CEIL, FLOOR, MOD…), date (SYSDATE, ADD_MONTHS, LAST_DAY…), conversion (TO_CHAR, TO_DATE, TO_NUMBER, CAST), null-handling (NVL, NVL2, NULLIF, COALESCE), and CASE / DECODE.
headings: Dealing with NULL: NVL, NVL2, NULLIF, COALESCE
pages.content: Character functions Number functions Date functions Conversion functions Dealing with NULL: NVL, NVL2, NULLIF, COALESCE CASE and DECODE A single-row function transforms one input row into one output value — clearly different from an aggregate many rows → one value, next page . These functions run per row, and they are where most formatting logic in real queries lives. Conversions turn data between types. The format masks are words Oracle recognizes — the format models page lists them: These functions replace or test for missing values — the practical keys to three-valued logic: CASE is the ANSI-standard conditional expression; DECODE is Oracle's older, terser equivalent. Both return a value, not run statements: COALESCE and NVL look similar, but COALESCE takes many arguments and short-circuits; NVL is the older, Oracle-specific two-argument form. NVL credit_limit, 0 prevents NULL from silently zeroing sums in aggregates; but on large tables it also blocks index use — the same note as implicit conversion. Oracle strings are 1-based , unlike most programming languages. SUBSTR 'ab', 0, 1 and SUBSTR 'ab', 1, 1 both return 'a' . Oracle performs implicit conversions when you mix types — a hidden VARCHAR2 → number conversion on every comparison against a numeric column kills index use see the performance page . Write the explicit TO_DATE / TO_NUMBER yourself, and store dates as DATE , not VARCHAR2 . Prefer CASE : it is standard, handles ranges and IS NULL cleanly, and reads better. Legacy Oracle code is full of DECODE — you must be able to read it, you do not need to write it. The one place DECODE shines is a quick equality lookup in a tiny expression. Function Returns Example UPPER s , LOWER s The string uppercased / lowercased UPPER 'tech' → 'TECH' INITCAP s Each word's first letter uppercase INITCAP 'hello world' → 'Hello World' SUBSTR s, pos, pages.title: Subqueries
pages.description: Single-row and multiple-row subqueries, correlated subqueries, nested subqueries, inline views, scalar subqueries, EXISTS/ANY/ALL, and the WITH clause (CTEs) — plain and recursive.
pages.content: Single-row vs multiple-row subqueries IN, ANY, ALL Correlated subqueries Nested subqueries Inline views FROM subqueries Scalar subqueries WITH clause / Common Table Expressions CTEs Recursive WITH queries A subquery is a SELECT used inside another statement — inside WHERE , FROM , or the SELECT list. Subqueries let one query be the answer to another's question: "orders bigger than the average order", "customers who never ordered", "the December per-region totals". What a subquery may return decides which operator you pair it with: Multiple-row subqueries pair with membership or quantified operators: Beware the NOT IN … NULL interaction from the filtering page — ALL and ANY share it. If the subquery's column can be NULL, "not bigger than all" never fires for that row. A correlated subquery references the outer query's row — it is re-evaluated per outer row, which is exactly the EXISTS pattern you saw earlier: Subqueries nest arbitrarily: "customers who ordered the product everyone orders". Each level simply answers the level above: Put a subquery in FROM and it becomes a derived table you can treat like any other table — the foundation of every "first compute it, then filter it" report: A subquery in the SELECT list that returns one row and one column becomes a scalar subquery — a computed column per row. If it returns no row it evaluates to NULL , so it never errors: The WITH clause names a subquery once and reuses it — cleaner than the same inline view twice, and it structures complex queries exactly like a packaged report's "extract the numbers first": A CTE can call itself, walking a hierarchy level by level — every employee's manager chain, a bill-of-materials, an org tree. Oracle also has the older CONNECT BY the Oracle-specific page covers it , but ANSI WITH RECURSIVE is standard and reads clearly: Correlated subqueries are powerful but run once per outer row, so on big tables they lean heavily on indexes see the performance page — this is where a missing index turns minutes of pain . "Biggest order per customer" is a canonical correlated query, but the analytic functions page shows the cleaner ROW_NUMBER way to do the same. If a "single-row" subquery returns more than one row, Oracle throws ORA-01427: single-row subquery returns more than one row . That is the error to expect when a label lookup stops being unique. Recursive CTEs must combine UNION ALL rarely UNION with an anchor , then a recursive term that stops when it matches nothing new. Missing stop conditions or cycles of the anchor-to-itself kind are the usual bugs — filter to a depth or use CONNECT BY NOCYCLE on the legacy side. Subquery returns Pair with Meaning Exactly one row, one column =, >, =, <= Compare a value to that single answer Many rows, one column IN, ANY, ALL, EXISTS Membership or quantified comparison Many rows, many columns IN / FROM inline view Row values, or a whole derived table Operator TRUE when… Cousin x IN sub x equals any returned value = ANY x > ALL sub x is bigger than the max returned > SELECT MAX … x > ANY sub x is bigger than the min returned > SELECT MIN … EXISTS sub subquery returns at least one row COUNT * > 0 SELECT order_id, total_amount FROM orders WHERE total_amount > SELECT AVG total_amount FROM orders ; -- returns exactly one number -- IN: customer is anyone in the returned list SELECT customer_name FROM customers WHERE customer_id IN SELECT customer_id FROM orders ; -- = ANY is identical to IN WHERE customer_id = ANY SELECT customer_id FROM orders ; -- > ALL: bigger than every returned value SELECT order_id FROM orders WHERE total_amount > ALL SELECT total_amount FROM orders ; SELECT c.customer_name FROM customers c WHERE EXISTS SELECT 1 FROM orders o WHERE o.customer_id = c.customer_id -- correlated: refers to outer c AND o.total_amount > 5000 ; SELECT customer_name FROM customers WHERE customer_id IN SELECT customer_id FROM orders WHERE order_id IN SELECT order_id FROM order_lines WHERE product_id = 7 ; SELECT cs.customer_name, totals.spend FROM customers cs JOIN SELECT customer_id, SUM total_amount AS spend FROM orders GROUP BY customer_id totals ON totals.customer_id = cs.customer_id WHERE totals.spend > 10000; SELECT c.customer_name, SELECT MAX o.order_date FROM orders o WHERE o.customer_id = c.customer_id AS last_order FROM customers c; WITH region_totals AS SELECT r.region_name, SUM o.total_amount AS revenue FROM orders o JOIN customers c ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id JOIN regions r ON r.region_id = c.region_id GROUP BY r.region_name -- "region_totals" is usable here and again below like a table SELECT * FROM region_totals WHERE revenue > SELECT AVG revenue FROM region_totals ; WITH emp_chain emp_id, emp_name, manager_id, depth AS -- Anchor: the top of the tree SELECT employee_id, full_name, manager_id, 1 FROM employees WHERE manager_id IS NULL UNION ALL -- Recursive part: one level at a time SELECT e.employee_id, e.full_name, e.manager_id, ec.depth + 1 FROM employees e JOIN emp_chain ec ON e.manager_id = ec.emp_id SELECT emp_id, LPAD ' ', depth-1 * 3 || emp_name AS tree FROM emp_chain;

pages.title: Transactions
pages.description: COMMIT, ROLLBACK, SAVEPOINT, read consistency, locks and concurrency basics, and the isolation model Oracle uses so that readers never block writers.
headings: Read consistency — the reader never waits
Isolation levels and what Oracle actually gives you
The DDL side effect: implicit commits
pages.content: The four isolation properties COMMIT, ROLLBACK, SAVEPOINT Read consistency — the reader never waits Locks and concurrency basics Isolation levels and what Oracle actually gives you The DDL side effect: implicit commits A transaction is a group of DML statements that must all succeed or all fail together. Oracle's model is simple: your DML starts a transaction implicitly, and it stays open until you COMMIT , ROLLBACK , or end the session. Nothing your coworkers see changes until you commit — and you can undo everything until then. Transactions guarantee ACID : A tomicity all-or-nothing , C onsistency a statement never sees a half-updated state , I solation concurrent transactions cannot corrupt each other , and D urability committed data survives a crash . Oracle's lock manager and redo log implement these — you mostly experience them as "why can't I commit if I have uncommitted work" and "why did my query show old data". The behavior that surprises everyone moving from another database: readers do not block writers . Oracle implements multiversion read consistency — a query sees the data as of the moment the query started , using an undo /rollback segment to reconstruct the older version of a row that some other session is busy updating. Consequences: Oracle's default READ COMMITTED is already very robust because of multiversioning — it is not "a plain snapshot per row" like some engines, so the "dirty read" and "lost update" anomalies that the ANSI docs warn about are largely engineered out. For true serializable reads of a changing table you opt in explicitly. This repeats the foundations warning because it is where the money disappears: CREATE / ALTER / DROP / TRUNCATE all commit your open transaction . Done need GRANT for many objects. If you batch 10,000 updates and then re-create an index, the updates are committed without you asking. A long-running report does not get partial updates: it sees a consistent snapshot. Rereading the same row inside one transaction can show different values if you explicitly want the newest — plain SELECT is statement-level read consistent unless you change it. In Oracle you cannot COMMIT inside a transaction that has only been started by SELECT in a read-consistency sense, and more practically: sessions with open transactions hold row locks that block other builders' UPDATE s on the same rows — and a hung session holding locks is a production incident. Commit promptly. The rules in practice: an UPDATE / DELETE locks the rows it touches until commit ; readers never lock; two sessions can update the same table but not the same row simultaneously; and a CREATE TABLE / DROP against a table being updated waits for the updater's commit. The “wait forever behind a zombie session” is why you see ORA-01555 snapshot too old and ORA-00054 resource busy in production. For long batches, practice commit in waves : FOR i IN 1 .. 99999 LOOP … IF MOD i, 1000 = 0 THEN COMMIT; END IF; END LOOP; . This bounds the undo/redo footprint and keeps the row locks short — the pattern every real ETL uses. Statement Effect COMMIT Makes all uncommitted changes permanent; releases locks; ends the transaction ROLLBACK Undoes all uncommitted changes; releases locks SAVEPOINT name Marks a point you can roll back to ROLLBACK TO SAVEPOINT name Undoes work since that marker, keeping earlier work Isolation level What it means Oracle default? READ COMMITTED Each statement sees data committed before it runs; no dirty reads Yes — Oracle's default SERIALIZABLE Read a single snapshot of the whole transaction — later commits invisible Available via SET TRANSACTION ISOLATION LEVEL SERIALIZABLE READ ONLY Guarantee only reads, for reporting Variant of serializable-oriented reporting SAVEPOINT before_split; UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance - 1000 WHERE account_id = 1; UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance + 1000 WHERE account_id = 2; -- something failed mid-way? Undo just the two updates ROLLBACK TO SAVEPOINT before_split; -- or keep them: make it permanent COMMIT; -- Session A UPDATE orders SET total_amount = 0 WHERE order_id = 5; -- row locked by A -- Session B separate window — BLOCKS here until A commits: UPDATE orders SET total_amount = 0 WHERE order_id = 5;

pages.title: Views
pages.description: Simple and complex views, updatable views, WITH CHECK OPTION, WITH READ ONLY, and materialized views with their refresh concepts.
pages.content: Simple vs complex views Updatable views WITH CHECK OPTION WITH READ ONLY Materialized views A view is a saved SELECT presented as if it were a table. It stores no data of its own — every query against it runs the underlying statement live. Views are the schema's two most useful magic tricks at once: shaping people see the columns they need, masked to what they may and decoupling the table behind can change without breaking every query above it . Believe it or not, UPDATE , DELETE , and INSERT through a simple view work — Oracle pushes the change down to the backing table. The practical rule: a view is updatable when it selects rows straight from one table WITH / DISTINCT / GROUP BY / set operators break it and contains no synthesized columns: The classic self-sabotage: insert a row through the view that fails the view's own WHERE — you wrote it in, but now you cannot see it. WITH CHECK OPTION bans that: A materialized view behaves like a view but physically stores the result — it is a snapshot table refreshed on a schedule. It trades freshness for speed: REFRESH FAST applies only logged changes and needs MV logs materialized view logs on the source tables; REFRESH COMPLETE rebuilds everything and is simpler. Use MVs for heavyweight joins you re-run constantly, dashboards, and cross-database replicas refresh on demand . Query rewrite can make the optimizer answer your query from the MV automatically — powerful, but a tuning chapter for the performance page . "Insertable" / "updatable" views are a genuine maintenance hazard: a view can be accidentally not updatable in subtle cases, and surprise-Oracle factors mean the safest contract is views are for reading . Use WITH READ ONLY below to harden that intent. The general ladder: a normal view when freshness matters and the base tables are small enough; a materialized view when the same heavy join runs every few minutes and a slightly stale number is fine. Federation and replication layers in Oracle 19c/23ai add "refresh on a schedule" variants of the same idea. Simple view Complex view Source One table Multiple tables / joins Functions & expressions Only character/number rows usually allowed as columns ANY expression, GROUP BY, DISTINCT, aggregates Rows updatable? Often yes Rarely; usually read-only in practice Example active_customers region revenue summary Regular view Materialized view Stores data No — runs live every time Yes — a physical snapshot Freshness Always current As of the last refresh Speed on big joins Repays each time Instant reads of the snapshot Refresh N/A ON DEMAND / ON COMMIT / scheduled CREATE VIEW active_customers AS SELECT customer_id, customer_name AS name, credit_limit FROM customers WHERE void_date IS NULL; CREATE VIEW region_revenue AS SELECT r.region_name, COUNT o.order_id AS order_count, SUM o.total_amount AS revenue FROM orders o JOIN customers c ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id JOIN regions r ON r.region_id = c.region_id GROUP BY r.region_name; UPDATE active_customers SET credit_limit = 100 WHERE name = 'Acme Corp'; -- propagates to customers.credit_limit for customer_id of Acme CREATE VIEW active_customers AS SELECT customer_id, customer_name, credit_limit FROM customers WHERE void_date IS NULL WITH CHECK OPTION CONSTRAINT chk_active_customers; -- This NOW FAILS ORA-01402 : it would create a row you can't see INSERT INTO active_customers customer_id, customer_name VALUES 999, 'Ghost' ; -- no void_date NULL -> violates the check CREATE VIEW report_customers AS SELECT customer_name, credit_limit FROM customers WITH READ ONLY; -- any DML through it -> ORA-42399 CREATE MATERIALIZED VIEW mv_region_revenue REFRESH COMPLETE ON DEMAND START WITH SYSDATE NEXT SYSDATE + 1 AS SELECT r.region_name, COUNT * AS order_count, SUM o.total_amount AS revenue FROM orders o JOIN customers c ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id JOIN regions r ON r.region_id = c.region_id GROUP BY r.region_name; -- Refresh manually: EXEC DBMS_MVIEW.REFRESH 'MV_REGION_REVENUE' ;

pages.title: Everything fails in one of three layers
pages.description: In Fusion there are only three ways data gets in or out: real-time REST, bulk FBDI, and scheduled ESS jobs. Every error you will ever see comes from one of them. Diagnose the layer first, then read the message — this section has a page for each layer and each Financials module.
headings: The same causes, over and over
pages.content: The diagnosis method The three layers The same causes, over and over Module-specific troubleshooting Next steps The diagnosis method Follow the same five steps for every failure — they resolve most issues before you ever open a log. Across all modules, most errors trace back to a handful of root causes. Check these before anything else: Each module has its own page of common failures: General Ledger — posting, periods, accounts, balances Payables — invoice validation, holds, suppliers, payments Receivables — AutoInvoice, receipts, customers Cash Management — statements, reconciliation, bank accounts Fixed Assets — depreciation runs, additions, retirements Expenses — approvals, card transactions, accounting Procurement — requisitions, purchase orders, receiving, suppliers Inventory — items, on-hand, transfers, counting Order Management — sales orders, fulfillment, shipping Start with the layer: REST , FBDI , or ESS . Learn the processes that fail: ESS , FBDI , REST . Before debugging a technical error, rule out the setup and data causes on this page. pages.description: Every REST failure is an HTTP status code plus an error body. Learn what the codes mean, how to read the body, and the five headers/details that cause most API problems.
pages.content: Reading the error body HTTP status codes Top causes & fixes OAuth & header checklist Prevention checklist Next steps Reading the error body Fusion REST errors return a structured body. Always read title and detail first — they are the human explanation. Additional hints arrive in o:errorDetails or the message field. Authenticate: username/password or OAuth 2.0 client credentials for integrations. Always send REST-Framework-Version e.g. 11.13.18.05 — it pins the resource behavior.
