pages.title: Advanced: JavaScript, Quick Starts & custom code
pages.description: When the visual designer is not enough, VBCS lets you drop in your own logic. This page covers custom JavaScript functions, importing third-party libraries, and the Quick Starts wizards that scaffold common page behavior in seconds.
headings: Quick Starts — build the scaffolding fast
pages.content: JavaScript functions Where modules scope your functions Third-party libraries Quick Starts — build the scaffolding fast Custom code beyond the editor Next steps VBCS is low-code, but not "no-code." At some point you need a JavaScript function to transform a value, validate a form, or load a library — and you want the boring scaffolding variables, types, action chains built for you. Both are first-class: custom functions for the logic, Quick Starts for the wiring. A JavaScript function is a reusable block of logic you define once and call from action chains, component bindings, or other functions. Define it in the code editor, then assign it where the visual designer reaches its limit. Functions live in modules , and the module decides where they are visible: You can import and reference third-party JavaScript libraries — functions, objects, and variables you want in your custom code. VB Studio also supports RequireJS , a module loader that simplifies managing library references. A Quick Start is a wizard that builds complex behavior for you. It lives in the Quick Starts tab of a component's Properties pane, and it wires what would otherwise take many manual steps: variables, types, action chains, and page events. Validation — check required fields or formats before a save. Calculation — compute totals, discounts, or concatenated labels. Transformation — reshape an object before it hits a service connection. Import the library as an app artifact, then reference it from your functions. Use RequireJS statements to pull libraries in cleanly. Web components — bring your own component or a third-party web component and use it on the page like a native component. Groovy on business objects — complex server-side logic lives in business object rules/triggers, not in page JavaScript see business objects . RequireJS modules — manage library references explicitly when your app grows past a handful of imports. Use the functions with data in UI components & patterns . Model the object your functions manipulate in business objects . Ship the custom code responsibly in deployment & lifecycle . Put truly reused logic at the AppModule level. Defining the same function in several pages guarantees they drift apart after the first edit. JavaScript runs on the client . Never hard-code credentials, certificates, or secrets in custom functions — once it is in browser code, it is exposed. Follow secure coding standards; keep secrets in service connections and OCI secrets, not in the page. A Quick Start often depends on the one before it — for example, Add Data must run before the create/edit/detail quick starts become available. If your endpoint isn't listed, use the Manual Setup of Endpoint icon in the wizard to configure it directly. When you customize a quick start's fields after the fact, you may need to re-edit the type Edit From Endpoint on the Types tab and the UI. For major changes it is often simpler to delete the component and re-run the quick start. Module Scope Use it when… PageModule One page only Load data on page load, page-specific validation FlowModule All pages in a flow Shared helpers across a multi-page process AppModule The whole application Reusable functions any page can call FragmentModule / LayoutModule Within that fragment/layout only Self-contained reusable components Quick Start What it scaffolds Typical next step Add Data Binds a table/list to an endpoint GET MANY Select which fields to display; add the create form Add Create Page A page to create new records from a form Wire the save action to POST Add Edit Page A page to update an existing record Add validation via a custom function Add Delete Delete action wired to DELETE Confirm dialog before delete List Creation / Detail Navigation Master-detail: selecting a row opens its detail Pass the selected row's id /** * Compute an order total including tax. * Called from an action chain: callFunction "computeTotal" */ function computeTotal lines const subtotal = lines.reduce sum, line => sum + line.qty * line.price , 0 ; const tax = subtotal * 0.10; return ; module.exports = ;

pages.title: Business Objects & REST
pages.description: VBCS business objects give you data without a backend: you define the object, VBCS generates storage plus a REST API, and your pages consume it with a few clicks. This page compares them with REST data sources and service connections.
headings: REST data sources vs business objects
Exposing your own REST with business objects
pages.content: What a business object is Fields & types Business object APIs REST data sources vs business objects Exposing your own REST with business objects Business rules Securing business objects Exposing objects to external clients Modeling objects with the diagrammer Import/export of business objects Next steps When you need data that has no home yet — a draft, a session preference, a lightweight list — you don't want to stand up a database. That is exactly the gap business objects fill: you declare the object and its fields in the designer, and VBCS creates the storage, the CRUD REST API, and the security around it. A business object is a VBCS-defined entity with a set of fields and an auto-generated REST API. VBCS provisions database storage for its rows, so reads and writes behave like a small database you never administer. From a page's point of view it is simply a REST endpoint — the same mechanism that talks to Fusion. Typical uses: Each field has a data type, an optional default, and resource flags. The same catalog powers generated form components, validation, and REST payloads: Business objects support resource associations — relationships exposed as REST sub-resources: For every business object VBCS generates a full REST API under your app's base URL, mirroring CRUD plus the associations above: A concrete call with basic auth, as it looks from curl: These concepts are frequently confused. A business object is VBCS-owned storage with a generated API; a REST data source describes an external JSON service as a schema for your pages; a service connection holds the URL and credentials for that external service. Because a business object is just a REST API, external consumers — a report server, another application, a scheduler — can read and write its data over HTTPS: A business object can carry server-side rules that validate data and react to changes. Because they run on the server, they apply no matter how the data arrives — through the REST API, a page form, or a script. Three kinds exist: By default an object is readable/writable by any user who can access the app. To restrict data, enable role-based security on the object: you get a matrix of user roles × operations view, create, update, delete and switch each cell on or off. External services Process Automation, OIC, report tools can read and write your business objects through their REST endpoints. VBCS exposes a catalog API describing every object's endpoints — one per app version Development, Staging, Live . The diagrammer gives you a visual data model: business objects as boxes and associations as lines. It is the fastest way to design interdependent objects before you build screens. Business objects travel with your application archive: definitions always export and the schema is recreated on import, but data is not moved by default — use the object's Export/Import Data action to move rows between environments. If dev and stage have drifted, reconcile definitions first; VBCS flags differences during import. Draft data — persist a half-filled form and restore it on the next visit. Session / preference state — bookmarks, filters, and "wizard position" that survive a browser refresh. Lookup tables local to the app status codes, country lists . Prototypes — build against a business object now, swap in Fusion REST later. Control who may call the object from its Endpoints settings. Use GET for read-only feeds and POST/PATCH for submission channels such as a supplier uploading a quote. Give consumers the full /mobile/custom/ /businessObjects/… URL served from VBCS's own domain. Operation-level — e.g. Viewers can read but not delete; Admins get everything. Row-level security — add conditions per operation via a query builder , such as "users can View/Update/Delete only rows they created" — perfect for draft or "my records" collections. New roles you add start with all operations disabled — you grant rights deliberately. From the app's Settings → Business Objects tab you can copy each URL and, under Security, choose to allow anonymous access to the Describe endpoint or enable basic auth for the object APIs. You can also click Get Access Token in the Security pane to obtain a bearer token for authenticated API calls from outside VBCS. Anonymous API access still requires an Authorization: Public header on requests — VBCS injects it automatically for its own pages; external clients add it manually. Right-click the canvas → + Business Object to create one; click its + Field to add plain or formula fields . Draw relationships between objects visually instead of typing association names. Select a field to edit its name, type, and properties in the Properties pane. Wire objects and Fusion! up in connecting to Fusion & OIC . Render your data on pages with UI components & patterns . Understand the underlying model in application & page model . See where objects fit in the stack on the architecture page . Think of a business object as "data-as-a-service with zero infrastructure." It is not the system of record — Fusion remains that. It is VBCS-owned scratch space: drafts, session data, app lookups, and prototypes you can later swap for a real service. You rarely write these URLs by hand. A business object can be consumed as a data source that fills a table or form, or wired into an action chain's Call Rest Endpoint step, which lists the object's endpoints in a dropdown. Do not store your "source of truth" in business objects — VBCS storage is not Fusion, and duplicated master data drifts. Keep real data in Fusion via OIC or REST and reserve business objects for ephemeral or app-local state. Rules can be defined visually conditions + actions in the trigger designer or as Groovy scripts for more complex logic. Both live on the object, so every consumer of the REST API gets the same behavior. Security changes apply only when you stage or publish the app. If the app is already live, you must create a new version, change settings, and stage/publish again for the new matrix to take effect. Field type Description Notes String Free text up to a configurable length Supports max length and pattern validation Number Integer or decimal values Quantities, prices, counts Boolean true / false flag Powers checkboxes and visibility conditions Date / Date-Time Calendar values with optional time Stored as ISO; rendered by date pickers Object A nested, single record e.g. an embedded address within an Order Array A list of nested records e.g. order lines inside an Order header File An uploaded attachment Download via the object's file endpoint Association Meaning REST shape One-to-many 1:∞ A parent owns many children Order → OrderLines GET /businessObjects/Order/child/OrderLines Many-to-many m:m Two objects share rows via a join Projects ↔ Tags GET /businessObjects/Project/child/TagMembership Self-referencing 1:1 An object points at another row of the same object e.g. an Employee's manager field bo-1m bo-mm bo-self Aspect Business Object REST Data Source / Service Connection Storage VBCS database auto-created None — reads external JSON API Generated CRUD REST by VBCS Uses the remote service's API Typical use Drafts, session data, app lookups Fusion / OIC / 3rd-party JSON Defined in Business Objects tab Service Connections tab schema fetch Rule type What it does Example Validators object/field Make sure field or record data is correct Credit limit must be ≥ 0; a valid email format Triggers object/field React to an event — insert, update, delete — with actions On insert, timestamp a 'createdBy' field Object functions Encapsulate reusable logic on the object A function that computes discounted total createdBy # List / create a business object collection GET /mobile/custom/ /businessObjects/Supplier POST /mobile/custom/ /businessObjects/Supplier # Single resource read / update / delete GET /mobile/custom/ /businessObjects/Supplier/ PATCH /mobile/custom/ /businessObjects/Supplier/ DELETE /mobile/custom/ /businessObjects/Supplier/ # Child resources associations, e.g. orders under a supplier GET /mobile/custom/ /businessObjects/Supplier/ /child/Order # Query with q, limit, offset, fields, and orderBy GET /mobile/custom/ /businessObjects/Supplier?q=Status%3D'ACTIVE'&limit=25 curl -u "user@example.com:password" \\ -H "Content-Type: application/json" \\ -X POST \\ -d ' ' \\ https:// /mobile/custom/MyApp_123/businessObjects/Supplier # → 201 with the new record's id in the body

pages.title: Application & Page Model
pages.description: How a VBCS application is assembled from web apps, flows, pages, business objects, service connections, and styles — and why every page is really just a small model of variables, action chains, and components.
pages.content: Application anatomy The page model Variables in depth Action chains Fragments Endpoints & service connections overview Next steps Scope Business-object variables Array and object shape An application is the top-level unit you export and deploy to other environments. Inside it sit web apps and flows navigation contexts with routes and layouts , and under each flow you find the pages users actually see. Alongside the pages sit the business objects , service connections , and styles those pages depend on. Picture a VBCS application as buckets hanging off one exportable unit: Every VBCS page has three parts, and everything you do in the designer touches one of them: Variables are typed — the type decides how VBCS renders them in forms and tables and how it converts values on assignment: A variable can live at page scope , flow scope shared by every page in the flow , or application scope . Narrower scope wins when names collide; use application scope sparingly — it is effectively global state. When data comes from a business object rather than an external REST service , the variable that holds its rows or a selected record is still just a page, flow, or application variable — but VBCS models it specially: a data provider or REST data source binds directly to the object's generated endpoint, so the variable tracks the record set, and per-row actions receive the selected object. This is the same variable machinery seen above, wired to a business object instead of a hand-built JSON call see business objects & REST . An array variable can declare an item shape so every element looks alike; when VBCS calls a REST endpoint it maps the JSON response onto that shape: An action chain is a named sequence of steps launched by an event : the page onLoad event, a uiAction from a component button click, table selection , or a timer . Inside a chain you read variables as and write them via generated getter/setters like . A fragment is a reusable page subset — a header, an address card, a tabular list — saved once and dropped into many pages. Template fragments declare input variables : the caller binds its input to an expression like ` ` , and the fragment re-renders when it changes. Inline fragments are copied in at design time and edited independently. Because a fragment is just another page model element, it can carry its own action chains and fire events back to the hosting page. Pages rarely own data; they fetch it. Service connections wrap an external REST endpoint with its URL and authentication basic, OAuth, or SSO and expose a friendly invoke-REST action plus data providers that feed tables and list views with lazy-loaded rows. Fusion, OIC, process tasks, and your own business objects all appear through the same mechanism — which is why connectivity deserves its own page. Web apps & flows define how users move around — each flow carries its own start page, navigation tabs, and layout templates. Pages are the leaf renderables: the actual UI the end user interacts with. Business objects give you database-backed data with a generated REST API, useful for local or draft data. Service connections point at external endpoints Fusion, OIC, third parties with their credentials attached. Styles application- or flow-level themes control fonts, colors, and spacing across every page that uses them. Variables — the page's working memory. A variable has a type string, number, object, array… , a scope, and a default value. The list of POs in your table is a variable. Action chains — the page's logic as an ordered sequence of steps triggered by an event "when the button is clicked, call the endpoint, assign the result, show a toast" . Components — the visible OJET widgets tables, buttons, charts whose properties are bound to variables. See how VBCS turns objects into REST in business objects & REST . Point your pages at real systems in connecting to Fusion & OIC . Learn what to place on those pages in UI components & patterns . Brush up the platform in the VBCS overview . You never edit raw files in VBCS. Everything — pages, flows, data objects, styles — lives as metadata in the design-time repository and is compiled into an OJET application when you publish. That is why the model concepts below matter: they are the only things you ever touch. Binding is the core idea: instead of writing , you point a component property at a variable with a double-mustache expression such as ` ` . When the variable changes, every bound component updates automatically. "All UI is data." Chains are synchronous by default; mark an invocation asynchronous , or wrap part of a chain in a Promise When action, for parallel calls. For long-running work, prefer calling OIC and showing a "processing" state. Type Holds Typical use Any Whatever you assign untyped Generic scratch buckets while designing String string Text; dates as ISO strings Labels, input fields, ids Number number Numeric values Quantities, totals Boolean boolean true / false Flags that flip visibility Object object A single structured record One form row, one API response Array array A list optionally of a typed item shape Rows feeding a table or list view Date date Temporal values Date pickers, time ranges v-str v-num v-bool v-obj v-arr v-date Action Purpose Call Rest Endpoint Invoke a service connection; put the response into a variable Assign Variable Set a variable from an expression or another variable For Each Loop over an array and act per item e.g. call a child endpoint If / Switch Branch the chain on a condition or a value Fire Event Trigger another action chain or page event Navigate Move to another page or flow, carrying parameters Reset Restore variable s to defaults e.g. clear a form Notification Show a toast or banner to the user vbcs Application the exportable, deployable unit Web Apps / Flows navigation, layouts, routes Pages variables + action chains + components neutral Business Objects & Service Connections the data the pages render Styles themes, skins, responsive rules accent Components tables, forms, charts bound to $variables Variables page state: strings, arrays, objects if, call, assign, for-each, navigate read / write events + setters "orders": , $variables.orders $page.variables.orders = response.body.orders

pages.title: Connecting to Fusion & OIC
pages.description: VBCS pages are only as good as the data behind them. Service connections point your pages at Fusion REST or OIC integrations with credentials attached — this page shows how to create them, secure them, and keep URLs environment-aware.
pages.content: Service connections 101 Connecting to Fusion REST Connecting to OIC Security tokens & OAuth Consuming process tasks Reacting to Fusion Business Events Environment-specific endpoints configuration Next steps Obtaining the OAuth token A VBCS page never hard-codes a URL or a password. Instead, every external system is reached through a service connection : a named object holding the base URL, the authentication scheme, and the credentials — created once in design time and reused by action chains and data providers across the app. Every connection has three parts you configure when you create it: Once created, a connection appears in two places: as a source for the Call Rest Endpoint action fetch into a variable and as a data provider you can drag onto a Table or List View for automatic lazy loading. Fusion exposes its business services through fscmRestApi ERP/SCM and hcmRestApi HCM , versioned under /resources/ " " . Create a connection with the Fusion base URL, choose basic a Fusion user or OAuth , and add the required REST-Framework-Version header so Fusion knows which resource version to serve. OIC integrations are exposed as REST endpoints under /ic/api/integration/v1/integrations/ " " /activate/invoke . Create a connection to that base, authenticate with OAuth 2.0 client credentials OIC issues you a client id/secret , and OIC returns a bearer token you send on every call. Notice the ' "request": ' envelope: app-driven OIC integrations expect their input wrapped in a request object, and return output under response . In your action chain, map the incoming page data into that envelope and read the reply from the body.response path. VBCS handles the token dance for you: the connection stores the client id and secret, VBCS calls the token endpoint …/oauth2/v1/token with grant_type=client_credentials , caches the access token, and refreshes it when it expires. You never see the secret in the browser. Human approval tasks from OIC Process Builder can surface right in your VBCS page. Point a connection at the OIC process/task API and authenticate with the logged-in user's session so each person sees only their own tasks; bind a Table to the task list data source title, assignee, priority, due date ; and per row, an action chain calls approve / reject / claim , then refreshes the table — the same pattern as any CRUD button. Fusion can notify when something happens — an invoice is approved, a PO is released, a worker is hired — via business events . The event itself is consumed in the integration layer OIC subscribes using the Fusion adapter's event subscription — see event-driven integrations . A VBCS page then has two clean ways to reflect that activity: Dev and production instances have different URLs. Rather than editing every connection on deploy, VBCS supports connection variables and environment inheritance : define the connection once with a placeholder like https:// " " /… , then set fusionHost per environment. The same archive then runs anywhere without code changes. Base URL — the root of the REST API e.g. https:// /fscmRestApi/resources/11.13.18.05 . Authentication — basic, OAuth 2.0 client credentials, or SSO, plus the secrets. Operations — the endpoint definitions paths, methods, schemas that show up as invokable actions and table data sources. Poll the result — the page's action chain calls the OIC endpoint or Fusion REST on a refresh/timer and re-renders the changed data. The page never subscribes to the raw event. Push via OIC → VBCS — OIC handles the event and updates data your page reads e.g. writes to a business object or an OIC REST endpoint the page exposes , and the page refreshes on its schedule or on user action. Build the data layer behind these connections with business objects & REST . Put the fetched data on screen with UI components & patterns . Keep credentials safe — see security & roles . Understand OIC's side of the call in the OIC overview . The rule that keeps VBCS portable: credentials live in the connection, not the code. When you later deploy to production, only the connection settings change — the pages, chains, and expressions stay identical. Direct Fusion calls are great for simple, read-mostly lookups . If the flow needs orchestration, scheduled sync, transformations, or a human approval, route through OIC instead and keep Fusion access out of your pages. Never paste client secrets, passwords, or private keys into page expressions, code snippets, or business object fields. Anything you put in the front end is visible in the browser. Secrets belong in the service connection's secure storage — VBCS then sends only tokens over the wire. The pattern to remember: the event fires in Fusion, OIC reacts, VBCS reflects. A VBCS page is a consumer of the result — it does not subscribe to Fusion business events directly. Keep event handling in OIC where the adapters and fault handling live and let the page stay a thin view. If you need "live" updates, route them through an OIC-sourced refresh or a polling timer on the page. Relying on a manually triggered refresh means users see stale data until they act — decide the acceptable delay per feature. Prefer environment-level variables over baking concrete hosts into connections. On import, the target environment's values take over automatically, so one archive, many environments — the key to a clean deployment story. Flow Who is identified Used for Secret location Authorization code The logged-in end user SSO session Fusion REST with the user's context, process tasks IDCS/OCI IAM; browser holds only the short-lived token Client credentials The application itself machine-to-machine OIC invoke endpoints, service-to-service calls Stored inside the service connection Basic A fixed user/password pair Legacy or simple Fusion read calls Stored inside the service connection or OIC connection vbcs VBCS Page Call Rest Endpoint / data provider oic Service Connection fscmRestApi base URL + credentials fusion Fusion Cloud fscmRestApi resources HTTPS + auth REST / JSON GET https:// /fscmRestApi/resources/11.13.18.05/suppliers/ Authorization: Basic REST-Framework-Version: 11.13.18.05 Accept: application/json # → 200 JSON: supplier record with links, flexfields, and children POST https:// /ic/api/integration/v1/integrations/ImportSupplier/activate/Invoke Content-Type: application/vnd.oracle.resource+json Authorization: Bearer "request": "supplierNumber": "SUP-10023", "payload": # → 202 Accepted — OIC processes asynchronously

pages.title: Deployment & Lifecycle
pages.description: How a VBCS app moves from a developer's browser to a live production system: development environments, export/import archives, and the optional VB Studio pipeline for team-scale delivery.
pages.content: Development environments From source to production Export/import archives Working with VB Studio VBSt Going live checklist Next steps VBCS apps are packaged , not compiled and shipped like traditional code. The lifecycle is a sequence of export, transfer, import, and configure — and, when you grow up to team development, a CI/CD pipeline in VB Studio that automates the whole thing. A typical OIC/VBCS setup provisions several environments, each a full instance of the platform: Every promotion repeats the same four steps: The archive is a zip of the whole application. What it carries — and what it doesn't — shapes your rollout plan: For solo builds, export/import in the browser is enough. As soon as multiple developers , version control , or release gates come into play, Oracle Visual Builder Studio VB Studio, VBSt is the companion service that brings engineering discipline to VBCS: Before you flip the production switch, walk this list — every item below has bitten someone: Development source — where the app is built and iterated; safe to break things. Stage — a near-production mirror for UAT: real Fusion/OIC endpoints, realistic data, role checks. Production — the live instance. Changes arrive only through the promotion path, gated by review/approval. Export the app from the source environment as an application archive .zip containing the app definition, pages, business objects, and connections . Transfer the archive download/upload, or push through VB Studio if a pipeline is wired . Import into the target environment — VBCS validates the archive against what already exists. Configure : re-point service connections to the target's endpoints, set environment variables, and assign roles before publishing. Git hosting — VBSt stores your VBCS metadata in a Git repository, so every change is a commit you can review, branch, and roll back. Build automation — a build job packages the app automatically on commit or on demand. Pipelines — CI/CD stages deploy the built archive to stage and then to production, optionally pausing for approval between stages. Integration with OIC — the same environment model that hosts VBCS also hosts OIC, so your integrations and app front ends can share a release pipeline. Validate endpoints — every service connection re-pointed to the production Fusion/OIC host; a test call run against each one. Configure environment variables — hosts, versions, and feature flags resolved per environment, none left pointing at dev. Point security roles — production users/groups assigned to the app roles; no test users carrying admin access. Test SSO — a full login through your corporate identity provider into the live app and, if ADV, through Fusion itself . Check performance — page sizes, lazy-loading behavior, and Fusion/OIC call latency under a realistic load, not a single user. Confirm business object data — reference/draft data seeded in production, since archives don't carry data. Make sure the production app is locked down — see security & roles . Re-check the connections you'll configure at deploy time in connecting to Fusion & OIC . Position VBCS in the wider landscape on the architecture page . The mental model: one app archive, many environments. You move the same .zip through dev → stage → prod, and each environment brings its own endpoints, credentials, and security settings along the way. The most common production failure is importing without reconfiguring. An archive that points at the dev Fusion host will happily run in prod — against the dev system. Add environment variables and a re-point checklist to your import routine. Adopt VB Studio before you need it. Retro-fitting version control to an app that was built ad-hoc is painful; starting a new app inside a VBSt project costs minutes and buys you history, reviewability, and automated deploys. Validate endpoints — every service connection re-pointed to the production Fusion/OIC host; a test call run against each one. Configure environment variables — hosts, versions, and feature flags resolved per environment, none left pointing at dev. Point security roles — production users/groups assigned to the app roles; no test users carrying admin access. Test SSO — a full login through your corporate identity provider into the live app and, if ADV, through Fusion itself . Check performance — page sizes, lazy-loading behavior, and Fusion/OIC call latency under a realistic load, not a single user. Confirm business object data — reference/draft data seeded in production, since archives don't carry data. Artifact In the archive? Notes Pages, flows, action chains, fragments Yes Definitions only; no runtime state Business object definitions Schema recreated on import; data not included by default Business object data No unless exported Use the data export/import feature to move rows separately Service connections Yes with values Credentials may need re-entering; URLs should use environment variables Styles / themes Imported as-is Roles & access settings Re-assign users/groups to roles in the target environment neutral Development build pages, objects, connections warning Stage test with prod-like data & config success Production live users, secured connections export archive approval gate MyApp.zip ├── metadata.json # app id, version, description ├── apps/ # web apps & flows │ └── web/flow/… # pages, fragments, action chains ├── resources/ # business objects, connections │ ├── businessObjects/ │ └── serviceConnections/ └── theme/ # styles & skins

pages.title: Walkthrough — enhance an Edit button and ship it to production
pages.description: The complete sequence for changing an existing VBCS app: understand the current flow, modify the business object, add a new option to the Edit button's action chain, harden security, test, stage, and publish to production — with a rollback plan at every step.
headings: Phase 1 — Understand the existing flow (do not skip)
Phase 3 — Add the new option to the Edit button
Phase 5 — Test in Development before touching prod
Phase 6 — Stage to a shared test URL
Rollback plan — the part everyone forgets
The full checklist (copy for your sprint)
pages.content: The journey at a glance Phase 1 — Understand the existing flow do not skip Phase 2 — Modify the business object Phase 3 — Add the new option to the Edit button Phase 4 — Harden security Phase 5 — Test in Development before touching prod Phase 6 — Stage to a shared test URL Phase 7 — Publish to production Rollback plan — the part everyone forgets The full checklist copy for your sprint Next steps This is the full workflow for the scenario we discussed: an existing VBCS app whose Edit button needs a new option, with the data living in a business object. Follow the phases in order — each one depends on the one before it, and each ends in a checkpoint you can verify before moving on. Every migration problem I have seen came from someone editing a chain they guessed at instead of read. Spend ten minutes here: Since the data lives in a business object, changes that the new option needs happen here first. In the Business Objects tab, select the object: With the object ready, modify the page. Decide the shape of the option first: The new option usually needs a permission decision, and since security only takes effect on stage/publish, do this before you leave Development: Staging produces a staged version others can reach without your developer session: If production regresses, roll back by re-publishing the previous version : Open the app in the Navigator , find the page with the Edit button, select it, and open Events → onClick . Read the action chain step by step — usually: open edit page → prefill from the selected row → on save, PATCH the business object. Note the variables, types, and service connections the chain uses. If an Edit page exists, open it and see what it writes back and which endpoint it calls. In the Business Objects tab, open the object behind the data: its fields, any rules/triggers , and whether role-based security is enabled. Menu on the button — replace Edit with an OJET menu/overflow; each item gets its own action chain. Extra step in Edit — insert steps into the existing onClick chain e.g. a confirmation Fire Notification Event , an extra Call Rest Endpoint , or an if branch on a page variable . Second button — add a new button bound to the same row with its own chain. If the page should be restricted, set the page's Access in its properties public / logged-in / role . If the option writes or reads more of the object, enable role-based security on the business object and grant the right roles the exact operations view/create/update/ delete — including row-level restrictions like "own rows only" if relevant. If anything must be public, review the anonymous access rules carefully see Security & Roles . Create a new version of the app first if the app is already published — never overwrite the live version. Stage the Development version top right, Stage button . You get a staged URL to hand to testers/business users. Have the business test the actual scenario: edit a record, use the new option, confirm the old behavior still passes. Keep the prior version available in the environment — do not delete it on publish. If the change added an object field , the rollback must also decide the fate of that field: a rolled-back app that still reads a new field can fail — plan to make the field optional or handle it in the older version. Business object security changes take effect on publish too ; a rollback to the prior version restores the prior security matrix. The object rules you may add are covered in Business Objects & REST . Chain steps and functions in Advanced: JavaScript & Quick Starts . Versions, staging and publishing in Deployment & Lifecycle . Record what you found before changing anything — a small note of "current chain: navigate → prefill → PATCH Supplier" is your safety net and your rollback reference. Object structure and rule changes typically do not touch existing rows , but a new required field with no default can break existing saves. Prefer an optional field or a default until you have migrated the data. If the option and Edit share logic, extract it into a page/flow JavaScript function and call it from both chains — see Advanced: JavaScript & Quick Starts . Never inject credentials or secrets into chain expressions or functions. Details on versions, archive export/import, and VB Studio integration are on Deployment & Lifecycle . If you use VB Studio , the promotion is CI/CD-driven; the business-object and chain changes still follow these same phases. A rolled-back app version cannot "unsee" a business-object field your new version created. If the field is not strictly needed to keep the old app running, keep it optional and unused during the rollback window rather than removing it in the same move. Change you need What to do Remember A new field e.g. 'Status' Add the field and set its type Pages using the object must be re-bound to see it; types may need Edit From Endpoint Default or derived value Set a default or add a formula field Formula fields are read-only, computed server-side Validation on the new data Add an object/field validator or trigger Rules run on the server for every write path REST, page, script Logic shared with the option Add an object function Groovy Keep business logic on the object, not in page JavaScript Status Check How Pass = The chain fires correctly Live view; click the modified button The new option runs end to end, old Edit still works The object write succeeds Create/update a record via the page Data persists; no validation surprise Access behaves Sign in as a low-privilege user Unauthorized users are blocked, authorized users pass Errors are visible Open the app's errors/logs in design time No unhandled exceptions in the chain Step Action Checkpoint 1 Confirm the staged build passed user acceptance Sign-off captured; edge cases tested permissions, offline, empty list 2 Record what changed object fields, chain, security A change note exists for rollback 3 Publish the staged version Production URL serves the new build 4 Smoke-test on production Edit works; new option works; no data corruption 5 Hand back to users / announce Business confirms the option is live # Done? Read the existing onClick chain and the business object — noted what they do ☐ Business object updated field/rule/security without breaking existing rows New option implemented in the chain menu / extra step / second button Shared logic extracted to a function no duplication, no secrets Security hardened: page access, object role matrix, anonymous rules if any 6 Tested in Development Live view end to end 7 Staged; business user-accepted the staged URL 8 Change note written object + chain + security delta for rollback 9 Published; production smoke test passed 10 Rollback plan recorded re-publish prior version; old field handling neutral 1 · Understand read the chain & the object vbcs 2 · Modify the object fields, rules, security 3 · Add the option action chain + function 4 · Test in Development Live view, Preview 5 · Stage shared test URL success 6 · Publish production, with rollback ready

pages.title: What is Oracle Visual Builder?
pages.description: Oracle Visual Builder (VBCS, Visual Builder Cloud Service) is Oracle's low-code platform for building web and mobile applications. It gives business-friendly developers a drag-and-drop design canvas, while still allowing custom logic and direct connectivity to Fusion and OIC.
headings: What you can build with VBCS
How a VBCS application is structured
The page model in one paragraph
How VBCS, OIC, and Fusion connect
pages.content: What you can build with VBCS Two flavours in Oracle's world How a VBCS application is structured The page model in one paragraph How VBCS, OIC, and Fusion connect Next steps VBCS is the front end of the Oracle stack. Where Fusion stores the data and OIC moves it around, VBCS is where people actually see and interact with that data — dashboards, extranet portals, self-service screens, and mobile apps. Oracle offers VBCS in two related forms. They share the same engine, so knowledge transfers directly between them: A VBCS app bundles several pieces that work together. You'll configure each in the design time the browser-based studio : In VBCS, every page has three linked parts. Variables hold page state e.g. the list of POs as a typed array . Action chains contain the logic — "when the button is clicked, call the service connection, store the result, then reload the table." Components are the visible OJET widgets tables, forms, charts whose properties are bound to those variables. You wire this together visually; VBCS writes the Knockout/OJET code underneath. Extranet portals — supplier or customer self-service that Fusion's own screens don't cover, or that must live outside the corporate firewall. Dashboards & reports — visual summaries of Fusion data open POs, expense status fetched through OIC or Fusion REST. Approval & task UIs — letting employees approve OIC process tasks from a friendly custom interface. Mobile apps — VBCS applications can be published as hybrid mobile apps Apache Cordova / OJET-based for iOS and Android. Extending Fusion itself — VBCS apps can appear inside the Fusion UI as "extensions," giving custom screens a single sign-on experience. Direct to Fusion: a service connection pointing at fscmRestApi / hcmRestApi with basic or OAuth credentials. Fast for simple reads. Via OIC: a service connection pointing at OIC's /ic/api/integration/v1/integrations/…/invoke endpoints. Use this when the flow needs orchestration, scheduling, or a human approval. Business Objects: VBCS's own REST-with-storage layer, handy for local, lightweight data drafts, session state or when you don't have a backend yet. Walk the application & page model in detail. Understand data with business objects & REST . Wire everything together in connecting to Fusion & OIC . VBCS rests on two big ideas: a visual page model you design the page, set variables and actions, and the framework generates the code and REST-first connectivity any REST API — Fusion's, OIC's, yours — can power a page with a few clicks . Oracle is converging these names — you will see "Oracle Visual Builder," "VBCS," and "Visual Builder Studio VB Studio for lifecycle management." For this guide, VBCS means the visual builder platform, and ADV means the copy embedded in Fusion. Under the hood, VBCS is built on Oracle JET — the same component library tables, forms, buttons, dialogs, charts, lists drives its design canvas. JET knowledge transfers directly: what you learn about a Table or Form in VBCS maps to the underlying oj-* component, which matters when you drop in custom HTML or read OJET docs. "All UI is data." The single most important VBCS habit is binding component displays to page variables rather than writing imperative DOM code. When a variable changes, everything bound to it updates automatically. Flavour Where it lives Use it when VBCS standalone A dedicated OIC/Building&Connecting environment You want a normal cloud app, maybe integrated via OIC ADV Application Development scope inside Fusion Embedded in the Fusion cloud, uses Fusion identity/vanity URL You build 'extensions' that appear inside Fusion itself extensions Layer Role Business Objects You define objects e.g. 'Supplier' , VBCS creates a REST API + DB tables to store them REST Data Sources JSON-shaped data from external services Fusion, OIC, 3rd-party Service Connections Named endpoints with security — how a page actually talks to OIC/Fusion Page Model Variables data , action chains logic , and the component tree UI Fragments Reusable chunks of UI used across pages Supplier vbcs Apps & Web Apps containers with pages, flows, styles Pages page model: variables, actions, components Business Objects / REST data sources behind the pages neutral OAuth settings for Fusion & OIC VBCS App your pages & business objects oic OIC Integration orchestration + process tasks fusion Fusion Cloud system of record REST via service connection FBDI / REST

pages.title: Progressive Web Apps (PWA)
pages.description: Turn a web application into an installable, app-like experience: a home-screen icon, a splash screen, offline fallback, and a QR code users scan to install. This page covers enabling PWA support, the manifest, branding, and offline behavior.
pages.content: Enabling PWA support The web manifest Branding and resources Offline fallback page Distributing a PWA Next steps A Progressive Web App PWA is a web app that behaves like an installed app: it can live on the home screen, launch with a splash screen, and degrade gracefully offline. VBCS enables this from the app's settings — no separate mobile build required. The manifest stores the configuration a PWA needs. You edit these settings in the Manifest Settings section of the PWA tab: Oracle provides Redwood-themed icons and splash screens as a starting point. From the Resources section you can download the pwabranding_redwood.zip sample, modify the images, and upload your branded set in its place. You can add an offline fallback page that appears when a user performs an action needing a connection while the device is offline: Once enabled, stage and publish the app like any web app. After publishing you can generate a QR code using your browser's native capabilities that users scan to quickly open and install the app on a laptop or device. Open your app in the web apps navigator, open the app artifact, and go to Settings . Select the PWA tab and click Enable Progressive Web App PWA . VBCS adds the required PWA resources to your project: a web manifest file a JSON configuration , required icons , and splash screens . Click Create next to Offline Fallback Page — VBCS adds a Redwood-themed offlinePage.html to your project. Open it in the designer and customize it message, retry button, links to fit your app. Design the responsive pages a PWA runs in — see UI components & patterns . Publish and distribute it in deployment & lifecycle . Control who reaches the installed app in security & roles . A PWA is still a web app under the hood — same VBCS pages, same service connections. The PWA layer adds installability and offline behavior around it, not a new technology stack. If you use adaptive icons Android 8.0+ , keep important content inside a "safe zone" — a circle with radius equal to 40% of image size . VBCS also documents the "purpose": "any maskable" setting for such icons. Offline means the shell and static resources may load, but data still comes from service connections that need the network. Plan what a user can realistically do offline — often "see that you're offline" is the honest, correct behavior. Mobile apps are no longer supported in VBCS — but you can convert an existing mobile app to a web app and deploy it as a PWA, keeping its reach on phones. Setting What it controls Application name Shown in the install prompt Short name Used on the home screen below the icon where space is limited Background / theme color The app's color treatment around the shell Icons & splash screens Branded assets shown at launch and on install "name": "Supplier Portal", "short_name": "Suppliers", "display": "standalone", "start_url": "/ic/builder/rt/supplier-portal/1.0/", "theme_color": "#0B5CAD", "background_color": "#0B5CAD", "icons":

pages.title: Security & Roles
pages.description: Who can see, build, and administer your VBCS app — and how it authenticates. This page covers SSO identity, application roles, page-level access, and the extra controls that appear when you embed an app inside Fusion.
pages.content: Identity & SSO Application roles Page & object access Embedded apps inside Fusion ADV Securing service connections Anonymous access Allowing access to your APIs Audit & entitlement basics Next steps VBCS separates who builds the app from who uses the app . Developers are managed in the environment's identity store; end users are managed through application roles that VBCS maps to your identity provider's users and groups. Understanding these two rails keeps your app both open to the right people and closed to everyone else. End users authenticate through the environment's identity provider — Oracle Identity Cloud Service IDCS or, on OCI, OCI IAM . VBCS issues a session token at login, which also seeds the SSO context used by service connections: Every VBCS app ships with a set of application roles . You assign provider users and groups to these roles, then control access by role. Two granular controls decide what a logged-in user can actually reach: When you build in Application Development scope inside Fusion ADV , your VBCS app becomes an extension hosted under Fusion's own vanity URL . The big payoff is identity: the app inherits Fusion's security context, so there is no separate login. Service connections hold credentials at design time and never expose them to the browser at runtime. Depending on the connection type: VBCS apps require sign-in by default. If a page must be public — a quote request form, a product catalog, a self-registration screen — you can turn on anonymous access : External clients — Process Automation, OIC, report tools — may need to read or update your app's business objects over REST. VBCS exposes a catalog API describing the endpoints of every business object, one per app version Development, Staging, Live : VBCS and the surrounding Oracle services record what happened and who is entitled to what: An audit event, as the identity provider would record it for one denied page access: Users sign in once; VBCS redirects them to the provider's login page or a corporate IdP via SAML federation and back with a validated identity. That identity is passed to Fusion and OIC, giving single sign-on across the whole stack — log into Fusion, click into the VBCS extension, no second password. Access control is role-based : VBCS maps the user's provider groups to application roles, and pages/objects check those roles. Page access — each page has an Access setting: public, logged-in user, or a specific role. Set it from the page's properties; unauthorized users get an access-denied screen or are redirected to login. Object access — business objects have their own read/write settings. You can even configure row-level security so users only see rows they own e.g. "my drafts" , not the whole collection. Users sign in to Fusion and reach your extension without a second authentication — true single sign-on . Roles can be aligned to Fusion job roles, so a Fusion user with "Manager" sees the extension's manager pages automatically. The extension appears inside the Fusion navigation a menu item , feeling native to Fusion even though it is a VBCS app under the hood. Basic — the username/password stays in the connection; the browser only sees the resulting Authorization header. OAuth client credentials — the client secret is stored securely; VBCS fetches and refreshes bearer tokens server-side. SSO — the token is tied to the user's session, so the backend sees who is acting, not one shared account. In the app's Settings → Security , deselect Require authenticated access . Visitors then get the Anonymous User authentication role automatically. Anonymous users are denied data by default — to let them read/write business objects, enable role-based security on the object and grant operations to the Anonymous User role explicitly. For service connections, enable Allow anonymous access to the service connection infrastructure and choose the authentication mechanism for anonymous users. You may need Override Security if the option is inherited and disabled. Open Settings → Business Objects to copy each version's catalog URL. The Staged and Live URLs only return data after the app is staged/published. Under Security , choose the access model: allow anonymous access to the Describe endpoint, or enable basic authentication for the object REST APIs. Click Get Access Token in the Security pane to obtain a bearer token for calls made from outside Visual Builder. Anonymous Describe access still requires an Authorization: Public header — VBCS injects it for its own pages; external callers add it manually curl example below . Entitlements — the environment itself is governed by OIC/VBCS service entitlements; only entitled users can even open the designer or publish. Audit trails — the identity provider logs sign-ins; Fusion logs changes to records your extension writes; OIC logs integration invocations. Together they let you answer "who did what, when." Review habit — periodically reconcile the app role list against reality: remove departed users, demote over-privileged roles, and confirm page access settings still match the business rules. Harden the connections your pages use — see connecting to Fusion & OIC . Model the data those roles protect in business objects & REST . Take the secured app live in deployment & lifecycle . A VBCS app is not a public website. By default it enforces login, and every user's identity — plus the roles attached to them — is checked on each page access. You decide how strict that gets. Don't hand out Administrators to everyone "to keep it simple." Keep design-time roles lean; give end users a custom role with access to just the pages they need. Least privilege scales and survives audits. A standalone VBCS app and an ADV extension use the same page model. The difference is where it is hosted and who authenticates it — which is why the same app can be republished either way. Treat the credentials in service connections as production secrets : export them only to trusted environments, restrict who can edit connections, and never paste a client secret or password into a page expression, a code snippet, or a business object field. Once a secret is in browser code, it is compromised. Allowing anonymous access to a backend exposes those endpoints without any authentication at a public URL. If you must do it: create a dedicated backend for the anonymous connections, and give it only the minimal read-only credentials those connections need. Do not hand the public the same backend your authenticated users use. Change takes effect on the next stage or publish — a live app needs a new version, the setting change, and re-publish before anonymous access actually works. Cross-origin callers may need to be added to the CORS allowlist by an administrator, and non-browser clients may need to send a matching Origin header or add CSRF headers to POSTs . If an external integration "works in the browser but fails from a server", CORS is the first suspect. Role Default capability Administrators Full app access: design, settings, role assignment, service connections Developers Can open the app in the designer and edit pages, flows, and logic Maintain_ Operational role: run the app, manage app data, access the object data pages Obligatory admin OIC-created Auto-created role that grants the app owner admin rights; never remove it Custom roles You define these and grant them specific page/object access in the app neutral User session signed in via IDCS / OCI IAM vbcs custom role per use case Page + Object access public / logged-in / role-based roles from groups checked per request # Anonymous access to the business objects catalog requires the Public header curl -v "https:// /ic/builder/rt/myapp/1.0/resources/data/describe?metadataMode=minimal" \\ -H 'Authorization: Public'

pages.title: UI Components & Patterns
pages.description: The VBCS canvas gives you Oracle JET (OJET) widgets out of the box. This page covers the component catalog, how to structure pages, and the binding patterns that keep your UI in sync with variables.
headings: What you get on the canvas
pages.content: What you get on the canvas Design page structure Binding components to variables Data providers & quota Validations & forms Notifications & UX patterns Next steps Everything you place on the VBCS canvas is an Oracle JET OJET component — the same widgets that power Fusion's own interfaces. That means accessibility, theming, and enterprise look-and-feel come free; your job is to pick the right widget, bind it to a variable, and wire up the action chain behind it. The common palette covers most business screens. Values flow into components through data binding item/text/selected = a variable or expression rather than imperative code. Every page has a content region you fill with rows and columns . Use page's structure pane to organize: Binding is the double-mustache " " expression syntax. Any component property — text, value, items, enabled — can be an expression that resolves against page scope: A Table's data comes from a variable populated by an action chain. Raw JSON from your service connection mapped onto a page variable might look like this: Instead of fetching everything into a variable, bind big lists to a data provider : an object that fetches rows on demand from a service connection and pages them automatically. Form fields declare validation like any other binding: mark inputs required , add pattern , min/max , and maxLength constraints, and give each field a message. Validation and disabled states are driven by variables — ` ` gates the Submit button, ` ` locks every field while an operation runs — and on submit an action chain Call Rest Endpoint s, checks the response, and shows a toast or navigates away. A handful of patterns keep the UI feeling alive without any custom JavaScript: Layout components — Columns, Flex, Grid, and Responsive containers hold the visible widgets. Regions — sticky header/footer bands page title, action bar, filters that stay put while content scrolls. Responsive behavior — columns declare breakpoints small/medium/large so a 3-column dashboard collapses to a single column on a phone. ` ` — bind a list to a Table/List View's data . ` ` — display a field of the selected row. ` ` — drive a spinner's visibility. Drag a REST data provider onto the page and point it at a connection operation e.g. Fusion GET /suppliers . The Table uses data = $page.dataProviders.supplierDP ; scrolling or the pager triggers lazy fetches. Fine-tune with limit / offset parameters, and re-query via the provider's refresh action after a create/update. Feed your widgets real data via connecting to Fusion & OIC . Model the state you bind to in application & page model . Keep the app secure as it grows in security & roles . The canvas reads like simple HTML: you drag a component , set its properties, and its bindings appear as expressions such as ` ` . VBCS compiles this into OJET/Knockout code for you — the designer is the code. Start with the Form + Create Page pattern : a Table bound to your data, an Add button that opens a Dialog with a Form Layout, and an action chain that calls the REST endpoint and refreshes the table. It covers 80% of commerce use cases. Because bindings are reactive , you never "refresh the UI."
